Shorter-billed than either Whiskered or Black Terns. Immature similar to non-breeding adult, but may have slightly more extensive dark cap and darker grey-brown back. Flight looks light and bouncy. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common passage migrant and winter visitor to inland lakes and dams in Aug–May, although a good number oversummer. Highly gregarious and may occur in flocks of many hundreds, especially on larger Great Rift Valley lakes. Much rarer at the coast, apart from on freshwater wetlands just inland.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Feeding parties utter short plik plik… calls.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: White-winged Black Tern

images.caption: White-winged Tern · Plate 81

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slightly larger and stronger-billed than White-winged and Black Terns. Breeding adult has black cap, white sides to face and dark grey underparts. Non-breeding adult has black patch behind eye and fine black streaking on rear crown (suggesting Sterna tern); rump, tail and back uniform pale grey. Beware confusing Sterna-like birds which lose grey underparts before moulting black cap. Immature similar to immature White-winged, but back is more boldly spangled brown and buff and rump is grey not white. Flight action stronger and steadier than White-winged Tern. In EA, race delalandii is a widespread resident, while slightly paler Palearctic nominate race has a larger white cheek and may be a visitor in Oct–Mar. White-cheeked Tern is similar but larger with a deeply forked tail, and is exclusively coastal.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common but not numerous on a wide range of fresh and alkaline waters inland, although breeding confined to only a few undisturbed areas in central Kenya and northern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Vocal, giving unpleasant low rasps and churrs, unlike most terns.

images.caption: Whiskered Tern · Plate 81

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has neat face pattern with vertical black stripe from forecrown to throat, and narrow black and white stripes curving above and behind eye. Underparts have narrow black breast-band above broader white band. Adult female is almost entirely barred, mottled and streaked except plain yellowish-buff lower face and breast-band. In flight grey-buff underwing contrasts with dark belly. Three races occur, varying mainly in general tone: ellenbecki in north and loveridgei in SWKe to CTz are paler than nominate birds in SKe and NTz.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are common in areas of dry open and bushed grassland from near sea level to 1,600m. Gathers at waterholes in early morning and late afternoon.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Flight call is an explosive wop’dela wiiiii, the last note being a fading whistle.

images.caption: Black-faced Sandgrouse · Plate 82

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather stout sandgrouse with extensive barring above and below. Adult male has black and white bands on forecrown, small white mark behind eye, and broad buff-brown breast-band traversed by two narrow black bands (one central, one below). Adult female is entirely barred with narrow blackish lines. In flight looks bulky, the pale inner wing contrasting with darker flight feathers. Race in EA is sukensis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are rather uncommon in the arid north, preferring stony and sparsely bushed country below 1,800m. Drinks before dawn or just after dusk.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Flight call is a high-pitched whistled and bubbling wicky-wi-wheo-wickiwicki-weeo… and also a low churr.

images.caption: Lichtenstein’s Sandgrouse · Plate 82

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large bulky sandgrouse. Adult male has pale yellow face and throat encircled by black band. Rest of upperparts rather plain grey-brown, with some dark spotting on scapulars and broad rufous fringes to wing-coverts; belly dark chestnut. Adult female is heavily mottled black, brown and buff, with paler yellowish face and throat, and dark chestnut belly. In flight, looks large and heavy with dark underwing and belly. Birds in EA are race saturatior.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs, small groups and occasionally larger flocks are locally common residents and wanderers on open short grassland and highland plains at 800–2,000m. Drinks in mid-morning.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Flight call is a strange musical cawing ah-oo-op-oo-ah-er-aap…

images.caption: Yellow-throated Sandgrouse · Plate 82

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A rather stout pigeon with eight races in EA. Basic adult plumage has green or yellow-green head, neck and breast, purple shoulder patch, and yellow belly with dark centres to undertail-coverts; tail grey or green. Six widespread races as described, while distinctive races granti (ETz) and delalandii (SETz) sometimes considered specifically distinct (Grey-breasted Green-Pigeon), and have mostly grey head, neck and underparts, with granti having a brighter yellow belly. Immatures of all races duller than adults and lack purple shoulder patch.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a wide range of woodland, forest edge, open country and cultivation at fruiting trees, from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very complex and un-pigeon-like call usually begins with a series of rising crackling notes, and continues with varied whinnying sounds and lower musical growls. Often several birds call together.

images.caption: African Green-Pigeon · Plate 83

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male appears all dark slate-grey with striking white half-collar on lower nape. If seen well shows iridescent green, purplish-pink and bronze sheen to hindneck. Adult female duller, lacks white collar, and is washed rufous-bronze on crown and nape. Immature similar to female, but darker brown above and dark rufous below. In all plumages bill dark with whitish tip. Race in EA is sharpei.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and flocks are locally common in highland forest mainly above 1,500m, with birds occasionally wandering to coastal forests.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Quite a complex call oo-oo-oo oo-oo-oo-oo-oo-oo-ah’ah’ah after three seesawing introductory notes, a descending series of oos followed by a more rapid series of deeper notes with a peculiar effect like a voice breaking.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Delegorgue’s Pigeon

images.caption: Eastern Bronze-naped Pigeon · Plate 83

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Robust grey and maroon-brown pigeon with conspicuous white spots on wing-coverts, bare red skin around eyes, and pink-and-white striated neck. In flight reveals distinct pale grey rump and broad black tip to tail. Immature is duller grey-brown with greyish eye-patch, broad brownish band around neck and plain grey-brown wings. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and common at 500–3,000m, in open country with cliffs and in many towns.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Two main calls; a throaty woopor…woooo, the first note rising then falling and last note falling and fading. Also a monotonous woo-woo-woo-woo… given for long periods.

images.caption: Speckled Pigeon · Plate 84

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very large, dark grey pigeon with bright yellow bill, eye-ring and feet. Conspicuously spotted white on wing-coverts and breast. Pale grey nape (sometimes very pale) may suggest White-naped Pigeon, but latter has plain dark wings and a yellow-tipped dark bill. Female slightly duller and immature rather browner. In flight, simply appears very dark and bulky with yellow bill and feet. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks are common in highland forest and woodland, as well as in adjacent country with isolated fruiting trees, mainly above 1,500m (but down to 700m in western Uganda).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A deep vibrating churr is followed by a sequence of rising oo notes.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Rameron Pigeon

images.caption: African Olive Pigeon · Plate 84

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: In EA, occurs as a highly variable introduced urban pigeon (Feral Pigeon); plumage ranges from grey with pale wings, glossed purple neck and two black wingbars, to patchy brown and white, all white, or sooty black. No wild Rock Doves occur in region.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks are widespread in cities, towns and larger villages throughout the region, nesting on buildings.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Bubbling rising and falling churr, interspersed by wing-clapping.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Feral Pigeon

images.caption: Rock Dove · Plate 84

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Typical wood-dove, grey-brown above, paler below with pinkish breast, and iridescent green spots on wings. Bill varies from blackish to dull dark red with black tip. Flaps noisily into flight, showing warm rufous panel in wing, two bold black bars on lower back and broad terminal tail-band. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are widespread and common in dry bush, scrub, woodland and cultivated land from sea level to about 2,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Long slow call of muffled poo notes lasting up to 10 seconds: first two or three are hesitant upslurs, then three seesawing notes, and a long slow series of 15 descending poo notes which accelerate as they fade.

images.caption: Emerald-spotted Wood-Dove · Plate 85

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Emerald-spotted Wood-Dove, but rather darker brown above and warmer buff below, with dark blue wing spots (can appear blackish) and purplish-red bill with yellow tip. In flight, overall tone is browner than Emerald-spotted. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common, generally in moister habitats than Emerald-spotted Wood-Dove including forest edge, woodland, gardens and secondary growth, from sea level to around 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Similar to Emerald-spotted, but final notes are all on one pitch, not descending.

images.caption: Blue-spotted Wood-Dove · Plate 85

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is rich dark rufous-brown above with a brilliant white face and underparts, and blue-black wing spots (very hard to see). Adult female is duller with whitish sides to face, mostly grey underparts, and white central belly. Immature similar to female but has duller head pattern, finely barred back, no wing spots and is brownish below. In flight, male appears dark brown above with rufous in wings and white below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are widespread and common in a wide range of forest, dense woodland and thickets, as well as gardens in wetter areas, from sea level to 2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Similar to Emerald-spotted Wood-Dove, but typically lacks slurred notes of introduction and all of the final poo notes are on same pitch not descending. NAMAQUA DOVE Only member of the genus Oena, a small long-tailed dove of arid and semi-arid county.

images.caption: Tambourine Dove · Plate 85

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Delicate, small dove with a long graduated tail. Adult male is black on face and upper breast with yellow-tipped purplish bill, two black bands on lower back and dark purple-black spots on wings. Adult female has pale buff-grey or whitish face and dark grey bill. Immature similar to female, but back and wing-coverts are spotted and edged pale rufous, grey, black and white. Flight is swift and direct, revealing rufous wings and long slender tail. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and common in drier bush and cultivated areas from sea level to 2,000m, rarely to 3,000m, but wanders widely.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a plaintive descending oooo given about every two seconds.

images.caption: Namaqua Dove · Plate 85

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Most common and widespread ring-necked dove. Basic appearance is brownish-grey (or grey) with small but prominent black eyes (obvious even at distance). Two races occur: widespread tropica is generally brownish-grey, while somalica in N and EKe and NETz is a cooler grey.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and flocks are widespread and may be very common at forest edge, in open woodland, dry bush and cultivation, mainly from sea level to 2,200m, less often to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A three-note oo-oo-rrooo repeated fairly rapidly (saying ‘ring-necked-dove’ or ‘work-harder’ over and over), as well as other coos and growling calls, and a nasal crooning err-waaaa on alighting.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Cape Turtle Dove

images.caption: Ring-necked Dove · Plate 86

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger and darker than Ring-necked Dove with dark red eyes surrounded by a small diamond-shaped area of dull maroon skin. Steep pale grey forehead contrasts with otherwise mainly plain brown upperparts and dark pinkish underparts. In flight rather dark and uniform above with broad grey band on tip of tail (lacking white). Immature has brown eyes, rufous-fringed upperparts and rather obscure hindcollar. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Lone birds and pairs, less often flocks, are widespread and common in moist forest, woodland and gardens from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call varies slightly, but typically a very rhythmical oo-oo-oo-oo-oo-oo (sounds like ‘I-am-a-red-eyed-dove!’) with the third and fifth notes lower. Also various other growling calls, and a single or double moaning uu-raaow on alighting.

images.caption: Red-eyed Dove · Plate 86

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A grey-brown ringed-necked dove with whitish or pale yellow eyes and narrow pink eye-ring. Three races occur and vary in overall tone: western logonensis is browner above and wine-pink below, central perspicillata is grey-brown above and pale pink below, and rather bleached eastern elegans is grey above and whitish below. Browner immature has dull brown eyes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and flocks are widespread and sometimes abundant in arid and semi-arid bush and wooded country, typically including acacias, from sea level to 1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Most distinctive call is a cheerful descending rolling churr rrrrrrrooooooo, and an oo-rrrrrrrr on landing with last note very tremulous and throaty.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: African Mourning Dove

images.caption: Mourning Collared Dove · Plate 86

spilopelia-senegalensis.ref: Plate 87: Laughing, Turtle And Lemon Doves
spilopelia-senegalensis.name: Laughing Dove

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Fairly small, slender pinkish dove, pale rufous above with pink and black mottling on upper breast and steel-blue wing-coverts (no black collar or neck smudge). Female slightly paler below. Appears slender in flight, revealing blue band on wings and white corners to tail. Immature significantly duller and plain below (lacks black breast mottling). Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: One of East Africa’s commonest and most widespread doves. Pairs and flocks are numerous in a wide range of habitats, usually below 2,000m, occasionally to 3,000m, including gardens, villages and towns.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a strange and laughing 5–6-note refrain, oo-oo-oo-oo-oo, with fourth note highest and fifth lowest.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Streptopelia.

images.caption: Laughing Dove · Plate 87

streptopelia-lugens.ref: Plate 87: Laughing, Turtle And Lemon Doves
streptopelia-lugens.name: Dusky Turtle Dove

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very dark grey dove with slightly paler grey face and distinct black patch on side of neck. Broad rich rufous edges to some wing-coverts and tertials give scaly effect. In flight, appears very dark with dull grey corners to tail. Immature paler with more extensive rufous feather edges. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles, pairs and flocks are widespread and sometimes common in the highlands at 1,800–3,200m, including forest edge, wooded areas, farmland and gardens. Birds wander widely, sometimes to lower altitudes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a very deep gargling and scraping oo-oo orrrrr-orrrrrr with all notes descending.

images.caption: Dusky Turtle Dove · Plate 87

aplopelia-larvata.ref: Plate 87: Laughing, Turtle And Lemon Doves
aplopelia-larvata.name: Lemon Dove

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Plump brown dove with greyish-white face and cinnamon-brown underparts. If seen well, shows green and purple sheen to nape and back, and small lemon yellow patch on side of neck. Sexes alike. Immature similar, but duller below with some rufous fringes to breast feathers. Two similar races occur: widespread nominate (as descibed), and jacksoni (WUg to WTz) with darker upperparts and a greyer breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are shy and uncommon (except locally), often walking on ground in shade of forest undergrowth and exploding into noisy flight when disturbed. Mainly in areas of dense highland forest at 1,800–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls with very low notes, either a pulsating poopoopoopoopoo… or a slow rising moan ooooo.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Sometimes placed in the genus Columba.

images.caption: Lemon Dove · Plate 87

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is mainly grey-brown on head and upperparts with a green (or bluish-green) rump and lower breast to vent, bright yellow band on forecrown, shoulders and underwing-coverts. Close views reveal all-dark bill and brown-red eyes. In flight clearly shows yellow underwing-coverts. Immature duller than adult and lacks yellow crown and thighs. Two races occur: saturatus (as described) is widespread, while in CTz race matschiei has blue-green breast and rump.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small parties are widespread and sometimes common in woodland, bushland, scrub and cultivation below 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Similar to Brown-headed Parrot, but screeches are less metallic and interspersed with slurred chattering.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Brown Parrot

images.caption: Meyer’s Parrot · Plate 88

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is mainly green (brighter on rump and lower breast to vent) with greyish-brown head; yellow confined to underwing-coverts (absent from crown, shoulders and thighs). At close range shows blackish upper and cream lower mandible, and pale yellow eyes. In flight, note bright yellow underwing-coverts and green rump. Immature duller. Birds in EA are race tanganyikae.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are rather local, but may be common residents in a wide range of well-wooded and baobab country throughout coastal Kenya and eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Makes a variety of loud, high-pitched and strangely metallic calls.

images.caption: Brown-headed Parrot · Plate 88

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is rather striking with broad bright orange band on breast, grey-brown head and blue-green rump and vent. In flight, adult male shows orange underwing-coverts. Adult female is very similar to immature Meyer’s Parrot, but lacks yellow on shoulder and has brown (not yellow) underwing-coverts. At close quarters note black bill and deep orange-red eyes. Immature is slightly paler than adult female. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are locally common in a wide range of semi-arid and arid bushed and wooded grasslands below 1,200m, often in areas with baobab trees.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Intermingles quiet chattering with rather muffled screeches.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Red-bellied Parrot

images.caption: African Orange-bellied Parrot · Plate 88

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large green parrot with a red forecrown, shoulders and thighs. At close range shows pale upper and dark lower mandible, and reddish-orange eyes. Sexes similar. In flight, appears largely green with dark flight feathers and bright red forecrown. Immature much duller with buff-brown forecrown, shoulders and thighs. Birds in EA are race massaicus.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and sometimes large flocks are common in highland forest (particularly Podocarpus and juniper) at 1,800–3,250m in W and central Kenya and northern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a shrill but not usually piercing warbling and chattering.

images.caption: Red-fronted Parrot · Plate 89

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Bright green with orange-red face, red bill, white eye-ring and yellow collar extending around hindneck and across breast; uppertail-coverts azure-blue. Sexes alike; immature duller. In flight looks bright green with orange-red face and blue rump. Introduced birds in Kenya frequently interbreed with Yellow-collared and show characteristics of both species. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to north-western Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi; pairs and flocks can be common in wooded grassland at 1,100–2,000m in northern Tanzania, including the Serengeti, occasionally west to Rwanda and Burundi. Escaped birds, around several towns in Kenya (including Nairobi, Naivasha, Kisumu and Mombasa), hybridise with Yellow-collared and are expanding their range.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Utters chattering squeaks, lacking any shrill notes (unlike hybrids).

images.caption: Fischer’s Lovebird · Plate 90

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Red bill, white eye-ring and blue uppertail-coverts similar to Fischer’s Lovebird, but head mostly dark brown, contrasting with broad rich yellow collar. Sexes similar; immature duller. In flight, appears much darker-headed than Fischer’s. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to Tanzania; pairs and flocks sometimes common in woodland and wooded grassland in north-central Tanzania at 1,100–1,800m to the east of Fischer’s (overlaps in some areas). Introduced birds in Kenya now hybridise with Fischer’s and are common there (see above).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls are similar to Fischer’s Lovebird, but more shrill and squeaky.

images.caption: Yellow-collared Lovebird · Plate 90

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Enormous, spectacular blue turaco; adult has red-tipped yellow bill and ragged black crest. Colourful, but rather muted blue from head to upper breast, upperparts and wings; lower breast greenish-yellow, belly to vent chestnut; long tail has yellowish-green side panels and broad black band near tip. Immature is duller with smaller crest. Great Blue does not have the red wing patches shown by other turacos. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small parties are locally common in good forest, relict forest patches, secondary growth and well-treed farmland nearby, at 700–2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Far-carrying hollow wooden rattle of rapid gonk-gonk-gonk-gonk- notes, which may continue for long periods, building to an excited crescendo with several individuals joining in. Also a loud rolling prrru call.

images.caption: Great Blue Turaco · Plate 91

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Deep blue turaco with bulbous bright yellow bill, yellow eye-patch, and brilliant crimson crest and outer wing. Immature duller with blackish bill and small dull frontal shield. In slow buoyant flight, reveals extensive crimson on wings. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles, pairs and small groups are widespread and locally common in riverine forest, forest edge, woodland and mature gardens at 700–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Often duets with a series of musical growls that slowly rise in tone to climax in a rolling bubbling for up to 15 seconds, which then descends before ending abruptly. GREEN TURACOS Eight mainly bottle-green and dark blue turacos which reveal scarlet wing patches in flight (five are on Plate 92). Colour and pattern of head markings aid identification. Sexes similar and immatures are like subdued adults. In wooded and forested areas, they run and bound through the canopy, often with their tails raised, before swooping to nearby trees. Their raucous calls are characteristic sounds of many forests.

images.caption: Ross’s Turaco · Plate 91

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive green turaco with white crested head, black forecrown, yellow bill and red eye-ring. Body largely bottle green with purple-blue wash to back, wings and tail. Monotypic

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are locally common in woodland (especially well-wooded valleys), thickets and bushed country at 1,000–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call starts with a single long laughing upslur and, after a short pause, continues with a rapid sequence of gruff khow notes that slur into each other.

images.caption: White-crested Turaco · Plate 91

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dark-crowned turaco with short, rounded blue-back crest, white oval loral spot, red eye-ring and white line below eye; bill dark red. Wings and tail rather dark violet-blue. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to East Africa; widespread and sometimes common, singles and pairs occur in a range of highland forests from massive blocks like Mt Kenya and Mt Kilimanjaro, to more isolated patches like the Taita Hills, Kenya, as well as well-wooded country and gardens, at 1,600–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls with loud, but gruff and muffled khaw notes, the first few quiet, rapid and ascending, then a set of 3–4 slower identical notes.

images.caption: Hartlaub’s Turaco · Plate 92

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Mainly green turaco with peaked crest edged white, bill appears all black in the field. White lines above and below red-ringed eyes. Wings dark green, tail often darker blue-green. Birds in EA are race emini.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are shy and hard to see, occupying dense forest canopy, at 700–2,800m. Although now rare in western Kenya, it can be common in the far west, including Rwanda and Burundi.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls a harsh roaring series of rrrerr notes, the first few slow and rising, then a long faster set of up to 15, slightly descending.

images.caption: Black-billed Turaco · Plate 92

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Livingstone’s, but has very long, white-tipped, floppy forward-pointing crest; also has bright red bill and white lines above and below red-ringed eyes. Wings green washed blue and tail glossed purple-black. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common in forest and riverine woodland in south-western Kenya and northern Tanzania, with a separate population in W and south-western Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a slightly descending series of growls preceded by an introductory growl and a short pause rrow… rrow- rrow-rrow-rrow-rrow.

images.caption: Schalow’s Turaco · Plate 92

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Attractive green turaco with peaked crest edged dull red and thinly fringed white (red on crest extends to nape); red bill and white lines above and below red-ringed eyes. Two races occur: nominate has blue-green wings and tail, and zanzibaricus (Zanzibar) has wings and tail violet-blue.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are locally common in dense coastal forest, woodland and remnant forest patches mainly in lowlands, but up to 1,500m in Usambara Mts, north-eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is similar to Schalow’s Turaco, but burrier; rising notes commence slowly and progress as a rapid series of up to 12 identical notes.

images.caption: Fischer’s Turaco · Plate 92

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large slender grey-and-white go-away-bird with tall grey crest. Grey upperparts, throat and breast are sharply separated from white lower breast to vent; long tail is grey, black and white. Sexes largely alike, but bill black in adult male and green in adult female. Immature duller than adult with plainer wings. In floppy undulating flight reveals white bars in wings and broad white band in tail. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family groups are common, widespread and often confiding in arid and semi-arid wooded and bush country to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls a repeated waah, a more rapid hollow wop-wop-wop… and occasionally a drawn-out ga-warr.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Corythaixoides.

images.caption: White-bellied Go-away-bird · Plate 93

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive bare-faced go-away-bird, largely grey-brown with contrasting white neck and breast. Two races occur, which are sometimes considered separate species: widespread leopoldi (Black-faced Go-away-bird) is black-faced with a green breast patch, while in extreme NKe the nominate race (Brown-faced Go-away-bird) has browner face and larger green breast patch. Sexes alike, but immature has duller face, brownish crest and lacks green on breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are locally common in open woodland, bush and cultivation, preferring wetter country west of White-bellied Go-away-bird, mainly below 1,400m, but occasionally to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a rather surprised corrr!, and less frequently heard is a loud, insane cackling duet.

images.caption: Bare-faced Go-away-bird · Plate 93

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Entirely dark ash-grey go-away-bird with a tall crest and long plain grey tail. Immature is paler grey-brown with shorter crest. Appears all grey in flight. Race in EA is molybdophanes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and groups are locally common in bushed grassland and woodland, including miombo, in S and south-eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a wonderful drawn-out gu’way (go-away); also a loud, harsh, pinched and interrogatory descending wherrrrrrrrr.

images.caption: Grey Go-away-bird · Plate 93

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Thickset grey-brown turaco with ashy head and shaggy white-tipped crest; conspicuous greenish-yellow or yellow bill. In rather ragged flight, reveals white bar in primaries and bold grey, black and white tail pattern. Immature like adult. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and groups are sometimes common in a wide range of wooded and bushed grassland, cultivation and gardens, at 700– 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls with loud, querulous and nasal notes which build up into a maniacal laughter.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Eastern Grey Plantain-eater

images.caption: Eastern Plantain-eater · Plate 93

clamator-glandarius.ref: Plate 94: Crested Cuckoos And Thick-Billed Cuckoo
clamator-glandarius.name: Great Spotted Cuckoo

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Largest crested cuckoo. Adult has shaggy pale grey crest, dark grey-brown upperparts with bold white spotting on wings, whitish underparts with buff-orange throat, and long, dark, graduated white-tipped tail. Strikingly different immature has black crown and cheeks, and chestnut primary patch in flight. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and sometimes common passage migrant to woodland, bushed and wooded grassland, and cultivation from sea level to 3,000m throughout the region, mainly Oct–Mar, with a notable passage through northern Tanzania, Jan–Mar. Some present throughout the year with scattered local breeding records.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Migrants are silent, but breeding birds give a loud woodpecker-like rattling chhhtrtrtrtrrr-titititititit.

images.caption: Great Spotted Cuckoo · Plate 94

clamator-jacobinus.ref: Plate 94: Crested Cuckoos And Thick-Billed Cuckoo
clamator-jacobinus.name: Jacobin Cuckoo

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to but smaller and shorter-tailed than Levaillant’s Cuckoo. Two races occur: widespread pica is black above and entirely white below (or hair-streaked) with a white wing patch and white-tipped tail. Light morph of southern race serratus is similar, but washed pale grey and finely streaked below. Dark morph serratus is jet-black (including tail ) except for white wing patch (dark morph Levaillant’s is larger with white tips to tail). Immature is brownish-black above and washed buff below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Sometimes common in bush, wooded grassland, scrub and cultivation from sea level to 3,000m, often in the rains. Breeds sporadically across the region. Migrations not well known, but race pica can be common moving south Nov–Jan and less common returning north in Mar–Apr. Southern serratus is uncommon Apr–Sep.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Migrants are silent, but breeding birds give squealed double and single notes, kwir’kik kwir’kik…kwir…kwir…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly known as Black-and-white Cuckoo Oxylophus jacobinus.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Pied Cuckoo

images.caption: Jacobin Cuckoo · Plate 94

clamator-levaillantii.ref: Plate 94: Crested Cuckoos And Thick-Billed Cuckoo
clamator-levaillantii.name: Levaillant’s Cuckoo

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large, crested black-and-white cuckoo with two distinct morphs: widespread light morph is black (glossed green) above and white below with heavy black streaking on throat and breast. Coastal dark morph is entirely black except for white patch at base of primaries and tips to tail. In flight, white wing patches and tail spots are conspicuous on both forms. Immature is dark brownish above, with throat and underparts washed buff. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Sometimes common intra-African migrant to moist woodland, bush and forest edge from sea level to 2,100m, shunning drier areas. Appears to be associated with the rains, not simply calendar months: from south-eastern Tanzania to Uganda birds occur Oct–Jun, and in western Kenya in May–Sep, with the black morph being mainly present in north-eastern Tanzania and coastal Kenya in Mar–Nov. Breeds sporadically throughout East Africa.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call comprises loud single-spaced squealed and rattled notes: ttttttttttt kweer kweer kweer tttttttt tttttt…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Oxylophus.

images.caption: Levaillant’s Cuckoo · Plate 94

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large grey cuckoo: adult male is grey above and on throat and breast, and thinly barred black and white below. From Common Cuckoo by more yellow-orange on bill (usually almost all basal half) and by complete white bars on two outertail feathers (usually very hard to see). Adult female is slightly browner above, with paler barred breast often with buff wash; very similar to adult female Common Cuckoo. Immature is barred throughout including rump. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and rather uncommon intra-African migrant to drier woodland, wooded and bushed grassland from sea level to 3,000m. Movements unclear, but records in all months in some areas, often during the rains, and birds may be overlooked when silent. Parasitises Fork-tailed Drongo.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a quiet repeated pooh-pooh which is very similar to African Hoopoe, but slightly slower.

images.caption: African Cuckoo · Plate 95

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Extremely similar to African Cuckoo but adult male has yellow-orange confined to base of bill and outer tail feathers spotted not barred (very hard to see). Adult female has two distinct colour morphs: either grey-brown (normal) or rufous (uncommon); both are barred below with strong rufous wash to sides of breast. Immature occurs in grey, brown and rufous morphs, all strongly barred like African, but rump plain (not barred). Two similar races occur: nominate as described, while subtelephonus is smaller and duller, with a paler throat, and more lighty barred underparts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and common Palearctic migrant to forest edge, woodland, wooded and bushed grassland on southward passage in Oct–Dec, and more common moving north in Mar–Apr (when it can be very common on the coast).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent in EA, but may call cuc-koo… in Mar–Apr.

images.caption: Common Cuckoo · Plate 95

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smaller and slightly more distinctly marked than larger grey cuckoos, but extremely similar to Madagascar Cuckoo. Adult male is grey above, on throat and breast, and well-barred black on white below, usually including undertail-coverts. Adult female has two distinct colour morphs: grey-brown with buff tinge to breast and flanks, or bright brick-red. Immature either grey-brown barred white and buff above, or much more rufous (hepatic morph). Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Migrates from South Asia, occurring Nov–Apr in forest edge, woodland and bush on coasts of Kenya and Tanzania (less commonly further inland). Sometimes common moving north in Mar–Apr.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent in region, but flushed birds may utter a loud staccato rattle.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly known as Asian Lesser Cuckoo.

images.caption: Lesser Cuckoo · Plate 95

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is dark grey above (sometimes paler on head), with grey throat, broad rufous band on breast, and black and white bands from upper breast to belly. Adult female is similar but has whitish-buff throat. Immature is charcoal-black above (with scaly pale fringes in fresh birds), with black throat and black and white bars below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread resident in forest edge, woodland and gardens, from sea level to 3,000m, wandering widely in rains, but also occurs as an intra-African migrant from the south to south-eastern Tanzania in Oct–Apr.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a familiar seasonal sound, usually three half-tone descending whistles, fwi-fwi-few (often rendered ‘it-will-rain!’); also a rising bubbling call, often partly in duet.

images.caption: Red-chested Cuckoo · Plate 96

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Variable dark cuckoo: most birds are often entirely black (blue-black in good light), but may show some pale barring below, especially on vent. Birds in the west commonly black above and rather dingy black and buff below, strongly washed rufous across breast and throat (formerly considered a race, gabonensis). Similar Red-chested Cuckoo has plain grey or whitish-buff throat. Sexes alike, immature duller. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread intra-African migrant to forest edge, woodland, wooded grassland and thickets, from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a three-note rising whistle, first two notes identical, third an upslur commencing a half-tone higher, for for-fier, sometimes leading into a cheerful rising bubbling call. LONG-TAILED CUCKOOS Three very similar-looking and elusive forest cuckoos with long graduated tails. All are extremely difficult to see and are best identified by call. Believed to parasitise akalats, illadopsises and ant-thrushes. Sexes alike.

images.caption: Black Cuckoo · Plate 96

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dark olive-brown and well barred rufous-buff above, whitish below and sharply barred black, with narrower denser barring on throat. Extent of buff on throat and vent varies. Immature similar, but more rufous fringes above and densely barred throat.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In the west, darker nominate race is resident and locally common in montane forest to 2,800m. In central Kenya and eastern Tanzania patulus inhabits montane and lower forest and woodland, and is present seasonally at the coast in Jun–Sep. Calls from canopy throughout the day, but forages at all levels.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Long sequence of slowly accelerating slurred and wheezy weeeyu weeeyu weeeyu… notes, then a more clipped wee-we’yu, wee-we’yu…, often ending with a fast wit-wit-wu wit-wit-wu (recalling Red-chested Cuckoo).

images.caption: Barred Long-tailed Cuckoo · Plate 96

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is metallic bronze-green above, with bold green-and-white face pattern, obvious red eye and white spots on wing-coverts. White below with barred flanks, and white spots in outer tail. In flight has entirely barred underwing. Adult female is brown and green above, with russet throat and upper breast, and densely barred flanks; eyes dull brown. Immature has two colour morphs: commonest is like adult female, but with rufous barring on upperparts and heavily streaked throat; rarer form is largely rufous above and below. Both have bright red bills. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common resident and partial migrant in a wide range of bushed and wooded grassland, and cultivation, from sea level to 2,200m, often appearing during rains.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Memorable onomatopoeic dee-dee-dee-dee-derik…, which can be clear, but is often wildly accelerated and slurred.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Dideric Cuckoo

images.caption: Diederik Cuckoo · Plate 97

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is iridescent bright green above, with uniform wings, small white bar behind dark eye, snow-white below with dark green patches on sides of breast. Adult female is bronze-green above with fine russet barring below; eyes pale brown. In flight, adult male has white underwing-coverts and largely white outer tail; female and immature also show white outer tail. Immature is similar to adult female, but more heavily barred above and below, with subdued bar behind eye and dark bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread resident in moister and often denser habitats than Diederik Cuckoo, including woodland, forest edge, bush and gardens, from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a repeated high-pitched slurred whistle, fwiii-fi, fwiii-fi…

images.caption: Klaas’s Cuckoo · Plate 97

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is a stunningly gaudy emerald-green and yellow cuckoo. Adult female is barred rufous and green above, and green and white below, and never has white flash behind eye of Klaas’s. Immature is like adult female. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Solitary, but widespread and common resident of moist forest, dense woodland and thickets, from sea level to 2,000m. Males call from high canopy and are hard to see despite bright colours.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very distinctive set of four whistles, whi’twau wor-wee (often translated as ‘hel-lo geor-gie’), with first two notes descending, a short pause, then two accentuated rising slurs.

images.caption: African Emerald Cuckoo · Plate 97

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Strange, long-tailed grey cuckoo with bright yellow bill, blue skin around red eyes, and a dark slaty-blue sheen on back, wings and tail. Sexes alike; immature duller with brownish throat, pale horn bill and brown eyes. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Dense thickets, forest patches and edges at 700–2,000m in the west.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a series of paired clicking notes that starts slowly and accelerates into a rapid series of descending tic notes, terminating in a long rattle, tic-tic, tic-tic, tic-tic, tictictictic tictrrrrrrrrr.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Blue Malkoha

images.caption: Chattering Yellowbill · Plate 97

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Chattering Yellowbill, but has a green sheen to back, wings and tail. Sexes alike; immature duller with brownish throat, pale horn bill and brown eyes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Mainly a migrant from the south to dense thickets, forest patches and edges, in coastal lowlands, less often inland, in May–Sep.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls a sequence of accelerating tic notes Chattering Yellowbill, as well as a loud shrill wailing k’weeeap k’weeeap k’weeeap k’weeeap…

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Green Malkoha

images.caption: Whistling Yellowbill · Plate 97

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three races and two distinct forms occur: paler-crowned nominate and brighter loandae share a long white supercilium, with fine pale streaking extending onto rufous-brown back; pale below, streaked and barred darker. Immature similar, but supercilium, streaking on upperparts and entire underparts suffused with buff. Race fasciipygialis (sometimes treated as a separate species, Burchell’s Coucal) has a blue-black crown and nape, rufous back and wings; immature similar to other races.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are widespread and common in rank vegetation, thickets, bushed and wooded grassland, often near water, from sea level to 2,300m, with nominate (north-eastern Uganda and Kenya), loandae (Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, south-western Kenya and Tanzania) and fasciipygialis (S and south-eastern Tanzania, including Mafia Island).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: The typical ‘water-bottle’ series of descending hollow notes is more hurried than other coucals; also has a variety of harsh kak notes.

images.caption: White-browed Coucal · Plate 98

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large, robust coucal with glossy blue-black crown extending over nape (may look black in field), off-white to buff below, with long black tail slightly glossed green. Immature is like adult, but has dull black faintly streaked crown, barred primaries, buffy underparts and black-brown tail. In the west, race fischeri is widespread; slightly brighter nominate race occupies WKe and CKe highlands.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Resident and locally common close to water in marshes, papyrus swamps and other densely vegetated wet areas at 700–2,000m, rarely to 2,700m. Also occurs in highland undergrowth in central Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a typical coucal descending series, lower and slower than White-browed.

images.caption: Blue-headed Coucal · Plate 98

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to White-browed Coucal race fasciipygialis, but rump and tail are plain black (not barred). Immature like immature White-browed, but has browner crown, only faint buff supercilium, and buffy (not grey-white) underparts. Blue-headed and Coppery-tailed Coucals are much larger. The nominate race is widespread; race flecki (with slightly blue-black crown) occurs in C and STz.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread resident of drier habitats, like forest clearings, thickets and bushed grassland (being the least water-dependent coucal).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call varies locally, but typical descending sequence follows an initial two-note introduction, ending on a higher series of identical notes.

images.caption: Senegal Coucal · Plate 98

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smallest coucal; breeding adult is highly distinctive being all black with chestnut wings. Non-breeding adult is heavily streaked buff and brown on head and upper back, barred rufous and black on wings and tail, and mottled brown and buff below. Immature is like non-breeding adult but has more extensive barring on crown (resembles White-browed but smaller and always lacks white brow). Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Generally uncommon and local in swamps, river valleys and flooded grassland from sea level to 2,700m. Mainly in the west and coastal lowlands, although wanders widely during the rains.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a regular, rather hollow-sounding kuk-uk kuk-uk kuk-uk…, the notes identical and rhythmic, and a subdued typical descending coucal series.

images.caption: Black Coucal · Plate 98

tyto-alba.ref: Plate 99: Barn Owls And Medium-Sized Owls
tyto-alba.name: Barn Owl

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Ghostly owl patterned golden-buff and pale grey above (finely speckled black and white), with small dark eyes set in a pale heart-shaped facial disc, and white to creamy-buff underparts. In buoyant flight, appears largely pale golden-buff and white. Birds in EA are race affinis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are uncommon but widespread residents from sea level to 3,000m, often near settlements, and in buildings, old wells and Hamerkop nests; tends to be absent from forest and arid country.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls frequently, although bird is usually unseen, a high-pitched screamed chrirrrr given singly or in series.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities treat the Asian and American populations as separate species, renaming this form as Western Barn Owl.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Common Barn Owl

images.caption: Barn Owl · Plate 99

asio-capensis.ref: Plate 99: Barn Owls And Medium-Sized Owls
asio-capensis.name: Marsh Owl

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Warm uniform brown above and on breast, and buff-brown below, with penetrating dark eyes set in a paler facial disc. Short ear-tufts sometimes visible at rest. In flight, resembles African Grass Owl but shows obviously larger rich buff patch at base of primaries. Vagrant Short-eared Owl is paler with yellow eyes. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and sometimes small groups are not uncommon in grassland, as well as moorland and marshes below 3,000m. Often active just before dusk and flushes easily in daylight.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Unusual call is a rising rasp krrrik or a series of rasps.

images.caption: Marsh Owl · Plate 99

strix-woodfordii.ref: Plate 99: Barn Owls And Medium-Sized Owls
strix-woodfordii.name: African Wood Owl

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Attractive round-headed owl without ear-tufts; lightly barred facial disc with dark brown eyes, underparts heavily barred rufous-brown and white. Three rather similar races occur: brighter nuchalis in the west, darker nigricantior in Ke and NTz, and nominate in SWTz.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in a wide range of forest and forest edge habitats, woodland, and mature gardens, from sea level to 2,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male gives a rhythmic oo-hoo-oohu-hu-hu-hu, female often replies with identical series at a lower tone. Male also gives a long rising and then falling slurred oo-ooooooo.

images.caption: African Wood Owl · Plate 99

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger, paler and greyer than scops-owls with eyes that can quickly change from yellow to red, and white face mask with black borders. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are local and rarely common residents in a variety of dry bush country (particularly acacia) up to 1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a hollow dove-like kuk-koo’ooh with the last note descending, although birds in EUg make a simple descending pooor.

images.caption: Northern White-faced Owl · Plate 100

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Almost identical to Northern White-faced Owl, but usually darker and greyer. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are local and generally uncommon residents from sea level to 1,700m, preferring dry woodland and bushed and wooded grassland.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a reverberating wu-wu-wu-wu-wu-wu-wu woo!, the last note explosive. SCOPS-OWLS Small owls with ear-tufts (though often lowered and hard to see). Cryptic plumage and habit of often roosting close to tree trunks makes them very hard to locate and when disturbed they may respond by raising their ears-tufts and adopting a thin elongated posture. Sexes and immatures are similar.

images.caption: Southern White-faced Owl · Plate 100

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Well camouflaged scops-owl entirely streaked and mottled grey-brown, but some are lightly washed warmer brown or pale rufous. Bright yellow eyes are set in narrowly black-edged grey facial disc, and underparts boldly marked, giving marbled effect. The nominate race is widespread, paler nivosus occurs in EKe.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common and widespread in dry bush and woodland, including large trees along river courses, from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls for long periods, a musical krrrou or krruuup, given at regular intervals of 4–8 seconds. Eastern birds tend to sound more reverberating than western populations.

images.caption: African Scops-Owl · Plate 100

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very slightly larger than African Scops-Owl with a longer primary projection and often a little browner and plainer. Most are the nominate race, but there are specimens of pulchellus (more spotted mantle) and turanicus (slightly paler).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles are scarce Palearctic migrants, but almost certainly overlooked in wooded habitats and forest edge, Nov–Apr. Scattered records are mostly in Kenya and Uganda, and one from Pare Mts, northern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent in region, but in Palearctic calls a repeated single hoo or peu.

images.caption: Eurasian Scops-Owl · Plate 100

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Tiny scops-owl with pale grey, grey-brown and bright rufous morphs. All are lightly speckled black and white above, and vermiculated and speckled black and white below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to coastal forest in Kenya and north-eastern Tanzania. Pairs are best known from red soil Cynometra forest of Arabuko- Sokoke Forest, Kenya, but also occurs further north in Dakatcha Woodlands, and at low densities up to 400m in foothills of the East Usambara Mts, north-eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Noisy, giving a hollow rather high-pitched and ventriloquial hooh at about 2-second intervals for long periods without pause. EN

images.caption: Sokoke Scops-Owl · Plate 100

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Brown above with small white spots on crown and back, larger white spots on scapulars (forming a white line), two dark eye spots (false eyes) on nape, and intimidating yellow eyes. Underparts variably streaked and spotted rufous-brown with broad streaking extending to lower flanks. Birds in EA are race diurnum.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are widespread and very common in bushed and wooded grasslands, preferring drier areas with acacias, mainly below 2,200m (sometimes to 3,200m).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call starts with a long series of short piped fwoo-fwoo-fwoo… notes that gradually rise in pitch and volume and, after a pause, a shorter sequence of whistled downslurs fweeu-fweeu-fweeu… often given in a seesawing duet.

images.caption: Pearl-spotted Owlet · Plate 102

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two similar races occur with brown heads, barred backs, and well-barred and spotted underparts, but differ in head pattern: scheffleri (EKe and ETz) has crown spotted with white dots; ngamiense (C and STz) has crown barred whitish.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs of scheffleri are local and uncommon in coastal forest and woodland, while ngamiense is widespread and common in interior woodlands.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Long series commences with regular identical piped downslurs then, after a pause, a set of peculiar vibrato downslurs that seesaw towards the end.

images.caption: African Barred Owlet · Plate 102

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather plain owlet with a greyish head, dark reddish-brown back and wings, rufous-washed chest and flanks (with variable dark spots), and boldly white-spotted tail. Two races occur: medje in WUg is darker above and more spotted below than more eastern elgonense.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are uncommon residents of forests in western Uganda above 700m, but more confined to highland forest in W and possibly central Kenya at 1,500–2,350m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Gives a piped series of 3–6 identical phoo-phoo-phoo… notes, and a regular high-pitched and descending slurred feeeeeeo.

images.caption: Red-chested Owlet · Plate 102

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Huge orange owl which is unlikely to be confused with any other bird. Bright orange-rufous above with dark barring. Slightly paler below, with variable dark spots and bars (usually more concentrated on flanks). Sexes similar but female is larger. Immature much paler orange-rufous, and juvenile leaves nest with much white on head and underparts. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are uncommon beside well-wooded slow-flowing larger rivers, as well as lakes and mangroves from sea level to 1,700m. Occurrence scattered, but ranges from Murchison Falls NP, western Uganda, to Ruvubu NP in Burundi, from the Maasai Mara Game Reserve, south-western Kenya to the Tana River in eastern Kenya, and on major rivers in southern Tanzania, like those in Selous Game Reserve.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Common call is a deep booming oom… oom… oom… at 4–5 second intervals; also an eerie downslurred scream.

images.caption: Pel’s Fishing-Owl · Plate 102

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Typical Caprimulgus nightjar; mainly differs from Slender-tailed and Long-tailed in square-ended tail. Males of all three have white spots on primaries (4–5 feathers in Square-tailed), white bar on lesser wing-coverts, narrow white outer tail, and white tips to secondaries forming a white bar along trailing edge of wing. Female has buff wing spots and outer tail. Two races occur: welwitschii occurs from WUg and SKe to STz (as described), while paler, greyer southern African griseoplurus is reported as an intra-African migrant to Ug and SKe in Jun–Sep.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in bushed grassland, clearings in woodland, and open cultivated areas, from sea level to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a long low continuous churring, typically about 20 notes per second, although often changes speed and pitch. Also gives a whoop or several a-whoop calls in flight. [Alt. Mozambique Nightjar] Slender-tailed Nightjar Caprimulgus clarus  28cm, 11" Similar to Square-tailed Nightjar, with white spots on primaries (6–7 feathers), white bar on lesser wing-coverts, narrow white outer tail, and white tips to secondaries forming a white bar along trailing edge of wing. Both sexes have elongated central tail feathers but these may wear or break, and are often hard to see on the female. Female has wing spots and outer tail buff. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in dry bush country, coastal scrub and fallow cultivation, often near water, from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a slow steady kwoikwoikwoikwoi… (like a pulsating generator); a rapid kwip-kwip or kwip-kwip-kwip is given in flight. Long-tailed Nightjar Caprimulgus climacurus  43cm, 17" Similar to Square-tailed and Slender-tailed Nightjars, with white spots on primaries (5 feathers), white bar on lesser wing-coverts, narrow white outer tail, and white tips to secondaries forming a white bar along trailing edge of wing. Both sexes have very long central tail feathers (up to 34cm, 13” in male), but moulting birds have shorter tails and are very similar to Slender-tailed. Female has buff wing spots and outer tail. Southern birds often washed rufous. Birds in EA are race sclateri.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Seasonally common in range, preferring bushed grasslands and semi-arid country, and breeds in northern Uganda during Mar–Jul.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a very fast and constant, almost reeling, churr of 40 plus notes per second (much faster than other churring nightjars), also a nasal chyaw flight call.

images.caption: Square-tailed Nightjar · Plate 103

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Quite similar to Square-tailed Nightjar, but male has broad white outer tail and lacks white bar on lesser wing-coverts and trailing edge of wing. Looks short-tailed in flight when male also shows white spots in primaries (4–5 feathers). Female has buff wing spots and outer tail. With good views, both sexes show dark cheeks and buff collar but overall coloration is yellowish-brown. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common with a preference for wet grassland and marshy areas at 600–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a repeated simple and monotonous chok-chok-chok…, and a melodious laughing whip hululululu in flight.

images.caption: Swamp Nightjar · Plate 103

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather dark nightjar with a rufous collar. Male has white spots on primaries (4 feathers) and almost all-white outer tail. Female has buffy wing spots and less white in outer tail. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in highlands, usually in vicinity of forest, but also in nearby farmland and well-wooded urban areas, mainly at 1,500–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A nasal ank-ank-ank often precedes a haunting high-pitched and whistled piiiyu-pirrrrr (first note is a falling then rising upslur, the last slightly falling and tremulous). Higher-pitched than Fiery-necked Nightjar.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Abyssinian Nightjar

images.caption: Montane Nightjar · Plate 104

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: In flight, male shows white spots on primaries (4 feathers) and large white tail corners (approximately one third). Rich rufous ear-coverts and hindcollar may be visible in daylight. Female has smaller wing spots and tail corners, sometimes washed buffish. In STz, a rufous morph with variable amount of cinnamon-rufous on head, back, tail and underparts occurs. Birds in EA are race shelleyi.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in forest and woodland (especially miombo) throughout the south and in coastal Kenya, from sea level to 1,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a slow woi- woi- woi-… preceding a dramatic whistled t’woy-wirrrrrr (the first note a falling then slightly rising upslur, the last very tremulous).

images.caption: Fiery-necked Nightjar · Plate 104

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Fiery-necked Nightjar with rufous hindneck, white spots on primaries (3–4 feathers) and fairly large white tail corners. Differs in being generally darker, including ear-coverts, with boldly marked black and buff scapulars, larger creamy-buff spots on wing-coverts, and a very different voice. Female has spots on wings and tail smaller and washed brownish. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common resident and migrant, most often found in grassland and on rocky slopes, but always with some cover. Mainly at mid-altitudes, but range extends from near sea level to 3,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a long series of deep hollow-sounding churrs, lacking any rising or falling inflection, and often commencing with a pair of hurried hiccup-like notes, kwi-kuk kwi-kuk.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly known as Dusky Nightjar.

images.caption: Sombre Nightjar · Plate 105

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Variable colour morphs complicate identification of this species even more than usual. Typical male is similar to Sombre Nightjar but paler, lacks boldly marked scapulars, and has slightly smaller white tail corners. In daylight often appears paler grey-brown, but in flight shows more rufous in wings and some have greyer central tail. Female has buffy and slightly smaller wing and tail spots. Rufous morph is washed rufous with deeper rufous wing spots; brown morph is darker brown, including central tail. Birds in EA are race torridus.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in dry bush and semi-desert in north and east at 600–1,250m. Exact status uncertain, but has occurred throughout the year, with most records in Nov–Mar.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call not recorded in region, but elsewhere gives a barking and paired wow-wow very similar to Freckled Nightjar (but less musical and more rushed).

images.caption: Nubian Nightjar · Plate 105

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A rather plain-looking nightjar with grey-brown, brown, and rufous morphs. All males have white spots on primaries (4 feathers), large white corners to tail, and no white on throat (may show small black spots on crown and scapulars like Star-spotted Nightjar). Females have buffy-brown wing spots and no white in tail. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Mainly a seasonally common non-breeding migrant, Oct–Apr. Others (possibly breeding birds) occur in the far north in May–Aug. Recorded from a wide variety of bush country and grassland, from sea level to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Mostly silent in EA, but gives a chuck call when flushed; breeding birds call with a long mechanical churr similar to but higher-pitched than Sombre Nightjar.

images.caption: Plain Nightjar · Plate 105

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Plain Nightjar, with similar plain overall appearance. Colour morphs include brown, grey-brown, rufous, and buff. Best identified from Plain by voice and smaller white corners to tail in both sexes. Day-roosting birds show white patches either side of throat (all brown on Plain) and very small black spots on crown and scapulars. Birds in EA are race simplex.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common up north, particularly in areas with lava and nearby sandy scrub, mainly at 350–1,000m, rarely wandering higher.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a steady yelping pweu, pweu, pweu…

images.caption: Star-spotted Nightjar · Plate 105

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small, boldly patterned nightjar with grey-brown and rufous morphs. In flight, shows white spots on primaries (4 feathers), and small white corners to tail in both sexes (slightly tinged buff on female). In daylight often shows large white throat patch and broad creamy-buff fringes to scapulars. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in dry bush country from sea level to 1,250m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a monotonous, whistled and rather tremulous t-weer-tweeu (first note a rising upslur, last notes descending).

images.caption: Donaldson Smith’s Nightjar · Plate 105

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large migratory nightjar. In flight male shows white spots on primaries (3–4 feathers) and white tail corners. Four races occur, varying mainly in overall tone, but always difficult to judge in the dark: nominate is grey-brown, meridionalis slightly smaller, unwini paler grey-brown and plumipes cinnamon-buff. In daylight, all show narrow black streaks on the crown, blackish-mottled shoulders and a pale bar on the lesser wing-coverts; lacks rufous hindneck of many nightjars. Females lack white or buff in wings and tail.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic winter visitor and passage migrant in a wide range of more open habitats during Oct–Apr, from sea level to 2,000m; tends to roost on branches during the day.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent in EA, but occasionally calls quoik when flushed.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Eurasian Nightjar

images.caption: European Nightjar · Plate 106

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large, dark grey-brown nightjar, mottled all over with fine greyish or buffy speckles. May show whitish throat markings. No rufous hindneck. In flight male shows white spots on primaries (4 feathers) and small white tail corners. Female has white wing spots but tail is barred dark brown on brown (no pale corners). Northern birds are the nominate race, while colder-toned granosus occurs in STz.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common on rocky hills and escarpments at 600–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Paired musical and whiplashed kow-wow…kow-wow… notes, often interspersed with irregular nasal upslurs, wup-wup-wup…

images.caption: Freckled Nightjar · Plate 106

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is unmistakable with broad white flash right across wing and long white wing-streamers (elongated second primary). Non-breeding male loses long pennants, but is still distinctive with broad white flash and black tips to wings. Female has rufous hindneck, and strongly barred blackish and rufous flight feathers and tail (no white); similar to non-breeding male and female Standard-winged Nightjar but larger. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Breeds in southern Tanzania (Aug–Mar) then migrates north where it may be locally common (particularly in west). Prefers bushland and bushed grassland at 1,000–2,800m, but may wander to near sea level.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Breeding birds utter a rapid insect-like chitchitchitchit… which is similar to but slower than Standard-winged Nightjar.

images.caption: Pennant-winged Nightjar · Plate 106

apus-affinis.ref: Plate 107: White-Rumped Swifts And Large Swifts
apus-affinis.name: Little Swift

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small swift with rectangular white rump patch (extending onto lower flanks), square-ended tail and white throat patch. Seems stocky in flight, with fairly broad wings, interspersing rather fluttery wingbeats with short glides. Birds in EA include the nominate race, and aerobates with darker wings and tail.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small to large flocks are common and widespread from the coast to 3,000m. Often seen in small screaming parties. Nests under bridges, in villages and towns, as well as in natural sites like cliffs and gorges. Widespread away from dry north-eastern Kenya, but local and uncommon in W, C and southern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A very noisy swift which frequently gives musical twittering downslurs.

images.caption: Little Swift · Plate 107

apus-horus.ref: Plate 107: White-Rumped Swifts And Large Swifts
apus-horus.name: Horus Swift

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Stocky dark swift with shallow-forked tail, broad white band on rump (wrapping around flanks like Little Swift) and large white throat (may extend to upper breast). In flight appears shorter-tailed than White-rumped Swift, and spread tail may seem only slightly notched. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are mainly intra-African migrants, present in East Africa during Mar–Sep, and breeding in unused holes in bee-eater colonies in the highlands at 1600–2,000m, occasionally to 3,000m. Wanderers may occur almost anywhere, but confusion with similar species means precise extent of range and seasonality are unclear.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Low-pitched, burry and downslurred screams have a unique nasal and pinched quality.

images.caption: Horus Swift · Plate 107

apus-caffer.ref: Plate 107: White-Rumped Swifts And Large Swifts
apus-caffer.name: White-rumped Swift

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slender and slightly longer-bodied than Little Swift, with forked tail and narrow crescent-shaped white rump (which hardly wraps onto lower flanks); throat clearly white. In fluid flight, looks slim-winged with pointed tail that only appears forked if spread (often while banking). Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: More solitary than Little Swift, but pairs and small flocks are common from sea level to 3,000m in villages and towns, as well as near rocky cliffs and gorges. Nests in crevices and often in old mud nests built by swallows. Widespread at low densities away from arid north-eastern Kenya, and largely absent from W and central Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Breeding birds give rapid short burry and buzzy rattled churrs; lower-pitched than most other swifts. LARGE SWIFTS Outsized swifts with broad wings and thickset bodies, and deep powerful flight (noisy at close quarters). Size of single Mottled Swifts can be hard to judge, and both species wander far from nest sites. Sexes and immatures are very similar. Both species were formerly in the genus Apus.

images.caption: White-rumped Swift · Plate 107

tachymarptis-melba.ref: Plate 107: White-Rumped Swifts And Large Swifts
tachymarptis-melba.name: Alpine Swift

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctively patterned huge swift: uniform brown above and largely white below with well-defined brown breast-band. Powerful in flight with deep wingbeats. Three races occur: the northern nominate is seasonal in Ug, darker africanus is a widespread resident, and darkest race maximus occurs in WUg, Rw and Bu.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or small groups are fairly uncommon away from their highland nesting sites, but are widespread and often associate with other swifts. Palearctic breeding birds occur in Uganda (Sep–Apr) and may wander elsewhere (but patterns poorly known).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: At breeding colonies gives a twittering trill and a soft trilled scream.

images.caption: Alpine Swift · Plate 107

tachymarptis-aequatorialis.ref: Plate 107: White-Rumped Swifts And Large Swifts
tachymarptis-aequatorialis.name: Mottled Swift

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very large grey-brown swift with mottled underparts (only visible at close range and in good light) and small dingy white throat. When close, striking and impressive with long wings and rather pointed forked tail. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Single birds to large flocks are common in the highlands to 3,000m, but birds wander widely, often feeding over wetlands.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Around breeding colonies gives dry twittering trills, almost always screamed in excited aerial chases.

images.caption: Mottled Swift · Plate 107

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dark blackish swift with slightly paler blackish-brown patch on inner upperwing (secondaries and greater coverts) that contrasts with darker body and rest of wing. Always has a dark forehead, with variable white or whitish-grey throat. Birds in EA are race roehli.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small parties and flocks are sometimes common (often with other swifts) in the highlands from western Uganda to Burundi, from north-eastern Uganda through Kenya to north-eastern Tanzania, and in south-western Tanzania, at 1,000–2,400m (but may wander to other areas).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Near breeding sites gives an excited rasping trill without any musical quality.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: African Black Swift

images.caption: African Swift · Plate 108

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Widespread nominate race is dark brown and similar to African Swift, but in good light is always obviously brown (not black). Contrasting paler inner wing patch on flight feathers from above (slightly more extensive than in African), and also visible from below; often appears translucent. Forehead dark brown, with variable but usually poorly defined whitish throat. Race somalicus is paler grey-brown with a well-defined white throat and is occasionally recorded in NKe.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small (sometimes large) flocks are locally common, often in drier country, breeding in rocky cliffs below 2,800m from north-eastern Uganda through W and central Kenya to northern Tanzania (abundant at roosts in Hell’s Gate NP, Kenya). Occasionally wanders.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In flight gives short dry and rasping trilled downslurs and high-pitched twittering notes.

images.caption: Nyanza Swift · Plate 108

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Nominate race is an entirely sooty black-brown swift, lacking the contrast in wings of African and Nyanza Swifts, with small but prominent white throat patch.
