Forehead dark (paler in immature). Eastern race pekinensis is paler sooty-brown, with a slightly larger, brighter throat patch.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic migrant occurring in small to sometimes huge flocks, often ahead of weather fronts. Main passage is Sep–Dec (south) and Mar–Apr (north), but also occurs Aug–Apr in areas with abundant insect prey, often over wet grassland. Race pekinensis has been recorded in Uganda and Kenya; its status is unclear but it can be common in coastal lowlands in Nov–Dec.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent in EA, but may give harsh high-pitched screams.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Eurasian Swift

images.caption: Common Swift · Plate 108

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A sooty-brown swift with a prominent white throat, either a white or dark forecrown, and faint scaly underparts (only visible at very close range). Dark-headed birds may be indistinguishable from pekinensis race of Common Swift (except by call). Individuals with a whitish forecrown are similar to immature nominate Common, but latter is overall blacker at all ages. Best identified from Black and Nyanza Swifts by more uniform mantle and upperwing. Birds in EA are the race bensoni.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small to large flocks visit coastal Kenya and northern Tanzania from breeding sites in NE Africa in Oct–May (often over forests like Arabuko-Sokoke and the Shimba Hills, Kenya).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In flight gives musical trilled downslurs.

images.caption: Forbes-Watson’s Swift · Plate 108

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very slim, uniform mouse-brown swift, with long scimitar wings and long, very deeply forked tail. Highly characteristic flickering flight, with tail invariably held closed and needle-like. Two races occur: western myochrous is lightly glossed green on wings and tail, while eastern laemostigma is slightly paler.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: More solitary than other swifts, but pairs and small flocks are common and widespread from sea level to 1,400m (less often to 2,000m), invariably associated with palm trees.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Breeding birds give thin high-pitched twittering and rattled trills. SPINETAILS Atypical swifts with broad wings and short tails; usually in pairs or small groups. Extent of white in plumage, range and habitat aid identification. Sexes and immatures similar.

images.caption: African Palm Swift · Plate 109

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Extremely short-tailed spinetail, with broad black wings (narrowing close to body), extensive white belly and narrow white rump contrasting with blackish-brown throat and upper flanks. Flight appears ‘uncertain’, fluttery and bat-like, with much slow wheeling and chasing, often low over canopy. Two races occur: pale-throated sheppardi in the lowlands of EKe and Tz, and the darker-throated nominate in WTz.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are local and uncommon in forest and woodland (including miombo), throughout coastal lowlands of Kenya and inland on major rivers, but much more widespread in Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Distinctive musical twittering.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Bat-like Spinetail

images.caption: Böhm’s Spinetail · Plate 109

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Closely recalls Little Swift, but white rump extends as narrow whitish band across lower belly (can be hard to see). Indistinct mottling on throat and breast also obscure in the field. Flight swift-like, without fluttering of other spinetails. Two races occur: blacker sharpei in W and SUg, and stictilaema elsewhere.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are rather uncommon and local residents over forests in W and southern Uganda, but more widespread over woodland, open forest and edges from central Kenya south into Tanzania (often near baobabs).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Gives a variety of rhythmic chitters and squeaks in flight.

images.caption: Mottled Spinetail · Plate 109

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is a scruffy, long-tailed, buff and brown bird with a brown crest, whitish cheeks, blackish patch around eye and fine dark barring on throat and breast. Bill is black above and pink below. Similar immature has shorter crest and paler duller bill. Nine similar and intergrading races occur, varying mainly in being lighter or darker brown, and presence or absence of barring on throat.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are widespread and common in a variety of moister bush from thickets to forest edge, including gardens, from sea level to 2,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Scratchy and unpleasant raspy churrs given when perched and in flight.

images.caption: Speckled Mousebird · Plate 110

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has a white crest and face, obvious small blackish mask, finely barred throat, hindneck and mantle, and grey-brown tail. Bill is pale with a dark tip. Immature has duller crest and less pronounced barring. Two races occur: turneri in NKe is darker with stronger barring than the nominate in SEKe and NETz.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks are rather uncommon in arid and semi-arid bush from sea level to 1,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls rapid, spitted metallic notes titititititititit…

images.caption: White-headed Mousebird · Plate 110

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slender, thin-tailed, crested adult is mainly grey-brown with a red mask, black-tipped red bill and blue nape patch. Immature is duller, with less distinct blue nape, greenish facial skin and pale bill. Four races occur and mainly differ in overall grey or grey-brown appearance.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks are widespread and common in arid and semi-arid bushland, woodland and sparsely bushed grassland from sea level to 1,900m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls a single loud and rather mournful piiiyew and softer short nasal slurred notes, which are rather shorebird-like in quality.

images.caption: Blue-naped Mousebird · Plate 110

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is vivid green above with green throat and upper breast, red belly, and blue-green tail with white outer tail feathers (tail looks all white from below). Adult female is duller and has cinnamon-brown (not green) forecrown, throat and breast. Immature is like adult female but has white tips to wing-coverts. Three races occur: nominate male as described (widespread), bluer-breasted brachyurum (WUg) and bronze-breasted coastal littorale (EKe to ETz).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are widespread and reasonably common residents in forest and richer woodland from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a pulsating, repeated and crooned krooo-krrrou with strong accent on the second note. Each long series commences with short purred notes and increases in volume.

images.caption: Narina Trogon · Plate 110

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to Narina Trogon, but rather darker with blue band on breast. From behind has narrowly barred black-and-white tail edges, and from below tail is entirely barred. Adult female has dull brown head and breast. Immature similar to adult female, but has pale-tipped wing-coverts. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are uncommon in highland forest at 900–2,600m (usually at higher altitudes than Narina Trogon where their ranges overlap).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a series of up to a dozen identical upslurred or downslurred reedy notes, fweu-fweu-fweu…, with pauses between each set, and also a single far-carrying yaow from high in the canopy.

images.caption: Bar-tailed Trogon · Plate 110

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large characterful black-and-white crested kingfisher. Adult male has two complete breast-bands; adult female has one broken band. Immature similar to adult female but has brown fringing to face and throat, and duller breast-band. Uniquely, fishes from hovering flight, thereby exploiting open water. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Highly social; singles and groups are widespread and common residents beside all types of water, from sea level to 2,300m, including coastal shallows.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls an explosive and rather tern-like chit-chit, which often breaks into a metallic, musical and rhythmic chittering with many birds joining in excitedly.

images.caption: Pied Kingfisher · Plate 111

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small, dumpy, rather drab kingfisher with dark eyestripe, whitish or buffy throat and collar, and variably streaked crown, lower breast and flanks. Bill black with red lower mandible. Sexes similar, although male has black band on underwing (seen when flashes open wings in display) and greyer crown than female. In rapid direct flight shows a turquoise-blue back, rump and tail. Immature has dull reddish bill, is less streaked and can be darkly scaled below. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common and widespread from sea level to 2,300m in a wide range of bushed and wooded grassland, often far from water.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Regularly repeated call is an emphatic isolated first note followed by a descending series of trills: fi-frrrrrrr… fi-frrrrrrr… fi-frrrrrr…

images.caption: Striped Kingfisher · Plate 111

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult of widespread nominate race has a pale grey head and breast, black upper back and bright blue lower back, wings and tail, with a red bill and chestnut belly. Sexes similar, immature duller with dusky barring on head and breast, very pale chestnut belly, and dark-tipped red bill. In Rw south to STz (and migrating east Apr–Sep) race pallidiventris has a greyer head and back, and paler chestnut belly; semicaerulea (visiting from SW Arabia, Aug–Mar) has a browner crown and deep chestnut belly; coastal hyacinthina has violet-tinged wings and tail.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common and widespread in a wide range of woodland, bush and cultivation, from sea level to 2,200m, often near water.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a rising, falling, then rising wave of notes that become very strident: ti-ti-ti-tit-tit-tit-tiu-tiu-tiu-ti-tit-tit-tit… Call is a series of identical sharp tchk, tchk, tchk… notes.

images.caption: Grey-headed Kingfisher · Plate 111

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Grey-headed Kingfisher but lacks chestnut belly. In EKe and interior Tz race prentissgrayi has faintly streaked brownish crown, a pale collar and pale buff belly, with buff-chestnut wash confined to flanks; bill bright red. Sexes differ: male has black back; female dark brown. Coastal race orientalis has a plainer crown (with no obvious collar) and plain buff flanks. Darker-billed immature has browner crown and light barring on breast. In flight, shows warm rufous-chestnut underwing.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are fairly common in bushed and wooded habitats mainly in the east from sea level to 1,800m, often away from water, with some local movements.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a monotonous repeated and whistled sequence of four descending notes with emphasis on the first, and next three gradually fading: wi-ti-ti-tu.

images.caption: Brown-hooded Kingfisher · Plate 111

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Spectacular massive kingfisher, blackish above with fine white speckles and bars. Adult male has broad chestnut breast-band; adult female has chestnut from breast to vent. In flight underwing-coverts are white on male, chestnut on female. Immature resembles adult, but chestnut bands are speckled and broken. Two races occur: nominate is widespread, while in WTz gigantea has plainer upperparts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs are shy and local, but widespread on highland lakes, rivers and streams, mainly at 1,500–2,700m, though also wanders widely, including to deeper coastal creeks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Loud, far-carrying raucous laugh followed by single notes, kiau-kiau-kee-ee-ee-ee-ee-ee- kiau-kiau-kiau-kiau… often given in flight.

images.caption: Giant Kingfisher · Plate 111

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather thickset kingfisher: adult nominate race is dove-grey, black and bright blue with a striking red-and-black bill, and no blue on breast. Migrant southern race cyanoleuca has grey head washed blue, and black extends slightly behind eye. Immature similar to adult, but has buff wash on head, lightly scaled breast and flanks, and dark bill.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are widespread and common in a range of wooded and bushed grassland, cultivation and gardens, mainly from sea level to 1,500m (but up to 3,000m). Race cyanoleuca breeds in southern Tanzania and migrates north (Apr–Sep).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a descending rattled series that starts with an explosive note, followed by a short pause, chit chtchtchtchttitititchrrrrrrr. Birds also call with a repeated musical rattled upslur.

images.caption: Woodland Kingfisher · Plate 112

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Woodland Kingfisher, but has slightly darker grey head and bright all-red bill. Immature duller than adult with buff-brown wash on head, breast and flanks, and dark bill. In flight, reveals a black carpal crescent on underwing. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common resident of coastal areas in a wide range of habitats from bush to forest, mangroves and gardens.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song similar in structure to Woodland, but after isolated introductory chink the series is much slower and more emphatic: chink trrt trrt trrt trrt trrt trrt trrt trt trtt trtrtrtrtrtrtrtrtrt.

images.caption: Mangrove Kingfisher · Plate 112

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is blue above, rufous below with slightly shaggy blue-green and black-barred crown extending down to eye, and bright red bill. Immature similar, with shorter black bill, brownish-rufous underparts and whitish belly. Race in EA is cyanostigma.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and singles are common and widespread throughout most of East Africa from sea level to 3,000m, occurring beside all types of water with fringing vegetation. Some local movements appear to occur, but are not well known.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a short sharp rather unmusical chht, which may run on into a dry chitter.

images.caption: Malachite Kingfisher · Plate 113

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Malachite Kingfisher but slightly smaller. Adult nominate race and darker ferrugina have small dark blue crown-stripe not extending down to eye, orange cheeks with purplish-pink wash on ear-coverts, and white neck spot. Immature like adult but duller, with darker face, breast scaling and shorter blackish bill. Southern race natalensis has paler belly and small blue patch above white neck spot.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Three races occur: nominate is widespread in Uganda, Kenya, and north-eastern Tanzania. often far from water, in forest and denser thickets in bushed and wooded grassland, and woodland, usually below 1,500m (less often to 2,000m), ferrugina in forests in far west, and migrant natalensis breeds in C and southern Tanzania in Sep–Apr, before moving north to forests in Uganda and central Kenya, and to dense coastal thickets in Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls a high-pitched tsi-tsi… and a squeaky chittering.

images.caption: African Pygmy Kingfisher · Plate 113

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small neat bee-eater. Adult is green above with rufous panels in wing and uppertail, yellow throat, well-defined black gorget, and dull cinnamon-rufous underparts. Three races occur: meridionalis (widespread) has short, narrow blue stripe just above mask and blue top edge to gorget; ocularis (NUg) is paler below; cyanostictus (Ke) has longer blue superciliary stripes joining over bill, and thin purplish-blue top edge to gorget. Immature duller and paler than adult, washed variably pale green below. Larger Cinnamon-chested Bee-eater is a much richer and darker bird of forests.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or family groups are common in bushed and wooded grassland, and more open woodland, from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a sharp high-pitched tsip tsip…; when excited these break into a long metallic sequence interspersed with some quite musical nasal skirls.

images.caption: Little Bee-eater · Plate 114

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Little Bee-eater but much larger. Darker green above and deeper rufous-cinnamon below (with variable white edge to rear of yellow cheek). Little or no blue above mask. Immature is paler, lacks black gorget and is variably washed green below. In flight, tail appears longer, broader and largely green from above, with broad black tip. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are common in highland forest, forest edge and gardens at 1,800–2,300m, generally perching high in canopy.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls from excited birds are a very varied mix of metallic chinks, slurs and trills, often rather cheerful in quality.

images.caption: Cinnamon-chested Bee-eater · Plate 114

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is a pale blue-green bee-eater with striking black-and-white head pattern, tawny nape and long central tail feathers. Sexes similar, but male has slightly longer tail-streamers. Immature is similar to adult, but has yellow wash over throat, is duller with many buff-edged feathers, and lacks tail-streamers. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common intra-African migrant from southern Sahara (rarely breeds in northern Uganda and Kenya). Highly gregarious and vocal flocks disperse to woodland, bush and grassland, as well as more open forest and gardens, mainly Aug–Apr, from sea level to 2,000m (less often 3,000m).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a rather harsh and throaty chep, which often breaks into musical slurs with several birds taking part in an excitable wader-like chorus.

images.caption: White-throated Bee-eater · Plate 115

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Washed-out, slightly unkempt bee-eater. Adult is pale blue-green above, with white throat and pale apricot underparts. Immature is duller version of adult. In flight, reveals silvery-blue rump and undertail-coverts. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are shy, solitary and sedentary residents below 1,000m in arid and semi-arid bushland in eastern Kenya (away from coast).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rarely heard call is a long ramble of musical and excitable but rather mournful chits and whistled slurs.

images.caption: Somali Bee-eater · Plate 115

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is largely dark blue with black-rimmed scarlet throat, paler blue forehead, and rufous-brown back and wings. Sexes alike, but immature is much plainer, duller blue-green below and lacks scarlet throat. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are uncommon residents in Kakamega and South Nandi Forests in western Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a repeated simple swir-swi swi starting with a raspy slur and interspersed by metallic tink notes, resulting in a medley punctuated with short pauses.

images.caption: Blue-headed Bee-eater · Plate 115

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Striking chestnut and golden bee-eater with yellow throat and pale blue underparts. In fresh plumage, adult male has broad golden sides to chestnut back; non-breeding male and female are much duller and greener above. At rest or in flight, adult shows projecting central tail feathers (slightly shorter in female), which are absent in young birds. Immature is greenish above, with brown-washed crown, dull green sides to back, pale yellow throat and blue underparts. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small to large flocks on passage are harbingers of Palearctic migration even in Jul, but main southbound movement is Sep–Nov, with a more sporadic northbound passage Mar–May. Prefers open country from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Far-carrying, loud and attractive calls are very fluid and deep throaty trills and churrs, prrutt, prrutt prrutt, often with many birds calling together.

images.caption: European Bee-eater · Plate 116

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slender, vivid emerald-green bee-eater. Adult has green crown, blue borders to mask, and yellow chin grading into orange-brown throat. Female has shorter tail-streamers. Immature is duller with less blue around eye and no tail-streamers. Shows obvious cinnamon underwing in banking flight (like Olive Bee-eater). Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small parties are regular throughout East Africa in Oct–Apr, preferring bushed and wooded grassland below 1,500m, often near water.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is an attractive fluid trill, preepp, preepp, preepp, which is repeated for long periods with slight changes in tone.

images.caption: Blue-cheeked Bee-eater · Plate 116

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Overall slightly duller than similar Blue-cheeked Bee-eater, with smoky olive-brown cap, white borders to mask, and dull brick-red throat. Female has shorter tail-streamers. Immature is much duller than adult and lacks bold head pattern. Very similar to immature Blue-cheeked, but less green with more uniform throat. In flight, shows plain cinnamon underwing like Blue-cheeked. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are non-breeding visitors from the south, mainly in Apr–Sep, below 1,500m (but up to 2,300m) in bushed and wooded country, often near water. Occasionally breeds in coastal lowlands, and some may be present year-round.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very like Blue-cheeked Bee-eater, but slightly higher-pitched and less fluid. [Alt. Madagascar Bee-eater] RED-THROATED BEE-EATERS Two closely related, attractive, resident, highly social and colonial bee-eaters, identified by head pattern and range. Sexes alike.

images.caption: Olive Bee-eater · Plate 116

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Colourful rather upright-perching bee-eater. Adult is mostly green above with white forecrown, black mask, and red throat bordered above with white; underparts warm buff-cinnamon with deep cobalt-blue vent. Immature is similar but more subdued, with orange-yellow (not red) throat. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks are widespread and sometimes common (notably in Rift Valley and southern Tanzania), associating with open water and rivers in bushed and wooded country to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls a distinct rather nasal and muffled gaaar, and a variety of other pinched slurred notes which may rise and fall.

images.caption: White-fronted Bee-eater · Plate 116

merops-nubicus.ref: Plate 117: Bee-Eaters Iv And Broad-Billed Rollers
merops-nubicus.name: Northern Carmine Bee-eater

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult bright carmine above, with turquoise-blue rump, lower belly and vent, well-defined green-blue crown and throat, and long central tail feathers. Immature is much duller with strong olive-brown wash, mottled head and throat, and short tail-streamers. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and flocks are regular visitors to bushed and wooded grassland, as well as cultivation, in N and eastern Kenya, northern Uganda and eastern Tanzania in Sep–Apr, usually below 1,200m. Sometimes very common in coastal districts and a few linger throughout the year. Occasionally breeds in extreme northern Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is an unattractive series of loud skirls, chitters and complaining notes, lacking the sweetness or variation of smaller bee-eaters.

images.caption: Northern Carmine Bee-eater · Plate 117

eurystomus-glaucurus.ref: Plate 117: Bee-Eaters Iv And Broad-Billed Rollers
eurystomus-glaucurus.name: Broad-billed Roller

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is a bright chestnut roller (variably washed lilac below) with broad yellow bill. Immature is much duller brown above with dusky-yellow bill and pale blue underparts. In flight, shows strong contrast between chestnut back and deep azure-blue outer wing and tail. In Ug and WKe, race afer is widespread, brighter suahelicus elsewhere.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles, pairs or small groups are sometimes common residents and intra-African migrants in bushed and wooded grassland, woodland and forest edge, from sea level to 2,200m. Mainly occurs in Tanzania Oct–Apr, but throughout the year elsewhere.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a deep and raspy single ahk or wak, and a uh-uh-uh-uhuhuhuhuh in rapid sequence.

images.caption: Broad-billed Roller · Plate 117

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Strikingly colourful roller. Nominate race has lilac throat and breast, olive-chestnut back, dark blue wing-coverts and deep blue underparts. Outer tail-streamers are slender and straight. Race lorti (Lilac-throated Roller) differs in having a small lilac throat patch. Immature is much duller than adult with olive-brown tinge to back, and no tail-streamers.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are widespread and common residents in open bush country, wooded grassland, woodland and cultivation, from sea level to 2,000m (less often 3,000m). Race lorti is largely confined to north-eastern Kenya, but wanders occasionally to northern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Displaying birds give loud dry rasps breaking into a long series that develops into a harsh rattle. Calls of race lorti similar but possibly more nasal.

images.caption: Lilac-breasted Roller · Plate 118

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slender vivid blue roller with rufous-brown back and very long outer tail-streamers (except in worn plumage). Appears bluer than other species, like a slim long-tailed European Roller. Immature duller than adult, with olive-brown tinge to back and square tail without streamers. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and less often small groups are common local residents and less common wanderers in semi-arid bush and woodland across northern Uganda and northern Kenya below 1,000m. One in Serengeti NP in Feb 2005 is only Tanzania record.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls are very harsh and unpleasant variable loud rasps.

images.caption: Abyssinian Roller · Plate 118

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Robust, thickset roller with blue head, chestnut-brown back, blue underparts and rather short square-cut tail (without streamers). On arrival in Oct, non-breeding adults and first-year birds are very pale with washed-out greenish-blue heads and underparts, and muddy brown backs. Prior to departure in Apr, adults are striking blue, with bright chestnut backs, and purplish-blue wing-coverts and rumps. Nominate race (as described) is widespread; paler semenowi also occurs.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic winter visitor and passage migrant, usually singly (but also moving together in loose associations) in Oct–Apr, typically in bushed and wooded grassland below 1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent in region, but may utter a deep croak.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Eurasian Roller

images.caption: European Roller · Plate 118

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Big-headed thickset roller which lacks blue underparts of other species. Adult has rufous crown with broad white supercilium and rufous-purple underparts streaked white. In flight, dark purple-blue flight feathers contrast sharply with rufous wing-coverts and greenish back. Immature similar, but duller and greener above and below. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are local and never numerous, often associated with rocky areas and large trees in drier wooded and bushed grassland to 2,000m (sometimes to 3,000m). Erratic and occasional influxes of non-residents occur.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a loud, harsh and throaty ouw, and in display flight a strident ak-ak-ak-aka-aka-aka-aka…kiau-kiau-kiau…

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Rufous-crowned Roller

images.caption: Purple Roller · Plate 118

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is a large red-billed iridescent bird with a white spot and bar in the wing, and long graduated white-tipped tail. Two races occur: widespread marwitzi is relatively easy to identify with a green head and back (although wings may shine violet and blue), while northern niloticus is generally more violet-blue and very similar to Violet Woodhoopoe, but will always show some green on head (if watched for several minutes). Immature is dull blackish, with brownish throat patch, straighter, shorter black bill, and dark legs.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Extended family groups are common and widespread in a wide range of wooded and forested habitats from sea level to 2,800m, with race niloticus in north-western Kenya south to Lake Bogoria.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Nasal bubbling and maniacal cackling in noisy group displays (calls perhaps indistinguishable from Violet and Black-billed Woodhoopoes).

images.caption: Green Woodhoopoe · Plate 119

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is very similar to Green Woodhoopoe race niloticus, but head, nape and back shine violet-blue, with green restricted to throat. Immature is duller with brown-buff streaking on throat and shorter black bill. In EA, race granti is sometimes considered distinct from the nominate race of SW Africa, and treated as Grant’s Woodhoopoe P. granti.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Family groups are local and uncommon in semi-arid and arid bush and woodland, often associated with rivers and doum palms.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Probably indistinguishable from Green Woodhoopoe.

images.caption: Violet Woodhoopoe · Plate 119

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Green Woodhoopoe, but has more violet and blue gloss, and black bill (sometimes with limited red at base, occasionally mostly red). Immature is duller with some buff on throat, shorter black bill and black legs. Birds in NEKe are the nominate race, while neglectus with a greener crown and nape may occur at Lake Turkana, NKe.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Family groups are fairly common in north-eastern Kenya, where they occupy semi-arid bushed and wooded areas, often in larger acacias and riverine woodland.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Probably not distinguishable from Green Woodhoopoe.

images.caption: Black-billed Woodhoopoe · Plate 119

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has variable amount of white on head, red bill, and blue-green glossed wings and tail without white spots. Immature has black bill and often a small amount or no white on head. Red bill and legs separate them from white-headed form of Forest Scimitarbill. Birds in EA are race jacksoni.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Family groups are common and widespread in forest at 900–3,000m in the west (but mainly restricted to highland forest above 2,000m in Kenya and extreme northern Tanzania).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Similar to Green Woodhoopoe, but notes are fuller, less nasal and more of a rattle.

images.caption: White-headed Woodhoopoe · Plate 119

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small and neat scimitarbill; adult has a sharply decurved bright orange-red bill and black glossed blue-purple plumage. Two races occur: widespread cabanisi is entirely blue-purple, lacking white in wings and tail; nominate in NEKe is similar but has a white wingbar. Immature is similar, but all brownish below with dull brownish-red bill.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are locally common but widespread in drier bushed and wooded grassland to 1,400m (less often 2,000m), including acacia scrub, preferring more arid and open areas than Common Scimitarbill.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a hollow rattle of identical notes, terminating on a single or double lower note, k-k—k-k-k-k-k-k-k-kiow, and a kreekreekreekree… given as a piercing burry scream.

images.caption: Abyssinian Scimitarbill · Plate 120

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger than Abyssinian Scimitarbill with a strongly decurved black bill, white bar across primaries and white tips to tail (may show a little white on primary-coverts). Often looks blackish but in good light shows violet-blue sheen. Immature is similar, but has shorter, straighter bill and less violet gloss. Race in EA is schalowi.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are fairly common and widespread in bush, woodland and riverine forest, from sea level to 2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a loud repeated downslurred sequence, quee-quee-quee-kirr-kirr-quee…, also a hollow wooden rattle and a high-pitched sisisisisisi while foraging.

images.caption: Common Scimitarbill · Plate 120

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three races occur: all are quite similar to African Hoopoe, but have bold white band across primaries and a narrow band of white (nominate) or pale buff (waibeli and senegalensis) below black tips of crest. Races differ in overall tones of head, back and underparts: waibeli is darkest, senegalensis intermediate and nominate palest. Immature is duller than adult.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Race waibeli is resident in extreme north-western Kenya, but migrates south as far as Entebbe, Uganda, and Nairobi, Kenya; senegalensis is resident in extreme northern Kenya; and nominate is an uncommon visitor from the Palearctic, south into drier areas of northern Uganda and northern Kenya, and rarely north-eastern Tanzania, in Oct–Mar.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls perhaps indistinguishable from African Hoopoe.

images.caption: Eurasian Hoopoe · Plate 120

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Typical bush hornbill easily identified by combination of banana-yellow bill and white-spotted wing-coverts. Adult male has slightly larger bill with thicker casque than female, and rich rose-pink rather than bare black throat patches. Immature has smaller dusky-yellow bill and is less clearly marked. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family groups are widespread at low density in semi-arid bush country and drier wooded grassland mainly below 1,400m. Form associations with groups of Dwarf Mongoose, acting as lookouts for birds of prey, and benefiting from the insects flushed.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Regularly calls a gently rising and falling series of very low-pitched and throaty rasping kruk-kruk-krukrukrukruk-krakrakrark-kerkrukrukruk… notes.

images.caption: Eastern Yellow-billed Hornbill · Plate 121

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Jackson’s Hornbill, but has a slender more decurved red bill (without creamy tip) and whiter face and neck. Adult male has slightly heavier bill than female, often with blacker base to lower mandible. Immature is duller, with buff spots on wing-coverts and smaller dull red bill. Two distinctive races occur which are sometimes considered to be separate species: widespread nominate (Northern Red-billed Hornbill) has pink orbital skin around brown eyes; ruahae in CTz (Tanzanian Red-billed Hornbill) (south of the dotted line on map) has a bold black mask around pale yellow eyes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs, family parties and sometimes larger flocks are common and widespread residents in dry bush and woodland up to 1,400m, less often 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a rather urgent rising and falling series of nasal kankankankankankank-kik-hahaha-kik-hahaha… notes, higher-pitched than other similar hornbills.

images.caption: Red-billed Hornbill · Plate 121

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Striking pied hornbill; similar to Jackson’s Hornbill but has unspotted black wing-coverts. Adult male has large red-orange bill with well-defined creamy-yellow tip; adult female has all-black bill. Immature resembles female but has duller blackish-brown bill and indistinct white spotting on wing-coverts. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family parties are widespread and common in dry bushed and wooded grassland from sea level to 1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a long series of low-pitched kuk-kuk-kukukukukukukuk-kuk… notes all on the same tone.

images.caption: Von der Decken’s Hornbill · Plate 121

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Von der Decken’s Hornbill but has boldly spotted wing-coverts. Adult male also has red bill with smaller less defined creamy tip; adult female has all-black bill. Immature is duller than adult. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family groups are common in semi-arid and arid country in north-western Kenya and north-eastern Uganda at 350–2,000m (where it replaces Von der Decken’s).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a long sequence of low rasping krukrukrukrukruk… notes all on much the same tone.

images.caption: Jackson’s Hornbill · Plate 121

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Relatively large, rather scruffy hornbill, which is blackish above with pale fringes to wings and dusky-red bill (brighter lower mandible in male, dusky-based in female). Immature similar to female. In buoyant undulating flight, appears dark above and mostly white below, with white stripes near edge of outer tail. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family groups are local in dry bush and woodland with rocky outcrops and cliffs at 950–1,300m in north-eastern Uganda and northern Kenya. Birds wander, but depend on rock crevices in cliffs and gorges for nesting.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a dramatic long series of loud whistled kek-kek-kek… notes that starts slowly, then accelerates into a frantic piping pip-pip-pip-pipip… ipipipipipi… before fading away.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Tockus.

images.caption: Hemprich’s Hornbill · Plate 121

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dull grey-brown hornbill with pale fringes to wings and long pale supercilium extending down side of grey-brown neck to nape. In the nominate race, adult male has dark bill with slender flat casque and striking creamy-white wedge at base; adult male of smaller race epirhinus has casque ending in slim raised tube. In both races, adult females lack casques, and have purplish-red bill tip and larger creamy-white wedge. Immature similar to adult, but duller with buff feather edges and smaller blackish bill. In undulating flight, reveals white corners to long grey-brown tail.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and groups are widespread and common residents in woodland, bushed and wooded grassland, from sea level to 1,700m. The nominate race in most of Uganda and Kenya, while epirhinus is widespread from southern Uganda through Tanzania into south-eastern Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a sharp pi pi pi… that accelerates and develops into a descending rather sad piping pipipipipipi pieu pieu. In flight, also often gives a single far-carrying pieu.

images.caption: African Grey Hornbill · Plate 122

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slender dark hornbill with bright red bill and long black tail with white corners. Western birds (formerly race geloensis) from Ug to CKe and NTz are darker-backed than eastern ones (former race suahelicus) in EKe and most of Tz; now considered monotypic. Despite name, no obvious crown, but white streaks behind eyes create dark-capped effect. Adult male is slightly larger than female with heavier casque. Immature similar to female, but duller with dull yellowish bill. In rather floppy undulating flight, shows obvious white tips to outer tail.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family groups are quite widespread and common in woodland and forest edges from the coast to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a very sharp high-pitched kip-kip-kip and a long piercing refrain that rises and falls, kwi-kwi-kwikwikwi, and is more musical than Congo Pied Hornbill.

images.caption: Crowned Hornbill · Plate 122

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Mainly glossy black above, with black throat and upper breast clearly separated from white lower breast and belly. Adult male has heavier bill and longer casque than adult female. Both sexes have bright pink eye-ring. Immature similar to female with insignificant casque. In flight, shows narrow white trailing edge to most of wing. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Groups are common in forest, woodland and mature gardens from the coast up to 1,650m (rarely to 2,200m), and often flock with Silvery-cheeked Hornbills.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A loud far-carrying, distressed braying (recalls a crying baby), naaay-naaaaaay-naaaaay-naaaay, which often weakens and dies away as if the bird has lost interest in calling.

images.caption: Trumpeter Hornbill · Plate 124

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger than Trumpeter Hornbill with white below confined to lower belly and vent. Face and ear-coverts tipped silvery in adult, but hard to see at distance. Adult male has massive bill and pale cream casque, which may extend beyond bill tip, and blue-grey eye-ring; adult female has casque confined to basal half of bill, and pinkish eye-ring. Immature is duller with smaller bill and brownish face. In flight, shows entirely black upperwing and white carpal patch in underwing. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Family parties are widespread and locally common in highland forest, woodland and mature gardens from sea level to 2,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Strident and loud goat-like braying wa-wa-wa-wa-wa and a longer rising and falling aah-aaaah-aaaah-aaah-aah-ah which lacks the pathetic crying edge and die-away effect of Trumpeter Hornbill.

images.caption: Silvery-cheeked Hornbill · Plate 124

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar size to Silvery-cheeked Hornbill but has more extensive white in wings. Adult male has a shorter bicoloured casque (blackish at front and pale behind); adult female has a smaller darker casque. Both sexes have a pinkish-grey eye-ring, brighter pinkish-red in female when breeding. Duller immature has smaller blackish bill lacking casque. In flight reveals broad white band at back of wing (most primaries and secondaries), and a black tail with white corners. Birds in EA are race subquadratus.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Groups may be common in mature woodland and forests including riverine areas, and in cultivated land with large trees at 700–2,600m in most of Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, as well as western Kenya and north-western Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Spectacular and musical bugled waah or waaaah develops into a cacophonous din when birds call together.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Grey-cheeked Hornbill

images.caption: Black-and-white-casqued Hornbill · Plate 124

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Huge shaggy-looking black bird with bright red eye and throat wattles, long heavy decurved bill and stout black legs. Adult male has eye and throat wattles all red, and bill has small casque at base of upper mandible; adult female is similar, but has patch of violet-blue in centre of throat; both sexes have pale yellow eyes. Immature duller and brown-tinged, with smaller bill, and rather yellowish-brown bare facial skin and throat patches. Birds prefer to slope off when disturbed, but in flight they reveal striking white primaries, which are hard to see in folded wing. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small groups are widespread, but often local, in moister bushed and wooded grassland to 3,000m, from central Kenya south into Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi. In many areas now uncommon due to human disturbance, accidental poisoning and lack of nest sites.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Often calls at dawn when the air is cool and still, and calls can carry over long distances; a very deep reverberant booming gump-rump-rumrumrump. VU

images.caption: Southern Ground-Hornbill · Plate 125

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has black head with two white stripes above and below eyes, yellow rump, two short bright yellow wingbars and yellow wing edges; throat white in all races (pale yellow in Yellow-throated Tinkerbird). Immature is like adult but duller with pale base to bill. Five races occur in two distinct groups: birds with lemon rumps (Lemon-rumped Tinkerbird) are leucolaimus (mid-altitude Ug and WKe) and mfumbiri (highlands of SWUg, WRw, WBu and WTz); races with golden rumps (Golden-rumped Tinkerbird) are jacksoni (highlands of Rw, Bu, NWTz, EUg and CKe), fischeri (coastal Ke and NETz) and nominate (SETz).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are widespread and common in forest, dense woodland, thickets and gardens from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Highland birds call a long series of random three or four note sets of metallic ponk-ponk-ponk-ponk; western races are similar, but higher-pitched and faster. Coastal race fischeri is very different: an introductory note is followed by a very rapid series of more than 20 ponk notes, almost trilled.

images.caption: Yellow-rumped Tinkerbird · Plate 126

pogoniulus-leucomystax.ref: Plate 127: Green Tinkerbirds And Duller Barbets
pogoniulus-leucomystax.name: Moustached Green Tinkerbird

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dull olive-green plumage with yellow wingbars and rump, and pale base to dark-tipped bill are all very similar to Eastern Green Tinkerbird, but has obvious pale greyish moustachial stripe. Immature is slightly yellower below. Usually considered monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common in highland forest at 1,400–3,000m in central Kenya to southern Tanzania (ranging down to 900m in the Usambara Mts, north-eastern Tanzania, where it overlaps with Eastern Green Tinkerbird).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a rapid series of dry chipping notes, tipipipipip…, varying in speed and tempo, some calls high-pitched and metallic.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Moustached Tinkerbird

images.caption: Moustached Green Tinkerbird · Plate 127

pogoniulus-simplex.ref: Plate 127: Green Tinkerbirds And Duller Barbets
pogoniulus-simplex.name: Eastern Green Tinkerbird

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small dull olive-green tinkerbird with yellow wingbars and rump, pinkish base to black-tipped bill; no moustachial stripe. Immature similar to adult but has more extensive pale base to bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are rather uncommon, mainly in coastal forest and woodland, but up to 900m (in Usambara Mts, north-eastern Tanzania).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a rapid tinny trill often followed by similar trills that drop in tone, and a fast musical poo-poo-poo-poo-poo-poo-poo of up to seven identical bell-like notes, similar to the coastal race of Yellow-rumped Tinkerbird but even more rapid. [Alt. Green Tinkerbird] DULLER BARBETS A varied group of dull green or dark brown barbets of woodland and forest which can be identified on colour and head pattern. Sexes are alike.

images.caption: Eastern Green Tinkerbird · Plate 127

cryptolybia-olivacea.ref: Plate 127: Green Tinkerbirds And Duller Barbets
cryptolybia-olivacea.name: Green Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Stocky upright dull olive barbet. Immature is similar to adult but duller. Four races occur: nominate (coastal Ke and NETz) is dull olive-green above, and dull olive or yellowish olive-green below, howelli (SC Tz) has blacker crown, woodwardi (SETz) has yellowish ear-coverts, and rungweensis (STz) is greyer below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs may be common in forest and woodland in coastal Kenya, but are more widespread in Tanzania up to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a sad repeated kwop-kwop-kwop-kwop-… often during heat of the day (like the distant sound of an axe within a wood).

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Stactolaema.

images.caption: Green Barbet · Plate 127

stactolaema-leucotis.ref: Plate 127: Green Tinkerbirds And Duller Barbets
stactolaema-leucotis.name: White-eared Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dark barbet with bold white stripe behind eye, and variable white to brown rump and belly. Two races occur: kilimensis (CKe to NETz) has a white stripe behind the eye and largely white rump; leucogrammica (highlands of CTz), sometimes considered a distinct species (White-lined Barbet), has a swollen stripe that almost encircles the eye and a brown rump. Immatures are similar, but have less defined face patterns, and pale bases to bills.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common but patchily distributed in forest and forest edge from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a loud kwi-kwi-kwi-…, either singly or in a rapid series.

images.caption: White-eared Barbet · Plate 127

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Red-fronted Tinkerbird, but has yellow-orange forecrown spot, and in widespread nominate race much stronger yellow wash on underparts. In STz race extoni has more golden-orange forecrown and greyer underparts. Immature similar to adult but lacks yellow forecrown spot.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are widespread and locally common in moister habitats than Red-fronted including forest edge, riverine woodland, thickets and mature gardens, from sea level to 1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Some calls are doubtfully distinguishable from Red-fronted Tinkerbird, but possibly faster and lower-pitched. Also utters a very fast trill when excited.

images.caption: Yellow-fronted Tinkerbird · Plate 128

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Stocky, robust barbet with long yellow-white supercilium and red forecrown spot. Two races occur: north of equator (NEUg to NKe) the nominate is creamy-white below with few spots on lower flanks, south of equator (CKe to CTz) massaica has heavier spotting on breast, belly and flanks. Immature is duller with just a little red and a paler bill.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread in dry bush and woodland at 600–2,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Wide vocabulary; usual calls are a rapid descending and hollow pooh-pooh-pooh-pooh, and a slow, nasal and pinched wah wah wah…

images.caption: Red-fronted Barbet · Plate 128

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has broad black bib tapering onto central breast and pale yellow-orange eyes (darker in female). Two races occur: nominate (NUg to EKe and NCTz) has boldly spotted buff-white flanks; radcliffei (WUg and Rw to CKe, and N and SCTz) has smaller round flank spots. Immature is greyer above with brown eyes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and sometimes common in wooded and bushed grassland, as well as riverine forest below 2,000m. Prefers rather moister habitat to similar Black-throated Barbet.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a long series of sharp kwek notes, commencing slowly and accelerating with a strange whiplash effect. Also a series of nasal weh weh weh…. and poop-poop…. notes similar to Red-fronted Barbet.

images.caption: Spot-flanked Barbet · Plate 128

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Widespread race stigmatothorax has a boldly striped head and long blackish-brown bib which tapers to a sharp point in centre of whitish belly, and no spots on flanks. In the Wembere area of NTz, distinctive race flavibuccalis has yellow head-stripes and a short bib terminating mid-breast. Immature is duller with pale bill.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs inhabit semi-arid bush and thorn-scrub country from near the coast to 1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a throaty hiau-hiau-hiau…, sometimes breaking into descending musical churrs and often in duet.

images.caption: Black-throated Barbet · Plate 128

buccanodon-duchaillui.ref: Plate 129: Woodland And Forest Barbets I
buccanodon-duchaillui.name: Yellow-spotted Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is a boldly marked blue-black forest barbet, extensively spotted and barred yellow, with a scarlet forecrown patch, and long curving yellow line from eye to hindneck. Immature similar, but less well marked, lacks red forecrown and black bill has pale base. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and small groups are common residents of western forests, being very active in the canopy and around fruiting trees, often in mixed-species flocks, at 1,150–2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typically gives a low purred snoring trill delivered from high in the canopy, prrrrrrrrrrr…, also a hooting boo-boo-boo.

images.caption: Yellow-spotted Barbet · Plate 129

tricholaema-hirsuta.ref: Plate 129: Woodland And Forest Barbets I
tricholaema-hirsuta.name: Hairy-breasted Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has a black head with two white stripes on each side, suggesting a giant tinkerbird. Greenish-yellow below with black streaks, becoming heavily spotted from mid-breast to vent (close views reveal long separated hair-like breast feathers). Immature similar, but more barred on flanks. Birds in EA are race ansorgii.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are locally common in forest, riverine forest and woodland at 700–1,800m in S and western Uganda, north-western Tanzania, and western Kenya (Kakamega only).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls with repeated low hollow identical-paced notes, pooh pooh pooh…

images.caption: Hairy-breasted Barbet · Plate 129

lybius-torquatus.ref: Plate 129: Woodland And Forest Barbets I
lybius-torquatus.name: Black-collared Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Colourful barbet: in two similar races red head and breast are separated from yellow belly by black breast-band. Race pumilio (SERw, Bu and WTz) has more orange-red head and breast than irroratus (EKe to CTz). Immature has black face with variable red-brown flecks, and is yellowish-white below with pale base to bill (black in adult). In SETz, distinctive race zombae has black head (with variable white speckles) and small white patch behind eye; pale buff-yellow below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are local in a range of woodland and forest edge, as well as gardens, from sea level to 1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls start with growled churrs and develop into a characterful bounding twi-popopop twi-popopop… (first note of each series is higher, last note rapid and identical, the whole effect being like a rolling wave).

images.caption: Black-collared Barbet · Plate 129

pogonornis-melanopterus.ref: Plate 129: Woodland And Forest Barbets I
pogonornis-melanopterus.name: Brown-breasted Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large eastern barbet with a red head (streaked black on nape), broad brown breast-band, white mid-breast to vent, and pale bill. Immature similar, but has much less red in the face, a grey-brown breast and darker bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs may be common in woodland and forest edge, as well as gardens and abandoned farms, along the coastal strip and inland, from sea level to 1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a repeated nasal and very pinched wek.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Lybius.

images.caption: Brown-breasted Barbet · Plate 129

lybius-leucocephalus.ref: Plate 130: Woodland And Forest Barbets Ii
lybius-leucocephalus.name: White-headed Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Handsome blackish-brown and white barbet with heavy black bill. Four races occur, which may be two distinct species; all have white heads and rumps, and three are dark below. If considered specifically distinct, the nominate race (Ug, NWTz and WKe), albicauda (SWKe to SEKe and south to NW and NTz) and lynesi (CTz) remain as White-headed Barbet. Nominate has extensive white fringes to wing-coverts, blackish lower breast to vent with fine white streaks and black tail; albicauda (SKe and NTz) is similar, but has white tail; lynesi (CTz) is also similar, but tail is dark at base and white at tip. In CKe highlands and Chyulu Hills, SEKe (east of the dotted line on map), distinctive race senex (Brown-and-white Barbet) is all white except for very dark brown mantle and wings. All immatures have brown-mottled head and brown tail, but otherwise resembles dull adult. Some races interbreed in areas of overlap.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Social; pairs and family parties are common and widespread in bushed and wooded grassland, as well as gardens, often near fruiting fig trees, from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Impressive range of loud growling, harsh gurgling and sharp very babbler-like chattering calls, often with exaggerated displays of bowing and gaping.

images.caption: White-headed Barbet · Plate 130

lybius-guifsobalito.ref: Plate 130: Woodland And Forest Barbets Ii
lybius-guifsobalito.name: Black-billed Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has bright red face, throat and upper breast, and black bill; similar Red-faced Barbet has less red on face and paler bill. Flight feathers edged pale yellow, upperwing-coverts edged whitish. Immature duller with brownish-black head and variable red mottling on face and throat. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small parties are widespread at low densities in drier bush and woodland over most of Uganda to extreme western Kenya at 600–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a mechanical rolling ki-twop ki-twop ki-twop…, first note of each series higher.

images.caption: Black-billed Barbet · Plate 130

pogonornis-bidentatus.ref: Plate 130: Woodland And Forest Barbets Ii
pogonornis-bidentatus.name: Double-toothed Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Impressive ivory-billed barbet, black above (with white centre to back) and bright red below with white crescent patches on lower flanks; creamy-white eyes are ringed by bare yellow skin; double notch on either side of upper mandible. Female is similar to male, but has a few black streaks on the red flanks. Immature duller, showing much less red below and greyish orbital ring around brown eyes. Birds in EA are race aequatorialis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family groups are widespread and common in a range of woodland, wooded grassland, gardens and cultivation with scattered fig trees at 900–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Loud song is a nightjar-like churring, but much raspier, and the call is a dry frog-like rasp erk or kerk.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Lybius.

images.caption: Double-toothed Barbet · Plate 130

trachyphonus-darnaudii.ref: Plate 131: Ground Barbets And Yellow-Billed Barbet
trachyphonus-darnaudii.name: D’Arnaud’s Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Speckled and spotted barbet with an orange vent. Three races occur, which may be two distinct species; all adults have pinkish bills, pale yellowish-orange tones to head, broken black breast-bands and orange-red vents. If considered specifically distinct the nominate race (NUg to NKe) and boehmi (EKe to NETz) remain D’Arnaud’s Barbet; nominate has crown speckled black, and a variable but small black bib; boehmi similar, but crown black. In CTz (south of the dotted line on map) the form emini (Emin’s Barbet), has a black cap and large black bib. Immatures similar, but duller than adults.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family groups are widespread and common in semi-arid bushed and wooded grassland from sea level to 2,000m. They are frequently seen on the ground near termite hills, or in rather weak low flight.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a mechanical duet accompanied by cocked and frantically waving tails; it comprises two rising and two falling notes repeated for long periods: kee-ta-ti-tootle kee-ta-ti-tootle…

images.caption: D’Arnaud’s Barbet · Plate 131

trachyphonus-erythrocephalus.ref: Plate 131: Ground Barbets And Yellow-Billed Barbet
trachyphonus-erythrocephalus.name: Red-and-yellow Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Stunning black, red and yellow barbet, with white-spotted upperparts, bright red bill and striking white comma on ear-coverts surrounded by red. Three races occur: adult male versicolor (NEUg to NKe) has red confined around white comma, no black throat-stripe, and mostly yellow breast; nominate race (SKe to NETz) has a black crown and throat-stripe, mostly red face and red-orange breast; shelleyi (NEKe) is much paler yellow below. Females in all races have yellow or red crown speckled black. Immature similar to adult, but duller.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family parties are widespread and locally common in dry bush and woodland with termite mounds below 2,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Performs spectacular loud rolling duets, with a musical and reverberating series of three descending notes repeated endlessly as a wave: teedle-kwau teedle-kwau teedle-kwau…

images.caption: Red-and-yellow Barbet · Plate 131

trachylaemus-purpuratus.ref: Plate 131: Ground Barbets And Yellow-Billed Barbet
trachylaemus-purpuratus.name: Eastern Yellow-billed Barbet

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Striking long-tailed forest barbet with a yellow bill and large patch of bare yellow skin around eyes; rest of upperparts blue-black, breast very dark maroon (often looks blackish in the field), lower breast to vent largely yellow, spotted yellow on black towards vent. Sexes alike. Immature duller without maroon on breast and more extensive yellow belly and vent. Birds in EA are race elgonensis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common and widespread in primary and secondary forest, including clearings, at 700–2,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a monotonous series of identical musical hollow poop poop poop notes given at about 1 per second, less often a paired cu-coop.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Now considered specifically distinct from West African populations; formerly known as Yellow-billed Barbet.

images.caption: Eastern Yellow-billed Barbet · Plate 131

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has pale pinkish bill, black throat and white ear patch. Rest of plumage dull brown with small yellowish shoulders (usually concealed); in worn plumage may show small whitish area on rump. White outer tail noticeable in undulating flight or when landing. Female is mostly dull brown above, with paler and greyer underparts and grey-brown bill. Immature is more olive-brown above than adult, with creamy-yellow throat and breast and small white area on lower rump. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in riverine and open woodland, bush country, and farmland with scattered large trees, from sea level to 3,000m. Perches upright in canopy, calling repeatedly, often from well-established song posts. Known to lead people to bees’ nests.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a far-carrying repeated and explosive wi-chew wi-chew wi-chew…, first note high, second lower, and also a rather complaining nasal chattering (which is used to attract honey hunters).

images.caption: Greater Honeyguide · Plate 132

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Mostly dull olive-green above with browner wash to head; forecrown, throat and breast are mixed dark grey and white giving scaly or mottled appearance. Mid-breast to vent is plainer dirty white, sometimes tinged yellowish. Immature similar but greener on upperparts and more heavily marked below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common but never numerous in a wide variety of habitats including forest, woodland, thickets and bush country from sea level to 3,350m. Rather shy and presence often first noted by hearing distinctive call.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a long rather purred and rising trill trrrreeeeeeeeeeeee, and also gives a complaining tew-tew-tew…

images.caption: Scaly-throated Honeyguide · Plate 132

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Classic common honeyguide: widespread race teitensis is medium-sized, with a grey head and underparts, and indistinctly streaked olive-green back and wings. Adult has medium grey underparts, small pale loral spot and dark grey malar stripe. Immature has uniform grey head, lacking both loral spot and malar stripe, and riggenbachi (WUg to Bu) is brighter above and slightly darker below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather active, common and widespread, in forest edge, open woodland, bush country and trees in cultivated areas, from sea level to 3,000m; usually avoids forest interior.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song starts with a short downslur and then, after a brief pause, continues as a series of dry chips, about 2 per second, tew chet-chet-chet-chet-chet-chet…, and also utters a nasal chittering.

images.caption: Lesser Honeyguide · Plate 133

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slightly smaller than Lesser Honeyguide with pale grey underparts, plainer back and smaller bill. Head pale grey accentuating small dark eyes, giving a beady-eyed look. White loral spot present (but often hard to see), no dark malar stripe. Immature is more yellowish-green above and slightly darker below. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Unobtrusive and uncommon, inhabiting woodland and clearings within forest from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a rising series of lispy upslurred notes starting with fwo and continuing fwee-tk fwee-tk fwee-tk…

images.caption: Pallid Honeyguide · Plate 133

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Brown and white honeybird with dull brown head, back and wings; tail of adult has black centre and terminal band. Breast brownish-grey, throat and belly paler dirty white. Immature similar, but slightly paler above and washed yellowish below, with all-white outer tail. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local and uncommon in open woodland and bush country from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a long very dry rattle.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Wahlberg’s Honeybird

images.caption: Brown-backed Honeybird · Plate 134

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Differs from Brown-backed Honeybird by olive-green back and wings (not brown). Outer tail plain white on adult, underparts greyish with paler belly. Immature similar, but paler and more buffy below, sometimes with small dark tips to outer tail. Two races occur: ellenbecki (Ke and NTz) is darker than nominate (SWTz).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather local at forest edge and in mixed woodland, from near sea level to 1,850m. Often joins mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Displaying birds fly low over treetops calling with a chittering high-pitched rattle and nasal zhwink.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Eastern Honeybird

images.caption: Green-backed Honeybird · Plate 134

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult of widespread nominate race has upperparts all finely mottled, barred and speckled brown, grey and black, with a series of darker spots forming a streak on nape and back. Throat and upper breast rufous, rest of underparts buffy, with fine brown streaks and bars and rufous wash to vent. Immature is darker than adult with more barred upperparts; rufous on throat and breast less extensive and finely barred. In NWUg race pulchricollis is more rufous above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread, but only locally common resident in open woodland, remnant forest edges and cultivated areas with scattered trees, at 600–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls include a raptor-like, piercing cor-quee-quee-quee-quee-quee and a chittering when excited.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Rufous-necked Wryneck

images.caption: Red-throated Wryneck · Plate 135

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Red-throated Wryneck being mottled, barred and speckled grey-brown with a blackish stripe down nape and back, but has dark streak through eye and no rufous on throat and breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In East Africa, the nominate race is a scarce Palearctic visitor to open woodland and bush country in Oct–Apr. One at Arusha NP in Jan 2010 is the only Tanzania record.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Silent in region. FOREST WOODPECKERS Three woodpeckers found only in forest. All have plain green or olive backs and barred or spotted underparts.

images.caption: Eurasian Wryneck · Plate 135

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two similar races occur: nominate (WUg south to WTz) is plain olive-green above with a red cap; sides of face and throat grey with fine dark barring, rest of underparts yellowish-green entirely barred dark olive. Adult female is similar but crown black with white speckles. Immature duller above and more heavily barred below. Race hausbergi (Ke to NTz) is more yellowish overall with narrower darker bars below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are locally common in montane forest at 1,600–3,000m. Frequently seen in mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A remarkably silent species, but infrequently gives a loud kweek-kweek-kweek…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Tullberg’s Woodpecker C. tullbergi.

images.caption: Fine-banded Woodpecker · Plate 135

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small woodpecker with a small bill. Adult male is olive-green above with an olive-brown cap and red restricted to nape; sides of face and throat pale yellow or greyish with fine dark streaks; rest of underparts dark olive, spotted on breast and barred on flanks with pale yellow. Adult female similar, but cap entirely dark olive-brown. Immature similar to female.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In East Africa, singles and pairs of race herberti are locally common in forest and thick secondary growth below 1,800m. Often joins mixed-species flocks, particularly in lower levels of tangled vines and undergrowth.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a well-spaced weeeoooooo rising towards the end, but also gives a burry downslurred pheeu.

images.caption: Buff-spotted Woodpecker · Plate 135

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is dark bronzy-olive green above, with brown crown, red hindcrown and conspicuous large chestnut-brown ear-patch; underparts are entirely spotted pale buffy-yellow on olive. Adult female similar, but crown all brown. Immature similar to female but greener above, with paler spots on underparts and some barring on belly. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs are locally common in forest and older secondary growth at 700–1,800m. Joins mixed-species flocks and usually feeds in middle and higher levels.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is an upslurred and descending weeeeeeeyu with a slight ascent in the middle.

images.caption: Brown-eared Woodpecker · Plate 135

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Common bush and woodland woodpecker, barred above and boldly spotted below. Adult male has red cap and malar stripe similar to several other species; ear-coverts narrowly streaked black and white, and throat white. Adult female has similar streaked ear-coverts and white throat but red is restricted to hindcrown and malar stripe is black speckled with white. Immature can be rather streaky on breast. Widespread nominate race is darker and has larger spots below than pallida in coastal Ke; intergrades occur in Tsavo, Ke.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in dry bush, acacia and wooded grasslands from sea level to 2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a long series of repeated hardly varying metallic tinkh-tinkh-tinkh-tinkh-tinkh… notes, which speed up and slow down with levels of excitement and are frequently given in duet.

images.caption: Nubian Woodpecker · Plate 136

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Golden tail is not distinctive. Both sexes differ from all preceding woodpeckers by streaked underparts (not spotted) and black throat with white speckles. Immature has variable barring on flanks and belly. Four races differ mainly in colour of upperparts; olive-brown in nominate (WUg south through WTz), greener in chrysura (WUg lowlands), olive-green in kavirondensis (ERw to SWKe and CTz) and yellowish-green in suahelica (CKe to STz inland).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in forest, riverine woodland and dense thickets below 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a rising and falling slurred tch’waaye, the first note harsh and grating, and the rest nasal and complaining.

images.caption: Golden-tailed Woodpecker · Plate 136

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A small green-backed woodpecker with spotted underparts. Three races occur: nyansae (SWUg to SWKe and south to SWTz) has fine short streaks above and barred flanks; nominate (coastal Ke and NETz) is spotted above and below; and loveridgei (E and SETz) is similar, but more barred above. Male has red crown and nape; female similar but with white-spotted black crown.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common but patchily distributed in forest and woodland from sea level to 2,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is an irregular, rather lazy upslurred ke-wiu or kiu-week.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecfic with Little Green Woodpecker, and called Green-backed Woodpecker.

images.caption: Little Spotted Woodpecker · Plate 136

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small green-backed woodpecker with entirely barred underparts. Male has red crown and nape; female similar but has white-spotted black crown.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Race permista is uncommon in forests of south-western Uganda.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a series of six or so piercing high-pitched upslurred ke-wii notes.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecfic with Little Spotted Woodpecker, and called Green-backed Woodpecker.

images.caption: Little Green Woodpecker · Plate 136

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Golden-tailed Woodpecker with streaked underparts; both sexes differ in whiter throat and very lightly speckled upperparts (may appear plain in the field). Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in forest and woodland in coastal Kenya and inland along the Tana River, and in north-eastern Tanzania to the Usambara Mts.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a rising and burry dry trill: whirrrrrr-whirrrrrr-whirrrrrr-whirrrrrr.

images.caption: Mombasa Woodpecker · Plate 136

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small woodpecker with lightly streaked sides to face, well-streaked underparts and spotted wings. Five races occur: adult male always has a mostly red crown, narrow black malar stripe, golden-yellow tail-shafts and well-streaked underparts; female similar, but crown blackish-brown. Four races have distinctly barred backs: hemprichii (NEUg to EKe) has a dark brown back with pale bars and white wing spots; massaicus (EUg to CKe and NTz lowlands) is similar but wing spots yellowish; hartlaubii (SEKe and most of Tz) is more olive-brown above with yellowish wing spots and yellowish underparts; centralis (WTz) is similar but browner above, and more yellow below. Distinctive race lepidus (Ug, Rw and Bu east to CKe highlands) has plainer olive-brown back (dark barring only visible at close range). Several races intergrade in contact zones.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
