sections.text: Most common and widespread woodpecker, in forest edge and clearings, open woodland, dry bush and cultivation, from sea level to 3,000m. Race lepidus prefers more forested habitats.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a very cross-sounding series of dry high-pitched and tuneless rattled churrs that change slightly in pitch.

images.caption: Cardinal Woodpecker · Plate 137

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Cardinal Woodpecker but ear-coverts dark brown encircled by white and tail brown with small white spots (no golden tail-shafts). Adult male has red restricted to hindcrown; adult female has crown and nape entirely brown. Three distinct races occur: nominate (in Ug) is brown above and faintly streaked below; ingens (NEUg, CKe and NTz) is darker above and more streaked below; and crateri (Crater Highlands, Tz) is blackish-brown above and heavily streaked below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are local and rather uncommon in a variety of woodland, forest edge and cultivated areas with large scattered trees, from sea level to 3,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a rattled musical chreetchee-chree-chee or variants; also a series of upslurred squeals, rather like a small raptor.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Picoides.

images.caption: Brown-backed Woodpecker · Plate 137

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large woodpecker with a bold black-and-white face pattern, finely barred dark olive back and wings, and narrowly barred, or broken barred and spotted, underparts. Adult male has black forecrown (with tiny white speckles) and red hindcrown; adult female is similar but lacks red on hindcrown. Immature has red speckles on crown in both sexes. Two races occur: in race schoensis (NWUg, NEUg, and NKe) black face-stripes join, and underparts are more grey-brown with variable bars and spots. In more southerly nominate race, face-stripes are separated and underparts more tightly barred. Races intergrade around the equator.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread, but rather local in variety of woodland and bush country with large trees, from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a long descending series of yelps kree-kree-kree-kreekreekree… that accelerates towards the end.

images.caption: Bearded Woodpecker · Plate 138

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Plain olive-green and grey woodpecker with a red rump. Adult male has red crown, small orange or yellowish patch on belly and faint barring on flanks. Adult female similar but lacks red on head. Immature duller than adult, without orange or yellow on belly. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a wide range of woodland, forest edge, bush country and farmland with trees, mainly to the west of Eastern Grey Woodpecker, and north of Eastern Grey where they meet in central Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Common call is a descending series of squealed kwikwikwi… notes, but also gives an upslurred musical and churred trrree’t’ri’tree.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecfic with Eastern Grey Woodpecker.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Grey Woodpecker

images.caption: African Grey Woodpecker · Plate 138

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to African Grey Woodpecker but slightly more golden-green above, with large red patch on belly.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In East Africa, race rhodeogaster occurs in a variety of woodland and cultivated areas with trees in the highlands of W and central Kenya to northern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Similar to African Grey Woodpecker.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered to be a race of African Grey Woodpecker.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Grey-headed Woodpecker, Mountain Grey Woodpecker

images.caption: Eastern Grey Woodpecker · Plate 138

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small and chunky with a black or dark grey crown, brown upperparts (some races streaked blackish); whitish or buffy underparts streaked black (either heavily or lightly); all have white back (obvious in display, but difficult to see when perched). Five similar races occur: those with heavily streaked underparts include meinertzhageni (Ug, Rw, Bu to WKe), albigularis (W, S and CTz) and suahelicus (coastal Ke and ETz). Lightly streaked races are medianus (C to SEKe and N to NETz) and cryptoleucus (STz).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread, but very shy, local and solitary in good forest from sea level to 2,150m. Sits upright and motionless for long periods, but then flies fast and direct, and is difficult to relocate.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls a quiet mewing huiii, huiii, but more frequently heard is a loud far-carrying, mechanical and vibrating br-er-errrrrrrr, slightly falling then rising, before falling to fade.

images.caption: African Broadbill · Plate 139

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very attractive and distinctive with a boldly marked head, green back, blue shoulders and red belly. In flight, shows white patch at base of primaries, and bright blue shoulders and rump. Best identified from Green-breasted Pitta by tawny-buff breast. Immature duller than adult with buffy-pink vent. Birds in EA are race longipennis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Extremely shy; often on the ground within dense cover and stands motionless for long periods. Breeds in south-eastern Tanzania Dec–Apr, elsewhere migratory occurring in small numbers north to western Uganda and coastal Kenya, May–Sep.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a loud far-carrying and explosive quoip (given from a lateral branch in mid-canopy and coinciding with a jump). Notes are identical and spaced every few seconds. On migration makes a low croaking sound.

images.caption: African Pitta · Plate 139

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Quite large, stocky and short-tailed, with obvious pale supercilium, conspicuous rufous wings in flight, and non-contrasting buffy outer tail; crown feathers often raised giving shaggy-headed appearance. In EA most of the seven races have little or no rufous on nape: athi (CKe to NTz) as described above is typical of most forms; harteri (SEKe) is overall more rufous; tropicalis (WUg south through WTz) is intermediate between athi and tropicalis; ruwenzoria (SWUg) is greyer above; transvaalensis (E and STz) is generally paler, with some rufous on nape; distinctive races nigrescens (Njombe, STz) and nyika (Mbeya, STz) are darker reddish-brown above (with black scaling) and finer bills, breast streaking on nigrescens extends to flanks.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: The most common and widespread lark, in grasslands with or without bush cover, and open farmland, at 1,000–3,000m. Sings from prominent perches including bushes, termite hills and fence posts.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Normal song is sii-su-eeeee with middle part falling and last part gently rising to fade. Many local variations based on this, also a monotonous piping. Often the most characteristic wet-season call of upland grasslands.

images.caption: Rufous-naped Lark · Plate 140

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The nominate race is similar to Rufous-naped Lark but larger with a longer tail, black spots at sides of breast usually form two small blackish patches (may be invisible on worn birds or immatures). Long heavy bill, rufous wings (particularly noticable in flight), buffy supercilium, slight shaggy appearance to crown and brown tail are all generally similar to Rufous-naped. Race kidepoensis (NEUg) is smaller and more rufous above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Occurs mainly N and E of Rufous-naped, from near sea level to 1,350m preferring drier areas with more bush cover. Often perches and sings from tops of small bushes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very fluty, rather chat-like song, with short varied phrases repeated monotonously. Usually given from a perch, but also in heavy laboured flight.

images.caption: Red-winged Lark · Plate 140

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Fairly small lark; generally brown (or rufous-brown) both above and below, with buffy-rufous outer tail; breast spotting varies from rufous to blackish. Three races occur: kawirondensis (WUg to WKe and NTz) is generally dark with heavy blackish streaking above; torrida (NUg to NKe and S to CTz) is more rufous; fischeri (coastal Ke and Tz) is either earth-brown or warm rufous above with less bold markings.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Often first encountered in display flight when it makes loud far-carrying prrrrrrrr-rrrp sound with its wings. On the ground rather shy, often crouching and keeping near cover. Inhabits grassland with or without scattered trees and bushes, from sea level to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rarely heard song from top of bush is a loud, piercing, serin-like rising and falling si-uu-si-si-uu.

images.caption: Flappet Lark · Plate 140

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smallish, size similar to Singing Bush and Flappet Larks. Two races occur (sometimes considered species): athensis (Athi Short-toed Lark) from SKe to NTz is grey-brown above with heavy blackish streaks and buffy fringes; pale supercilium and eye-ring and a pale pinkish bill are distinctive at close range. Wings lack rufous patches, tail dark with buffy-white edges. Breast to vent washed pale brown, with short heavy dark streaks on breast, throat whitish. Race megaensis (Somali Short-toed Lark) in NKe (within dotted line on map) is similar, but general tone more sandy-buff. Flappet is much browner below, while Singing Bush has an obvious white outer tail and rufous wing patches.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in flocks on open ground with short grass cover at 1,200–1,850m. Generally uncommon away from Athi Plains, Kenya, and Arusha area, northern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sings in high display flight a series of fast, complex, rising and falling notes incorporating mimicry, vaguely like a smoother version of an Acrocephalus warbler. Flushed birds call trrrit.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Calendrella.

images.caption: Somali Short-toed Lark · Plate 141

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to White-tailed Lark but with dense black spotting across upper breast contrasting with whiter throat (especially when singing). Also shows more boldly patterned upperparts, and in flight brighter rufous wing patches. White outer tail is obvious in Melodious, White-tailed and Singing Bush Larks. Presently considered monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Generally uncommon in grassland with or without open woodland at 600–2,000m; particularly attracted to black cotton soil.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Flight songs vary from a complex rambling of harsh and sweet notes which include much mimicry, often given for long periods in cruising flight. Also calls from bush tops or termite hills a chattering ch-ch-ch-ch-ch.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Since 2020 birds that appear to be Melodious Larks (song similar to those in southern Africa) have been found to be resident in the Maasai Mara, Ke, and Serengeti, Tz. Previously these were overlooked or considered to be an undescribed form of White-tailed Lark.

images.caption: Melodious Lark · Plate 141

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Fairly small grey-brown lark with dark streaking; buffy supercilium accentuates dark ear-coverts; bill dark above, pinkish below. Underparts buffy with small streaks on sides of breast; throat white. In distinctive hesitant flight (shared with White-tailed and Friedmann’s Larks) shows rufous wing patches and obvious pure white outer tail feathers. Birds in EA are race marginata.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in bush country with sparse grass cover from sea level to 1,800m. Also appears in flocks in seasonal grasslands during the rains. Flies up and then dives into cover when flushed.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sings in high circling flight or from bushes, a continuous rather monotonous series of repeated notes, preceded by slower slightly lower notes.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities consider this species to be a race of Horsfield’s Bushlark M. javanica.

images.caption: Singing Bush Lark · Plate 141

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Singing Bush Lark, but overall tones are more rufous and bill is slightly larger; best identified by voice and puffy white-throated appearance when calling. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Little known; most records occur during the rains in the Tsavo region of Kenya, where it may breed. Likes open bush country with short grass cover at 600–900m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls from tops of bushes and in flight, a rising and falling reedy whistled whooyu, repeated at about 2-second intervals.

images.caption: Friedmann’s Lark · Plate 141

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slim appearance and bill give rather pipit-like impression. Upperparts lightly mottled grey-brown with greyer crown; sides of face, throat and breast mottled pinkish-brown, like no other lark or pipit. No white in tail or rufous in wings. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in bush country with little ground cover at 150–1,800m, where frequently perches on tops of bushes with a horizontal stance.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Monotonous descending hissed song is given from small trees (similar to song of overlapping Ashy Cisticola). Also calls an occasional single squeaked tseet from the ground.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Mirafra.

images.caption: Pink-breasted Lark · Plate 142

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Sandy grey-brown lark with a long pointed crest, often raised or blown up by wind, but not always immediately obvious. Underparts very pale sandy with dark brown streaks on breast. Birds in EA are race somaliensis. Very similar Thekla’s Lark is darker above with heavier short spots on breast. Sides of tail and underwing-coverts pinkish-cinnamon (noticeable in flight).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in range, particularly in sandy desert with sparse cover at 400–900m. Usually in pairs, but more may gather at waterholes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Long rambling song, usually from the ground or low perch, consists of many randomly introduced rather scratchy notes.

images.caption: Crested Lark · Plate 142

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Crested Lark but bill and crest slightly shorter, and darker above with shorter heavier spots on breast. Underwing-coverts greyish or pinkish-grey. Combination of dark-toned upperparts and breast spotting accentuates whiteness of throat. Birds in EA are race huriensis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in pairs and loose flocks in rockier areas than Crested Lark. Very common in lava deserts east of Lake Turkana, Kenya, at 400–1,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sings from rocky ground, a short series of sweet notes recalling a bunting. More complex series including mimicry in flight.

images.caption: Thekla’s Lark · Plate 142

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: An attractive and distinctive lark, mostly bright cinnamon-rufous above, with a lightly streaked black-and-white hindneck. Black band across base of neck separates white throat from rufous mottling on upper breast. In flight rufous upperparts and wing-coverts contrast strongly with white-tipped blackish flight feathers and tail. Immature is more scaly above, blackish breast-band indistinct. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common within a very limited range on red sandy soil with Acacia turnbulliana trees, at 100–1,350m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song comprises a few introductory notes followed by a loud drawn-out plaintive rising whistle, often given from a bush top with the crown slightly raised; also sings in flight.

images.caption: Collared Lark · Plate 142

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Singing Bush and White-tailed Larks but less heavily streaked above. Two colour morphs occur: both are comparatively plain above (except for crown streaking) and have long pale superciliary stripes. Dark morph is blackish-brown above with dark pectoral patches, and dark chestnut and black mottling and streaking on breast and flanks; rufous morph is rufous-brown above, with rufous-brown pectoral patches and sparse dark rufous-brown streaks on breast. In rather strong and direct flight both show rufous wing patches and white outer tail feathers. Bill is pale greyish, or pinkish above and white below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic; known only from the Dida-Galgalu desert area and between Isiolo and Garba Tula, Kenya. It inhabits rocky lava desert with short grass cover at 600–1,350m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is thin and rather scratchy, with random loud sharper notes towards the end.

images.caption: Williams’s Lark · Plate 142

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive lark with bright rufous cap (sometimes raised) and rufous patches on sides of breast; bold white supercilium and unstreaked whitish underparts. When flushed, shows very dark tail with narrow white sides. Two races occur: western and southern saturatior as described, williamsi in CKe highlands is greyer and more streaked above. Immature is very different, with dark blackish-brown upperparts finely spotted white on crown, white fringes to mantle and blackish-brown spots on sides of breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and common but patchily distributed, sometimes gathering in large flocks on short grasslands at 950–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In circular flight utters a continuous rhythmical and monotonous song based on one note. Single liquid chirrup given when flushed.

images.caption: Red-capped Lark · Plate 143

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Boldly marked, rather long-billed, short-tailed lark, with a distinctive black crescent below eye and vertical bar on cheek. Prominent streaking on breast often shows as dark patches at sides of neck. In flight, short square tail has white outer feathers. Race megaensis (NKe) as described above; delamerei (SKe and NTz) is greyer and also has an uncommon rufous morph.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Resident and erratic wanderer usually in small flocks on dry soils with short grass, and on burnt grassland, at 1,000–1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Distinctive song is an attractive jumble of rising and falling notes with minor-key intrusions. From the ground, calls a variety of chips and explosive downslurs.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Pseudalaemon.

images.caption: Short-tailed Lark · Plate 143

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive lark with grey-brown upperparts, a striking black face mask and a stout pale pinkish or horn-coloured bill. Underparts unstreaked with small whitish throat grading into greyish breast and rufous belly. Tail dark brown with buff outer feathers. Sexes alike. Three races occur: yavelloensis (NKe) is greyer above, mcchesneyi (Marsabit, NKe) is browner above, and intensa (CKe) more richly coloured below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common within restricted range, inhabiting black lava desert with sparse grass cover, at 400–1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Various calls described in flight and on ground include a rolling tew-tew-tutew-tew and a high-pitched treeeeeeee. SPARROW-LARKS Small chunky sparrow-like larks with heavy conical bills, usually found in flocks. Sexually dimorphic: males are boldly marked on head and underparts; females and immatures are much drabber.

images.caption: Masked Lark · Plate 144

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has blackish-brown facial markings adjoining paler brown (or chestnut-brown) crown and nape; no white on crown. Facial pattern extends as stripe from chin to vent, sides of breast and flanks buffy-white. Back and wings dull grey-brown, and no white on tail. Adult female has medium-brown upperparts, with pale rufous-brown sides to neck and a dark blackish-brown stripe on the belly. Immature is like dull female with more mottled upperparts; small dark mark on belly hard to see. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread up to 2,000m in dry grassland, on airstrips and in semi-arid areas. Mainly found to the west of other sparrow-larks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call from perched or flying bird is a double, quite explosive tsi-sit, the song being an embellishment of these notes and rather sparrow-like.

images.caption: Fischer’s Sparrow-Lark · Plate 144

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male of the nominate race similar to Fischer’s Sparrow-Lark, but cleaner looking; black or dark chestnut facial markings encircle white patch on crown. Cheek patch very white. Facial pattern extends as black vertical stripe from chin to vent (broader than Fischer’s); sides of breast and flanks white. Back and wings pale grey-brown, narrow white tail edges. Adult female has brown crown, pale rufous superciliary and buffy-white cheeks. Immature is like poorly marked female with dull broad streaking on breast. Race harrisoni in north-west of range is greyer above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a variety of arid and semi-arid habitats including lava rock and sandy desert, open stony areas with some bush cover, and short dry grassland from sea level to 1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call consists of spaced piping notes, some similar to Lesser Striped Swallow. Song is a series of repeated and rising mournful notes.

images.caption: Chestnut-headed Sparrow-Lark · Plate 144

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is distinctive with a rich chestnut back and wings, bold black-and-white head pattern and mostly black underparts (with white vent). White on ear-coverts and nape, but not on crown. Whitish lower rump and outer tail in flight. Adult female is duller with variable (but usually extensive) black mottling on head and underparts, and chestnut wing-coverts. Immature is like pale female, but may show distinctive chestnut patch on wing-coverts. Birds in EA are race madaraszi.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather local in range and subject to erratic wandering. Can occur in large numbers, particularly on black soils and recently burnt grassland, between sea level and 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is more complex than that of other sparrow-larks, a mournful series of slurs and chips delivered in flight and from the ground.

images.caption: Chestnut-backed Sparrow-Lark · Plate 144

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Plain brown above, white below with a brown breast-band, uniform brown underwing and slightly forked tail. Similar Banded Martin is much larger with white underwing-coverts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Nominate race is a common Palearctic visitor from Sep to early May between sea level and 1,800m. Sometimes appears in flocks of thousands, which travel fast and direct on migration.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Series of churrs on different notes resulting in a formless song that is twittering and rather lark-like in quality.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Bank Swallow, Collared Sand Martin

images.caption: Sand Martin · Plate 145

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Entire upperparts, throat and breast are brown; belly white. Widespread race ducis is darker and has less white on the belly than the nominate in STz.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread, and often occurs in large flocks over water in the highlands, but is not restricted to specific altitudes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a harsh rasping churr from a perch and in flight.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Brown-throated Martin, Plain Martin

images.caption: African Plain Martin · Plate 145

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Sand Martin but much larger, with a short white stripe in front of eye, white underwing-coverts and square-ended tail. Widespread race suahelica as described, less common erlangeri in NEUg, NKe and EKe has centre of breast-band extending towards belly.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or small flocks occur over grassland from sea level to 2,500m. Flight is low and slow with frequent glides.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Musical notes given in descending series, with a twangy, nasal, rather lark-like quality. Calls in flight, but song is usually delivered from top of low vegetation.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Riparia.

images.caption: Banded Martin · Plate 145

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather stocky blue-black martin with white rump and underparts; tail forked, but not elongated like some pale-rumped swallows. Immature is duller and browner with grey-tinged underparts and rump. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic visitor in Sep–Apr.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In flight gives a pleasant, short, buzzy chirp, often with many calling simultaneously.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Common House Martin

images.caption: Northern House Martin · Plate 145

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger and bulkier than Red-rumped Swallow, but has similar blue-black cap down to eye and rufous ear-coverts. Pale throat contrasts with richer rufous breast and rufous (not black) undertail-coverts. Easily identified in flight by white underwing-coverts contrasting with blackish flight feathers. Race monteiri (Tz and EKe) has white spots on tail, while saturatior (elsewhere) has an all-dark tail; intergrades occur.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or small loose flocks are widespread from sea level to 2,600m, occurring in all but the most arid areas.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is loud and rambling, given either perched or in flight. Notes are drawn-out nasal slurs, very similar in quality to Grey-backed Fiscal.

images.caption: Mosque Swallow · Plate 146

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Blue-black cap extends below eye and over ear-coverts; chin to undertail-coverts and underwing-coverts rufous. Adult in fresh plumage has very long tail-streamers giving a slim elegant appearance. Birds in EA are race gordoni.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are generally uncommon, in wooded grasslands and cultivated areas at 700–1,700m in the west.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a hurried nasal jumble, ending with a high-pitched drawn-out descending seeeeuuu. Can be given frequently, usually from the vicinity of a termite mound, but also in flight.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Red-breasted Swallow

images.caption: Rufous-chested Swallow · Plate 146

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Strongly marked, richly coloured swallow with an extensive bright rufous head and rump, and heavy black streaking on white underparts. In flight, shows pale buffy underwing-coverts and heavily streaked underparts. Birds in EA are race unitatis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are widespread and common from sea level to 2,200m, occurring in a wide range of habitats except very arid country.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Cheerful ramble of rising and falling nasal chips and twitters, terminating in a louder and deliberate, well-spaced series of descending nasal notes. Usually given from a perch, but will sing in flight.

images.caption: Lesser Striped Swallow · Plate 146

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has blue-black upperparts and breast-band, chestnut forecrown and throat, and white or buffish underparts (grey in Angola Swallow). Tail is deeply forked with white spots on shorter central feathers. Immature variable, duller and browner above, with less chestnut on head and throat, and shorter tail. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common Palearctic visitor in Aug–Apr, throughout from sea level to 3,000m. Sometimes migrates and roosts in huge flocks. A few birds stay year-round.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually fairly silent in the region, but song delivered in flight or perched is a continuous rambling and cheerful twitter, with a finch-like quality.

images.caption: Barn Swallow · Plate 147

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Barn Swallow but upperparts brighter blue, breast-band narrow and incomplete in centre, rest of underparts grey; tail short and forked with obvious large white spots. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common mainly west of the Great Rift Valley, but also locally in eastern Tanzania. Occurs in villages and a wide variety of open country at about 700–2,600m, often nesting under bridges.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song given from a perch consists of loud squeaky, rather unpleasant notes. Flight calls have the same squeaky quality.

images.caption: Angola Swallow · Plate 147

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Barn Swallow with chestnut forecrown, but throat is buff in widespread nominate race, or white in coastal amadoni; narrow blackish breast-band is incomplete. In good light looks blue above and very white below. Forked tail has large white spots and is shorter than adult Barn Swallow.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Although found in a wide variety of open country, it is only common along Kenya coast, occurring elsewhere in scattered pockets to 1,900m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Most calls are nasal and harsh, but infrequently heard song given in flight consists of many sweet cadences and trills.

images.caption: Ethiopian Swallow · Plate 147

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is shiny blue above, very white below, with a neat chestnut cap; small dark breast and flank patches visible at close range. In good plumage white spotted tail has long very thin wires, but hard to see at any distance and sometimes broken. Immature has dull brown crown and no tail wires. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: A fast-flying common and widespread swallow, usually in pairs and often near water, from sea level to 2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rather quiet, the song is a subdued twittering similar to Barn Swallow, but of shorter duration.

images.caption: Wire-tailed Swallow · Plate 147

psalidoprocne-pristoptera.ref: Plate 148: Saw-Wings, Blue Swallows And Pseudhirundo
psalidoprocne-pristoptera.name: Black Saw-wing

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Four races occur: typical adult male is black (with a slight green gloss) and a broad-based deeply forked tail; female and immature duller with less deeply forked tail. Adult of race ruwenzori (WUg to NWTz) is shorter-tailed than widespread massaica (Ke to NETz) while holomelas (coastal Ke and Tz) is smaller overall. If seen well, all show silvery grey-brown underwing-coverts. Adult of distinctive race orientalis (Eastern Saw-wing) (south of dotted line on map) has pure white underwing-coverts; immature is duller, browner and shorter-tailed with greyish underwing-coverts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are common, mainly in highlands, but range from sea level to 3,500m (sea level to 1,800m for orientalis). Often in clearings in forest or over riverine woodland, and regularly perches on treetops.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Frequently utters seemingly random soft nasal squeaks, weeu, see, in flight and when perched.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Eastern Saw-wing was previously considered to be a distinct species.

images.caption: Black Saw-wing · Plate 148

psalidoprocne-albiceps.ref: Plate 148: Saw-Wings, Blue Swallows And Pseudhirundo
psalidoprocne-albiceps.name: White-headed Saw-wing

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very distinctive with pure white head and narrow black eyestripe. Adult female has dark ashy grey-brown head and whiter throat. Immature is dull dark brown with slightly paler throat (hard to see in field). Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common at 700–2,400m, in a wider variety of habitats than other saw-wings, including forest clearings, open woodland, bushed grassland and cultivation.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Similar to Black Saw-wing but is more hissing and breaks into a quiet chatter. Calls less frequently than most swallows, but will do so, especially during aerial chases. BLUE SWALLOWS Two distinctive, glossy dark blue swallows.

images.caption: White-headed Saw-wing · Plate 148

pseudhirundo-griseopyga.ref: Plate 148: Saw-Wings, Blue Swallows And Pseudhirundo
pseudhirundo-griseopyga.name: Grey-rumped Swallow

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slim swallow with pale grey rump and grey-brown crown; underparts white. Sexes alike. Immature is duller with browner rump and shorter tail. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Commonly seen in flocks, but rather local at 900–2,200m over open grassland and burnt areas. Uniquely breeds in rodent burrows.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls are harsh and burry, more like a Sand Martin than other swallows; flocks utter low churrs while feeding.

images.caption: Grey-rumped Swallow · Plate 148

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Only very black-and-white wagtail in region; adult is without grey or brown in plumage, and has comparatively broad breast-band. Immature is brownish-grey above. All ages are separated from Cape and White Wagtails by extensive white wing patches. Birds in EA are race vidua.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Most common and widespread resident wagtail, from sea level to 3,000m along riverbanks, lakeshores, in cultivated areas and forest glades, as well as towns.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sweet calls are frequently paired notes, which become an attractive complex and warbled song.

images.caption: African Pied Wagtail · Plate 149

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Non-breeding male has crown, nape and breast-band black, giving white-faced appearance, even more obvious in breeding plumage when throat is also black. Non-breeding female and first-winter rather dingy: crown to rump grey, face washed pale olivaceous, and dark narrow breast-band, rather similar to immature Cape Wagtail, but greyer above (not brown). Breeding female is similar to breeding male but not quite as clean-looking, with some grey on crown.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or small groups of the nominate race are scarce Palearctic migrants in Nov–Mar, mainly around the northern lakes and on isolated pools from sea level to 1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Does not sing in region, but often calls with an urgent dry paired chh-tit in flight or on the ground.

images.caption: White Wagtail · Plate 149

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Elegant and proportionately longer-tailed than other wagtails. Adult is largely clear grey above and white below with neat narrow black breast-band. Immature is similar, but washed brown above, with indistinct breast-band. Birds in EA are race torrentium.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are widespread residents along rocky fast-flowing rivers and at forest edges; although commonest in the highlands, they may occur down to 500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very vocal. Simple song is usually three notes siiiii seee-uu (first rising, then last notes falling to fade). Alarm and contact calls are a strange metallic explosive chit, which can break into complex whistles and descending trills with a buzzing quality.

images.caption: Mountain Wagtail · Plate 149

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is olive-brown above without obvious white panel in wing (although may show pale feather edges); creamy-buff underparts and narrow dark breast-band. Immature has buffy fringes to wing-coverts; washed yellowish-buff on underparts. Birds in EA are race wellsi.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are resident but rather local near lakes and ponds at 900–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls with an upslurred interrogatory siuweeee and chweet-chweet mainly in flight, but may also mix these calls into a simple song.

images.caption: Cape Wagtail · Plate 149

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slim, graceful wagtail with long tail. Non-breeding plumage varies but typified by grey upperparts with yellow rump, variable yellow underparts (may be restricted to vent), whitish throat and no breast-band. Breeding male has yellow underparts and black throat. Female has white throat and yellow breast to vent.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: The nominate race is a Palearctic migrant that mainly occurs in small numbers along highland streams from late Sep to Mar, but ranges down to sea level on passage.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a loud, harsh and explosive ti-titt. Infrequently heard song is the call interspersed with a loud siiii.

images.caption: Grey Wagtail · Plate 149

motacilla-flava.ref: Plate 150: Yellow Wagtails And Golden Pipit
motacilla-flava.name: Western Yellow Wagtail

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: On arrival in East Africa the plumage of Western Yellow Wagtails is highly varied and for many birds racial separation is impossible. Typical individuals are brownish above with variable yellow below, often strongest on belly and flanks. Adult males have most extensive yellow below, but note their distinctive head patterns. Females and first-year birds have olive-brown or plain brown upperparts and usually show some yellow on belly, but may have all-white underparts. From January males (and some females) acquire distinctive head patterns and become greener above and all yellow below (except for whitish throat on females). Six races and one named intergrade occur; males are described below: M. f. feldegg has completely black top of head. [Alt. Black-headed Wagtail] M. f. thunbergi has dark grey crown blending into blackish face. [Alt. Grey-headed Wagtail] M. f. flava has blue-grey crown and darker cheeks separated by distinct white supercilium. [Alt. Blue-headed Wagtail] M. f. beema has pale grey crown and darker cheeks separated by distinct white supercilium. [Alt. Sykes’s Wagtail] M. f. lutea has head mostly yellow, variably washed green on crown and ear-coverts. [Alt. Yellow-headed Wagtail] M. f. leucocephala has almost entirely white head. [Alt. White-headed Wagtail] M. f. ‘superciliaris’ has black head (like feldegg) with white supercilium (like flava); hybrid. Since hybrids are not uncommon, some individuals are impossible to assign racially. Differs from larger Grey Wagtail in all plumages by never having a grey mantle.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common Palearctic migrant in Sep–May, with several different races often occurring together, sometimes in flocks of thousands. Birds favour lakeshores, swampy land, short grassland and open cultivation, frequently associating with cattle and plains game, from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very vocal: call in flight and on the ground is a rising sweeep, softer than other wagtails in the region. The race feldegg sounds considerably harsher.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly known as Yellow Wagtail. GOLDEN PIPIT Golden Pipit resembles some of the longclaws (see Plate 151), but is particularly distinctive in flight when the male suddenly reveals striking bright yellow wings.

images.caption: Western Yellow Wagtail · Plate 150

tmetothylacus-tenellus.ref: Plate 150: Yellow Wagtails And Golden Pipit
tmetothylacus-tenellus.name: Golden Pipit

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male in breeding plumage is streaked and mottled dark brown, olive-yellow and buff above, and brilliant yellow with a neat black breast-band below. In flight, bright yellow wings with black tips and bright yellow outer tail are distinctive. Adult female is more like a typical pipit, but has dull yellow edges to primaries and outer tail, and is mainly plain buff below with pale yellow restricted to belly; underwing-coverts pale yellow. Non-breeding male resembles female but tinged brighter yellow. Immature is browner and even more pipit-like with streaked breast, but may show yellowish wing edgings. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are sometimes common in bushed and wooded grassland in dry country from sea level to 1,800m. Local movements occur, often in response to rains.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent, but can be very vocal after rains when the complex whistled song has a weaver-like quality.

images.caption: Golden Pipit · Plate 150

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is boldly marked blackish-brown above with buff fringes giving a heavily mottled appearance. Supercilium and underparts bright yellow with a broad black breast-band and short black streaks on sides of breast (breast-band may be less extensive on female). In gliding flight shows conspicuous white corners to tail. Immature is paler and browner with buffy throat and breast, and variable short blackish streaks on breast; pale yellow is restricted to flanks and belly. Two races occur: western nominate as described; tertius (coastal Ke, E and STz) is slightly smaller and brighter.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Most common and widespread longclaw in grassland, open bush country and cultivated areas from sea level to 2,300m. Feeds on the ground, but frequently perches on tops of bushes and fence posts.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Quite a varied repertoire, commonest calls consist of a whistled drawn-out seeueeeee, or a rapid wi-pi-pi-pi-pi-pi usually given in laboured flight.

images.caption: Yellow-throated Longclaw · Plate 151

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smallest longclaw; adult male is very boldly marked above with yellow underparts and black streaks on breast and flanks (no solid black breast-band). Adult female is similar but slightly duller. In flight, shows white along outer tail feathers (not just corners). Immature is paler than adult and largely buff below with variable brown breast streaking; pale yellow from lower breast to vent. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to montane grasslands from Mt Elgon to Mt Kenya at 1,850– 3,400m. Generally uncommon, and prefers grazed open grassland and short moist tussock grass.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent, but has a varied repertoire. In flight, sings a rhythmical warble and a wi-wi-wi-wi-wi-wi-… accelerating in tempo as the bird descends earthwards. Sometimes gives a harsh repeated pipit-like sit. EN

images.caption: Sharpe’s Longclaw · Plate 151

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is similar to Yellow-throated Longclaw, but throat usually orange or orange-yellow bordered by narrow black necklace (but note that female and older immature may have yellow throats). Centre of breast to belly yellow with extensive black streaking extending to tawny-buff flanks. Immature has ill-defined breast-band and mainly buff underparts with some yellow on breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in generally dry bushed grasslands to the east from sea level to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Not so vocal; call is a varied drawn out and whistled siuuweeeee rising then falling and rising to fade.

images.caption: Pangani Longclaw · Plate 151

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slender longclaw very boldly scalloped above with blackish and creamy-buff. Adult male is unmistakable with bright rosy-red throat and black breast-band; central breast to belly with variable amount of rosy-red. Female similar but rosy underparts much paler. In distinctive fluttery flight, slender tail shows white edges (not just corners). Immature is boldly marked above like adult, but buffy-brown below with blackish streaks on breast (very pipit-like); red confined to centre of belly (difficult to see). Two races occur: wintoni (CKe to NTz) as described; altanus (SWTz) is slightly more heavily streaked above and on sides of breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in open damp grassland at 600–2,200m. Shyer than other longclaws, often running on ground within cover.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song varies slightly from place to place, but most commonly heard phrase is su-su-su-su-su-su-su-su-su-seeeeeeeee, with the last note higher.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Rosy-breasted Longclaw

images.caption: Rosy-throated Longclaw · Plate 151

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The commonest grassland pipit throughout most of range. Six races occur: widespread lacuum (SEUg, WKe south to CTz) is mid-brown above with darker streaks on crown and mantle, a strong facial pattern with obvious buffy supercilium, and dark malar stripe. Lower mandible is yellowish, legs pinkish with long hindclaw. Buffy-white below with short dark streaks on breast; flanks usually plain. In flight, extensive white in outer tail. Race annae (SEKe to NETz) is slightly paler and greyer; lichenya (WUg south to WTz) is darker and more heavily streaked above, richer buff below; winterbottomi (STz) is whiter on throat and belly; spurium (SETz) is greyer above. In SUg and NWTz distinctive race latistriatus (Jackson’s Pipit) is much darker than other forms with blackish-brown upperparts, and rich cinnamon underparts contrasting with whitish throat; blackish streaks on breast and flanks. Lower mandible and legs pinkish.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common in open country from sea level to 3,400m, except desert areas, although it occurs in coastal dunes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varies regionally: typical song is a repeated trrlit-trrlit-trrlit, flight call a repeated trit. Race latistriatus sings a rapid-fire tit-it-it-it-it-it-it followed by a sweeter trit-rit-rit-rit-rit and ending in a similar, but longer descending series. Flight call chrit.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Grassland Pipit

images.caption: African Pipit · Plate 152

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Widespread race hararensis is a large-billed, long-tailed, comparatively uniform pipit (plainer and darker in worn plumage) with a whitish throat, buffy underparts and light streaking on the breast. In flight, tail shows buffy-white outer tail feathers. From Nairobi to Chyulu Hills, Ke, chyuluensis (Nairobi Pipit) has all-buff outer tail, and distinctive habit of flying into trees and walking on branches when flushed (like Woodland Pipit). Race dewittei (SWUg, Rw and Bu) is similar to hararensis, but slightly smaller and darker.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Lone birds or pairs are widespread but never numerous in rocky country and along escarpments.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a lazy series of four notes repeated randomly chrit…swit…chweep chreer…, and flight call is a muffled trrit-tip.

images.caption: Long-billed Pipit · Plate 152

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to African Pipit, but streaking on underparts bolder and more extensive especially on flanks; obvious yellow base to lower mandible and rich orange-yellow legs. In flight, shows white outer tail.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: The nominate race is restricted to coastal grassland and saltpans mainly north of Malindi, Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a rapidly delivered continuous series that is softer than other large pipits; flight call shreep.

images.caption: Malindi Pipit · Plate 152

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Boldly marked pipit with long buffy-white supercilium; streaks on underparts dark and long, extending well onto flanks and belly. Green-tinged primary edges distinctive (but not always easy to see). In flight, shows striking white outer tail feathers. Birds in EA are race stygium.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and single birds inhabit rocky hills with open woodland and cultivation below 2,000m. Feeds on the ground but flies to small trees and bushes if disturbed.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Most attractive pipit song with rapid varied and sweet bunting-like descending notes that can carry a considerable distance.

images.caption: Striped Pipit · Plate 152

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small, rather plain-faced pipit with an indistinct supercilium and no malar stripe. Warm brown above with darker streaking, and whitish below, finely streaked dark brown on breast and flanks; white outer tail. Tree Pipit is larger with dark malar stripe and heavier streaking below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Race blayneyi is local and uncommon in bushed and wooded grassland from near sea level to 2,200m. Feeds on the ground and often flies into trees when disturbed.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Quiet for a pipit, but song is a nasal and monotonous wii-zhweep given from top of a small bush, the effect being rather seesaw-like.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Bushveld Pipit

images.caption: Bush Pipit · Plate 152

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Much plainer than African Pipit with unstreaked or only lightly marked back; pale buffy or cinnamon-buff below with indistinct streaks on breast; malar stripe indistinct, lower mandible yellowish-pink (pink on Buffy Pipit). In flight, tail looks uniform dark brown with buff edges. Three races occur: zenkeri (Ug to Bu, NWTz, and WKe) is quite dark above and deep buff below; bohndorffi (SWTz) is paler, especially on underparts; and goodsoni (CKe to NTz) is paler and sandier, and sometimes considered a race of Buffy Pipit.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in short grassland with or without trees at 700–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A rather monotonous song like Long-billed Pipit, but notes scratchier and less distinct.

images.caption: Plain-backed Pipit · Plate 153

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Heavily streaked above and below including rump and flanks; outer tail white. Adult has brick-red face, supercilium and upper breast, but extent and intensity varies; this plumage can be seen in all months. First-winter and some females lack red and are best distinguished from Tree Pipit by whiter underparts with heavier black streaking, and whitish stripes on darker mantle. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic passage migrant and visitor to marshy grassland and lakeshores in Oct–Apr, from sea level to 3,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In flight, invariably gives a single high-pitched sharp zeeez.

images.caption: Red-throated Pipit · Plate 153

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Olive-brown and heavily streaked above with a plain rump, buff supercilium and narrow dark malar stripe. Warm buff on breast and flanks (but whiter on belly) with long dark streaks on breast (less distinct on flanks). White on outer tail feathers. Non-breeding Red-throated Pipit is darker above and whiter below with heavier streaking.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: The nominate race is a common Palearctic visitor and passage migrant Oct–May, mainly at 700–3,000m, favouring a wide variety of open wooded areas.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Commonly gives a distinctive nasal eeez.

images.caption: Tree Pipit · Plate 153

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small richly marked forest pipit; boldly streaked above with warm buff and blackish-brown and often prominent whitish wingbars; below white with bold black streaks on breast; outer tail edged white. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to largely undisturbed coastal forests in Kenya and Tanzania. Shy and very difficult to see while feeding in leaf litter, but flies into trees if disturbed.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls from ground or tree, a strong repeated high-pitched and rising tseeeee. Song given in a high undulating aerial display above the canopy is a repeated seueeeee falling then rising to fade. EN

images.caption: Sokoke Pipit · Plate 153

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is wholly glossy blue-black with a small orange-yellow gape; some have yellow shoulder patches. Adult female is olive-brown above with blackish barring and obviously yellow-edged wings and tail. White below washed yellow on sides of breast and extensively barred with small black crescents; much yellow on undertail. Immature is similar to female but has very heavy barring. Monotypic, but occasionally hybridises with Red-shouldered Cuckooshrike.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and common in woodlands, forest edge and scrub, from sea level to 3,000m. Numbers increase greatly in Apr–Sep when birds from the southern tropics arrive.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rather quiet unless breeding: commonest call is a repeated insect-like trill lasting about 2 seconds; a louder descending shree-shree-shree is heard less frequently.

images.caption: Black Cuckooshrike · Plate 154

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very similar to Black Cuckooshrike, but slightly stockier with smaller orange-yellow gape. In good light purple throat and breast contrast with otherwise glossy blue-black plumage. Adult female has a greyish head contrasting with quite uniform olive-green upperparts and dull green wings. Bright yellow below, with variable but usually indistinct dusky bars to breast; throat whitish. Immature is like female but has brownish head and heavier barring above and below. Widespread race martini as described, male of scarce muenzneri (ETz) has a steel-blue throat.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather uncommon in mid-levels and upper canopy of highland forest and forest edge at 1,700– 2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls varied, but based on a short sharp downslurred siu, given in series or repeated emphatically.

images.caption: Purple-throated Cuckooshrike · Plate 154

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to Black Cuckooshrike but has large and conspicuous orange-yellow gape wattles. Adult female is similar to female Purple-throated Cuckooshrike but brighter yellow on rump with black barring; blackish wings have bright yellow edgings. Underparts bright yellow with variable black barring especially on breast. Immature similar to female, but can be virtually unbarred above and more heavily barred on breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in the west, inhabiting mid-levels and canopy of good forest at 1,400–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a strong, rhythmical whistled series, sisisi-seeuu, the first notes identical, the last note falling in tone.

images.caption: Petit’s Cuckooshrike · Plate 154

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is almost uniform medium-grey (wings slightly darker), with blackish lores and chin, conspicuous large dark eyes and whitish eye-ring. Adult female is similar but lacks dark lores and chin. Immature is finely barred greyish-brown and white, with a darker tail. Birds in EA are race purus.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and common in canopy of highland forest, typically above 1,500m. Also montane and hill forests nearer the coast where it is occasionally recorded to near sea level.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Contact call is a high-pitched hissing; song is a high-pitched and complex jumble of twitters and squeaks.

images.caption: Grey Cuckooshrike · Plate 155

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is olive-green above with obvious creamy-yellow spots on wing-coverts and secondaries; underparts are pale grey-brown to whitish with a yellowish vent. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common but very difficult to see, inhabiting forest, patches of woodland and other dense cover in the east, from sea level to 1,900m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very vocal, invariably from dense cover, with a loud song that starts hesitantly with yu-ik-wit-wer-trrr and bubbles into a jumbled cho-chou-choou-chueeee. Call is a repeated sharp tuk.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Yellow-spotted Nicator

images.caption: Eastern Nicator · Plate 155

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slim brownish bird with a blackish head (may show slight crest), brown breast, pale belly and bright yellow vent. Three races occur: tricolor (Dark-capped Bulbul) (Ug to SWTz and CKe) has head and breast plain dark blackish-brown; similar layardi (SKe to ETz and SETz) has a blacker crown and face contrasting with browner back and breast; dodsoni (Dodson’s Bulbul) (N and EKe to NETz) has variably distinct white ear mark and pale feather edgings to neck and breast. Races may hybridise in contact zones.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Extremely common and widespread in virtually all habitats throughout the region from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sings a fairly slow deliberate set of descending notes, accelerating as birds become excited. Also varied chatters given at all times.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities consider race dodsoni as a distinct species.

images.caption: Common Bulbul · Plate 156

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dull olive-green with distinctive bright yellow whiskers at sides of throat (sometimes flattened and appearing yellow-throated); lower breast and belly yellow (not always obvious in field); reddish-brown tail. Immature is all dull olive-brown (similar to Little Greenbul) but bill has orange-yellow base and legs are bright orange-yellow. Widespread nominate race described above, possible race australis (Ufipa Plateau, SWTz) is paler and has a different voice.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common within range, in highland forest, forest strips and wooded gardens at 700–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls and sings throughout day, a dull ramble of chirrup, chup and chop notes, with an occasional burst of higher-pitched chattering; australis is reported to call zik zik zik…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Andropadus.

images.caption: Yellow-whiskered Greenbul · Plate 156

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small totally dull olive greenbul with short rather stout dark bill, dull yellowish-brown legs and reddish-brown tail. Immature is like adult but washed brown above; legs dull yellowish-brown. Three races occur: nominate (Ug to Bu and WKe) as described, zombensis (SEKe to STz) is generally brighter and paler; and zanzibarica (Zanzibar Island) is less yellow below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Patchily distributed, but common in range from sea level to 1,800m (mainly below 1,500m). Prefers thick secondary growth and forest edge where it is very noisy, but solitary and shy.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Persistent songster throughout day, and most musical of the genus, call notes being sweet and pure. After identical introductory chup notes, the song is a fast run of numerous bubbling notes, ending in a complex flourish of chatters and whistles.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Andropadus.

images.caption: Little Greenbul · Plate 156

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive slim greenbul with plain olive upperparts and pale grey underparts; bill is comparatively slender. Two races occur: nominate (Ug to WKe) is olive-brown above; percivali (CKe) has olive-green upperparts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in forest and forest edge canopy, often in fruiting trees, at 700–2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Noisy; commonest call is an upslur followed by a more tremulous downslurred sweeyu. The rarely heard song is a subdued and varied chattering.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Andropadus.

images.caption: Slender-billed Greenbul · Plate 156

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather plain olive-brown greenbul with obvious creamy-white eyes. Two races occur: widespread insularis is yellowish-olive below (with brownish wash to throat and flanks); hypoxanthus (SETz) is greener above and yellower below. Immature similar, but has dark eyes and small yellowish eye-ring.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common throughout coastal region, and rather less common in central Kenya highlands to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls throughout day from bush tops or telephone wires, a fast rising and falling series of cheerful notes with quality of Common Bulbul.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Zanzibar Sombre Greenbul

images.caption: Sombre Greenbul · Plate 156

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A grey-headed greenbul with a small broken eye-ring, fine whitish lines on ear-coverts, olive-green upperparts and variable grey or yellowish-green underparts. Three races occur: distinctive kikuyuensis (Olive-breasted Mountain Greenbul) in WUg, Rw, Bu and CKe has plain grey head and throat, and yellow-green underparts; nominate (SKe to NTz) has blackish crown and mostly grey underparts; usambarae (NETz) has black superciliary stripes and mostly grey underparts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in highland forest and nearby secondary growth, at 1,350–3,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a deep throaty delivery of clear notes, most phrases rising, some with cat-like calls. Calls include a grating churr. Race nigriceps also gives a repeated nasal ewat-ekeek.

images.caption: Eastern Mountain Greenbul · Plate 157

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Fairly large greenbul, olive-green above and olive-yellow below (bright in sunlight) with white-streaked dark ear-coverts and usually pale eyes. Two races occur: nominate (SEKe to Udzungwa Mts, Tz) as described; olivaceiceps (Mt Rungwe area, STz), which is sometimes considered to be a separate species (Olive-headed Greenbul), is duller, darker above and greener below with brownish eyes. Immature duller with little streaking on sides of face.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a variety of forest types at 150–1,850m, but mainly in highlands. Most frequent in midstorey and canopy.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song has same deep throaty quality of Eastern Mountain Greenbul, but with a slow and deliberate delivery that varies locally. Common call is a rapid monotonous wikawikawikawika…..wik!

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with extralimital Stripe-cheeked Greenbul A. milanjensis.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Olive-headed Greenbul

images.caption: Stripe-faced Greenbul · Plate 157

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dull olive greenbul with narrow broken whitish eye-ring and no obvious contrast between crown and nape with rest of upperparts; underparts paler dull olive with slightly contrasting grey-olive throat. Eyes red-brown, legs blue-grey or dull greenish. Two races occur: nominate (Mt Rungwe, SWTz) as described; roehli (NE to STz) is similar but has greyer sides to head, and paler greyer throat. Race roehli does not forage on tree trunks.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are fairly common in forest interior (mainly in highlands) at 500–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a diagnostic high upslurred qui-qui-qui-qui…, similar to a slowed-down version of Red-throated Wryneck.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Andropadus and considered conspecific with Kakamega Greenbul.

images.caption: Shelley’s Greenbul · Plate 158

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Quite thickset large greenbul of the south and east. Two races occur: centralis (Ke and ETz) is dark olive above with a darker olive-brown head and ruffled crown (often raised as shaggy crest), obvious white crescent above red-brown eye, yellow underparts, paler on throat; occidentalis (W and STz) is more olive-green above, brighter yellow below with variable paler throat and brownish wash on breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common in all types of thick cover, from sea level to 2,100m (on Mt Kilimanjaro, northern Tanzania).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Basic song is five slow, rather halting, nasal notes, eh… eh…uh…eeh…eh (first two and final note identical, third lower, fourth higher than first), often initiated with rather angry slurred churr calls.

images.caption: Yellow-bellied Greenbul · Plate 158

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Terrestrial Brownbul, but slightly smaller and slimmer; more russet above, with a russet-brown rump and tail; buffy-white throat contrasts slightly with rest of greyish-brown underparts. Eyes brown or reddish-brown; Fischer’s Greenbul has pale eyes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are common in thicker cover within semi-arid areas in the north and east, and also in coastal lowlands from near sea level to about 1,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Parties maintain a continuous rather nasal and pinched chatter from mid-canopy (recalling larger babblers).

images.caption: Northern Brownbul · Plate 159

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small warbler-like greenbul with grey crown, greenish back and wings, and whitish underparts with variable yellowish streaks. Race rabai (coastal Ke and lowland ETz, has mostly grey head contrasting with greenish back, wings and tail; pale greyish-white below with whiter throat and variable yellow streaking on belly. Bill grey, eyes variable but usually creamy-white or yellowish, darker on immature. Nominate (SETz) is similar, but underparts whiter and yellow on belly paler (hard to see in field). Immature has olive-green wash to crown.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are local and uncommon in undergrowth and mid-canopy of coastal forest and woodland from sea level to 450m in Shimba Hills Kenya, and up to 300m in East Usambara Mts, Tanzania. Often joins mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A remarkably loud low-pitched nasal and rhythmical song, including a bubbling trill and urgent na’na’na’ nya-na…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Montane Tiny Greenbul.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Tiny Greenbul

images.caption: Lowland Tiny Greenbul · Plate 159

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A slim, slender-billed greenbul with greenish-olive or olive-brown upperparts and a creamy-yellow, or creamy-white, throat. Three races occur: westerly sucosus (Ug, Rw, Bu, NWTz and WKe) is greenish-olive above with a rufous-brown tail; pale-yellow throat and belly contrast with darker olive breast and flanks; nominate (W and SWTz) is similar, but paler yellow on throat and belly. In Ke east of Great Rift Valley, and N, E and STz distinctive race placidus (Placid Greenbul) is dull olive-brown above with a warm russet-brown tail; creamy-white throat contrasts with greyish-olive breast and flanks. Differs from rather similar Grey-olive Greenbul by blue-grey legs and feet (not pale pinkish).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Noisy small flocks occur in a variety of dense undergrowth, mainly in highland forests, but down to 600m in north-eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song starts as low-pitched chatter and breaks into a higher seesawing wii-werr…, a second bird accompanying with regularly spaced growls. Race placidus is similar but grating.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities split the two western races as Cabanis’s Greenbul P. cabanisi, and the eastern race as Placid Greenbul P. placidus.

images.caption: Cabanis’s Greenbul · Plate 160

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Extremely similar to Little Grey Greenbul, including small white eye-ring and gingerish belly and flanks; best identified by olive-grey (not yellow) belly. Two races occur: nominate (SWUg) as described; kavirondensis (WKe) slightly browner above and greyer below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In East Africa known only from the Bwindi-Impenetrable Forest south-western Uganda, and Kakamega Forest, western Kenya, where singles and pairs are common but unobtrusive. Likes to forage in mid-levels and on open branches in lower canopy.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A three-note querulous wee-wer-weet (middle note slightly lower than others) and a harsh rapid trill ritittitititititit.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Andropadus.

images.caption: Ansorge’s Greenbul · Plate 160

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to several other greenbuls with olive upperparts and dull reddish-brown tail; paler olive-grey-green below with slightly browner flanks and yellowish belly (hard to see in field). Slender bill separates from similar Eurillas greenbuls. Sympatric Cabanis’s Greenbul has creamy-yellowish throat and darker olive breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small parties are shy and uncommon, keeping to undergrowth and mid-strata tangled vines within primary forest at 700–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song starts with descending, often paired burry notes, followed by loud descending shreee-shreee-shreee-shreee-shreee, like a scold in response to the first notes.

images.caption: Toro Olive Greenbul · Plate 160

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Drab and nondescript with small greyish-white eye-ring, reddish-brown tail and yellowish belly all similar to several other greenbuls; short bill eliminates Phyllastrephus species. Best identified by grey throat contrasting slightly with darker olive head and breast. Similar Little Greenbul has plain olive underparts. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in undergrowth, lower mid-levels and at fruiting shrubs in primary and secondary forest at 700–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a three-note wit-woo-werrrr, the last slightly falling and tremulous.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Andropadus.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Cameroon Sombre Greenbul

images.caption: Plain Greenbul · Plate 160

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large greenbul, bright yellowish olive-green above and largely yellow below, variably washed greenish on sides of breast and flanks. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common within a patchy range, occurring in noisy active flocks moving through the midstorey and lower canopy of primary and secondary forest at 1,400–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very vocal with a striking and memorable song: proclaims a cheerful and explosive fwit-fwit-fwit… before a rapid and exuberant sequence that ends in a set of squeaky wi-wi-wi-wi-wi-wi-wi… notes.

images.caption: Joyful Greenbul · Plate 162

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dark olive above, with patch of pale blue-grey skin above eye; tail plain red-brown, often obvious in flight. Below mainly yellow, with yellow throat contrasting with more olive breast. Immature russet-brown above with yellowish-green skin around eye; variably washed rufous on sides of breast and flanks. Birds in EA are race woosnami.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common but shy in dense forest undergrowth at 700–2,150m. Usually seen alone or in pairs foraging along quiet trails at dawn and dusk; often attends ant swarms.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Vocal throughout day, song typically involves long, low tremulous whistles run together, either descending or ascending. Alarm is a loud rapid and continuous tip-tip-tip-tip.

images.caption: Red-tailed Bristlebill · Plate 162

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large, dull and olive-grey-brown above with contrasting pale creamy-yellow throat. Eyes vary from dark to dull yellowish, or pale greyish. Often looks rather dishevelled. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are common and noisy in a variety of thick undergrowth including along wooded streams, thickets and overgrown cultivation, at 900–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varies locally, but typically sings a rather excitable babbler-like chattering, commonly made in flight.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with West African Yellow-throated Greenbul (or Yellow-throated Leaflove) Chlorocichla flavicollis, but now regarded as specifically distinct and both forms placed in the genus Atimastillas.

images.caption: Pale-throated Greenbul · Plate 163

pogonocichla-stellata.ref: Plate 164: Small Robins And Akalats I
pogonocichla-stellata.name: White-starred Robin

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Seven very similar races, varying slightly in size and tone: typical adult has a slate-blue head, greenish back and bright yellow underparts; tail yellow with black central feathers and terminal band. White spot in front of eye and on breast are often concealed. Only race elgonensis (Mt Elgon, Ug and Ke) differs markedly in having an almost plain black tail. Immature is olive-green above, dull yellow below, tail pattern as adult but duller. Juvenile is dark olive above with pale spotting, underparts yellow with bold scaly black markings.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common but rather shy, in undergrowth of highland forest and bamboo usually above 1,600m, but down to 300m in eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varies racially and often mimics, but strong song is typically six rising then falling whistles (more frequently heard subsong is similar but muffled). Call is a seesaw piping pi-pi pi-pi…

images.caption: White-starred Robin · Plate 164

sheppardia-aequatorialis.ref: Plate 164: Small Robins And Akalats I
sheppardia-aequatorialis.name: Equatorial Akalat

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Upperparts olive-brown with slightly more rufous tail; lores and around eye greyish, but difficult to see in dull light of forest undergrowth. Underparts rufous-orange with white belly. Juvenile dark brown above with pale rufous spotting, mottled black and tawny below. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Not uncommon, but a shy resident of undergrowth and mid-levels in highland forest at 1,600–2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Quiet for a forest chat, song is rather like the repeated call of African Scops-Owl, a burry prrru-prrru on the same note.

images.caption: Equatorial Akalat · Plate 164

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Olive-brown above with blue-grey supercilium and wing-coverts; throat, breast and flanks orange-yellow, belly and vent white. Displaying bird may show a white supraloral spot. Juvenile is olive-brown above with pale spots, underparts buff-brown with darker brown scalloping on breast. Two races occur: sokokensis (coastal Ke and Tz below 300m) as described; alticola (Nguu Mts, ETz, above 1,150m) has very little white on belly.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very local and shy akalat of dense forest undergrowth.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Seasonally vocal. Song can be strong or muffled and difficult to pinpoint. After a few piping notes, gives a variable liquid rising and falling werwiderly-widerly…, with all of the notes running into each other and often repeated for long periods.

images.caption: East Coast Akalat · Plate 165

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Five very similar races occur: adults have blackish, dark brown or grey-brown heads contrasting slightly with dark chestnut-brown or dull brown backs and wings. Dull white supercilium can be obscure but usually obvious in front view. Underparts dingy-white, whiter on throat and variably washed grey-brown on breast and flanks. Juveniles are dark brown above with orange spotting, buff and grey below with black fringes to breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in forest at 700– 2,800m, but more typically at higher altitudes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Quiet for an alethe, song is an infrequently heard series of whistled downslurs. Utters harsh notes at ant swarms and a nasal alarm similar to Grey-chested Illadopsis.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Alethe.

images.caption: Brown-chested Alethe · Plate 166

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Paler than most other robin-chats with orange throat and breast contrasting with grey flanks and belly.
