Grey crown, white supercilium and blackish face (not as boldly marked as most robin-chats). Juvenile is brown above with buffy spots, pale brown below with dark scaling. Widespread race iolaema as described, kivuensis (SWUg to SBu) is brighter below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a wide variety of habitats including moorland, forest edge, cultivation and gardens at 1,600–3,400m (occasionally as low as 500m in Tanzania).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A very thrush-like songster, with short varied phrases repeated after brief pauses.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Cossypha.

images.caption: Cape Robin-Chat · Plate 167

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Boldly marked and entirely bright rufous-orange below. Crown and sides of face black with a long white supercilium. Tail rufous-orange, usually with olive-brown central feathers. Juvenile heavily spotted, with less pronounced supercilium and rufous-brown underparts with dark scaling. Two races occur: nominate (widespread) as described, and similar but slightly smaller intermedia (coastal Ke and Tz).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Most widespread robin-chat in the region, common in many habitats from sea level to 2,200m, but avoids forest interior and desert-like country. White-browed prefers lower altitudes and more open habitats than Rüppell’s Robin-Chat.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song variable, but is usually a simple refrain of repeated high notes, followed by lower notes, with each sequence increasing in volume and becoming more rapid and urgent. Alarm call is a loud but wooden takata-kata-kata.

images.caption: White-browed Robin-Chat · Plate 167

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to White-browed Robin-Chat, but tail rufous-orange with blackish central tail feathers. Juvenile similar to juvenile White-browed. Two races occur: intercedens is widespread, and smaller nominate (with more olive upperparts) occurs at Moyale and Marsabit, NKe.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Much more of a highland forest bird than White-browed Robin-Chat, but also occurs in overgrown gardens, at 1,400–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A most accomplished songster. Basic song is a musical warbled, thrush-like refrain given either continuously or in short bursts. Often mimics birds, other small animals and human whistles in its neighbourhood. Sings continuously from cover, particularly before dawn and at dusk, and often repeats a monotonous rrri-pru-ru.

images.caption: Rüppell’s Robin-Chat · Plate 167

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smaller than White-browed Robin-Chat with blacker wings, small bright steel-blue shoulder patches and paler yellow-orange underparts. Tail rufous with a black centre. Juvenile resembles other juvenile robin-chats, but immature quickly gains blue shoulder patch. Birds in EA are race bartteloti.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Generally uncommmon in thick forest undergrowth at 700–2,000m, where it is very shy and difficult to observe.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A most accomplished mimic incorporating human whistles and the sounds of many other forest inhabitants in its song. Picks up refrains very quickly, but lacks the sweetness of Rüppell’s Robin-Chat and tends to ramble.

images.caption: Blue-shouldered Robin-Chat · Plate 167

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large robin-chat with white stripe over crown (can be difficult to see); large black patches on sides of head and rufous collar often more obvious. Mantle and wings slaty; central tail black. Juvenile similar to other juvenile robin-chats but larger. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Not uncommon, but shy in forest, remnant woodland and thickets at 900–2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually heard at dusk, the rapidly delivered strong and varied song has a fluty quality. Birds incorporate much mimicry, but most of the song is their own. Common call is a repeated mournful piping fweeeeo…

images.caption: Snowy-crowned Robin-Chat · Plate 167

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Only robin-chat with a rufous-orange head (sometimes browner on crown); if seen well beady black eyes are conspicuous. Mantle and wings blue-grey, tail rufous with black centre. Juvenile is mottled black and rufous above, paler below with dark scaling. Birds in EA are race intensa.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: A shy but common bird of forest undergrowth and thickets from sea level to 2,200m. Resident and intra-African migrant populations (from the southern tropics) occur, but movements poorly understood. Numerous in the west and coastal regions from May to Nov, while smaller numbers of residents occur in scattered locations throughout the region.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: An accomplished mimic, bouts of singing can last many minutes. Quality is drunken or lazy compared to other robin-chats, notes are slurred and not very pure. Commonest call is a monotonous, distinct and endlessly repeated preeep-prooop.

images.caption: Red-capped Robin-Chat · Plate 168

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small robin-chat with a dark grey crown, white supercilium (finely streaked black) and narrow black eyeline. Wings olive-brown with blue-grey shoulders; tail plain rufous-brown; underparts rufous-orange with whitish belly. Juvenile is brown above with rufous spots, short rufous supercilium, blue-grey patch on wing-coverts, and plain pale rufous underparts. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather local in forest undergrowth and thickets along streams at 1,100–2,150m. Often on the ground in leaf litter, being shy and difficult to observe.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Some local variation and mimicry; songs can be slow sweet refrains or rapid high-pitched and regular musical phrases.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Juvenile plumage and plain tail suggest this species may be an akalat, and then known as Grey-winged Akalat Sheppardia polioptera, but voice (including mimicry) is much more robin-chat like.

images.caption: Grey-winged Robin-Chat · Plate 168

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Six races differ mainly in tone, with those at higher altitudes (particularly on isolated mountains) generally darker than the more widespread nominate form. Nominate adult (throughout Ke highlands, NEUg and NTz) is dark olive-brown or grey-brown above, with an orange bill and small orange eye-ring; greyish-brown breast, and rufous-orange flanks or belly. Other races differ as follows: baraka (Rwenzori Mts, WUg) has streaked throat and lower breast, and tawny belly; bambusicola (SWUg, Rw, Bu) has throat and breast ash-brown; oldeani (Crater Highlands NTz) is darker sooty-grey, flanks grey-brown; deckeni (mainly Tz highlands east of oldeani) is darker than nominate; and nyikae (highlands of E and STz) has dark breast and flanks.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: The most common and widespread thrush in the highlands, occupying a wide range of habitats including heath, forest edge, gardens and cultivation, at 1,500–3,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song consists of short typical thrush-like phrases followed by a pause, each phrase ends with a short series of repeated subdued notes like an echo.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Olive Thrush T. olivaceus of southern Africa.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Mountain Thrush

images.caption: Abyssinian Thrush · Plate 169

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very dark above, with virtually black head and breast, bright red-orange bill and eye-ring; lower breast to vent white with bright rufous flanks. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to the Taita Hills, south-eastern Kenya, where it is rare and confined to the interior of tiny remnant forest patches. Shy and feeds amongst leaf litter.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sings from concealed mid-level perches. Much richer and slower than Abyssinian Thrush, with similar very quiet hissed notes ending each phrase.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Abyssinian Thrush. CR

images.caption: Taita Thrush · Plate 169

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Abyssinian Thrush, but paler with pale yellow-orange bill and lightly streaked throat. Two races occur: centralis (Ug and WKe) has pale ashy-brown breast, with pale buff-orange sides and flanks; graueri (Rw, Bu and WTz) is browner above with orange flanks and belly.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Largely replaces Abyssinian Thrush in the west, being common and widespread in forest edge, thickets, gardens and cultivation. In areas of overlap with Abyssinian Thrush, African occupies lower altitudes, but can reach 2,000m where Abyssinian is absent.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: More varied than Abyssinian Thrush, with a completely different structure of various repeated phrases given for long periods without pause, and no softer terminal calls. May mimic other birds.

images.caption: African Thrush · Plate 169

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Grey above, with an orange bill, diamond-shaped patch of bare orange-yellow skin around eye and white throat strongly streaked black; breast grey, lower breast and flanks rufous. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common but retiring resident of generally drier areas including coastal scrub, riverine vegetation and wooded bushland from sea level to 1,750m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is similar, but louder and slower than Abyssinian Thrush, incorporating a diagnostic rapid bubbly pi-pu pi-pu pi-pu which has a peculiar nasal quality, and is also given in alarm.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: African Bare-eyed Thrush

images.caption: Bare-eyed Thrush · Plate 169

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Orange Ground-Thrush, but has a large white eye-ring and orange-brown forecrown (and crown in the west); upperparts warmer russet-brown. Five similar races differ mainly in tone. Most distinct race tanganjicae (Kivu Ground-Thrush) is brighter, with entirely orange-brown crown and nape.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread in forested highlands across N, W and central Kenya, and Nguruman Forest in southern Kenya. Abyssinian overlaps with Orange Ground-Thrush on Mt Kenya but occurs mainly above 2,300m, Orange below 2,000m. Occurs in Tanzania on Kilimanjaro, Loliondo and Magaidu; in Uganda separate populations on Rwenzori Mts (western Uganda), Mt Moroto (north-eastern Uganda) and distinctive tanganjicae occurs at 1,500–2,900m in south-western Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is similar to Abyssinian Thrush, but richer and flutier, albeit not usually as rich and varied as Orange Ground-Thrush. Race tanganjicae sings melodic, slow, loud and deliberate notes, with a fluty delivery.

images.caption: Abyssinian Ground-Thrush · Plate 170

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Abyssinian Ground-Thrush, but has a narrower broken white eye-ring, olive-brown crown and forecrown, indication of dark mark below eye and greyish patch on ear-coverts. Three similar races occur: chuka is slightly larger with olive-brown upperparts (Mt Kenya and south Aberdares, CKe); raineyi slightly smaller and paler (Taita and Chyulu Hills in SEKe, and NTz); and otomitra (E and SWTz) is similar to chuka but slightly smaller and more grey-brown above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Only ground-thrush in much of Tanzania, from 450m in the East Usambara Mts to 2,400m on Mt Meru. In Kenya it occurs on Mrima Hill in SE (at only 300m), in the Chyulu and Taita Hills, and on the wetter N, E and S slopes of Mt Kenya below 2,000m. Overlaps with Abyssinian Ground-Thrush at Kieni Forest, central Kenya, but is rare there.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Musical fluty song is slower than that of Abyssinian Ground-Thrush, and some phrases are identical to those of Taita Thrush.

images.caption: Orange Ground-Thrush · Plate 170

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dark brown above with a blackish tail, broadly tipped white on outer corners (not obvious when perched); in flight, shows broad rufous wingbar. In WKe typically dull and dark below, but birds in Ug, Rw and Bu have brighter rufous underparts and are very similar to Red-tailed Ant-Thrush if white tail corners not seen. Birds in EA are race praepectoralis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Shy, but locally common in forest undergrowth at 700–2,520m (often on ground near ant swarms).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Commonest call is a loud spitted tuneless trtttt, often given in flight and followed by a single rising or falling downslur.

images.caption: White-tailed Ant-Thrush · Plate 171

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rich rufous ant-thrush with slightly duller brown head and mantle, and rufous-brown tail (slightly darker in centre). Very similar to Rufous Flycatcher-Thrush, but has more typical thrush-like horizontal stance, smaller rounded head and longer bill. Immature is like adult but duller. Two races occur: gabunensis (WUg) has grey on breast, and nominate (coastal Ke and Tz) is plain rufous below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Two widely separated populations in forest undergrowth from sea level to 900m in the east, and 700–1,400m in the west.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Western and coastal birds differ: in the west, the call is a sharp crack followed by several rising and falling whistles, ending in a chatter; coastal birds give a ratchet-like trrrt, often followed by a long falling whistle fweeeeeee.

images.caption: Red-tailed Ant-Thrush · Plate 171

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Olive-brown above with vertical black bands through eye and ear-coverts; white spots on wing-coverts form two bars; underparts white with heavy black spots. Sexes alike. Birds in EA are race fischeri.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Uncommon intra-African migrant from the south to coastal Kenya and north-eastern Tanzania, but only regular at Gede and Arabuko-Sokoke in Mar–Oct. Small population breeds on Rondo Plateau, southern Tanzania. Solitary, feeds in leaf litter where hard to see in dappled forest light.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Loud, melodic and varied song, but migrants are usually silent, possibly uttering a thin whistle.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Zoothera. EN

images.caption: Spotted Ground-Thrush · Plate 172

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has head, throat and upper mantle blue-grey with a white patch on the back, rest of underparts orange-red; tail orange-red with darker central feathers. Non-breeding male is mottled and scaly all over with a rufous tail and some rusty feathers on flanks. Female and first-winter similar to non-breeding male, but generally browner, rufous limited mainly to tail, but lower underparts also washed pale rufous. Longer-billed and shorter-tailed than other rock-thrushes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread Palearctic passage migrant and winter visitor in Oct–Apr. Favours open woodland, bush and sparsely vegetated semi-arid country, where they perch upright and are conspicuous.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Silent and unlikely to sing in EA, but may utter a soft tak.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Common Rock-Thrush

images.caption: Rufous-tailed Rock-Thrush · Plate 172

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smaller, slimmer and longer-tailed than Rufous-tailed Rock-Thrush; like a small robin-chat. Adult male is brownish-grey above, without white back of Rufous-tailed and with blue-grey extending over head onto upper breast. Bold blackish central tail and tips form distinctive inverted ‘T’. Miombo Rock-Thrush has rufous upper breast and totally different range. Female is duller and paler than male. Immature is spotted buff above, scaly blackish on buff below. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs occur patchily within range, on rocky escarpments and in broken hill country with some trees.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sings from tops of small trees, a simple but sweet thrush-like refrain, ending each phrase with a double zi-zit, rather like ‘is-it’ at the end of a sentence.

images.caption: Little Rock-Thrush · Plate 172

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Appears all dark brown when perched, but large whitish patches in primaries are obvious in flight. Sexes alike. Immature is slightly scaly on throat and breast. Race in EA is cryptoleuca.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family groups are common in open country and farmland mainly above 1,500m, often on the ground or perching on low bushes, fences and termite mounds.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Loud, rolling and musical but rather monotonous song repeated at length with little variation (several birds may sing together).

images.caption: Northern Anteater Chat · Plate 173

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to Northern Anteater Chat but much blacker with white wing patch confined to the shoulder (not primaries). Immature male is like dull adult male. Adult and immature females are sooty-brown without white in wings. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in lightly wooded grasslands from sea level to 1,700m, mainly west and south of Northern Anteater Chat.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Much more melodic and varied than Northern Anteater Chat, often with mimicry in long refrains, and regularly given in a parachuting song flight.

images.caption: Sooty Chat · Plate 173

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is an attractive black and rufous chat with white shoulder patch and narrow whitish breast-band. Adult female has similar basic pattern, but is grey and rufous without any white. Immature is dull version of adult. Race in EA is subrufipennis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are widespread, but patchily distributed, frequenting rocky gorges and hillsides at 600–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Complex song with much local variation is long, rambling and rather thrush-like, but notes are more spitted out and interspersed with sweet warbling and flourishes recalling song of White-throated Robin; frequently amplified by rocky gorge habitat.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Myrmecocichla.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Cliff Chat

images.caption: Mocking Cliff Chat · Plate 173

saxicola-torquatus.ref: Plate 174: Open-Country Chats And African Wheatears
saxicola-torquatus.name: African Stonechat

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Four races occur: typical adult male has a black head and throat, chestnut or black on breast (varying in size), white patches on sides of neck, wings and rump, and blackish tail. Adult female is streaked brown and buff with indistinct supercilium and white wing stripe; brown throat contrasts slightly with pale rufous-brown breast. Immature is like female but duller. In race axillaris (widespread, most of Ug, Rw, Bu, Ke and Tz) male has deep chestnut breast patch; promiscuus (ETz) has a paler breast patch; stonei (SWTz) has extensive pale chestnut underparts; and distinctive albofasciatus (NEUg) is entirely black and white (with no rufous).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and common at 500–3,200m, generally in highlands, but at lower altitudes and in marshes in Tanzania. Perches in open on fence posts, tree stumps and small bushes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Attractive, repeated, short scratchy warbling may be sung for long periods without much variation.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities consider all of these races to be conspecific with Common Stonechat S. rubicola.

images.caption: African Stonechat · Plate 174

saxicola-rubetra.ref: Plate 174: Open-Country Chats And African Wheatears
saxicola-rubetra.name: Whinchat

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has distinctive long white supercilium and blackish ear-coverts; washed buffy-orange below, with small white patches on wing-coverts and white sides at base of tail. Non-breeding male, female and first-winter resemble female African Stonechat; best distinguished by well-defined buffy supercilium and white base to outer tail. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Palearctic passage migrant, in Oct–Apr, which can be common in the west. Perches on small bushes and trees in grassland and cultivated areas.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent, but may sing occasionally, similar to African Stonechat. AFRICAN WHEATEARS Medium-sized chat-like birds mostly with white or buffy rumps and an inverted black ‘T’ on the tail. Mainly ground-dwelling in open country.

images.caption: Whinchat · Plate 174

oenanthe-pileata.ref: Plate 174: Open-Country Chats And African Wheatears
oenanthe-pileata.name: Capped Wheatear

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has a narrow white band on forecrown, white supercilium, white throat and broad black breast-band. Immature is similar to female Northern Wheatear but spotted buff above and washed yellow-brown with darker brown mottling below. Birds in EA are race livingstonii.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread on short grassy plains mainly above 1,400m, but migrants may occur down to 450m. Stands very upright, often on fence posts and other low sites.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a mix of harsh and sweet notes in short bursts, often with mimicry, and sometimes in a low song flight. Alarm call is a muffled tik.

images.caption: Capped Wheatear · Plate 174

oenanthe-lugubris.ref: Plate 174: Open-Country Chats And African Wheatears
oenanthe-lugubris.name: Abyssinian Wheatear

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is blackish with pale dingy grey-brown crown, white belly and unique cinnamon-buff rump and undertail; tail orange-buff with inverted black ‘T’. Female has rump and tail similar to male, rest of plumage mostly dark brown with whitish lower breast and belly. Immature is like dull female with buff speckles. Two races occur: schalowi (as described) is endemic to Rift Valley area of CKe and NTz; nominate, on Mt Kulal, NKe, has buffy-white in outer tail.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are fond of rocky hillsides with some grass and scattered bushes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song comprises short bursts of identical muffled but sweet refrains.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Taxonomy unresolved with some authorities considering this species as conspecific with extralimital Mourning Wheatear O. lugens, whereas others consider race schalowi to be a separate species, Schalow’s Wheatear O. schalowi.

images.caption: Abyssinian Wheatear · Plate 174

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is distinctive with grey crown, nape and mantle, broad black mask and black wings, and buffy throat and breast. Terminal tail-band broader than Pied and Black-eared Wheatears. Female and non-breeding male are earth-brown above, with pale supercilium and buffy underparts. In flight, dark wings contrast strongly with paler brown mantle and white rump. First-winter has buffy wing edges like Isabelline Wheatear, but tail-band always narrower. Two similar races occur: nominate as described, male libanotica has a whiter supercilium, paler grey upperparts and less buff on throat and breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread passage migrant and winter visitor to a wide range of open habitats in Sep–Apr.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent, but may sing before departing EA a mix of rapid scratchy and sweet notes. Alarm call is an oft-repeated tchak…

images.caption: Northern Wheatear · Plate 175

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to female Northern Wheatear but often stands very upright and is slightly larger, stronger-billed and generally paler with pearly-buff underparts. Supercilium whiter in front of eye (whiter behind it in female Northern). Wings have broad buffy feather edges and in flight appear more or less uniform with mantle; dark alula often conspicuous on closed wing. Terminal tail-band broader than in Northern. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common passage migrant and winter visitor in Oct–Mar, generally preferring dry country, but can turn up in any open area within wintering range.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent; but song consists of a complex warble of scratchy and nasal twanging. Call is a harsh tchak…

images.caption: Isabelline Wheatear · Plate 175

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Only black-and-white white-rumped wheatear likely to be seen. Breeding male has black on face, upper breast, mantle and wings, with crown and nape white or silvery-grey in fresh plumage, and narrow terminal tail-band (sometimes broad). Breeding female is cold earth-brown above with buffy supercilium and warmer cheeks. Fresh-plumaged birds in Oct are like female, but dark grey-brown is finely scaled and blackish wings have prominent pale fringes; male is dark-faced with pinkish-brown on breast. An uncommon white-throated form ‘vittata’ also occurs. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common winter visitor with a preference for dry country; often perches on small bushes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent in EA, but song is a short sweet refrain interspersed with harsh chak notes. Call is a soft, muffled chat repeated frequently.

images.caption: Pied Wheatear · Plate 175

luscinia-megarhynchos.ref: Plate 176: Migrant Nightingales, Chats And Scrub-Robin
luscinia-megarhynchos.name: Common Nightingale

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Unstreaked rufous-brown chat with warm rufous rump and tail. Differs from very similar Thrush Nightingale in plain underparts (not mottled) and stronger contrast between rump and tail and rest of upperparts. Three races occur and differ mainly in colour of upperparts: nominate (mainly western) is mostly warm rufous-brown above; africana (mainly central) is duller brown on back and wings, and golzii (mainly coastal) is colder brown-grey above, with rufous restricted to rump and tail. All have dark eyes and narrow whitish eye-ring. Sexes alike. First-winter is like adult but has pale tips to tertials and wing-coverts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic migrant and winter visitor mainly across Uganda and Kenya. Wintering birds (Oct–Apr) occur in similar habitat to Thrush Nightingale.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a loud and harsh tk-tk-trrrrrrk (like running a stick along a fence), but also utters a muffled tuk tuk in alarm, and a strong whistled wheet at dawn or as a prelude to song. Song is a loud complex warble of mainly sweet notes, with a pause between each sequence.

images.caption: Common Nightingale · Plate 176

luscinia-luscinia.ref: Plate 176: Migrant Nightingales, Chats And Scrub-Robin
luscinia-luscinia.name: Thrush Nightingale

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Common Nightingale but generally duller brown above with less contrasting rump and tail. Dingy pale grey-brown below with variable mottling on breast, faint malar stripe and whiter throat; smudgy spots on undertail-coverts diagnostic if present. Sexes alike. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic migrant in Oct–Dec and Mar–Apr, preferring thickets and leafy bush country below 1,500m, mainly east of the Rift Valley (but more widespread in southern Tanzania). Small numbers winter in E and central Kenya and south-western Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Two frequent calls (similar in Common Nightingale) are a whistled weeep and harsh takk. Often sings a loud rather strident musical refrain of sweet and harsh notes, continuing for long periods without pause (not as pure or disjointed as Common Nightingale). Also lacks slow introductory whistles, but song ends in a rising series of dry tocky-tock-tock notes. [Alt. Sprosser] MIGRANT CHATS AND SCRUB-ROBIN Rufous-tailed Scrub-Robin is the only migrant scrub-robin and closely related to the species on Plate 177. The other two species here are grey, black and rufous migrant chats from the Palearctic.

images.caption: Thrush Nightingale · Plate 176

irania-gutturalis.ref: Plate 176: Migrant Nightingales, Chats And Scrub-Robin
irania-gutturalis.name: White-throated Robin

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is boldly marked: blue-grey above with all-black tail contrasting with black-and-white head pattern and rich rufous-orange breast. Female is rather plain grey-brown above with blackish tail, whitish throat, scaly buff and grey breast, and flanks washed pale rufous-orange. First-winter is like female, but has browner wings and lightly spotted greater coverts. Black tail is obvious when birds fly into cover. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather scarce and local Palearctic migrant to thickets, dense bush and gullies at 500–1,400m in eastern Kenya and Tanzania, where easily overlooked.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sings regularly from Feb until departure, a loud musical warble, not unlike a speeded-up version of Thrush Nightingale. Alarm is a throaty trrrr (similar to but quieter than Common Nightingale).

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Irania

images.caption: White-throated Robin · Plate 176

phoenicurus-phoenicurus.ref: Plate 176: Migrant Nightingales, Chats And Scrub-Robin
phoenicurus-phoenicurus.name: Common Redstart

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Male in Jan–Apr is grey above with white forehead, black face, bright orange-red underparts and bright rufous tail with dark brown centre; in Oct–Dec has pale fringes on head and breast giving frosty, mottled appearance. Female is grey-brown above with a narrow pale eye-ring, buffy below with paler throat and buffy-orange breast; tail as male. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Reasonably regular Palearctic visitor to northern Uganda and north-western Kenya in Oct–Apr, favouring wooded areas and thickets. Slim with quick movements and often first noticed when it flashes rufous tail.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent, but occasionally calls a soft tik.

images.caption: Common Redstart · Plate 176

cercotrichas-galactotes.ref: Plate 176: Migrant Nightingales, Chats And Scrub-Robin
cercotrichas-galactotes.name: Rufous-tailed Scrub-Robin

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Brown above with dark eyestripe and long off-white supercilium, no bold white pattern in wing, rufous rump and tail broadly tipped black and white (most visible when tail cocked and spread); pale unstreaked underparts. Sexes alike. Birds in EA are race familiaris.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic winter visitor in Nov–Apr, mainly below 1,000m in dry bush country in the north and east.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent, but may call a quiet and hesitant seeep.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Rufous Bush Chat, Rufous Scrub Robin

images.caption: Rufous-tailed Scrub-Robin · Plate 176

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Six races in two distinct groups: white-winged forms inhabit drier areas mainly to the north and east, and red-backed forms are found in higher country and wetter coastal Ke. White-winged forms (White-winged Scrub-Robin) are typically paler-backed, with a lighter streaked breast, greyer crown and nape, earth-brown mantle, and broad white edges to wing-coverts and inner secondaries forming large white patches. Red-backed forms (Red-backed Scrub-Robin) are darker-crowned with white edges to wing-coverts often forming two bars, and heavily streaked underparts. All races have rufous rump and mainly rufous tail with blackish subterminal spots and white tips.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a wide variety of habitats (except forest and barren desert) from sea level to 2,200m. Often keeps to cover unless singing, when displays repeatedly from bush tops.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: An accomplished and persistent songster which varies locally and individually; the usual song consists of loud phrases repeated over and over again, with or without modification.

images.caption: White-browed Scrub-Robin · Plate 177

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to White-browed Scrub-Robin, but has darker brown crown and back, dark- brown wings edged white on greater and lesser coverts forming two bars. Whitish underparts lightly streaked grey-brown; lower rump and tail rufous with broad blackish subterminal band and white tips. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are patchily distributed, being more common in the west, in forest edge, open wooded or bush country with long grass and edges of cultivation, at 900–2,200m. Sings from bush tops, but otherwise shy and retiring.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is sweeter than that of White-browed Scrub- Robin, but lacks the variety of phrases.

images.caption: Brown-backed Scrub-Robin · Plate 177

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather plain olive-brown above with bold face pattern, pale buffy-orange breast and flanks, white wing flashes, warm rufous rump and blackish-brown tail with white tips. Two races occur: nominate (as described) is widespread in the east, greenwayi (Mafia and Zanzibar Islands, Tz) is greyer above and very pale below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Often shy and difficult to observe, keeping to thick cover in forest, wooded valleys and thick scrub from sea level to 1,000m (occasionally 1,800m).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A persistent singer, particularly at dawn and dusk, with pleasant and varied whistles, and often repeating favoured phrases. Alarm is a harsh chrrrt.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Eastern Bearded Scrub-Robin

images.caption: Bearded Scrub-Robin · Plate 177

cichladusa-guttata.ref: Plate 178: Palm-Thrushes And Dull Resident Chats
cichladusa-guttata.name: Spotted Palm-thrush

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Uniform brown or rich brown above with white supercilium and rufous-brown rump and tail. Whitish below with black malar stripe extending as spots on breast and elongated streaks on flanks. Immature duller. Three similar races occur: nominate (Ug and NWKe) as described; intercalans (CKe to CTz) is more heavily spotted below; rufipennis (EKe to NETz) has smaller breast spots.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common and widespread in coastal thickets, wooded grasslands and semi-arid bush, often feeding on the ground in vicinity of cover.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Characteristic song of dry scrub, given throughout day and on moonlit nights. Flutier than scrub-robins, almost thrush-like, usually consists of short repeated or alternating phrases, with some mimicry.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Spotted Morning-Thrush

images.caption: Spotted Palm-thrush · Plate 178

cichladusa-arquata.ref: Plate 178: Palm-Thrushes And Dull Resident Chats
cichladusa-arquata.name: Collared Palm-thrush

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Mostly warm russet-brown above with pale cream eyes; creamy-white throat bordered by narrow black bib; sides of neck, breast and flanks grey, grading to pale rufous vent. Immature lacks black collar, and is variably streaked above and below with black and brown. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are rather shy and associated with palms and nearby undergrowth, being common in some coastal areas, and patchily distributed in suitable habitat in the west.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: May sing for long periods; song is similar to Spotted Palm-thrush, but more varied and scratchy. DULL RESIDENT CHATS Tame, subdued, dull-plumaged chats which frequently flick their wings after landing or while foraging on the ground. Sexes alike. All three species were formerly in the genus Cercomela.

images.caption: Collared Palm-thrush · Plate 178

oenanthe-familiaris.ref: Plate 178: Palm-Thrushes And Dull Resident Chats
oenanthe-familiaris.name: Familiar Chat

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather uniform drab brown chat with rufous rump and outer tail; central tail and terminal band blackish, forming inverted ‘T’. Ear-coverts tinged rufous; narrow white eye-ring; throat and breast paler grey-brown. Immature is spotted buff above, mottled buff and dark brown below. Two similar races occur: falkensteini (SUg and Tz) as described; omoensis (NEUg and NWKe) is slightly darker.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are local away from southern part of range, in open woods and bush country often in rocky areas.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sings from bush tops, a tuneless scratchy warble incorporating its call, a repeated wii cha-cha.

images.caption: Familiar Chat · Plate 178

oenanthe-scotocerca.ref: Plate 178: Palm-Thrushes And Dull Resident Chats
oenanthe-scotocerca.name: Brown-tailed Chat

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Familiar Chat but no rufous in plumage except for slightly warm-brown ear-coverts (only visible at close range). Recalls Grey Flycatcher, but typically has more horizontal chat-like posture and distinctive habit of flicking wings on landing. Immature like adult. Birds in EA are race turkana.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local in rocky semi-arid bush country where it feeds among boulders and sings from dry acacia bushes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Repeated wispy song starts wip, followed immediately by a burry rolling liquid shrerererererereep.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Brown-tailed Rock Chat

images.caption: Brown-tailed Chat · Plate 178

pinarochroa-sordida.ref: Plate 178: Palm-Thrushes And Dull Resident Chats
pinarochroa-sordida.name: Moorland Chat

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dumpy, short-tailed chat with a wheatear-like tail pattern (white sides and inverted black ‘T’ shape). Three similar races occur: ernesti (Ug and Ke) is dark brown above and buffy-brown below; hypospodia (Mt Kilimanjaro, Tz) has darker crown and greyer underparts; and olimotienis (Crater Highlands, Tz) is intermediate. Immature is lightly scaled above, speckled below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in giant heather and on moorland above treeline, occasionally occurring lower along vehicle tracks or in forest clearings. Tame and inquisitive, hopping on ground and perching on low vegetation.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a formless and unattractive series of various sparrow-like chirps, interspersed with squeaks.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Alpine Chat

images.caption: Moorland Chat · Plate 178

iduna-natalensis.ref: Plate 179: Yellow And Acrocephalus Warblers I
iduna-natalensis.name: African Yellow Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two races occur: adult massaica (widespread) is olive-brown above with darker blackish-brown crown (rear may appear slightly crested), yellow supraloral stripe and all-yellow underparts; nominate race (STz) has crown only slightly darker than mantle. Immature is tawny-brown above and yellow below with tawny wash.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are widespread, inhabiting undergrowth and dense vegetation, often near water at 800–2,300m. Sings frequently from cover, but also on exposed perches at dawn.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varied song commonly begins with a few chips and continues with either a rather urgent tp…wi-chi-wi-chi-wi-chi-wi-chi or a nasal weeeez.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Dark-capped Yellow Warbler

images.caption: African Yellow Warbler · Plate 179

iduna-similis.ref: Plate 179: Yellow And Acrocephalus Warblers I
iduna-similis.name: Mountain Yellow Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is similar to African Yellow Warbler but uniform olive-green above including crown. Immature slightly darker above and more buffy below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in forest and bamboo at higher altitudes, 1,800–3,400m. Rather active, climbing around in middle and lower levels of any forest vegetation, singing from within cover and while on the move.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Beautiful songster, with a long, varied, sweet and repeated refrain characteristic of the bamboo zone. Phrases begin wee-weeu before breaking into a medley of chips and flourishes with twanging notes.

images.caption: Mountain Yellow Warbler · Plate 179

acrocephalus-gracilirostris.ref: Plate 179: Yellow And Acrocephalus Warblers I
acrocephalus-gracilirostris.name: Lesser Swamp Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Typical Acrocephalus warbler: size midway between Greater Swamp Warbler and African Reed Warbler. Three races all have long thin bills and whitish throats contrasting with darker breasts and flanks; wings more rounded (shorter primary projection) than Basra Reed Warbler. Race jacksoni (Ug to WKe) is greyish-brown above and below, with whiter belly; parvus (CKe to NTz highlands) is tawny-brown above with slightly rufous rump and greyish-brown breast and flanks; leptorhynchus (EKe and ETz lowlands) is tawny above, with brighter rufous rump and paler tawny-buff breast and flanks. All have short pale supercilium and dark grey legs.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common, widespread resident of waterside vegetation, reedbeds and papyrus.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Loud, frequent and fluid songster mixing melodious phrases with subdued chattering. Commonest calls include a seesawing and rapidly delivered interrogatory wee-ter-ree-ter-ree-ter-reet.

images.caption: Lesser Swamp Warbler · Plate 179

acrocephalus-rufescens.ref: Plate 179: Yellow And Acrocephalus Warblers I
acrocephalus-rufescens.name: Greater Swamp Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger than Lesser Swamp Warbler and more uniform darker earth-brown above (albeit slightly tinged rufous on rump); whitish throat blends gradually into grey-brown underparts. Bill noticeably large and strong; short indistinct supercilium, and greyish legs. Birds in EA are race ansorgei.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common resident within range, inhabiting papyrus swamps at 600–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Unlike any other Acrocephalus, the slow deliberate song is a deep, gravelly and rhythmic wer-ker-chi-chuk-chuk-chuk-chuk-chuk, regularly interrupted by erk notes and a liquid donk, or variations.

images.caption: Greater Swamp Warbler · Plate 179

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: In EA, race fuscus is grey-brown above, with grey-olive tones to head and nape; whitish underparts. Extremely similar to Marsh Warbler, but has slightly rufous-washed rump and whiter underparts. Some individuals are warmer brown above with more russet tones to rump, and whitish below with buffy-brown sides to breast and flanks. Head appears flat-topped (not rounded). Legs usually dark brownish.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Palearctic winter visitor in Oct–Apr which is widespread (but only common west of the Rift Valley) and inhabits thickets, bush, rank vegetation and cultivation.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Classic Acrocephalus song is given for long periods without pause: most notes rather scratchy, twangy and unmusical. Alarm is a repeated harsh burry cherrr.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities consider Eurasian Reed and African Reed Warblers to be conspecific, and call them Common Reed Warbler A. scirpaceus.

images.caption: Eurasian Reed Warbler · Plate 180

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Extremely similar to Eurasian Reed Warbler, but uniform cold olive-brown above and whitish below with buffy-yellow tinge; plumper with more rounded head and slightly shorter bill than Eurasian Reed. Legs pale pinkish-brown (but can be dark in first-year). Both species have short pale supercilium and small eye-ring. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common Palearctic migrant in Oct–Apr to a variety of bush country and overgrown cultivation, mainly east of the Great Rift Valley; uncommon elsewhere.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Not particularly vocal in EA (but heard from Feb to departure). Full song includes mimicry and is rich and melodic for an Acrocephalus, but still scratchy. Call is a soft tuk.

images.caption: Marsh Warbler · Plate 180

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very large, warm brown above with distinct buffy supercilium, strong bill and long wings. Below whitish with strong tawny-buff wash on sides of breast and flanks. Legs usually pale brownish. The nominate race seems most numerous, but zarudnyi with more greyish-olive upperparts and whiter underparts also occurs.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather local Palearctic winter visitor from Oct to early May, but more numerous in Apr east of the Great Rift Valley. Inhabits rank vegetation and thickets.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is much slower than smaller Acrocephalus, but still typical: a loud, deep scratchy and croaking medley. Call is a single chakk.

images.caption: Great Reed Warbler · Plate 180

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger than Eurasian Reed Warbler but smaller and slimmer than Great Reed Warbler with distinctive long slim bill and long wings. Cold olive-brown above with obvious whitish supercilium above broad dark loral line, and dark tail; white below, faintly washed buff on sides of breast and flanks. Legs grey. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Palearctic visitor in Nov–Apr, mainly in east, but occasionally in the Great Rift Valley, occurring in marshy areas and damp thickets.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: May be heard prior to departure and, while obviously an Acrocephalus song, it is coarse and tuneless with rather similar notes that sound like a protracted scolding. EN

images.caption: Basra Reed Warbler · Plate 180

acrocephalus-schoenobaenus.ref: Plate 181: Acrocephalus, Locustella And Bradypterus Warblers
acrocephalus-schoenobaenus.name: Sedge Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Streaked above with a distinctive bold creamy supercilium, whitish below with buffy-rufous flanks. In flight, shows contrasting uniform rusty-orange rump and dark tail. First-winter may show hint of pale crown-stripe. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic visitor to reedbeds, marshes and lakeside vegetation in Nov–Apr. Wintering birds are most numerous in the west, but there is also a strong and widespread northerly passage in Apr.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Often heard, but typical song is subdued, sweeter and far less scratchy than other small Acrocephalus. Call is a harsh rolling chirrr. LOCUSTELLA WARBLERS Shy brown warblers with rather weak bills, indistinct superciliary stripes, strongly graduated tails and very long undertail-coverts (can be mottled or streaked). Sexes alike. Palearctic migrants, two of them are extremely rare.

images.caption: Sedge Warbler · Plate 181

locustella-fluviatilis.ref: Plate 181: Acrocephalus, Locustella And Bradypterus Warblers
locustella-fluviatilis.name: River Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Cold olive-brown and unstreaked above, with narrow supercilium and diffusely mottled breast; long and conspicuously pale-tipped undertail-coverts appear marbled. Legs pink. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Not uncommon Palearctic passage migrant, Nov–Apr in eastern Kenya, but shy and difficult to observe. Inhabits thick scrub and undergrowth.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rarely heard song is a protracted rattling zri-zri-zri-zri-zri… (like Yellow Bishop); call is a soft irregularly repeated tak.

images.caption: River Warbler · Plate 181

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Four races occur: widespread nominate (SWUg to Bu, Ke, N and NETz) is uniform rufous-brown or dark brown above, with a long buffy supercilium, white throat and belly, and bright warm rufous breast and flanks; cavei (NEUg) is darker; mildbreadi (Rwenzori Mts, WUg) is more richly coloured above; and nyassae (E and STz) duller and paler, with a buffy throat and buff-brown breast. Immature is duller above with yellowish wash to throat and belly.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In undergrowth, forest edge and bracken, mainly above 1,000m (often above 2,000m). Creeps around in thick cover, and usually first located by its loud song, or flash of rufous as it flies. Where sympatric, Evergreen Forest Warbler is in forest interior and Cinnamon Bracken at edge.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varies a little locally, but typical loud song is an introductory wii followed by 3–6 identical explosive spitted notes. Call is a nasal pink.

images.caption: Cinnamon Bracken Warbler · Plate 182

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Fairly uniform grey-brown above (no wing panel) with a short pale supercilium and paler creamy-buff underparts. Outer tail narrowly edged whitish (hard to see in the field). Lower mandible is pale yellowish-horn, easily noticeable as bird is usually seen from below. Legs pinkish, or brownish-grey. Race in EA is elaeica.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread passage migrant and winter visitor from sea level to 1,900m in Oct–Apr. Always on the move, often dips its tail while calling, and is particularly fond of canopy in large acacia trees.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Regularly calls a fairly harsh chk, and also often sings a soft Acrocephalus-like refrain.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly called Olivaceous Warbler Hippolais pallida.

images.caption: Eastern Olivaceous Warbler · Plate 183

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger than Eastern Olivaceous Warbler and greyer above with whitish supercilium; duller white below with pale-buff or buffish-grey flanks. Narrow white edges to longer and much darker tail easily seen (as it is frequently waved or slightly fanned). Wings also darker with pale panel on secondaries when fresh, but less distinct than on Olive-tree Warbler. Lower mandible pinkish; legs pinkish-grey. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Fairly uncommon winter visitor in the east from Nov to early Apr, and occasional in Great Rift Valley on passage. Dry bush country from sea level to 1,200m, tending to keep to cover and occasionally feeds on the ground.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Unlike Eastern Olivaceous Warbler, call is a soft nasal chah-chah-chah…, repeated rapidly and for long periods if agitated.

images.caption: Upcher’s Warbler · Plate 183

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Largest Hippolais warbler; grey-brown above with short narrow whitish supercilium, whitish underparts with variable pale grey wash. Bill noticeably long and strong with yellowish-horn base to lower mandible. Long wings are darker than mantle and in fresh plumage pale-edged secondaries form pale panel. Tail very dark, with narrow white edges to outer feathers. Strong blue-grey legs. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Much less common than Upcher’s Warbler, occurring mostly on passage in Oct–Dec and Mar–Apr, but a few winter in southern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a harsh tak; rarely heard song is Acrocephalus-like, but deeper and more musical, not scratchy.

images.caption: Olive-tree Warbler · Plate 183

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather uniform greyish-brown warbler with an indistinct short buffy supercilium, narrow pale eye-ring and noticeable dark eye; some birds show pale grey patch on sides of neck. Underparts buffy-brown with grey-brown legs. Well-rounded head and short bill distinguish it from similar Hippolais warblers. Two similar races occur: nominate as described; woodwardi is slightly colder, greyer above and paler below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread Palearctic visitor in Oct–Apr (wintering from central Uganda southwards). Occurs in a variety of woodland, from forest edge to lush bush country and gardens, at 800–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a varied continuous warble similar to Eurasian Blackcap, but lacks scratchiness and is more muffled and sweeter. Call is an abrupt and repeated teck.

images.caption: Garden Warbler · Plate 184

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large and rather long-tailed, grey or grey-brown above with narrow whitish wingbars and variable barring below. Adult male is well barred on underparts with distinctive pale yellow eyes. Adult female is browner above and less barred below. First-winter shows only a hint of barring (often restricted to flanks and vent); eyes dark resembling Garden Warbler, but Barred identified by larger size, longer tail and pale-tipped wing-coverts. Both nominate race and merzbacheri occur. Pure merzbacheri are paler and browner above with less barring below, but many are intergrades.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic migrant from Oct to Apr, mainly in north and east. Prefers thick cover in bush country from sea level to 1,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a repeated dry chek-chek-chek, and its seldom-heard song is a rich and varied sweet warbling.

images.caption: Barred Warbler · Plate 184

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is grey-brown above and paler grey below with a striking black cap. Adult female slightly browner above and buffier below, with rusty reddish-brown cap. First-winter similar to female but duller. Two similar widespread races occur: nominate as described and paler dammholzi.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common Palearctic winter visitor, occurring in a wide variety of habitats in Oct–Apr, including scrub and forest edge, but mainly in highlands above 1,600m (from 1,000m in north-eastern Tanzania).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a hard, sometimes rapid tak tak tak; song is a scratchy melodious warble, often heard from Jan until departure. [Alt. Blackcap] PHYLLOLAIS A small pale warbler of Acacia country.

images.caption: Eurasian Blackcap · Plate 184

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very small, slim pale warbler, uniform olive-grey or grey-brown above and pale creamy-yellow below, with very narrow white edges to tail; pink lower mandible and legs obvious in the field. Sexes alike, immature more yellowish below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small groups of 2–6 are common within range at 600–2,000m; usually in acacias where they forage busily in the canopy. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Parties are noisy and frequently call a spitted chittering tit-tit-tit-tit-tit…, which often breaks into a dry trill.

images.caption: Buff-bellied Warbler · Plate 184

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two races occur: widespread acredula is dull olive above and pale yellow below, with a long pale yellow supercilium and dark line through eye. First-winter is greener above and yellower below. Less common race yakutensis is grey-brown above, greyish-white below (no olive or yellow tones) with a whitish supercilium. Both races usually have pale yellowish-brown legs, but dark on some birds. Song is best distinction from Common Chiffchaff.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common Palearctic visitor from late Sep to early May in a wide variety of bush and woodland from sea level to 3,000m. Usually at lower altitudes than Common Chiffchaff.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a silvery descending cadence terminating in a flourish; call is a short interrogatory, disyllabic hooweet which ends abruptly.

images.caption: Willow Warbler · Plate 185

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Extremely similar to Willow Warbler, but has more rounded crown, less distinct supercilium, slightly shorter and darker bill, shorter primary projection and usually very dark legs. Birds in EA are race abietinus with greyish-olive or olive-brown upperparts and whitish or buffy underparts. Only safely separated from Willow Warbler by song.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Generally uncommon Palearctic visitor, mainly to highland forest above 2,000m, in Oct–Apr.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually located by song, its onomatopoeic chiff-chiff-chaff-chiff-chaff… is distinctive and heard from Jan until departure. Call is an upslurred hweet, a little shorter and higher-pitched than Willow Warbler.

images.caption: Common Chiffchaff · Plate 185

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Brightly coloured leaf warbler, with olive-green upperparts, yellow supercilium, sides of face, throat and vent; rest of underparts whitish or very pale grey. Races vary in colour of crown and nape: olive-brown in minullus (Taita Hills, SEKe, south to Uluguru Mts, ETz), orange-brown in johnstoni (Mt Rungwe, STz); ochrogularis (Mahari Mts, WTz) is like johnstoni, but has face and throat washed orange-yellow.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common within range, inhabiting canopy and mid-levels of highland forest at 800–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Some local variation in song which is generally a strong but not particularly sweet, descending and seesawing ter-twi-ter-ter, or twi-te-twi-te-twi-te-twi-te twi. Call is a high-pitched seeu.

images.caption: Yellow-throated Woodland-Warbler · Plate 185

phylloscopus-budongoensis.ref: Plate 186: Phylloscopus Warblers Ii, Hylia And Hemitesia
phylloscopus-budongoensis.name: Uganda Woodland-Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small leaf warbler with olive-green upperparts, a strong white supercilium and narrow black line through eye. Underparts whitish with grey-washed flanks. Immature is washed pale olive on breast and flanks. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Single birds inhabit canopy and mid-levels of primary forest at 1,200–1,900m, where they are constantly on the move and call frequently while feeding.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A short rising and falling series of 4–7 distinct silvery notes si-wi-si-wi-wi-si.

images.caption: Uganda Woodland-Warbler · Plate 186

phylloscopus-umbrovirens.ref: Plate 186: Phylloscopus Warblers Ii, Hylia And Hemitesia
phylloscopus-umbrovirens.name: Brown Woodland-Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: In our area much browner than other leaf warblers with wings and tail edged green. Five races are accepted, but the differences are mostly clinal, and the following three are the most distinctive: widespread mackenzianus is warm brown above with long buffy supercilium and dark eyeline; alpinus (WUg) is similar, but more grey-brown above and greyer on the flanks; fugglescouchmani (Uluguru Mts, ETz) is entirely rich brown below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in many highland forests above 1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Variable and complex song of sweet seesawing notes followed by trills and flourishes, with very brief pause between each phrase.

images.caption: Brown Woodland-Warbler · Plate 186

hylia-prasina.ref: Plate 186: Phylloscopus Warblers Ii, Hylia And Hemitesia
hylia-prasina.name: Green Hylia

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Mostly dark olive-green plumage may suggest a dull warbler. Better views reveal dull olive-green upperparts and grey-green underparts, with a long curved buffy supercilium and short black slightly decurved bill. Immature is darker olive below than adult with yellowish bill. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Fairly common but often overlooked in mid- and higher levels of primary forest at 700–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Extraordinary song is a strong obtrusive ratchet like tr-rr-rt, followed by a long pause of up to four seconds, then two whistled downslurs, feeew-feeew, the second slightly lower than the first.

images.caption: Green Hylia · Plate 186

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two distinct races occur: both have a curving white supercilium, chestnut eye-line and pale grey or olive underparts with yellow undertail-coverts. Nominate (WUg and Ke) has crown and nape chestnut-brown, a very white supercilium and pale grey underparts; chloronota (SWUg to WTz) has rusty-brown ear-coverts and greener upperparts. Nominate immature has indistinct supercilium and brownish throat, breast and flanks; immature chloronota is similar but washed rusty above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Inhabits highland forest above 1,550m, including canopy, tangled vines and undergrowth.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varies locally, but always reminiscent of woodland-warblers; typically, nominate song is a rolling, distinct sequence of clear notes with no embellishment, si-si-si-su-si-si-si-su-si-si-su-su-si, while chloronota tends to sing a silvery rising and falling series.

images.caption: White-browed Crombec · Plate 187

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Uniform grey above with a dark eyeline and tawny-buff supercilium and throat (but chin whitish). Underparts buffy-cinnamon with whitish belly. Immature is like adult but with buffy tips to wing-coverts. Birds in EA are race carnapi.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common resident of woodland, gardens and bush country at 600–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually a simple repeated phrase, like a lisping version of Green Crombec.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly included Eastern Crombec.

images.caption: Northern Crombec · Plate 188

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slightly larger than Northern Crombec with similar grey or grey-brown upperparts; sides of face, throat and most of underparts plain cinnamon (lacks dark eyeline). Four races occur: loringi (NEUg to NKe) is more olive-brown above with a whitish belly; jacksoni (Ug to CKe and NTz) is richly coloured grey and rufous; minima (coastal Ke and ETz) is palest, and nominate (STz) is like jacksoni but rather paler. All races intergrade, but generally those in Ug, WKe and WTz are more richly coloured, while northern and eastern birds are paler. Immature has buffy tips to wing-coverts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread resident in a wide variety of woodland and bush country from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Differs locally, but usual song is a variation of a loud, repeated rolling si-si-siu si-si-siu si-si-siu si-si-siu.

images.caption: Red-faced Crombec · Plate 188

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Pale buffy-grey crombec with a long bill and whitish supercilium; very pale buffy-white below, palest on throat. Immature similar but lightly mottled on throat. Pale underparts and sunbird-like slightly decurved long bill distinguish it from all other crombecs in region. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Generally uncommon in dry bush country of NE and eastern Kenya below 1,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a typical crombec tichi tichi tichi ri-ti-chu, the last note lower. In flight, call is a sharp chik.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Somali Long-billed Crombec

images.caption: Somali Crombec · Plate 188

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Short-tailed eremomela with grey upperparts, whitish throat and breast, and yellow from breast or lower breast to vent. Three races occur: abdominalis (NKe to NTz) has extensive bright yellow on belly; griseoflava (NUg, NW and SWKe, ERw and NWTz) has paler and less yellow on belly, and polioxantha (E and STz) has a greyer breast. Immature is variably washed olive above; yellow on underparts paler and often restricted to ventral area (very similar to Yellow-vented Eremomela).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are widespread in open woodland and bush country to 1,900m. Often found in mixed-species flocks with white-eyes, penduline-tits and crombecs.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rather crombec-like, but more penetrating; song is a variable rising and falling or rolling series of distinct notes, typically t’tri-t’ri-t’tri. A nasal contact note is also used in display.

images.caption: Yellow-bellied Eremomela · Plate 189

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slightly smaller than Yellow-bellied Eremomela, with very short tail and pale yellow restricted to vent (can be difficult to see). Immature has just the faintest yellow wash to vent. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Restricted to north and east in dry bush and semi-desert country below 1,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Differs from Yellow-bellied Eremomela in the scratchiness of its song, a loud and burry ser-si-ser’si-sit.

images.caption: Yellow-vented Eremomela · Plate 189

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Greyish above with olive-green or yellowish-green crown, yellow supercilium and blackish lores; eyes pale yellow. Three races differ mainly in colour of underparts; citriniceps (WUg and SWKe to SWTz) has yellow throat and breast and greyish-white belly; kikuyuensis (CKe) is similar but belly is very pale yellow; nominate (EKe, E and STz) is entirely pale yellow below. Immature is paler than adult with olive wash to upperparts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather local with patchy distribution from sea level to 1,800m. More common in the west and south where small flocks are common, particularly in Brachystegia woodland.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Contact calls consist of continuous guttural short churrs and a low chatter srrrrr-srrrr-srrrrr…

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Greencap Eremomela

images.caption: Green-capped Eremomela · Plate 189

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Bright attractive warbler. In EA the nominate race is olive-green above with a well-defined grey crown and nape, and broad dark mask through eye; very white throat and upper breast contrast with bright yellow breast to vent. Eyes yellowish, legs orange-pink. Immature is like adult but duller and paler.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: A localised species found in small flocks in open bush and woodland at 600– 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: An effervescent rambling series of excitable musical chips and churrs and louder wi-chi-chit phrases.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with West African Senegal Eremomela E. pusilla.

images.caption: Green-backed Eremomela · Plate 189

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Rufous-crowned Eremomela, but chestnut restricted to forecrown. Immature is very plain, washed olive above and creamy-yellow below. Two races occur: nominate (WKe) as described; kalindei (SWUg) is paler with darker wings.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Uncommon in East Africa, being known from forests around Kakamega, western Kenya, and near Kigezi, south-western Uganda, at 1,500–1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Highly vocal giving repeated chichichichichichi…, the notes often interspersed with soft chipping resembling a rattle.

images.caption: Turner’s Eremomela · Plate 189

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is unlike any other bird in EA being bright chestnut with a broad black vertical stripe on face, throat and breast. Adult female has similar black vertical stripe but is mainly olive-grey. Immature is plainer dull olive-grey, with random patches of rufous on male. Birds in EA are race vulpinus.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common but very shy and restricted to undergrowth in primary forest of the west, at B 700–2,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Often duets; male sings a monotone piercing piping, and female accompanies Ruf with a rattling doubled or tripled chlt-chlt. Foraging or alarm call is also this note, repeated by the group.

images.caption: Black-faced Rufous Warbler · Plate 190

curruca-boehmi.ref: Plate 191: Parisomas, Grass Warblers And Grauer’S Warbler
curruca-boehmi.name: Banded Parisoma

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is greyish-brown above with pale eyes, white wingbars and a fairly long white-edged dark tail; below it has a distinct black breast-band and tawny-buff flanks and vent. Three races occur: nominate (widespread) as described; marsabit (NKe) is paler; somalica (NEKe) has heavier throat spotting. Immature is washed brownish above, with buffy wingbars and no black breast-band.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs occur in acacia country and open woodland, usually below 1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Attractive loud rolling and rattling song begins with a reeling fluid trill and continues chip-chit-wurr-chewy-chewy-chewy.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Banded Warbler

images.caption: Banded Parisoma · Plate 191

catriscus-brevirostris.ref: Plate 191: Parisomas, Grass Warblers And Grauer’S Warbler
catriscus-brevirostris.name: Fan-tailed Grassbird

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Resembles a dark-coloured, short-billed Eurasian Reed Warbler, with a long broad black tail (obvious in flight). Immature is washed pale yellow below. Birds in EA are race alexinae.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Resident of moist grassland, marshy meadows and overgrown wet cultivation at 800–2,150m. Hard to see unless flushed, but will perch on exposed grass stems, and performs a flight display.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a simple short, metallic piping ping ping ping… Alarm and contact notes are a sharp tak-tak-tak…

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Broad-tailed Warbler

images.caption: Fan-tailed Grassbird · Plate 191

melocichla-mentalis.ref: Plate 191: Parisomas, Grass Warblers And Grauer’S Warbler
melocichla-mentalis.name: Moustached Grass Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Bulbul-sized warbler which is plain rich brown above, with chestnut-washed forecrown and pale yellow eyes; paler rufous below. Face pattern distinct, with white supercilium, white throat and narrow black malar streak. Immature is like dull dark-eyed adult. Two races occur: amauroura (Ug to SWTz and Ke to NTz) as described; orientalis (NETz to STz) has paler upperparts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs inhabit thick cover along streams from sea level to 2,500m, where shy but vocal, singing frequently from concealed perches.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: One of the best songsters of rank herbage. Basic song begins with a series of tip tip tip… notes breaking into a varied and complex falling flourish, ending tweedle-iddle-ee. Also a nasal scolding chahhchahhchahh… and a capable mimic.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: African Moustached Warbler

images.caption: Moustached Grass Warbler · Plate 191

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three very similar races occur: all are small with a very short, blackish, white-tipped tail and no obviously contrasting coloured rump. Breeding male has unstreaked central crown and blackish lores; often has darkish patches at sides of breast. Non-breeding male and female have forecrown to tail evenly streaked; no loral spot or breast patches.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in grassland at 1,400–2,000m in Kenya, 1,400–2,500m in Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In high-level display repeats a soft chht…chht…chht…, often preceded by a wing-click, before plummeting earthwards with accelerating chht notes ending abruptly on apparent impact, or continuing in a low wavering flight over the grass. Neither calls nor wing-snaps relate to changes of direction. Also utters a soft tic.

images.caption: Pectoral-patch Cisticola · Plate 192

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Typical small cisticola with streaked upperparts; slightly paler nape collar and plain rufous-buff rump (most obvious in flight); tail mid-brown with dark subterminal spots and pale tips. Two races occur: uropygialis (widespread) as described; terrestris (Bu to STz) is darker. On Pemba Island, Tz, a rich rufous form of uropygialis occurs.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in both damp and dry grasslands from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Cruises in a display-flight calling zit…zit…zit… (hence name) at top of each of a series of undulations, never wing-snaps.

images.caption: Zitting Cisticola · Plate 192

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Like Zitting Cisticola but rufous-buff rump is paler, uppertail tail blacker with white tips. Pectoral-patch Cisticola has similarly patterned but shorter tail and lacks rufous rump. Immature has whiter underparts. Birds in most of range are race tanganyika, while in NKe greyer birds are intergrades with Ethiopian lavendulae.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in short dry open grassland (not restricted to desert areas) from sea level to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a high-pitched plaintive p’ink… p’ink… p’ink…, at half-second intervals either from a perch or in low display flight, usually with a wing-snap accompanying each note.

images.caption: Desert Cisticola · Plate 192

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is very small and short-tailed, heavily streaked above with a dark crown, contrasting rufous rump and blackish white-tipped tail. Non-breeding male and female are slightly longer-tailed. Pectoral-patch Cisticola lacks rufous rump. Zitting Cisticola has longer and browner tail. Four similar races vary mainly in overall tone.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Inhabits open grass and moorland, common down to 1,200m in the west, but mainly above 1,800m in Kenya and south-western Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Display flight includes spates of wing-snapping and erratic manoeuvres, often very high and out of sight, while singing varied sweet short phrases.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Ayres’s Cisticola

images.caption: Wing-snapping Cisticola · Plate 192

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has plain rich rufous crown and nape, very heavily streaked back, rich rufous rump and short very dark pale-tipped tail; flanks washed rufous. Non-breeding male has heavily streaked crown separated from back by rufous nape collar; tail longer. Female similar to non-breeding male but shorter-tailed. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Uncommon in both short and seasonally flooded grassland at 900–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Displays like Pectoral-patch Cisticola, including wing-snapping, but song is a burry repeated phrase, tlii-tlii-tlii tlu-tlu-tlu… with some variation.

images.caption: Black-backed Cisticola · Plate 192

cisticola-nana.ref: Plate 193: Small Rufous-Crowned And Stout Cisticolas
cisticola-nana.name: Tiny Cisticola

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small short-tailed cisticola with bright rufous crown, plain greyish-brown back (may look very lightly streaked at close range) and buffy-white underparts; can show short pale line in front of eye. Immature is mostly rufous above and buffy-yellow below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are rather local in dry woodland and acacia, often with mixed-species flocks, from near sea level to 1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a rather prinia-like monotonous series of seesawing notes or a musical chittering from the tops of bushes and trees. Also a rapidly delivered set of cht notes in alarm. STOUT CISTICOLAS Rather stocky cisticolas with males noticeably larger than females. Immatures are washed yellowish below. Stout Cisticola Cisticola robustus  14cm, 5.5" Two races of this distinctive large cisticola occur: adult of widespread race nuchalis has rufous crown thinly streaked black, unstreaked bright rufous nape (which can ‘bleach’ with wear) and heavily streaked back; wings edged dull brown and tail blackish with obvious white tips. Female is similar but smaller. Race awemba (Ufipa Plateau, SWTz) is more red-brown above with a different dialect. Immature (both races) is yellow below, with streaked nape.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and groups (often many birds together) are common in open long grassland, or grassland with scattered bushes, at 1,200–2,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a dry, rattling monotone wind, with introductory notes (lacking in Winding Cisticola) trt-trt-trrrrrrt. Also calls a drawn-out nasal upslurred zweeenk given singly, and a loud repeated pip-pip-pip-pip… Song of race awemba lacks introductory notes and is slower, and it has a call of short sharp tsip notes. Croaking Cisticola Cisticola natalensis  14cm, 5.5" Large bulky cisticola with thick slightly decurved bill; streaked dark brown on paler brown above without bright rufous in plumage, although some races have rufous tones on nape and wing edgings; tail brown with dark subterminal spots and white tips. Four similar races differ mainly in tone, but with many intergrades.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
