sections.text: Pairs are locally common and widespread in tall grassland with scattered bushes from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Unique among cisticolas; a drawn-out nasal call terminating in a short explosive note, tk’weeeeeeee-chunk, and a repeated seesawing metallic tink-tonk…, with the first note higher. VU Aberdare Cisticola Cisticola aberdare  14cm, 5.5" Very similar to Stout Cisticola, but black streaking on crown extends over nape (therefore nape does not contrast so strongly with back), wing edgings rufous-brown; tail appears longer and blacker with buff tips. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to high grasslands either side of the Great Rift Valley in Kenya, at 2,300–3,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls chwichwichwichwi followed by varied bubbly throaty churrs, which are very different from Stout Cisticola.

images.caption: Tiny Cisticola · Plate 193

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The most common and widespread cisticola of bush country. Crown and nape only lightly washed dull rufous and usually (but not always) streaked, medium to densely streaked back, no obvious rufous wing panel; tail brown with dark subterminal spots and whitish tips. Ten races vary mainly in tone, and intergrade in areas of overlap. More distinctive are races heterophrys (coastal Ke and Tz) and emendatus (SETz), which are both almost plain-backed with dull rufous wing panels.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family parties inhabit acacia country, open woodland and cultivation from sea level to 2,100m. Usually in cover near ground, but scolds and calls from bush tops, and virtually always responds to pishing.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varies locally, but distinct rattling always present; it can be musical or dry. Song is 3–5 squeaky downslurs followed by a lower scolding rattle: wiu-wiu-wiu-chuchuchuchuch. Call is a rather nasal tit-like chht.

images.caption: Rattling Cisticola · Plate 194

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Extremely similar to Rattling Cisticola, but crown plain dull brown, back not as heavily streaked as most races of Rattling. Best identified by voice. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are very local within range, occurring on rocky hillsides with some bush and cover at 850–2,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is distinctive, fast and clear, commencing with chik-chik-chik followed by a liquid descending chewewewewewewe.

images.caption: Boran Cisticola · Plate 194

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slim ashy-grey or greyish-brown cisticola, uniformly streaked above and lacking rufous on crown or wing panel (although these areas can appear slightly browner in worn plumage); underparts whitish to pale greyish-buff, tail brownish with dark subterminal spots and white tips. Birds in EA are race schillingsi.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in dry bush country at 300–1,300m, perching openly on low bushes to sing.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a pretty, liquid descending, whistled refrain: si-swi-si-swi-siwoo. Calls a pinched nasal tsit and tseent.

images.caption: Ashy Cisticola · Plate 194

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Boldly streaked above with obvious rufous crown and wing panel; tail grey or brown with dark subterminal spots and white tips. Three races vary mainly in tone, and intergrade in areas of overlap.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common in reeds, sedges and rank vegetation away from coastal lowlands up to 2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is like a ratcheting fishing-reel rrrrrrrrrrrrrrr, but varies locally from complex and musical winds to much simpler trills, often with a set of squeaky upslurs, wiii wiii wiii…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly known as C. galactotes, but this name is now assigned to Rufous-winged Cisticola in southern Africa.

images.caption: Winding Cisticola · Plate 195

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Paler than Winding Cisticola with much duller crown, paler face and dull rufous wing panel. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In Kenya restricted to edges of wetlands, bushland, dunes and cultivation in coastal lowlands, but extends inland to low bushy foothills in eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A short monotonous raspy trill, similar to a prinia, and a variety of tic tictic notes when excited.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Winding Cisticola C. (galactotes) marginatus.

images.caption: Coastal Cisticola · Plate 195

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Winding Cisticola but brighter and more boldly marked. Crown, nape and wing panel are rich bright rufous, back very heavily streaked black; tail rufous with blackish central feathers and white tips. Two races occur: oreophilus (Ke) as described; shiwae (SWTz) has a darker crown.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in tall grass and reedbeds in highland swamps at 2,000–3,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a hurried, musical refrain given at intervals of 2–3 seconds, a descending wit-chup followed by an ascending chererrerrerrit.

images.caption: Levaillant’s Cisticola · Plate 195

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Winding Cisticola, but crown chestnut-brown, wing panel dull brown (not bright rufous); uppertail mostly blackish apart from white tips. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common but restricted to papyrus swamps around Lake Victoria, and in other wetland vegetation in south-western Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, at 700–2,200m. Frequently calls at dawn while flying across gaps in papyrus beds.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: An explosive machine-gun burst of identical notes lasting 2–3 seconds, but with long gaps between each series.

images.caption: Carruthers’s Cisticola · Plate 195

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has rufous crown and wing panel contrasting with uniform grey-brown back; underparts whitish washed buffy on sides of breast. Immature is slightly more rufous above. Three races occur: belli (Ug, NWTz and WKe) and slightly larger pictipennis (CKe to NETz) are both as described; muenzneri (E and STz) is darker above with a brighter crown in non-breeding adult.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common and widespread in fairly dense vegetation at forest edge, around cultivation, in rank undergrowth and gardens, from sea level to 2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Despite name, song is very simple; typically male delivers loud chips followed by an explosive paired whi-chip whi-chip…, and female joins in with dry raspy churr notes or the same.

images.caption: Singing Cisticola · Plate 196

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Singing Cisticola but adult has variable rusty wash extending over face and ear-coverts, grey-brown crown more uniform with nape and back than Singing, and no contrasting rufous wing panel; variable below from buffy-brown to pale rufous. Immature is more rufous-brown above. Two races occur: widespread sylvia as described; nyasa (STz) has richer redder face.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in luxuriant vegetation, often near streams or lakes, from sea level to 2,300m, but also in cultivated land in Rwanda and Burundi.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a complex rather rhythmic duet; generally male gives nasal zwink and chip-wee notes, and female utters rising piping squeaks, hoo-hoo-hoo-wiwiwi.

images.caption: Red-faced Cisticola · Plate 196

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is dull brown with slightly contrasting chestnut-brown crown, dark lores, brown back with variable but generally indistinct darker streaking (only visible in good light); underparts greyish with whiter throat. Immature is warmer brown above. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to East Africa, small parties inhabit overgrown cultivation, remnant valley herbage, forest edge and giant heather in highlands at 1,550–4,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a loud far-carrying, excited and highly distinctive musical duet from bush tops. One bird gives a rising and falling rolling trill, tweetrrrrrr tweetrrrrrr… while another (or more) joins in with see-tuit…

images.caption: Hunter’s Cisticola · Plate 196

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Hunter’s Cisticola, but adult has black lores and brighter rufous crown contrasting with totally unstreaked grey-brown back; underparts creamy-buff with whiter throat. Immature is duller than adult. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups have a mainly westerly distribution at 1,600–2,500m, overlapping with Hunter’s on Mt Elgon where Chubb’s is found below and Hunter’s above 2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Duetted song is a repeated descending and explosive series of three notes; wi-ti-chiow, wi-ti-chiow, wi-ti-chiow…

images.caption: Chubb’s Cisticola · Plate 196

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is rather plain with dull chestnut-brown crown contrasting only slightly with brown back, no obvious wing panel; underparts whitish with pale grey flanks; tail has dark subterminal spots and pale tips. Female is smaller and slightly brighter on crown. Immature much more rufous above and yellow below. Two races occur: nominate (WUg and Rw east to SWKe and across NTz) as described; lufira (Bu and WTz) is warmer brown above and very buffy-brown below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in a wide variety of grassland with scattered bush and trees at 900–2,000m, and in miombo in Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Unique song is a musical trill rising to a crescendo and lasting 3–4 seconds, trrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr, with long pauses. Call is a series of hollow scolds: tyap-ayap…

images.caption: Trilling Cisticola · Plate 197

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather drab and variable species (with a beady-eyed look) best identified by song. Six races vary slightly in density of streaking on upperparts, which also varies seasonally, being indistinct in breeding (especially western) and usually heavier in non-breeding plumages. Very dull or no rufous on crown or wing. Underparts buffy with whiter throat, tail dull brown with dark subterminal spots and white tips. Immature is pale yellow below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread but inconspicuous, frequenting bushed grassland and open forest edge from sea level to 2,200m, often singing from tops of small trees.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Quiet and high-pitched song varies locally, but is usually a repeated series of three or more sibilant descending notes: si-si-siu si-si-siu…

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Siffling Cisticola

images.caption: Short-winged Cisticola · Plate 197

cisticola-angusticauda.ref: Plate 198: Plain-Backed Cisticolas Iii And Prinias I
cisticola-angusticauda.name: Tabora Cisticola

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Uniquely long-tailed cisticola. Breeding adult has bright rufous crown contrasting with plain grey-brown back; tail long, dark and narrow with white tips. Non-breeding adult has a shorter tail. Immature is duller and browner above, washed pale yellow below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or small parties occur in acacia grassland below 1,800m; constantly on the move, working through low bushes and on the ground.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a repeated soft piping delivered from a perch or in display flight; call is a harsh repeated chipping.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Sometimes considered conspecific with Piping Cisticola but has different wing formula and slightly different song.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Long-tailed Cisticola

images.caption: Tabora Cisticola · Plate 198

prinia-rufifrons.ref: Plate 198: Plain-Backed Cisticolas Iii And Prinias I
prinia-rufifrons.name: Red-fronted Prinia

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small slender warbler with variable amount of rufous on forecrown or crown, ashy-brown back and whitish underparts; long tail is blackish and narrow with white tips and is habitually cocked and waved from side to side. Immature lacks rufous on forecrown. Two races occur: smithi (NEUg, Ke and NETz) as described, and rufidorsalis (apparently confined to Tsavo East NP, SEKe) with back washed rufous and sometimes a blackish breast-band.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family parties are common in dry bush at 400–1,300m, endlessly searching for insects in low dry vegetation, rarely far above ground.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Lively song is a long and varied medley of nasal buzzes and chips (each note repeated many times before the next). Call is a harsh repeated nasal slur.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Spiloptila.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Red-fronted Warbler

images.caption: Red-fronted Prinia · Plate 198

prinia-subflava.ref: Plate 199: Prinias Ii And Grey-Capped Warbler
prinia-subflava.name: Tawny-flanked Prinia

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Most common and widespread prinia with five very similar races. Seasonal and racial differences mainly in tone of upperparts. Typically pale brown or grey-brown above, with an obvious pale supercilium, narrow darker eyeline, off-white throat and breast, and pale tawny-buff wash to flanks. Immature is washed yellowish below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in a wide variety of habitats including gardens, bushed grassland, overgrown cultivation and clearings in forest, from sea level to 2,300m. Shuns forest interior and arid areas.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Simple unmusical song consists of a rapid-fire tititititititititit… or a rasping zhertzhertzhert… Also a buzzy scolding call, jeee jeee…

images.caption: Tawny-flanked Prinia · Plate 199

prinia-somalica.ref: Plate 199: Prinias Ii And Grey-Capped Warbler
prinia-somalica.name: Pale Prinia

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Tawny-flanked Prinia but generally paler; whiter underparts lack tawny wash on flanks. Immature is washed very pale buff on breast and flanks. Race in EA is erlangeri.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs inhabit dry bush country, with or without grass cover. In drier habitats than Tawny-flanked where ranges overlap.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song differs from Tawny-flanked Prinia, being a rattle of dry, cricket-like notes lasting 4–5 seconds: zherzherzherzherzher…

images.caption: Pale Prinia · Plate 199

prinia-fluviatilis.ref: Plate 199: Prinias Ii And Grey-Capped Warbler
prinia-fluviatilis.name: River Prinia

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Extremely similar to Tawny-flanked Prinia, but ranges do not overlap in our region. From Pale Prinia by slightly darker grey-brown upperparts, shorter supercilium finishing just behind eye (not longer and fading) and buffy tinge to flanks and undertail-coverts. Most safely distinguished by voice. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs inhabit seasonally dry riverbeds on plains east of Lokichokio in extreme north-western Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a piercing repeated downslurred metallic siet-siet-siet-siet… and, in duet, female answers with a buzzy trill.

images.caption: River Prinia · Plate 199

schistolais-leucopogon.ref: Plate 199: Prinias Ii And Grey-Capped Warbler
schistolais-leucopogon.name: White-chinned Prinia

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Mostly grey warbler with a creamy-white throat, darker grey ear-coverts, red-brown eyes and pink legs; tail broader than genus Prinia. Sexes alike; immature is slightly paler below. Birds in EA are race reichenowi.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small groups are common in secondary forest, forest edge and thick cover along streams, at 1,100–2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: An energetic and excitable song of rapid chips and squeaks, variously chippity-chu-chu chi-chu-chi-chi… given in duet.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Prinia.

images.caption: White-chinned Prinia · Plate 199

prinia-bairdii.ref: Plate 199: Prinias Ii And Grey-Capped Warbler
prinia-bairdii.name: Banded Prinia

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive prinia with blackish-brown upperparts, white-spotted wing-coverts, long white-tipped tail, and strongly black and white banded underparts. Three races occur and are sometimes considered to be two species: nominate (Banded Prinia) at 700m in Semliki Forest, WUg, has banding throughout underparts. At 1,550–3,000m in the highlands, obscura (WUg, Rw and Bu) and melanops (EUg and WKe) (Black-faced Prinia) have a blackish face and throat. Immatures are browner above and less distinctly barred below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in parts of range, but shy and difficult to see in dense forest undergrowth.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is usually given as a duet; male repeats series of high nasal rhythmical notes, ch’zi-ch’zi-ch’zi-ch’zi-ch’zi…, while female peeps plaintively piu piu…. GREY-CAPPED WARBLER A large and distinctive warbler – the sole member of the genus Eminia.

images.caption: Banded Prinia · Plate 199

eminia-lepida.ref: Plate 199: Prinias Ii And Grey-Capped Warbler
eminia-lepida.name: Grey-capped Warbler

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive warbler with grey and green plumage, black band around crown and chestnut throat patch. Immature is duller with less chestnut on throat. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Shy, but very vocal, with pairs inhabiting a wide variety of thick undergrowth, including gardens, forest edge and river courses at 800–2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Loud often duetted song is variable but easily recognised as notes are slow, strong and fluty, typically wer-wi-wi… whii-chutchutchutchutchutchutchutchut… (with male trilling and female adding rising nasal upslurs).

images.caption: Grey-capped Warbler · Plate 199

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Eight races occur in two distinct groups; grey-backed birds are mainly in the west and central regions, although they reach the Ke coast north of Mombasa. Green-backed birds occur in coastal SEKe south to E and STz. Several races are known to intergrade. If considered specifically distinct, grey-backed races become Grey-backed Camaroptera C. brevicaudata and green-backed races become Green-backed Camaroptera C. brachyura. Both are grey with green wings, but the brachyura group has green (not grey) backs. Races within groups are similar but some are browner above when breeding; underparts vary from grey to pale greyish-white. Immature is variably washed yellow below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common in undergrowth and lower levels of forest, dense bush, gardens and cultivation, from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Musically versatile although all calls are simple. Frequently heard is a very nasal pinched wheezy bzeeee (often described as a bleat). Song is a loud whip-cracked t’chk t’chk t’chk, and also a nasal wiwiwiwiwiwi…

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Green-backed Camaroptera, Bleating Camaroptera

images.caption: Grey-backed Camaroptera · Plate 200

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dull drab camaroptera of forest interior. Adult has olive-brown upperparts with slightly greener wings; face and breast dull tawny-brown contrasting with whiter belly and vent. Immature is generally greener and variably washed yellowish below. Birds in EA are race toroensis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Lone birds or pairs are common in tangled vines and undergrowth in primary forest at 700–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a soft weep weep… which often leads into an unusual high-pitched and insect-like piping on one note: ee-ee-ee-ee-ee-ee-ee-ee-ee-ee…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities consider the race in Ug and WKe specifically distinct as Tawny-breasted Camaroptera C. toroensis.

images.caption: Olive-green Camaroptera · Plate 200

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: All dark grey-brown with a broad tail which is often cocked and waved. At close range may show slightly speckled throat and some indistinct barring on belly. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in acacia scrub and bushed savanna at 100–1,300m. Usually seen moving slowly low down in bushes, or on the ground below them, but moves to tops of small trees when calling.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is an explosive repeated chup, chup, chup given for long periods at a rate of about one note per second.

images.caption: Grey Wren-Warbler · Plate 200

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is grey-brown above (paler than Grey Wren-Warbler), dingy greyish-white below with narrow darker grey-brown barring on throat and breast, variably extending onto flanks. Immature is slightly paler and can have a cinnamon wash on the flanks. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Favours open grassy hills with scattered bushes and trees (particularly miombo) at 900–1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rather like a musical sparrow, calling for long periods about once per second, cherp cherp cherp….

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities consider this species conspecific with Stierling’s Wren-Warbler as they hybridise in a small area of Zambia.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Pale Wren-Warbler

images.caption: Miombo Wren-Warbler · Plate 200

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Complex species with races variously placed in two groups based on tail colour and voice. All are greenish above with varying amounts of grey on crown, and a yellow breast-band with or without a small black breast bar or spot. In NEUg and NKe race flavocincta (Brown-tailed Apalis) has a grey forecrown, no black breast patch and brown uppertail with yellowish edges. Elsewhere, races have green uppertails and also vary as follows: caniceps (Ug to WKe) has grey crown and no black on breast; pugnax (CKe highlands) has mostly green crown and black breast spot in both sexes; golzi (SEKe to CTz) is similar but has grey crown; and neglecta (coastal Ke to STz) has grey crown and variable black spot or bar in male, none in female.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common and widespread in woodland, bush and cultivation from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Race flavocincta sings a monotonous dry rasping duet, the male giving a krik-krik-krik… and the female very quiet throaty growls. Green-tailed birds have a slower more distinctive rhythm, like a galloping horse, the male calling chirrit-chirrit-chirrit-… and the female a rising nasal eek eek eek eek…

images.caption: Yellow-breasted Apalis · Plate 201

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has brown crown contrasting with greyer mantle and wings (less so in female); white outer tail feathers easily distinguish this species from Brown-headed Apalis. Very similar Kungwe Apalis is colder grey above, without any hint of brown on crown. Immature is washed olive above and very pale yellow below. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in highland forests of Kenya and lower altitudes in the west, at 1,200–3,000m. Primarily a canopy species but forages at lower levels at forest edge.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male calls a monotonous chip-chip-chip…, often accompanied by wing-snapping, while the female gives a frequent high-pitched rattle.

images.caption: Grey Apalis · Plate 201

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive with ash-grey upperparts, short white supercilium, obvious white patch in inner secondaries, creamy-white underparts and a white outer tail. Sexes alike. Two races occur: nominate (NEUg) as described; stronachi (NTz and SWKe) male is more brownish-grey above without short white supercilium and greyer flanks; female paler.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: A little-known, local and uncommon East Africa endemic, with three populations centred on Mt Moroto to Kidepo NP in north-eastern Uganda; the Wembere–Serengeti area, north-central Tanzania; and eastern Maasai Mara, south-western Kenya at 900–1,800m. Particularly fond of whistling thorn Acacia drepanolobium where up to six have been seen together.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a duet of repeated musical phrases: wee tou wee tou wit too. Calls dwe dwe dwe and a raspy jirrrr. VU

images.caption: Karamoja Apalis · Plate 202

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A black and white or very dark brown and creamy-white apalis with a white-tipped tail. Four races occur: males of nominate (coastal Ke to East Usambara Mts, NETz) and muhuluensis (STz) are very black above; moschi (SEKe and NETz highlands) has dark grey crown and upperparts with black restricted to sides of face; and nigrodorsalis (CKe highlands) is very dark blackish-brown above. Females are slightly paler than males with an olive wash to upperparts. Immatures are variably washed pale yellow below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs may be common in canopy and mid-levels of eastern forests, frequently in mixed-species flocks from sea level to 2,150m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a typical monotonous apalis-like chipping, but with some geographic variation; a sibilant tiree-tiree-tiree-tiree… repeated 4–5 times, and then again after a pause of varying length.

images.caption: Black-headed Apalis · Plate 202

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Predominantly grey apalis with paler underparts and a small clear-cut chestnut throat. Tail grey with inconspicuous whitish tips. Immature is washed pale yellow on throat, sides of face and belly. Two races occur: nominate (widespread) as described; affinis (SWUg) has darker chestnut throat and paler underparts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and singles are common in the canopy of highland forest at 1,700–3,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Unique-sounding apalis; male sings a set of two ringing dry trills on one level, similar to an old-fashioned telephone, t-t-trrriiii trrrriiii, and female accompanies with rapid seeping notes. Male also calls short chip chip chip notes.

images.caption: Chestnut-throated Apalis · Plate 202

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male of race nigrescens (all of range apart from SWUg) is blackish-brown above, pale creamy-white below, with a dark tail and four pairs of white outer tail feathers (very obvious in flight). Adult female has tawny-buff throat to upper breast. Immature is olive-grey above with yellow wash to throat and breast. In Bwindi-Impenetrable Forest, SWUg, race kigezi is greyer above in both sexes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in forest canopy in W and southern Uganda at 700–1,800m, and less numerous in north-western Tanzania and western Kenya between 1,200 and 2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a monotonous repeated two-toned chipping, ch’rip-ch’rip-ch’rip-…, often accompanied by wing-snaps.

images.caption: Buff-throated Apalis · Plate 203

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Boldly marked attractive apalis which is wholly dark grey above, with white outer tail feathers, and white underparts with distinct black collar and bright chestnut flanks. Sexes alike. Immature is paler with dark grey breast-band. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are common in forest undergrowth and tangled vines at 1,550–2,400m, being most numerous in western Kenya, less so in central Kenya highlands.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song consists of repeated sets of paired, pinched, nasal notes on alternating seesawing tones, zeeu-zeeu-zeeu…, usually 4–7 paired notes per series.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Apalis.

images.caption: Black-collared Apalis · Plate 203

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Five distinct races occur, all with a narrow black band below throat, but differ in colour of crown, back and underparts. Race griseiceps (Chyulu Hills, SEKe, NTz and Udzungwa Mts, ETz) has a brownish cap, yellowish-green back, white throat and yellow lower breast to vent; murina (NE to STz) is grey-brown above and mostly white below with yellow on belly; pareensis (South Pare Mts, NTz) is similar but yellow restricted to vent; uluguru (Uluguru Mts, ETz) is like griseiceps but yellow extends from breast-band to vent; youngi (Ufipa Plateau, SWTz) is grey-brown above and all white below except for black band below throat.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in undergrowth and mid-levels of forests at 1,300–3,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Complex, with songs varying almost as much as the birds do in plumage; race murina has a descending dry trill, uluguru a two-tone repeated chipping, griseiceps and youngi are similar to uluguru but more rapid. Females often accompany males with a dry rattle.

images.caption: Bar-throated Apalis · Plate 203

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Totally dark brownish-grey above with narrow white edges to tail; throat to upper breast blackish, lower breast to vent off-white with very pale yellow wash. Sexes alike. Monotypic. SH. A Critically Endangered endemic restricted to forest remnants on higher slopes of the Taita Hills, SEKe, where probably fewer than 250 individuals survive.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male gives a fast chipping while the female accompanies with metallic tink notes. CR

images.caption: Taita Apalis · Plate 203

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Bright attractive apalis; adult male has black throat and sides to face separated by broad white malar stripe; rest of upperparts include dark grey crown, green back and dark grey wings with variable whitish edges to inner secondaries; below bright yellow washed greenish on flanks. Adult female is similar, but has greyer crown and throat. Immature male is duller with greenish crown and greyish throat; immature female has yellowish throat. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in the canopy of highland forest at 1,200–2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song differs from all other apalises in sounding musical, hollow and metallic: a seesawing two-tone call repeated for long periods: t’link-t’link-t’link-…

images.caption: Black-throated Apalis · Plate 204

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three races occur: all have a distinctive blue-grey, black-tipped bill. Nominate race (NEUg, Ke and NETz) is dark blue-grey above and paler below (grading to whitish on belly) with a conspicuous broad white eye-ring and blue-grey bill with a black tip; nyikensis (highlands of Tz away from NE) is more slate-grey with a small eye-ring; and toruensis (WUg, Rw and Bu) is blue-grey like the nominate race, but has a very inconspicuous eye-ring. Immatures are spotted buffy-white above, mottled and scalloped blackish on breast and flanks.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread at forest edge, in wooded glades and gardens at 1,350–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rarely heard song consists of a sibilant hissing and clicking interspersed with very loud and explosive swee-wi-yu calls. More common call is a complaining trrr-trrr. BLACK FLYCATCHERS Three similar-looking flycatchers best identified by overall colour, eye colour, song and range. Typical flycatchers perching quietly with an upright posture for long periods. Sexes alike. Also consider other black birds like cuckooshrikes (Plate 154), boubous (Plate 238), and drongos (Plate 244).

images.caption: White-eyed Slaty Flycatcher · Plate 205

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is very similar to Northern Black Flycatcher, but glossy blue-black (not dull black), eyes dark brown. Immature dull black, spotted above and scalloped below with buff. Up to five races described, but all are poorly defined and most authorities consider the changes clinal.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in a wide variety of drier woodland, bush and cultivation from sea level to 1,800m. In Kenya occurs mainly east of Great Rift Valley, but widespread in Tanzania and extends west to Burundi and Rwanda and southern Uganda.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is very complex, sweet and warbler-like.

images.caption: Southern Black Flycatcher · Plate 205

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two races occur: lugubris (widespread in Ug, WKe and NWTz) is totally dull slate-black with dark brown eyes; schistacea (Moyale, NKe) is dull dark grey-black. Immature is streaked tawny on crown, more heavily spotted with tawny elsewhere. Southern Black Flycatcher is more glossy black.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread north and west of the range of Southern Black, occupying woodland, dry bush country and cultivated areas. In Kenya it is common mainly west of the Great Rift Valley at 400– 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is very different from Southern Black Flycatcher, being rather slow and sibilant, with many long drawn-out burry slurs and occasional soft nasal chips.

images.caption: Northern Black Flycatcher · Plate 205

bradornis-microrhynchus.ref: Plate 207: Grey And Brown Flycatchers I
bradornis-microrhynchus.name: African Grey Flycatcher

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Pale Flycatcher, but usually a little smaller and greyer; best identified by grey-brown plumage with fine blackish streaks on crown, and from Spotted Flycatcher by absence of breast streaking. Four similar races occur: neumanni (NEUg to N and EKe) is slightly smaller and browner than others; burae (EKe) is smallish and paler grey; taruensis (SEKe) is similar but darker; and nominate (SWKe and Tz) is slightly larger and greyer.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in dry bush and open wooded acacia country from near sea level to 2,000m; where ranges overlap, Pale Flycatcher occupies more verdant habitat.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is rarely heard, a complex, variable and continuous warble with mostly harsh and scratchy notes. Commonly heard alarm is a rather nasal scraping, a paired shree-shree.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Greyish Flycatcher

images.caption: African Grey Flycatcher · Plate 207

agricola-pallidus.ref: Plate 207: Grey And Brown Flycatchers I
agricola-pallidus.name: Pale Flycatcher

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three similar races and two additional distinct races (both perhaps separate species) occur: most are best separated from African Grey Flycatcher by at least slightly larger size, overall browner plumage and uniform brown crown without streaking. Races parvus (NWUg), murinus (widespread in Ug, Ke and NTz) and griseus (SEKe to STz) are all similar and as described. In dry scrub in NEKe bafirawari (Wajir Grey Flycatcher) is paler grey-brown, with distinct short white supercilium. In coastal Ke and NETz subalaris (East Coast Flycatcher) is smaller and paler sandy-brown.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Generally in more lush and wooded habitats than African Grey Flycatcher, from sea level to 2,000m. Wajir Grey Flycatcher unique in preferring dry thorn scrub.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a spitted note, extremely similar to Yellow-spotted Bush-Sparrow, and often followed by a scratchy shrehh. Rarely heard song is a harsh rather unmusical warbled treet-etreet-et-ti-cherr et-ti-cherr…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Bradornis.

images.caption: Pale Flycatcher · Plate 207

muscicapa-striata.ref: Plate 207: Grey And Brown Flycatchers I
muscicapa-striata.name: Spotted Flycatcher

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Medium-sized slim grey-brown flycatcher with a streaked crown and breast (often indistinct on latter), and black bill. Rear crown often appears peaked; wings are pointed and long, reaching halfway down tail. Most belong to the slightly greyer race neumanni, but browner nominate race also occurs.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread Palearctic passage visitor from late Sep to Apr and can occur in any habitat from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is not heard in EA, but still quite vocal; frequent call is a harsh chick.

images.caption: Spotted Flycatcher · Plate 207

muscicapa-gambagae.ref: Plate 207: Grey And Brown Flycatchers I
muscicapa-gambagae.name: Gambaga Flycatcher

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Spotted Flycatcher, but head appears rounded with a plain forecrown, indistinctly streaked hindcrown, browner more diffuse streaking on breast and yellowish base to lower mandible. Closed wing does not extend beyond base of tail. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Solitary and very uncommon in dry bush and open wooded country below 1,600m in northern Uganda and northern Kenya. Usually flicks its wings when landing after short flights.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call consists of a repeated series of paired and single clicks, like a dry twig snapping, t’lik t’lik…, unlike anything produced by Spotted Flycatcher.

images.caption: Gambaga Flycatcher · Plate 207

muscicapa-adusta.ref: Plate 208: Grey And Brown Flycatchers Ii
muscicapa-adusta.name: African Dusky Flycatcher

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small rather dumpy brown flycatcher. Adult is typically uniform dark brown above and variably paler brown or grey-brown below; some show variable whitish throat and or belly, and have very light streaking on breast. Five similar races vary slightly in general colour, but one soon learns this common, mainly highland, species.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common and widespread in forest, riverine woodland and gardens at 900–3,200m. Most numerous in high country, but down to 900m in western Uganda. Typical flycatcher behaviour, making short flights and returning to a favourite exposed perch.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a high-pitched continuous series of varied unmusical squeaks and hisses, sounding a little chat-like.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Dusky-brown Flycatcher

images.caption: African Dusky Flycatcher · Plate 208

muscicapa-aquatica.ref: Plate 208: Grey And Brown Flycatchers Ii
muscicapa-aquatica.name: Swamp Flycatcher

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Uniform dark earth-brown above and white below with broad brown breast-band and flanks; throat appears very white. Immature is heavily spotted above with buff, breast-band indistinct, mottled brown and white. Birds in EA are race infulata.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Restricted to west where pairs are common around swamps, papyrus beds and along lakeshores, mainly at 700–1,400m, but rarely to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varies locally, but calls are high-pitched, chat-like, and given in snatches punctuated by short pauses; typical call is a hissed sisisisi at end of each series, but a long, complex and sweet ramble with almost Serinus-like phrases is also given.

images.caption: Swamp Flycatcher · Plate 208

fraseria-caerulescens.ref: Plate 208: Grey And Brown Flycatchers Ii
fraseria-caerulescens.name: Ashy Flycatcher

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slim ash-grey or blue-grey flycatcher with narrow dark eyeline, short whitish supraloral line and small indistinct broken eye-ring; greyish-white below, paler on throat and belly. Three races occur: brevicauda (Ug to Bu and WKe) is mostly blue-grey; cinereola (EKe and ETz) is paler ashy-grey; and impavida (WTz) is palest with whitish underparts. Similar Grey Tit-Flycatcher has horizontal posture and white outer tail.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs are widespread, but only locally common in canopy and mid-levels of forest edge, clearings and along well-wooded rivers from sea level to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a descending series of spaced, harsh but musical chips, trit tit tit it, which may break into a flourish. Song is a sweet, chat-like warble.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities place in the genus Fraseria.

images.caption: Ashy Flycatcher · Plate 208

fraseria-plumbea.ref: Plate 208: Grey And Brown Flycatchers Ii
fraseria-plumbea.name: Grey Tit-Flycatcher

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Blue-grey or ashy-grey above with short whitish supercilium and greyish underparts; blackish central tail and white outer tail. General appearance very similar to Ashy Flycatcher but moves with horizontal posture while frequently waving and fanning its tail. Three races occur: nominate (WUg to NWTz and east to Rift Valley, Ke) as described; orientalis (SEKe to ETz) is paler bluish-grey; and catoleucus (C to STz) is much whiter below. Immatures are washed brownish above, with small buffy spots on wings.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are widespread but local and generally uncommon in the canopy of a variety of woodland from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Far-carrying song consists of long pure burry notes. Coastal birds tend towards wi-wi-oo, the first two notes on same higher tone; inland birds start with a long note, followed by a higher one.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Sometimes placed in the genus Fraseria.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Lead-coloured Flycatcher

images.caption: Grey Tit-Flycatcher · Plate 208

fraseria-lendu.ref: Plate 209: Western Grey And Brown Flycatchers
fraseria-lendu.name: Chapin’s Flycatcher

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather dingy flycatcher; uniform olive-brown above with indistinct greyish loral line (hard to see on birds high in the canopy) and pale greyish-brown underparts with a lighter throat and belly. Bill mostly blackish and in close views may show bare yellowish skin near base. Immature is spotted buff on mantle and wing-coverts, with darker spotting on breast. African Dusky Flycatcher is smaller and darker brown. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rare and little-known bird of the forest canopy where it behaves like a typical Muscicapa. Restricted to Bwindi-Impenetrable Forest, south-western Uganda, and Kakamega and North Nandi forests, western Kenya, at 1,500–2,150m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rarely heard song is very lively, hurried and fairly sweet. Commonest call heard is a spitted t’t’t’t’t’t’t’t’… very similar to Little Grey Greenbul.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities place in the genus Fraseria. VU

images.caption: Chapin’s Flycatcher · Plate 209

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has grey crown and small white nuchal spot, narrow white supercilium (usually prominent) and fairly broad breast-band (narrower in similar male East Coast Batis). Adult female has sharply defined dark chestnut breast-band and throat spot (paler tawny and less well-defined in female East Coast Batis). Two races occur: widespread puella as described, palliditergum (STz) is slightly paler.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Most common and widespread batis, though uncommon in south-eastern Tanzania; pairs inhabit a wide variety of woodland, thickets and gardens at 500–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Commonest songs are two well-spaced pure whistles pii… poo, or a three-note pii-pii-poo, the second and third notes becoming progressively two tones lower. Female often calls in duet with snappy nasal notes and wing burring.

images.caption: Chinspot Batis · Plate 210

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very similar to Chinspot Batis but has narrower breast-band and overall slightly paler appearance. Adult female differs in having throat and breast-band paler tawny and less sharply defined. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are local in Brachystegia (miombo) and other woodland, mainly in coastal lowlands but up to 1,000m in East Usambara Mts, north-eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male call is a simple well-spaced piping of pure notes, pyi-pyi-pyi-pyi…, often accompanied by the slightly nasal female.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Pale Batis

images.caption: East Coast Batis · Plate 210

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small, rather short-tailed batis: adult male has grey crown and short white supraloral stripe (sometimes hard to see). Adult female has similar supraloral, rufous-tawny breast-band, and white (or very faint buff) throat. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in semi-arid acacia bush country below 1,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a loud high pure piping of identical notes, hi…hi…hi…, which can recall Desert Cisticola.

images.caption: Pygmy Batis · Plate 210

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has black crown, long white supercilium and a fairly narrow black breast-band. Adult female has dark chestnut breast-band. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and locally common in a variety of woodland and open bush in the west at about 700–1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varies locally; song is a series of identical pure piping notes, hi-hi-hi-…, at intervals of a little more than one per second and sometimes followed by a series of peculiar paired nasal downslurs.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Eastern Black-headed Batis.

images.caption: Western Black-headed Batis · Plate 210

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very similar to Grey-headed Batis but crown is very dark grey (or blackish). Best identified from Western Black-headed by crown colour, if dark grey, and range. Adult female has slightly narrower breast-band than female Grey-headed. Birds in EA are race suahelica.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Generally uncommon in coastal scrub and woodland, entering drier bush country further inland, from sea level to 950m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Some variation but usually a series of pure piping notes in groups of 2–4, slightly slower and longer than Western Black-headed. Also a buzzy call.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Western Black-headed Batis.

images.caption: Eastern Black-headed Batis · Plate 210

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A short-tailed, red-eyed batis with two races in EA. Males have red or orange eyes and a broad breast-band; but race ultima (coastal Ke) has an indistinct narrow white supercilium; nominate (NETz) has none. Female ultima has frosty pale cinnamon throat and breast; female nominate is darker and brown-eyed, with short supercilium and rich chestnut throat and breast. Both females have much rufous in the wing.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In Kenya pairs are shy (but not uncommon) residents in lower strata of dense coastal forest, but in Tanzania they inhabit mid-levels and high canopy at 300–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Significant variation; common call of the nominate is a slow monotone piping at mid-range, ultima has a lower-toned piping, and some regular raspy nasal notes.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Short-tailed Batis

images.caption: Forest Batis · Plate 211

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is a striking black and white bird with red or dark orange-red eyes. Perches upright and gently waves tail from side to side; similar puffbacks have white or grey on wings and a horizontal posture. Adult female is brown above, washed rufous on rump and vent, broadly streaked dark brown and white below. Immature is like dull female. Birds in EA are the race aequatorialis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are local and generally uncommon in the canopy of primary forest and tall secondary growth at 700–2,150m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual song consists of cheerful, scratchy, rhythmical rising or falling slurs, often given in triplets or pairs, . Contact and flight call is a repeated very high-pitched sit-sit-sit...

images.caption: African Shrike-flycatcher · Plate 211

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has a bright red wattle above eye and white wingbar; white throat and black breast-band resembles batises. Adult female is greyer above with dark maroon-brown throat and upper breast. Immature is brownish-grey above, with tawny-buff wingbar, throat and upper breast. Birds in EA are race nyansae.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in middle strata and canopy of thick bush, woodland and forest edge at 600–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A unique syncaphonic sound, usually three minor-key descending notes preceding a series of up to five descending minor-key notes. Some notes are burry and scratchy. Pair may duet, the female giving a scratchier accompaniment.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Common Wattle-eye

images.caption: Brown-throated Wattle-eye · Plate 212

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to Brown-throated Wattle-eye with a bright red wattle above eye but no white wingbar; white throat and narrow black breast-band resembles a batis. Adult female has throat and upper breast black. Immature is browner above than adult, with tawny edges to wings and buffy wash to throat. Two races occur: mentalis (west of Rift) has upperparts glossed blue-black; cryptoleuca (east of Rift) is glossed greenish-black above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread but patchily distributed and not numerous in a wide variety of forest and woodland from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Some variation; song is a monotonous repeated series of rhythmic scratchy notes followed by a nasal buzzy seesawing ch’ch’ch’ch’… in-cherin-cherin-cherin-cherinch…, often in duet.

images.caption: Black-throated Wattle-eye · Plate 212

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Tiny wattle-eye often appearing black and white in the field with huge turquoise eye wattles, a chestnut patch on side of neck and dark green gloss to upperparts visible in good light. Sexes similar but female is greyer above. Immature is similar to female but has pale chestnut throat and upper breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Not uncommon in western forests at 700–2,300m, but always difficult to see in dense undergrowth.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varies locally, but common call is an extremely high-pitched and piercing pi-pi piii often accompanied by loud wing-rattling.

images.caption: Jameson’s Wattle-eye · Plate 212

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dumpy sexually dimorphic wattle-eye with a very short tail and purplish eye wattles (can be difficult to see in the field). Male is black and white with broad black breast-band. Female is distinctive; bright chestnut with grey crown and white lower breast and belly. Immature is similar to female but has grey and pale chestnut mottling across breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Unobtrusive quiet little birds of tall undergrowth and mid-levels of forests at 700–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very wide vocabulary though all calls consist of identical repeated notes: can be a pinched pee-pee-pee…, a strange note like a distant whiplash, or a metallic tinkerbird-like tonk-tonk-tonk…

images.caption: Chestnut Wattle-eye · Plate 212

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is dull olive-green above and bright yellow below with huge apple-green eye wattles. Adult female is similar, but more grey-green above with strong wash of orange-chestnut across throat and upper breast. Immature is like pale male, washed greyer above, with buffy tips to wing-coverts and greyish eye wattles. Two races occur: graueri (SWUg to Bu and east to WKe) as described; in distinctive kungwensis (Kungwe Wattle-eye) (Mahale Mts, WTz) male is slate-grey above and pale yellow below with bluish eye wattles.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Shy and uncommon in dense tangled vines and undergrowth of primary forest at 700–2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a very rhythmical series repeated without variation, with three higher identical notes, two descending notes, and terminating in a rising whiplash wi-pipi wi wu kwip!

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities consider this form specifically distinct from West African Rufous-bellied Wattle-eye, and name EA birds D. ansorgei.

images.caption: Yellow-bellied Wattle-eye · Plate 212

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive flycatcher with silvery-grey upperparts and rufous-orange underparts. Sexes alike. Immature is heavily spotted above with creamy-buff and black, and mottled below with orange, buff and brown. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or single birds are locally common in wooded acacia and bushed grassland, and edges of cultivation, at 400–2,300m. Perches in the open and drops to feed on the ground.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sings infrequently, but is the sweetest-sounding of the flycatchers; song consists of random short phrases with a thrush-like pattern but chat-like delivery, swi-sisi sir wi-wir…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities now place this species in the genus Melaenornis.

images.caption: Silverbird · Plate 213

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Black-and-white crested-flycatcher with white in wings and uniform dark tail. Adult male has long pointed crest, glossy blue-black head and upper breast, dark blue-grey mantle, and white lower breast to vent. Two races occur: male vivax (SWUg to WTz) has two narrow whitish wingbars; male bivittatus (C and EKe, and ETz) has a prominent white wing patch. Females of both races are grey above, with mottled grey and white breasts and two narrow pale greyish-white wingbars. Immature like female but has buffy edges to wing-coverts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are locally common in undergrowth and denser midstorey of forest from sea level to 2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Vocal and noisy: usual call is several rising nasal and scratchy slurs (similar to African Paradise-flycatcher), often followed by a run of rapid, pure and rather hollow bell-like notes: wiu-pupupupupupupu….

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities consider EA races distinct from southern African birds as Eastern Crested-flycatcher T. bivattatus.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: African Crested-Flycatcher

images.caption: Blue-mantled Crested-flycatcher · Plate 214

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is a blackish crested-flycatcher (slate-grey on back) with a white belly and very conspicuous broad white tips to all but central tail feathers (obvious as it frequently jerks and fans its tail). Adult female and immature are duller slate-grey. Two races occur: nominate (Ug to Bu, Ke, and Ufipa Plateau, SWTz) as described; subcaerulea (E and STz) is paler.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in all levels of highland forest (mainly up to 2,700m, but down to 900m in Tanzania).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Complex warbling song consists of deliberate pure notes that rise and fall, and incorporates phrases of other crested-flycatchers, as well as mimicry of other birds.

images.caption: White-tailed Crested-flycatcher · Plate 214

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very similar to White-bellied Crested-flycatcher with dark slate-grey plumage (slightly blacker head, wings and tail) but differs in lacking white on belly. Sexes similar but adult female is duller. Immature similar to female but browner. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Shy but locally common in dense forest undergrowth at 700–2,150m, where its quiet and retiring nature make the species difficult to detect.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: An infrequent singer, most calls are harsh and scratchy, but also an accomplished mimic incorporating many species’ calls into a long rambling refrain.

images.caption: Dusky Crested-flycatcher · Plate 214

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A slim cerulean-blue monarch-like bird, with slightly crested head, black lores and whitish underparts washed pale blue-grey across the breast; plain blue graduated tail. Immature is greyer than adult, with buffy fringes to upperparts. Birds in EA are the race teresita.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common in the west in riverine woodland, forest, gardens and cultivation at 800–2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Long and complex warble of sweet and harsh notes, sometimes very metallic chits and tinks, and canary-like flourishes. A metallic chink is also used as a contact and alarm call.

images.caption: African Blue-flycatcher · Plate 215

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Plain yellowish-olive above with conspicuous dark eyes (narrowly ringed yellow), rather obvious pink lower mandible and bright yellow underparts. Immature is very similar to adult but slightly paler. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or small flocks are common in coastal and eastern lowland forests from sea level to 1,000m, usually in the high and middle canopy, often in mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Despite diminutive size, a noisy species, with a complex and pretty chittering song that breaks into a silvery descending series of clear notes.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Yellow Flycatcher

images.caption: Little Yellow Flycatcher · Plate 215

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Underparts are pale olive-brown with very narrow dark feather edges giving a scaly lace-like pattern on well-marked birds, but often difficult to see, and not present at all on some individuals. Throat and belly are pale grey, legs pale pinkish. Birds in EA are the race barakae.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Lone birds or pairs are common in the interior of good forest with ample leaf litter, at 700–2,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Distinctive song consists of a subdued chattering that breaks into two or three slowly delivered rising notes, tiu teu tii.

images.caption: Scaly-breasted Illadopsis · Plate 216

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Pale greyish-white throat (can look whiter when calling) contrasts with grey breast and rich brown flanks and vent. Legs purplish-grey. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in highland forest undergrowth (including remnant patches), mainly at 1,500–2,800m but down to 1,300m in western Tanzania. Often in groups of 4–6, but also in pairs. Likes dense leafy undergrowth and stays within 1.5m of the ground, only occasionally venturing higher in vine tangles.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls are similar to Brown Illadopsis but higher-pitched, and song tends to be a more rambling trrtrrtrr…ti-ti tiu tiyu.

images.caption: Mountain Illadopsis · Plate 216

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two races which may be separate species occur. In Ug and Kakamega, WKe, nominate (Pale-breasted Illadopsis) has a whitish throat contrasting with pale olive-brown breast, flanks and vent, and whitish belly; legs darker than in Scaly-breasted, grey or purplish-brown. At Ol Doinyo Orok, SKe, and in Usambara, Uluguru and Nguru Mts, Pugu Hills and on Zanzibar in NETz distans (Grey-breasted Illadopsis) has a pale grey breast contrasting slightly with olive-brown flanks and vent.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or small groups are shy, generally uncommon and patchily distributed in dense forest undergrowth and leaf litter, from near sea level to 1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song of the nominate race is similar to Brown Illadopsis but notes are generally higher-pitched and pinched, not clear. While one bird (or the group) chatters, the male sings a descending series with a hiatus before the final notes, titititi titityu. Race distans is more varied with more notes per phrase; male also calls a rising and falling explosive nasal tyah tya!

images.caption: Pale-breasted Illadopsis · Plate 216

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three distinct races are sometimes considered to be two species: in WUg, Rw and Bu, race atriceps (Rwenzori Hill-babbler) has an all-black head; in NEUg, Ke, N and SWTz the nominate race has a grey head and breast, and stierlingi from the Uluguru Mts to STz has a black face and black-streaked throat. If atriceps is considered specifically distinct, nominate and stierlingi are known together as African Hill-babbler.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and singles are common in highland forest in tangled vines and undergrowth at 1,500–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a variety of repeated thrush-like rich fluty warbles, but the notes are often slurred together.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities place this species in the genus Sylvia.

images.caption: African Hill-babbler · Plate 216

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Uniform brown above with very fine crown streaks, pale yellow eyes, a pale yellow or brownish bill, and russet-brown underparts (variably plain or paler on throat and belly). Four races occur: nominate (NEUg and Ke except SE) as described; sharpii (NEKe) is larger; heuglini (coastal Ke and NETz) is darker above, brighter below; and emini (NTz inland) has bolder silvery crown streaking.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in a variety of dry bushed habitats and nearby riverine vegetation, from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Unlike babblers, chatterer calls are more subdued, quieter and higher-pitched; group members keep in touch with excited piercing squeaks. Song is similar, but many notes are downslurred, louder and purer with irregular chittering, and interspersed with a louder downslurred seeeu.

images.caption: Rufous Chatterer · Plate 217

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dull brown above, with a small mask of grey skin around yellowish eyes and rather long decurved pale horn bill. Feathers on throat and breast have dark centres and pale fringes giving a scaly appearance. Three similar races occur: boranensis (NKe) has darker crown and stronger scaly underparts; keniana (EKe to NETz) is overall richer brown; and mentalis (NCTz) is more ash-brown.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small groups are local and uncommon in thick bush country, particularly Commiphora, from sea level to 1,500m, and usually in drier areas than Rufous Chatterer.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A high-pitched metallic, scraping and ratchet-like noise is the usual call, often given excitably by all members of the group.

images.caption: Scaly Chatterer · Plate 217

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Grey-brown babbler with yellow eyes (in west and north) or orange-red (more southerly); underparts, including lores and chin, grey-brown with small pointed arrow-shaped tips to feathers of throat and breast. Two races occur: emini (west of the Rift) is darker on the head than kirkii (more easterly), but they intergrade.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in range, but distribution is patchy, inhabiting a variety of bushed and wooded country with undergrowth, from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call varies locally; starts almost mechanically with alternated nasal notes, leading to all members giving a raucous cackling which develops into long nasal whining downslurs tyah tyah tyah…

images.caption: Arrow-marked Babbler · Plate 217

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Arrow-marked Babbler with yellow eyes, but lores and chin whitish. Pale tips to feathers of throat and breast similar to Arrow-marked but not as pointed. Birds in EA are the race cinerea.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Groups are common in bushed and wooded country at 600–2,000m, mainly to the north of Arrow-marked Babbler but overlapping in western Uganda where it prefers moister habitats.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A very loud, raucous, wooden-sounding chatter breaks into a scolding k-tchah k-tchah k-tchah…

images.caption: Brown Babbler · Plate 217

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Differs from Arrow-marked Babbler in having white eyes and black lores. Two distinctive races occur: widespread nominate (Sharpe’s Babbler) is speckled with pale fringes to throat and breast; in Nanyuki area of CKe race vepres (Nanyuki Babbler) is darker brown above with a pure white throat (variably extending to belly as a mix of white and brown streaks on some birds).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Groups are common in a wide range of more open bushed and wooded country at 1,000–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls are higher-pitched than most typical babblers with a slightly insane and hilarious laughing quality; race vepres is similar.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: In the Ndutu area of Serengeti, NTz, babblers with white eyes, whitish throats and variably blotched creamy and brown wings and underparts may be an undescribed race.

images.caption: Black-lored Babbler · Plate 217

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dark olive-brown babbler with very dark lores and ear-coverts, and pale fringes to crown, throat and breast giving a scaly appearance; eyes orange-yellow. Two races may occur: nominate in coastal Ke; while in extreme NEKe, birds with variable white head markings and creamy-white eyes are possibly Ethiopian carolinae.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Groups are shy, keeping to coastal brush and other thick cover.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: One of the most grating and toneless calls of any passerine, with a typical babbler pattern. Group keeps up a continuous rasping noise with a peculiar undulating quality. Single call is a ti-yor ti-yor ti-yor…

images.caption: Scaly Babbler · Plate 218

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Brown above with dark lores and conspicuous white eyes; underparts mostly white with brown breast patches and flanks. Two races occur: nominate (CKe to extreme NTz) as described; rufuensis (NTz) is more grey-brown with pale scaly fringes to the crown and often more extensive breast patches.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: East Africa endemic: locally common in woodland, acacia country, bush and gardens, mainly at 1,000–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Group members give single high-pitched explosive downslurs and unique long scolding nasal notes that lack the unpleasant churring of other babblers.

images.caption: Northern Pied Babbler · Plate 218

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Plumage highly variable, but typically a scaly-looking red-eyed babbler with broad black and white fringes to throat and breast. Large parts of the plumage are often dark brown (or blackish) with smaller patches of tawny-rufous and white; rump, flanks and vent frequently rufous-brown. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local and threatened Kenya endemic: population centred around Mt Kenya, where it mainly survives in steep-sided valleys within cultivated areas at 1,300–1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is similar to Scaly Babbler, a very harsh scolding chatter which breaks into a rapid downslurred iyor-iyor-iyor… VU

images.caption: Hinde’s Babbler · Plate 218

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Boldly marked black, white and grey tit with a black cap, bib and collar encircling white cheeks; vertical black line on throat and breast. Birds in EA are the race barakae.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in a variety of dry bush country (particularly acacia) below 1,600m in the north.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls and scolds are similar to White-bellied Tit, but harsher with more a vibrating ratchet-like quality: chrrrt-chah, chrrt chah-chah.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Northern Grey Tit, Acacia Tit

images.caption: Somali Tit · Plate 219

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is all sooty-black with red eyes (may slow slight greenish gloss to upperparts in fresh plumage); female is similar but slightly greyer. Immature is like female, but has small white tips to wing-coverts and dark eyes. Typical tit-like behaviour helps identify this species from other black forest birds. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in the canopy of primary and secondary forest at 900–2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical call is a musical chi-chyu with last note downslurred, but also tends to babble with a mixture of harsh tit-like notes, sweet whistles and slurs.

images.caption: Dusky Tit · Plate 219

melaniparus-albiventris.ref: Plate 220: Tits Ii, Spotted Creeper And Tit-Hylia
melaniparus-albiventris.name: White-bellied Tit

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Black head and upperparts contrast with white lower breast and belly; wing-coverts and outer tail also edged white. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are common in a wide variety of habitats including forest edge, open woodland and bush country at 900–3,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Some variation, but mostly a typically tit-like harsh, nasal and scolding si-chah-chah-chah that may break into a scratchy medley.

images.caption: White-bellied Tit · Plate 220

melaniparus-fringillinus.ref: Plate 220: Tits Ii, Spotted Creeper And Tit-Hylia
melaniparus-fringillinus.name: Red-throated Tit

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Face, nape, throat and upper breast pale rufous (so not very well named) contrasting with slaty-grey crown and back; wings blackish broadly edged white. Immature is browner with scaly rufous and grey crown. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: East Africa endemic: pairs and family parties are local and generally not numerous in acacia woodland at 1,000–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song contains sweet downslurs and rhythmical phrases, and the call is a rather harsh chi-chr’chr’chr’chr’chr or ti-tchah-tchah-tchah-tchah-tchah. SPOTTED CREEPER Unlike any other bird in East Africa, the sole representative of the family Certhiidae in the Afrotropical region.

images.caption: Red-throated Tit · Plate 220

salpornis-salvadori.ref: Plate 220: Tits Ii, Spotted Creeper And Tit-Hylia
salpornis-salvadori.name: African Spotted Creeper

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A well-camouflaged mottled brown and white creeper with a slender decurved bill. Two races occur: nominate (Ke and Tz) has larger white spots on upperparts than emini (NWUg).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Lone birds or pairs are locally common in miombo (Brachystegia) woodland in Tanzania, and rare elsewhere, where they prefer large acacia trees and remnant woodland at 600–2,300m. Always busy, climbing up trunks or large limbs in the canopy before swooping to the bottom of another tree and working upwards again.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Frequently heard call is a high-pitched si si si si… and the song consists of different high-pitched toneless and rhythmical slurs: si sisi siu siu seeu seeu.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Now considered a separate species from Indian Spotted Creeper S. spilonota. TIT-HYLIA Distinctive, tiny birds variously placed in no fewer than six different families at one time or another, most recently in Scotocercidae.

images.caption: African Spotted Creeper · Plate 220

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Six races occur and can be assigned to four groups: roccatii (Ug, WKe, Rw, Bu and NWTz) has yellowish forecrown, olive upperparts and pale yellowish underparts; pallescens (WTz) and rhodesiae (SWTz) are similar but whitish or buff below; and robertsi (coastal Ke and ETz) is greyish above and pale yellowish or buffy below. Races sylviella (CKe to NTz) and sharpei (SWKe to NWTz), often considered a separate species (Buff-bellied Penduline-tit), have a buffy forecrown, grey upperparts and cinnamon-buff underparts, richer and darker in sharpei (encircled by a dotted line on the map).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local and uncommon in a variety of open woodland from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical call is a rapid high-pitched and squeaky si-si-si-si…, but buff-bellied races are slower and also give a rhythmical tit-like ti-chi-wee ti-chi-wee ti-chi-wee…

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: African Penduline-tit

images.caption: Grey Penduline-tit · Plate 221

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Grey Penduline-tit, but grey-brown above and very pale grey-brown below. Also compare with Yellow-vented Eremomela (especially immature which lacks pale yellow vent). Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread but never numerous in dry bushland mainly to north and east of Grey Penduline-tit, at 400–1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical call is a repeated si si si si si si si si si si, and a more complex warbled series of high squeaky and spitted notes.

images.caption: Mouse-coloured Penduline-tit · Plate 221

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Seven similar races occur, with many intergrading where they meet; typically green above and bright yellow below with narrow white eye-ring. Kenya White-eye has paler yellow underparts. Some races of African Yellow White-eye have green sides to breast and flanks, and are similar to Mbulu White-eye, but are brighter yellow below with a largely different range and prefer lower altitudes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: The only white-eye in Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and much of Tanzania where it inhabits a variety of moorland, forest, woodland, gardens and cultivation, from sea level to 3,400m. In Kenya it is common in the west and highlands in the north, east to Nairobi.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: An attractive songster; a series of typical white-eye slurred notes, but some have a rather burry quality.

images.caption: African Yellow White-eye · Plate 221

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to African Yellow White-eye but paler, with clear pale powder-yellow underparts and a small eye-ring. Two races occur: nominate (widespread) as described; jubaensis (Ethiopia border south to Mt Kulal) is duller.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Inhabits a variety of woodland and bush country from sea level to 1,800m, often in drier areas than other white-eyes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is an excitable collection of squeaks and descending slurs put together in a random pattern; call is a burry descending seeu.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered a race of Abyssinian White-eye Z. abyssinicus.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Pale White-eye

images.caption: Kenya White-eye · Plate 221

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A green and yellow white-eye with a large white eye-ring, broad yellow forecrown, black lores, and greenish underparts with a yellowish throat and vent. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to the central Kenya highlands, where it is common and widespread in forest, edge, secondary growth and gardens, from Meru, Mt Kenya, and the Aberdares to Nairobi.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a rising and falling jumble of often-slurred notes, with a rather mournful quality, and calls are a downslurred seyuuu and piu given while foraging and moving in flocks together.

images.caption: Kikuyu White-eye · Plate 222

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to South Pare White-eye, but has a very broad white eye-ring and no yellow on forecrown, darker green upperparts, largely grey underparts (with no belly stripe), and a yellow throat and vent. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: A Kenya endemic that is common in highland forest on the Taita Hills and Mt Kasigau, south-eastern Kenya).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is similar to Kikuyu White-eye, but has a more pinched quality; calls are also similar. EN

images.caption: Taita White-eye · Plate 222

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has an iridescent green head which often shines blue leading to confusion with Blue-throated Brown Sunbird; back and wings matt moss-green, lower breast to vent grey with creamy-white pectoral tufts (usually concealed); eyes brown.
