No non-breeding plumage. Adult female has iridescent blue-green cap and entirely grey underparts. Immature is dark olive above, yellowish below, with black face and upper breast. Race in EA is viridisplendens.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in highland areas at 1,200–2,500m, inhabiting forest edges, secondary growth, gardens and cultivation.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call consists of explosive loud chit notes and a drawn-out chiawee. Song starts with these notes and then breaks into a loud, energetic rolling flourish unlike any other sunbird.

images.caption: Green-headed Sunbird · Plate 224

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has a fairly narrow red breast-band bordered above by a thin blue band; steel-blue uppertail-coverts and light olive-yellow belly. In areas of overlap best identified from Northern Double-collared Sunbird by narrower breast-band, more golden-green sheen to upperparts, and slightly longer bill. Female is dull olive-brown above, paler plain yellowish-olive below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in highlands of Kenya and northern Tanzania, east to Kilimanjaro and the North Pare Mts in heath, forest, bamboo and gardens at 1,800–3,700m. Wanders seasonally to lower altitudes but usually at higher altitudes than Northern in areas of overlap.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song commences with a few loud hissed notes, immediately followed by a rolling, rattled prinia-like si-si-si turilirilirilirilirili.

images.caption: Eastern Double-collared Sunbird · Plate 225

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very similar to Eastern Double-collared Sunbird but red breast-band is broader bordered above by a thin violet band; violet uppertail-coverts and olive-brown belly. Usually shines more blue-green and bill slightly shorter than Eastern. Female is very similar to female Eastern, but slightly darker and shorter-billed. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and in similar habitats to Eastern but in areas of overlap usually found at lower altitudes. In the east typically at 1,700–2,800m, but in the west down to 1,250m. Its upper altitude limits are restricted by presence of Rwenzori Double-collared Sunbird on some Albertine Rift mountains.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A few introductory dry chipping notes precede a sweet rolling warble that ends in a series of identical chips.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly known as C. preussi.

images.caption: Northern Double-collared Sunbird · Plate 225

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to several previous species, but lacks thin blue or violet line above red breast-band; uppertail-coverts greenish-blue, belly dark olive. Adult female is dark olive above with a short supercilium; paler throat grades into indistinctly streaked yellowish-olive breast and flanks. Birds in EA are the race orphogaster.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a variety of lush habitats including forest edge, moist bush and cultivation at 700–1,750m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a dry rattle preceded by a rather tuneless warbled trtrtrtr trilitrilitrilitrilit.

images.caption: Olive-bellied Sunbird · Plate 226

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has a small purple cap and bluish uppertail-coverts; broad red breast-band, yellow pectoral tufts (usually concealed) and a black belly. Adult female is mostly brownish-grey above, with long whitish supercilium and blackish tail very narrowly edged white; underparts paler. Immature is like female with a blackish upper breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Race turkanae feeds on aloes and flowering acacias in northern semi-arid bush country at 400–1,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is 4–5 distinct similar or rising and falling chips. Song is a rather monotonous, but musical two-tone seesawing like a slow trill.

images.caption: Shining Sunbird · Plate 227

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very similar to Hunter’s Sunbird with scarlet breast and small iridescent green cap; chin and throat iridescent green. Three races occur: lamperti (most of Ug to WTz and east to CKe) has tiny blue bars across scarlet chest (visible at close range); gutturalis (elsewhere in Tz, and coastal Ke) is similar but has a small violet shoulder patch; acik (NUg) is slightly paler with no violet shoulder patch. Adult female is dark brown above with dark mottled throat and upper breast, becoming streaked on paler yellowish belly. Immature male is like female with dull red feathers on breast. Immature female is like female with blackish throat.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Inhabits forest edge, woodland, gardens and cultivation from sea level to 2,150m. Usually in pairs, but sometimes in large numbers at Leonotis flowers.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a short series of loud explosive notes, interspersed with monotonous, complex chips and scratchy notes.

images.caption: Scarlet-chested Sunbird · Plate 227

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very similar to Scarlet-chested Sunbird but throat black bordered with narrow iridescent green malar stripes (difficult to see); purple rump and shoulder spot. Breast scarlet, but can show a few tiny blue bars at edges. Female and immature female similar to Scarlet-chested but not as dark brown and slightly paler below. Immature male is like female but has some red on breast. Two races occur: nominate (widespread) as described; race siccata (NWKe) has breast more orange-red.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and singles are widespread and locally common in semi-arid bush country from near sea level to 1,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is very different from Scarlet-chested Sunbird, a rapidly delivered and energetic rolling warble.

images.caption: Hunter’s Sunbird · Plate 227

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male sometimes appears all black, but in good light shows small iridescent blue-green cap and amethyst-purple throat patch; small patch on bend of wing is iridescent fiery amethyst. Adult female is olive-brown above with narrow white supercilium; underparts pale yellowish with extensive dusky-brown streaking. Immature is like female with dark throat. Birds in EA are the race kirkii.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in a wide variety of habitats including forest edge, woodland, moist bush and gardens from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call consists of both scratchy chirps and sweeter seet notes, and song is not unlike a small Acrocephalus warbler in quality.

images.caption: Amethyst Sunbird · Plate 228

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is mostly black with an iridescent green cap and throat (narrow violet edges to both are hard to see in the field). Adult female is brown above with narrow creamy supercilium; underparts pale yellowish, heavily streaked brown. Immature like female but has dark throat patch, and some iridescent green spots on throat of immature male. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in the west, in forest and nearby secondary growth at 700–1,800m, with a preference for the midstorey and canopy.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varied song can be a rambling mixture of sweet and harsh twitters, or 4–6 loud rising and falling chips followed by a rising, rapidly spitted sequence, chu chu chu chu chi tttttt. SHORT-BILLED FOREST SUNBIRDS WITH GREEN UPPERPARTS Two fairly similar sunbirds with totally separate ranges.

images.caption: Green-throated Sunbird · Plate 228

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large, long-billed, all-olive sunbird with variably paler underparts. Bill black but sometimes shows a smidgen of orange at base of lower mandible. Six races differ mainly in tone, and are sometimes placed in two groups; race ragazzii (Ug to WKe and south to WTz) and granti (Pemba Is, Tz) have yellow pectoral tufts in males only; neglecta (CKe to NTz), changamwensis (coastal Ke to NETz), olivacina (coastal SETz) and alfredi (STz) have yellow pectoral tufts in both sexes. Immature resembles adult.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in forest interior, less so at edge, from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A very noisy and musical song that starts slowly, then accelerates up and down the scale. Call is a dry persistent high-pitched raspy chip.

images.caption: Olive Sunbird · Plate 229

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Olive Sunbird in structure, but plumage mostly cold grey with a darker tail. At close range, shows an oily-blue sheen on shoulder, very narrow black malar stripe and red pectoral tufts. Sexes alike. Two races occur: fischeri (coastal Ke and Tz) as described; zanzibarica (Zanzibar Island, Tz) is paler below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs inhabit woody thickets, coastal scrub and mangroves where generally uncommon.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a harsh and tuneless scratchy note, but the song is an attractive and simple refrain of well-emphasised rather indignant notes, tu-ti-tu ti-tu-tu, which rise and then fall.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities use the name C. veroxii.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Grey Sunbird

images.caption: Mouse-coloured Sunbird · Plate 229

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has fiery copper head, mantle and breast, with gold, ruby, green and purple reflections, wings and tail blacker. Non-breeding male is much duller, with iridescent wing-coverts, often blacker on underparts with a few scattered iridescent feathers. Female is olive-brown above with blackish tail; dull yellow below. Immature like female, but with dark throat on immature male. Two races occur: nominate (Ug to WKe and south to NWTz) as described; chalceus (SWTz) is more greenish-bronze on head and back.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in lightly wooded areas, bush country, the fringes of swamps and cultivation, at 700–1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: One song is like a bouncing ball, tit tit tit tit tttttttttt, and there is also a similar series that breaks into a twittering flourish.

images.caption: Copper Sunbird · Plate 229

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male above may shine golden-green in certain lights; broad maroon breast-band bordered above with blue; no pectoral tufts. Two races occur: northern osiris (NEUg to NKe) has a black belly, and suahelicus (most of range) has a greyish-black belly. Larger and longer-billed than similar Purple-banded Sunbird. Female is greyish-brown above with an indistinct supercilium, yellowish below with dark streaking and paler throat. Immature is like female but has blackish throat and mottled breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in open woodland and bush country at 800–2,000m, but exact range uncertain because of confusion with Purple-banded Sunbird.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Strong call is a rapid nasal chipping, often given in long complaining series, while the song incorporates the call together with some loud sweet warbled chipping notes.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Marico Sunbird

images.caption: Mariqua Sunbird · Plate 230

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to Mariqua Sunbird but has small violet forecrown and orange-yellow pectoral tufts (usually concealed). Adult female is olive-brown above with a faint supercilium; yellowish below (may show very indistinct dusky streaks). Immature like female; immature male has blackish throat and random iridescent feathers. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather uncommon in forest edge, secondary growth and at flowering trees in nearby cultivation at 700–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Unique song commences with a long dry rattle that breaks into a sweeter sitisitisitisiti.

images.caption: Orange-tufted Sunbird · Plate 230

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is extremely similar to Mariqua Sunbird but is more blue-green, slightly smaller and shorter-billed; maroon breast-band bordered above with violet-blue, belly black. Breast-band violet and maroon. Non-breeding male is like female with black throat and some iridescence on wing-coverts. Female is grey-brown above with a fine supercilium; underparts pale yellowish finely streaked dusky. Immature is like female with a dark throat. Birds in EA are the race microrhynchus.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in woodland, thickets and seasonally wet bush country in the west, and moist coastal scrub in the east, but exact range uncertain because of confusion with Mariqua Sunbird.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a distinctive sip sip, while the song commences with the call and breaks into a complex musical rolling twitter.

images.caption: Purple-banded Sunbird · Plate 230

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is very similar to Purple-banded Sunbird but maroon breast-band narrow, bordered above by a thin line of blue. Female is grey-brown above with a pale supercilium and darker tail; underparts pale yellowish streaked dusky. Immature is like female with dark throat. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Largely confined to the dry hinterland of Kenya and extreme north-eastern Tanzania where it prefers dry Acacia and Commiphora scrub. Range intersects the moister habitats preferred by Purple-banded Sunbird; common in the Tsavo area, in Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a rapid chuchiti-tsi-tsi-tsi-tsi-sitisee-see-see-see-chitisee…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Purple-banded Sunbird.

images.caption: Tsavo Sunbird · Plate 230

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to Purple-banded Sunbird but has broad band of iridescent violet from lower throat to breast. Slightly larger and longer-billed than Purple-banded Sunbird, and lacks maroon on breast and pectoral tufts. Female is grey-brown above with a pale supercilium; plain grey below with pale yellowish belly. Immature male is like female with blackish throat. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather uncommon in coastal bush country.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls tsik, tsik, tsik, or chee-chee-chee; song is a thin high, hurried tsewtsi-tse-tseep-sisisi-tsewtsi-tsi-tsi and a short trill.

images.caption: Violet-breasted Sunbird · Plate 230

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three races with variable colour on underparts occur: breeding male igneiventris (Ug south to Mt Mahari, Tz) is mixed orange-red and yellow below, with red pectoral tufts; falkensteini (most of Ke and Tz) is yellow to orange-yellow below; albiventris (NEKe) is white below; both falkensteini and albiventris have yellow pectoral tufts. All three races have violet-blue throat and upper breast. Non-breeding male is similar to female with scattered iridescence. Adult female igneiventris and falkensteini are olive-brown above with blue-black tails, and plain yellow below; female albiventris is greyer above and whiter below. Immature male is similar to female with blackish throat.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Yellow-bellied races are common and widespread, particularly in the highlands in a variety of woodland, bush and cultivation; albiventris occurs in semi-arid bush in north-eastern Kenya. From sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a harsh nasal scraping note, while among a wide variety of songs, a si-sit-swit chichichchi is most common.

images.caption: Variable Sunbird · Plate 232

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has head and upperparts iridescent green; iridescent green throat and upper breast is bordered below by a narrow violet band; mid-breast to vent yellow. No pectoral tufts. Adult female has similar iridescent green upperparts; underparts including throat and breast plain yellow. Immature is like dull pale female. Three similar races vary mainly in tone.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common and widespread from sea level to 2,800m in a wide range of fairly lush habitats, including forest, bush and coastal lowlands.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a repeated slightly lisping but penetrating seeyu seeyu seeyu…, while song is a repeated si-si-sut seeu seeu seeu seeu seeu seeu… Pygmy Sunbird Hedydipna platura  18cm, 7";  9cm, 3.5" Breeding male is like Collared Sunbird but has very long thin tail-streamers. Non-breeding male is like female with some iridescence. Adult female is greyish-olive above, plain yellow below with whitish chin. Immature is like female, with blackish throat in male. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local in north-western Uganda in semi-arid bush and wooded grassland. Erratic in north-western Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a downslurred pinched seea seea seea, while song begins with these notes and continues with a high-pitched series of hissed notes breaking into a flourish.

images.caption: Collared Sunbird · Plate 232

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very dark bottle-green above including head, throat and upper breast (can appear black); pectoral tufts orange (usually concealed), lower breast to vent white. Adult female is grey-brown above with narrow whitish supercilium; white below. Immature is like pale female. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: East Africa endemic. Local in forest canopy from sea level to 900m, in Arabuko-Sokoke Forest, Kenya, and in East Usambara and Udzungwa Mts, Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a penetrating twee-twee (first note upslurred, second downslurred). Song is a long complex high-pitched twittering incorporating harsh chittering notes. EN

images.caption: Amani Sunbird · Plate 232

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is dull plain green above and yellow below with a dark iridescent blue-black forecrown, throat and upper breast; pectoral tufts yellow. Adult female is plain olive-green above with a narrow supercilium; yellower below, paler on throat. Immature is like female but more olive-brown above. Birds in EA are the race yokanae.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are local and generally uncommon in thick coastal forest, but ascend to 1,000m in the East Usambara Mts, Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a loud nasal repeated tyow tyow tyow…, or a higher-pitched rapidly repeated nasal upslur. Song is a distinctive, regularly repeated, descending series. VIOLET-BACKED SUNBIRDS Males are all similar with short bills, violet upperparts, small turquoise patches near bend of wing, and whitish underparts, best identified by range, habitat and association with more distinctive females.

images.caption: Plain-backed Sunbird · Plate 233

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is violet-blue above with slightly contrasting turquoise-blue rump and white underparts. May look black and white in poor light. Yellow pectoral tufts usually concealed. Warbler-like adult female is brown above with a bold white supercilium and iridescent dark blue uppertail; entirely white below. Beware pollen-stained individuals with orange throats that have been feeding on aloes. Immature similar to female but may have a faint yellow wash to belly. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in semi-arid areas from sea level to 1,300m where they are particularly fond of acacia and Commiphora bush, when flowering aloes and Loranthus are plentiful.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a scratchy complaining downslur, given irregularly when feeding or repeatedly when excited.

images.caption: Eastern Violet-backed Sunbird · Plate 233

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Largest fiscal with long broad all-black tail and white rump. Black cap contrasts with dark grey back and scapulars; all other similar but smaller fiscals have white scapulars. Female is similar but has small chestnut flank patch. Immature similar to other immature fiscals but larger. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and sociable with groups of up to 10 birds interacting noisily in wooded grassland, acacia country and coastal bush from sea level to 1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Groups call noisily together from the tops of bushes; a lazy, liquid simple sequence of 3–5 notes mixed with a throaty churr.

images.caption: Long-tailed Fiscal · Plate 234

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male appears stocky and short-tailed with black crown and nape contrasting with pale grey back. Very similar to Somali Fiscal, but secondaries all black (without white tips). Adult female has small chestnut flank patch. Immature is dark grey-brown above and white below, finely barred throughout. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs are common in dry open grassland and bush country from sea level to 1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rarely heard song is a simple but very liquid and rhythmic wi-tirir-chh, wi-tink-tink, repeated monotously. Alarm is a nasal buzz.

images.caption: Taita Fiscal · Plate 234

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slightly slimmer than very similar Taita Fiscal and best identified by white tips to secondaries which appear as a narrow white trailing edge in flight. Sexes alike (female lacks chestnut on flanks, unlike most other fiscals). Immature shows fine barring on grey-brown upperparts and whitish underparts. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are fairly local and not common in arid and semi-arid areas of northern Kenya at 400–1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rarely heard song is quite different from Taita Fiscal, having a scratchy rather than a liquid quality wir-chi-ri-ri; the rising notes are repeated for long periods.

images.caption: Somali Fiscal · Plate 234

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A slim narrow-tailed fiscal with grey upperparts, black mask through eyes (narrowly bordered above with white), white V on back, and plain black wings. Grey-backed Fiscal is much larger, with black forecrown and much white in tail. Adult female is similar with chestnut flank patch. Immature is browner above, with light barring above and below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Solitary or in pairs, a quiet bird of forest edge, woodland and lush gardens at 700–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a quiet sometimes subdued but attractive warble which sounds rather like a slow Sylvia warbler.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Mackinnon’s Fiscal

images.caption: Mackinnon’s Shrike · Plate 235

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is a large bulky shrike with broad black mask (including across forecrown), grey upperparts and large white patches at base of tail. Adult female is similar but has small chestnut flank patch. Immature is grey-brown above with much fine dusky barring. Three similar races occur: nominate (widespread in Ug to W and CKe) as described; intercedens (WKe) is similar but larger; and boehmi (SWUg, SWKe and WTz) is darker grey above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in open woodland, acacia country and cultivated areas, often near water, and mainly at 600–1,900m, rarely to 3,000m. Small sociable groups are conspicuous and noisy, often gathering to display and wave their broad tails.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Several group members sing together a sequence of liquid but raspy descending slurred scraping notes. Call is a harsh schaah.

images.caption: Grey-backed Fiscal · Plate 235

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Palearctic migrant mainly in Mar–May when in very clean adult plumage with dove-grey upperparts, broad black mask extending across forecrown, white throat and pale pink breast. Non-breeding adult and first-year (rare Oct–Dec) are whiter below and lack black on forecrown. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common passage migrant which can appear almost anywhere from sea level to 3,000m and like a typical shrike perches conspicuously in the open.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Frequently calls a sharp scolding chek, but is otherwise rather quiet. In Apr–May, prior to leaving, may sing a sweet Acrocephalus-like song with a strange throaty quality.

images.caption: Lesser Grey Shrike · Plate 235

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is black and white with pale apricot flanks unlike any other shrike. Adult female is similar but slightly paler and browner above. First-winter is grey-brown above with scaly fringes and a pale-faced appearance. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Scarce Palearctic visitor in Oct–Mar, with most records from Lake Baringo, Kenya. Only record from Tanzania is one on Pemba Island in Nov 2003. Shy, perching in canopy of acacia trees, then dropping to the ground to feed.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent in the region, but occasionally calls a harsh tthek.

images.caption: Masked Shrike · Plate 235

lanius-phoenicuroides.ref: Plate 236: Lanius Shrikes Iii And Long-Tailed Shrikes
lanius-phoenicuroides.name: Red-tailed Shrike

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is reddish-brown above with brighter rufous crown and tail; prominent black mask bordered above by white supercilium, small white primary patch and whitish underparts. Female and first-winter are like dull version of male, with browner less bold mask. Distinguished from similar plumages of Red-backed Shrike by plainer back and rufous tail above and below. Doubtfully separated from female and immature Isabelline, but usually whiter below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common winter visitor from Palearctic, occurring almost anywhere on passage in Oct–Apr, but commonest in eastern Kenya and eastern Uganda. Prefers open bush country from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a harsh chack or quiet repeated ch-ch-ch…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Taxonomic status controversial, being sometimes considered conspecific with Isabelline Shrike. Moreover, in small area of overlap on breeding grounds, Red-tailed hybridises with both Isabelline and Red-backed Shrikes.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Turkestan Shrike

images.caption: Red-tailed Shrike · Plate 236

lanius-isabellinus.ref: Plate 236: Lanius Shrikes Iii And Long-Tailed Shrikes
lanius-isabellinus.name: Isabelline Shrike

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has crown and mantle uniform greyish-brown with rufous rump and tail; black mask bordered above by narrow white supercilium (often indistinct), small white primary patch and buffy underparts. Female and first-winter are like dull version of male, with a browner less bold eye mask. Distinguished from similar plumages of Red-backed Shrike by plainer back and rufous tail above and below. Doubtfully separated from female and immature Red-tailed Shrike, but usually more buffy below. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Winter visitor from Palearctic in Oct–Apr. Less common than Red-tailed Shrike, being most frequently found in open bush country in eastern Kenya, although smaller numbers may occur further west.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Similar to Red-tailed Shrike.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Taxonomic status controversial, being sometimes considered conspecific with Red-tailed Shrike. Moreover, in small area of overlap on breeding grounds, Isabelline hybridises with both Red-tailed and Red-backed Shrikes.

images.caption: Isabelline Shrike · Plate 236

lanius-collurio.ref: Plate 236: Lanius Shrikes Iii And Long-Tailed Shrikes
lanius-collurio.name: Red-backed Shrike

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is distinctive with blue-grey crown, neat black mask, chestnut wings, blue-grey rump and black tail with white patches at base. Three forms vary in colour on back (grey or chestnut) and forecrown (grey or whitish), with much variation although species is usually considered monotypic. Female and first-winter are very similar to Red-tailed and Isabelline Shrikes and best identified by more heavily barred underparts and grey undertail. First-winter is also more heavily barred above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common, widespread and conspicuous Palearctic migrant and winter visitor from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Makes tak or chack calls which are higher-pitched than Isabelline Shrike, but may also sing a rather sweet Sylvia-like song prior to departure.

images.caption: Red-backed Shrike · Plate 236

urolestes-melanoleucus.ref: Plate 236: Lanius Shrikes Iii And Long-Tailed Shrikes
urolestes-melanoleucus.name: Magpie Shrike

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large, very long-tailed shrike. Adult male is predominantly black with white scapulars forming conspicuous white V across back, greyish-white rump, and variable white wing patches. Adult female is similar, but has white flank patch. Immature is dark blackish-brown with dusky barring. Birds in EA are race aequatorialis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Highly sociable shrike usually found in small groups of up to 10 in open acacia woodland at 800–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is an attractive, extremely liquid rambling refrain, repeated for long periods without pause. Call is a harsh chahh-chahh-chahh…

images.caption: Magpie Shrike · Plate 236

corvinella-corvina.ref: Plate 236: Lanius Shrikes Iii And Long-Tailed Shrikes
corvinella-corvina.name: Yellow-billed Shrike

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A long-tailed, dull brown shrike with conspicuous yellow bill. Closer views reveal broad dark brown band through eye, numerous narrow black streaks above and below, and in flight rufous patches in the primaries. Sexes alike. Immature is similar, but duller with much barring. Birds in EA are the race affinis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small groups of 4–8 are locally common in woodland and bush country at 600–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Social and noisy; call is a very harsh tik-chahh or tik-tik-tik-chahh which is often repeated.

images.caption: Yellow-billed Shrike · Plate 236

laniarius-major.ref: Plate 237: Boubous, Gonoleks, Bushshrikes And Brubru
laniarius-major.name: Tropical Boubou

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Black and white boubou washed very pale pink on the breast. Three races occur: nominate (Ug east to Great Rift Valley, Ke, and south to STz) has a long white wing stripe; ambiguus (highlands of NKe to NTz east of the Rift) has a short white bar restricted to the wing-coverts; and mossambicus (SETz) is like nominate but washed stronger pink below. Immature duller, with variable fine barring above and below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in forest undergrowth, bush and gardens from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Pairs usually call a melodic antiphonal duet, perfectly timed to sound like one bird, wii-hoo wii-hoo or wii-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo are typical but there are many variations. Calls include a harsh tchik and coarse scolds.

images.caption: Tropical Boubou · Plate 237

laniarius-sublacteus.ref: Plate 237: Boubous, Gonoleks, Bushshrikes And Brubru
laniarius-sublacteus.name: East Coast Boubou

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Differs from Tropical Boubou in uniform black wings. Immature has buffy barring above and white underparts. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Inhabits forest undergrowth and thick scrub, mainly in coastal lowlands of Kenya and north-eastern Tanzania, but ascends to 1,800m in the Uluguru Mts.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls a repeated melodic hoo-he-ooh and harsh scolds.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Tropical Boubou.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Zanzibar Boubou

images.caption: East Coast Boubou · Plate 237

laniarius-erythrogaster.ref: Plate 237: Boubous, Gonoleks, Bushshrikes And Brubru
laniarius-erythrogaster.name: Black-headed Gonolek

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is striking black and scarlet with creamy-white eyes and a buffy vent. Immature is blackish-brown above, pale dirty yellow below with extensive dark scaling and random red spots. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common but rather shy in woodland, thickets and cultivation at 600–1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male calls a loud, rather oriole-like note and female may answer with a harsh ratchet-like tchtchtchtchtch.

images.caption: Black-headed Gonolek · Plate 237

laniarius-mufumbiri.ref: Plate 237: Boubous, Gonoleks, Bushshrikes And Brubru
laniarius-mufumbiri.name: Papyrus Gonolek

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Black-headed Gonolek but has golden-yellow crown, narrow white wingbar and orange-red underparts. Immature is duller than adult with dingy olive crown, dull yellowish throat and dirty pinkish-orange underparts. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in dense papyrus swamps at 1,100–1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male calls a musical wi-onk wi-onk or chonk-chonk (sometimes in a rhythmical series), and female may answer with similar antiphonal notes or a harsh chh-t-chh.

images.caption: Papyrus Gonolek · Plate 237

laniarius-ruficeps.ref: Plate 237: Boubous, Gonoleks, Bushshrikes And Brubru
laniarius-ruficeps.name: Red-naped Bushshrike

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Black, white and grey bushshrike with an orange-red crown or nape. Two races occur: kismayensis (NEKe) has entirely rufous crown; rufinuchalis (NEKe to Tsavo, SEKe) has rufous hindcrown. Female similar, but duller with olive-grey back. Immature lacks rufous on crown; grey above and greyish-white below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Shy and local in thick semi-arid bush country from sea level to 1,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male calls a nasal, burry frog-like upslur and female answers with loud ratchet-like antiphonal notes, or a series of four identical descending ratchet-like rasps. Other calls include harsh tik and deep clicks.

images.caption: Red-naped Bushshrike · Plate 237

nilaus-afer.ref: Plate 237: Boubous, Gonoleks, Bushshrikes And Brubru
nilaus-afer.name: Brubru

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small black-and-white bushshrike with chestnut flanks. Four races occur: three are similar with male having bold white supercilium; nominate (NUg) has centre of mantle and wing stripe rich buff; minor (N and EKe to NETz) has mantle and wing stripe whiter; and massaicus (Ug, Rw, CKe and NTz) has mantle and wing stripe creamy pale rufous with darker chestnut flanks. Female is similar but more blackish-brown above; some show dark streaks on throat. Immature is dark brown, mottled creamy-buff above, and lightly barred below. In distinctive race nigrotemporalis (Tz apart from north) male lacks white supercilium; female has short supercilium and black speckles on breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs are widespread, common and vocal in canopy of open woodland and acacia country from sea level to 2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a loud, very burry, gently rising and rather telephone-like slur brrrrrrrrp; also utters loud scraping notes.

images.caption: Brubru · Plate 237

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Only black boubou of bush country. Adult is dull dark slate-grey. Immature is finely barred dark brown and black. Two races occur: nominate (widespread); degener (coastal Ke and Tz) is slightly smaller and paler.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in semi-arid bush in north-eastern Uganda and Kenya, although in south-western Uganda and most of Tanzania in moister woodland, undergrowth and thickets in cultivation, from sea level to 2,200m. Invariably in pairs and rather shy, often on the ground, but calls from bush tops in early morning.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Duets: male mainly calls a loud shhhhhhh or clicking followed by coco-weet, the weet rising as an interrogatory slur. Also varied nasal, gruff and reverberating calls accompanied antiphonally by the female.

images.caption: Slate-coloured Boubou · Plate 238

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: All-black boubou with a glossy sheen and red-brown eyes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Restricted to coastal Somalia and Kenya north of Lamu and Manda Islands. Little known, except on Manda where reasonably common in thick coastal scrub.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A variety of far-carrying ringing melodic notes and a deep throaty churr.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered to be a black morph of Tropical Boubou.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Manda Black Boubou, Black Boubou, Coastal Boubou

images.caption: Manda Boubou · Plate 238

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two similar and one distinctive races occur, with intergrades in areas of overlap: in hamatus (SWKe and most of Tz) adult male is black above, with bright red eyes, and a pure white rump, scapulars and wing edgings; nairobiensis (inland EKe and NETz) is similar, but with more black in wings. Female has short white stripe before eye, a greyer rump and off-white underparts. Immature is similar to female but duller above with buffy underparts and wing edges. Distinctive race affinis (Zanzibar Puffback) (coastal Ke and Tz south to Rufiji River), has plain black wings on both sexes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common in forest edge, woodland and gardens from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male gives a short click followed by a rising upslurred whiplash note, to which the female frequently answers with a harsh paired ssssshh ssssshh. In display flight also gives a loud abrupt chow-chow-chow-chow-chow-…, up to 10 times, and a rapid tik-weeu- tik-weeu- tik-weeu…

images.caption: Black-backed Puffback · Plate 239

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two races occur: adult male of widespread malzacii is very similar to male Black-backed Puffback, but pale grey on scapulars and rump with slightly heavier bill; eyes orange-red. Adult female is earth-brown above with buffy wing edges; tawny-buff below. Immature is similar to female but has buffy fringes above. In race erythreae (Moyale, NKe) female is like male, but dark chocolate-brown above and creamy-white below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in a variety of woodland and dry acacia country at 900–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls shorter, much harder and delivered more rapidly than Black-backed, often tik-teek or tik-tik-teek, and in display flight a strident chok-chok-chok-chok-chok.

images.caption: Northern Puffback · Plate 239

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to other male puffbacks but much smaller, with pale base to lower mandible, and pale grey scapulars and rump; eyes red. Adult female and immature are pale grey-brown above with a whitish loral spot, narrow white eye-ring, and pale dirty-white underparts. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In East Africa pairs are restricted to semi-arid and arid bush at 200–1,200m, particularly in Commiphora and acacia woodland.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: During display flight male repeats a downslurred cheow-cheow-cheow-cheow, female sings a subdued and complex warble incorporating clicks and strange mewing sounds.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: At 1,600–1,750m on south side of Ngong Hills, Ke, males have a black crown that contrasts with a silver-grey (not black) back and much greyer wings, and may represent an undescribed race.

images.caption: Pringle’s Puffback · Plate 239

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has black cap, grey back and paler grey rump, all contrasting slightly with darker grey wings; very pale grey below. Adult female has distinctive grey crown contrasting with earth-brown back and wings; rich tawny-buff below with white belly. Brown eyes and pink legs and feet in both sexes. Immature is like dull female. Two races occur: nandensis (WUg to WKe) as described; kungwensis (Mt Kungwe, WTz) male has greyer crown.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Restricted to primary forests of the west where it prefers the canopy and midstorey tangled vines at 900–2,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Common call is a very harsh, grating and ratchet-like trrrrrrrrr.

images.caption: Pink-footed Puffback · Plate 239

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is larger than similar Brown-crowned Tchagra with a broad black crown-stripe. Immature duller with mottled brown and black crown-stripe; lacks narrow black edges to crown-stripe of Brown-crowned. Two races occur: armenus (widespread) as described; orientalis (coastal Ke and ETz lowlands) is slightly paler.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread from sea level to 2,100m inhabiting cover within open woodland, bushed grasslands and dry country.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a loud far-carrying fluty and thrush-like whistled song unlike any other tchagra. Calls include a wide variety of harsh and hollow-sounding tak notes and churrs.

images.caption: Black-crowned Tchagra · Plate 240

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has brown crown-stripe narrowly bordered black (sometimes giving impression of black crown). Immature is like adult but duller with more buffy-brown underparts. Two races occur: emini (Ug to NWTz, and east to CKe) as described, minor (EKe and most of Tz) is paler brown above, whiter below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Similar to Black-crowned Tchagra with no obvious habitat differences and often occurs in same areas, from sea level to 2,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song, often given in a parachuting display flight, is a rapidly delivered series of sweet descending downslurs, tiu tiu tiu tiu tiu… Also a variety of both harsh and musical churrs and sharp tak notes.

images.caption: Brown-crowned Tchagra · Plate 240

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small slim tchagra with three narrow black stripes on head, one through each eye and one on centre of crown. Immature is similar to adult but crown-stripe is shorter. Two races occur: nominate (NEUg to EKe) as described; mandanus (Manda and Lamu Islands and Tana River Delta, Ke) is paler and more sandy with a broader crown-stripe.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Usually solitary but may join mixed-species flocks in dense cover in dry bush and semi-desert country from sea level to 1,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Parachuting song flight is similar to Brown-crowned Tchagra but slightly higher-pitched, slurring a more distinct tui tui tui tui tui…

images.caption: Three-streaked Tchagra · Plate 240

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slender, long-legged, and striking bushshrike with patches of brilliant carmine-pink in plumage. Two races occur: male hilgerti (mainly north of equator) has a brilliant carmine stripe from throat to lower breast (without any black); male cathemagmenus (south of hilgerti) has similar carmine stripe and black band around throat. Both have bright carmine-pink rumps. Females of both races have whitish throat edged with black gorget and bright pink breast stripe. Immature is duller than adult and pale-fringed above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in pairs and small groups in semi-arid bush country at 150–1,600m. Calls from open bush tops and frequently runs on the ground.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Race hilgerti song is a loud far-carrying high-pitched and metallic peeee-yng, dropping and fading at the end, frequently given in duet, or sometimes with a distant female replying with a lower note. Race cathemagmenus is similar, but call is lower-pitched.

images.caption: Rosy-patched Bushshrike · Plate 240

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has a narrow yellow supercilium separating the grey crown from the black mask. Bright yellow below with broad wash of orange over breast. Immature lacks black on face, has a whiter throat and plain yellow underparts. Two similar races occur: nominate (WUg) as described, similis (elsewhere) has greyer ear-coverts. Grey-headed Bushshrike is much larger with yellow or orange eyes, a huge thick bill and no black on face.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in a wide variety of woodland, thickets and acacia country, from sea level to 3,000m, often in mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varied song is typically a repeated series of high bell-like notes which fade at the end, whi-wi-whi-whi-whi-wherrr. Also pupupupu and assorted harsh scolds.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Sulphur-breasted Bushshrike

images.caption: Orange-breasted Bushshrike · Plate 241

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large, bulky, grey-headed bushshrike with a massive black bill and yellow eyes, whitish loral spot not always obvious, underparts variable with rufous-orange wash across breast. Three races occur with many intergrades: catharoxanthus (Ug to WKe) is plain yellow below; approximans (Ke to NTz) has rufous-orange on breast to flanks; hypopyrrhus (Rw to STz) has less extensive rufous on breast. Immature is paler with dark eyes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and common at forest edge, in woodland and acacia country from sea level to 3,000m, often in same areas as much smaller Orange-breasted Bushshrike.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a slowly repeated hollow whistle, either whoo-whooik, whoo-whooik… or either note repeated alone. Also makes loud clicks and a screeched ereeek, ereeek, ereeek…

images.caption: Grey-headed Bushshrike · Plate 241

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive bushshrike with rufous-chestnut crown, throat and breast. Immature is olive above with pale yellow spots and stripe on wing (reminiscent of nicators on Plate 155), dull yellow below with fine barring. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather secretive in undergrowth and tangled creepers in forest and densely wooded valleys at 700–2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male calls a long, strange deep vibrating note worrrrk to which female responds with a harsh tkk, or a long kssshshssssh. Also gives a variety of harsh notes.

images.caption: Lühder’s Bushshrike · Plate 241

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has a broad black stripe through the eye and across the forecrown (without a white border); tail is green with small yellow tips. Four colour morphs differ in colour of underparts, which may be yellow, red, buffy-apricot with a white throat, or rarely (in East Usambara Mts) black on throat and breast. Immature is paler than adult without black mask. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Fairly common and widespread in highland forest at 900–2,300m, occasionally down to 300m. Most frequent in the canopy and often with mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Commonly gives a rising nasal snore, or varied but clear hollow ringing notes including whoop-wah, with second note lower, or a repeated ooo.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Sometimes considered conspecific with Many-coloured Bushshrike.

images.caption: Black-fronted Bushshrike · Plate 242

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to Gorgeous Bushshrike but forecrown bright red, with no red below black breast-band and a black tail. Adult female is similar but breast-band narrower and tail more olive-green. Immature is mostly dull green above, with yellowish-olive wash to underparts, all extensively finely barred blackish and buff; vent dull red. An extremely rare morph with yellow forecrown and throat is also known. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Reasonably common, but shy and difficult to observe in the undergrowth of highland forests at 1,600–3,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: High distinctive and far-carrying repeated wick, wick wick-wick-wick…

images.caption: Doherty’s Bushshrike · Plate 242

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is blackish above (greyer on back and wings) with bold white forecrown and supercilium; underparts white with faint creamy wash. Immature is barred above with buff and black, pale yellowish with grey fringing below. An aberrant form with a broad black breast band is known from Kakamega, WKe. Birds in EA are the race jacksoni.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in canopy at forest edge, in secondary growth and nearby forest thickets at 1,100–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In the west commonly calls a repeated rhythmical wi-chuk-a-chuk wi-chuk-a-chuk, while more easterly birds give a high whistled and rhythmic descending sequence of notes, pipipipi piu piu piu piu.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Grey-green Bushshrike

images.caption: Bocage’s Bushshrike · Plate 242

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Stocky and thick-necked with a white crown, blackish mask and dark brown wings and tail; white rump is conspicuous in flight. Immature is finely barred above, with a scaly brown crown, broad white nape collar, and buffy-brown breast; bill yellowish. Usually considered monotypic although birds in NEKe are slightly larger.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or small flocks are common in bush country from sea level to 2,300m; they perch in trees and fly down to the ground to feed.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Group frequently calls together, a series of pinched, nasal complaining notes and harsh chatters, also querulous loud squeaks in flight. [Alt. White-rumped Shrike] HELMETSHRIKES Previously placed in no fewer than five different families, they are now considered a subfamily of Vangidae. Helmetshrikes are active, social and vocal birds that travel slowly in loose flocks, often snapping their bills. Sexes are alike.

images.caption: Northern White-crowned Shrike · Plate 243

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Widespread black and white helmetshrike. Four variable races occur: concinnatus (NWUg) and cristatus (most of Ug to NWKe) are large with long curly white crests; closed wing of concinnatus has a long white stripe, cristatus is almost plain blac k; vinaceigularis (N and EKe to NETz) has a straight white crest and no white in closed wing; poliocephalus (SWUg and SKe south through Tz) has a short straight grey crest and long white wing stripe. All races have yellow eye wattles and, in flight, a conspicuous white bar across primaries. Immature is similar to adult but dingy, with dark eyes and no wattles.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and locally common in open woodland and bush country from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Flocks frequently call long burry downslurred notes, kirro, kirro, kirro, often accompanied by bill snaps and chattering.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: White Helmetshrike

images.caption: White-crested Helmetshrike · Plate 243

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger than White-crested Helmetshrike with long, pointed grey crest extending back from centre of crown; eyes yellow (without wattles); black patches on sides of breast. Immature is similar but has shorter crest and dark eyes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to East Africa, this uncommon helmetshrike occurs in acacia and leleshwa bush country at 1,200–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Complex calls are deeper and more guttural than White-crested Helmetshrike, but also include typical helmetshrike bill snapping and harsh churring notes

images.caption: Grey-crested Helmetshrike · Plate 243

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Grey-brown helmetshrike, darker on head and wings, with whitish vent and corners to tail; forecrown has rectangular patch of velcro-like chestnut bristles; eyes yellow with blue-grey wattles. Three similar races occur: keniensis (CKe, rare) lacks pale band behind chestnut forecrown; kirki (coastal Ke) is slightly paler and browner than nominate (coastal Tz). Immature is dull brown, dark-eyed and lacks bristles on forecrown.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Groups of up to 50 (but often far fewer) are locally common in woodland and forest canopy from coastal lowlands to foothills of north-eastern Tanzania. Often joins mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very noisy, roving groups give frequent high-pitched upslurred trilled rattles trrrrrrrrrt trrrrrrrrrt, and song consists of these rattles mingled with tit-like whistles.

images.caption: Chestnut-fronted Helmetshrike · Plate 243

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Chestnut-fronted Helmetshrike but larger and much blacker with a bright red bill and eye wattles, and yellow eyes. Two races occur: graculinus (Ke and NETz) has a distinct crest; tricolor (SEBu and Tz) has a shorter crest. Immature is duller and browner with short crest.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are widespread but only locally common in a variety of woodland from sea level to 1,900m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Mobile flocks give a range of strange burry, buzzy calls and a loud descending sequence of piercing whistles tiyui-tiyui-tiyui-tiyu-tiyui-tiyui… accompanied by rasping notes and bill snaps.

images.caption: Retz’s Helmetshrike · Plate 243

dicrurus-adsimilis.ref: Plate 244: Drongos, Piapiac And House Crow
dicrurus-adsimilis.name: Fork-tailed Drongo

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is glossy black (blue-black in good light) with a deeply forked tail and red eyes.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: that moulting birds can show strange-looking double-forked tails. Inner webs of flight feathers ashy, often making wings look pale silvery in flight. Immature has brown eyes, buffy speckling on wings, fine grey and black barring below, and a less deeply forked tail. Two races occur: fugax (widespread) as described; divaricatus in NUg and NKe has a shallower-forked tail (intergrades occur).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common and widespread at forest edge, woodland, semi-arid bush and cultivated areas from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Highly variable song, a long rambling and rather coarse mix of nasal, twangy notes, none of which are clear or pure. Often mimics other species. Calls are rather harsh.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities treat race divaricatus as a separate species, Glossy-backed Drongo.

images.caption: Fork-tailed Drongo · Plate 244

ptilostomus-afer.ref: Plate 244: Drongos, Piapiac And House Crow
ptilostomus-afer.name: Piapiac

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Unusual, unmistakable crow; slender adult often appears all black with a long graduated tail, but at close range may show dull brown wings and tail edges. In flight, pale grey-brown translucent primaries visible. Bill black in adult, bright pink with a black tip in immature. Eyes violet-purple. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are locally common at 600–1,500m in open country near Borassus palms. Invariably associated with cattle or large game, where they run about to flush and catch insects.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Noisy, especially at dawn and dusk, when parties maintain a cacophony of loud, squealing skweeer or pee-ip note HOUSE CROW An introduced, invasive crow.

images.caption: Piapiac · Plate 244

corvus-splendens.ref: Plate 244: Drongos, Piapiac And House Crow
corvus-splendens.name: House Crow

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slim black crow with variable (light or dark) grey neck and breast, and longish, slightly decurved bill. Immature is duller than adult with brownish cast. The nominate race is common, while intergrades with other (uncertain) races probably account for variation of paler and darker birds.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: An introduced crow from the Indian subcontinent. Numerous and regarded as a serious pest along much of the coast where it destroys nests of smaller birds and competes with the resident Pied Crow.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very noisy, calling a short, hurried kwaa kwaa…

images.caption: House Crow · Plate 244

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slim-looking, all-black crow with noticeably narrow bill and lax throat (feathers appear shaggy). Adult may show bluish or purplish sheen in good light, but in worn plumage is often rather brown. Immature has dull brownish wash on head and underparts. Race in EA is kordofanensis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks occur commonly in Kenya highlands and parts of northern Tanzania, mainly favouring open country and farmland below 2,500m, although a separate population occurs in semi-desert in northern Kenya at about 400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In addition to typical crow-like caw, makes a variety of strange throaty and liquid calls, the notes tending to slur together: kwah kworlik kworlik koh.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Cape Rook

images.caption: Cape Crow · Plate 245

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Boldly marked black-and-white crow: white hind-collar extends around sides of neck and across breast. Immature is similar to adult, but duller. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs to large flocks are common and widespread in all but the driest areas, as well as towns and open country from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Variable calls include both long and short caw in flight, while perched birds may utter a deeper call or a quiet musical hollow clork clork…

images.caption: Pied Crow · Plate 245

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather stocky glossy black crow with a thick bill and short tail that stops well before wingtips at rest. In flight, tail looks very short and wings appear broad. Head usually black (like body) but may be dark brown and thus similar to Somali Crow (which has a longer tail). Immature is duller and browner than adult. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and small flocks are common across northern Kenya at 400–2,600m in dry bush country with cliffs.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical calls are varied but rather high-pitched caw, although also has a quiet subsong of sweet notes usually given from shade during the heat of the day.

images.caption: Fan-tailed Raven · Plate 245

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Fan-tailed Raven but has slimmer bill, usually (but not always) a brown head and nape, and tail extends near to wingtips. In flight has obviously longer slimmer tail than very short rounded tail of Fan-tailed Raven. Immature is paler and browner especially on the head. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and small flocks are common in semi-desert country of northern Kenya from 200m to about 1,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varied caw and kwaar-kwaar notes, plus a throaty rolling krrrrrrrr.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered a race of Brown-necked Raven C. ruficollis of North Africa and the Middle East.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Dwarf Raven

images.caption: Somali Crow · Plate 245

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very large black raven (sometimes browner on head) with broad white collar at base of hindneck, and thick white-tipped black bill. Immature is duller than adult. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks prefer vicinity of cliffs and mountains, but wander widely down to 400m in eastern Kenya and as high as 5,800m on Mt Kilimanjaro, northern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a rather high-pitched kerrrrrh, with a more purring tremulous quality than other ravens and crows.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: White-naped Raven

images.caption: White-necked Raven · Plate 245

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Black-headed oriole with upperside of central tail feathers olive-green, greater coverts greenish-yellow, outer secondaries black broadly edged whitish and inner secondaries black broadly edged yellow. Immature has head and breast streaked blackish or dark green (and can be mistaken for Green-headed Oriole). Four similar races differ mainly in minor variations in yellow or golden tones.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in woodland, forest edge, gardens and bush country from sea level to 2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typically calls a hurried set of 4–6 mainly slurred notes lasting about 2 seconds, tiau…tor…te…wah wee…o, repeating the same sequence monotonously, and at times mimicking other species softly.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: African Black-headed Oriole

images.caption: Eastern Black-headed Oriole · Plate 246

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Eastern Black-headed Oriole but upperside of central tail feathers black, greater coverts bright yellow, outer and inner secondaries largely black with narrow yellow-olive edges, thus wings look overall blacker than Eastern Black-headed. Immature is streaked blackish on head and upper breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common, largely replacing Eastern Black-headed in highland forest at 1,500–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A very simple repeated song of four mainly slurred notes, wi te-wor who, is typical, but also a long, rambling and complex whistled sequence that may be given as a duet.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Hybrid larvatus × percivali with mixed tail patterns occur occasionally in central highlands of Ke.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Montane Oriole, Black-tailed Oriole

images.caption: Mountain Oriole · Plate 246

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Eastern Black-headed Oriole with upperside of central tail feathers olive-green, greater coverts dull greenish-grey, outer secondaries edged dark grey (not whitish), and inner secondaries dull olive-green (not yellow). Immature is much duller than adult with dark olive-green mottled head and breast. Birds in EA are the race laetior.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in forest and forest edge in Uganda and forest interior at Kakamega, western Kenya, at 700–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Simple song consists of 3–4 loud and distinctly separated notes, or hor wah hor wi wah, or wi wor hor wah, with the last note higher.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Western Oriole

images.caption: Western Black-headed Oriole · Plate 246

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Unique oriole with plain moss-green head, throat and upper breast; back, wing-coverts and uppertail also moss-green, wings largely plain grey without white spots on primary-coverts. Beware head can look dark when birds are high in the forest canopy. Immature is duller, streaked green on underparts. Birds in EA are the race amani.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local but not uncommon within its restricted range, from sea level to 1,800m in forest, mature woodland and well-established secondary growth.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a typical oriole-like hor weeeu, but also commonly makes a strange burry cat-like upslur nraaaaaah.

images.caption: Green-headed Oriole · Plate 246

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is only likely to be confused with Eurasian Golden Oriole, but has longer black streak extending behind eye and broad yellow edges to most wing feathers. Adult female is similar to male but duller and washed olive above. Immature has dark bill, greenish-yellow edges to wing-coverts, and pale yellow and whitish underparts streaked black. Two similar races occur: notatus as described; and nominate with narrower yellow edges to wing feathers.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Nominate race (Uganda to western Kenya) is mainly a non-breeding visitor from the northern tropics Jun–Feb. Race notatus (southern Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Kenya and Tanzania) is a non-breeding visitor from southern Africa mainly in Mar–Sep. Seasonally widespread and particularly common in Tanzania and coastal Kenya. Inhabits forest, woodland, lush gardens and moist bush country from sea level to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rather forced but typical oriole-like song, wee ah hah waah, but also commonly gives a burry extended miaowing upslurred nahararahhhhh.

images.caption: African Golden Oriole · Plate 247

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has a short black eyestripe extending from base of bill to eye, and mostly black wings. Adult female is highly variable, like the male, or with white from throat to vent, or like immature with red bill. Immature differs from immature African Golden by having slightly darker, plainer wings. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common passage migrant and less common winter visitor in Oct– Apr. Can occur anywhere on passage, but may be numerous along the coast in Apr.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Most frequently heard call is a harsh scolding miaowing kree-er, but in Apr may also give a fluty and rolling ori-ori-ori-ole. OXPECKERS Endemic to Africa and now placed in their own family, Buphagidae. The two species differ mainly in bill, eye, eye wattle and rump colour. Often called tick birds, they are mainly seen feeding on large wild mammals or cattle. Flocks roost together in dead trees. Sexes are alike.

images.caption: Eurasian Golden Oriole · Plate 247

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult differs from Yellow-billed Oxpecker by entirely red bill, red eye with bright yellow eye-ring, and plain brown rump (uniform with back, wings and tail). Immature is similar to immature Yellow-billed but more uniform dark brown above and may show reddish base to bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread from sea level to 3,000m wherever wild mammals and undipped cattle occur. Overlaps with Yellow-billed in many areas but usually more numerous.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is softer than Yellow-billed Oxpecker, a ssshhhhhh all on one tone, and often accompanied by spitted notes and clicks, tsik, tsik…

images.caption: Red-billed Oxpecker · Plate 247

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult has a bulbous bright yellow red-tipped bill, bright red eyes and pale creamy-buff rump that contrasts with darker back, wings and tail (obvious even at distance). Immature has bill and eyes dark brown and slightly less obvious pale rump. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Fairly common (but less so than formerly) from sea level to 3,000m. Typically in small loose flocks, feeding around a variety of larger mammals, and being particularly fond of buffaloes, giraffes and hippos.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls are harsh rasps, rraaah, given both perched and in flight.

images.caption: Yellow-billed Oxpecker · Plate 247

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Stunningly beautiful starling: iridescent blue, green and purple above, with a very long narrow graduated tail and bright golden-yellow breast and belly. Sexes alike. Immature is much duller, with head, mantle and upper breast mainly dull olive-brown, and breast to vent pale yellow. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in dry bush country in the east, from near sea level to 1,200m (and rarely to around 1,800m). Usually in small flocks, restlessly moving through low bushes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a simple, repeated and complaining downslurred rranyh.

images.caption: Golden-breasted Starling · Plate 248

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is all black with grey eyes. Adult female is dark slate-grey with large chestnut patches in the primaries. Immature is a duller version of respective adult. In the field difficult to distinguish from Stuhlmann’s Starling but ranges do not overlap. When perched high in the canopy can also be confused with Waller’s Starling, but latter is larger and stockier with chestnut wing patches and red eyes in both sexes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to East Africa; flocks are fairly common but local in the canopy of montane forests in central Kenya and north-eastern Tanzania at 1,000–2,500m (but down to 450m in East Usambara Mts, north-eastern Tanzania).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a warbled drongo-like refrain; call is a repeated pleep note.

images.caption: Kenrick’s Starling · Plate 248

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male appears all black in the field (blue-black in good light) with brown eyes and a very narrow pale yellow eye-ring. Adult female is dark slate-grey with large chestnut patches in the primaries. Immature is like dull female. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in the canopy of highland forest in the west at 1,500–2,600m, but also in the Tugen Hills in the Great Rift Valley, Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Flocks are very vocal, especially in flight, a simple but musical tuweet…

images.caption: Stuhlmann’s Starling · Plate 248

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is a large blackish starling (appears blue-black in good light) with chestnut primaries, and long and pointed but not particularly well-graduated tail. Adult female has greyer head and neck with some dark grey and violet streaking. Immature similar, but duller. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are common, usually in the vicinity of rocky hills or cliffs, but also in towns, at 500–4,100m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is an attractive loud, oriole-like, fluty wi-tyuor, either repeated when perched or as a single downslur in flight.

images.caption: Red-winged Starling · Plate 249

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smaller than Red-winged Starling with a shorter tail and red eyes. In good light, adult male shows blue-black and sometimes greenish reflections. Adult female has dark grey head and breast with some dark greenish-blue streaking. Two races occur: nominate (highlands of Ke east of the Great Rift Valley, south to STz) as described; elgonensis (highlands of Ug to WTz and Ke west of the Great Rift Valley) female has grey restricted to throat. Immature is like dull adult.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are widespread and common in the canopy of highland forests mainly at 1,500–3,000m, but down to 300m in the East Usambara Mts, north-eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call is a loud far-carrying wee-tyur (the first note short and rising, the second descending and fading away), given when perched and in flight.

images.caption: Waller’s Starling · Plate 249

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Red-winged Starling but slimmer with a well-graduated tail and slender bill. Adult male has deep violet-blue-black gloss. Adult female is duller, with a scaly grey head and breast (sometimes very pale). Immature is like dull adult. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are locally common, particularly around highland forest and on alpine moorland, but are not restricted to high elevations and wander widely at 1,400–4,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Perched flocks give a loud but rather tuneless warble which may continue for long periods without pause. In flight, flock members give harsh slurred notes, teeeo or teeoo.

images.caption: Slender-billed Starling · Plate 249

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Largest of the red-winged starlings with a very long graduated tail and a small spiky cushion of feathers on the forecrown. In good light shines glossy blue-black. Sexes similar, immature duller. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are sometimes common but rather local in the north, where restricted to semi-arid country below 1,300m. Often associated with cliffs and gather to feed in Salvadora bushes.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual flight call is a loud, spitted, rising swi-chit or a more subdued but fluty weeo which perched birds may develop into a long but simple medley.

images.caption: Bristle-crowned Starling · Plate 249

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The most widespread blue starling. Two races occur: cyaniventris (Ug except SW, Ke except SE, and NTz) all iridescent blue-green (including tail) with ear-coverts appearing as a dark blue or blackish patch, and yellow or occasionally orange eyes; sycobius (SWUg, SEKe, and Tz) is smaller and greener with magenta-violet flanks and belly, and is very similar to Lesser Blue-eared Starling. Immature has dark eyes, is uniform dull blue-black above and sooty-brown below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks occur in a wide variety of habitats including woodland, bush country, cultivation and gardens from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a very complex and varied, somewhat drongo-like warble, incorporating harsh and sweet notes. Call is a characterful, nasal, cat-like mew myaaah, which is often given in flight.

images.caption: Greater Blue-eared Starling · Plate 250

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Greater Blue-eared Starling but smaller, smaller-billed and shorter-tailed; dark mask through eye narrower. Often looks very green, but this is not a reliable field character. In some lights, flanks and belly shine purplish-blue like sycobius race of Greater Blue-eared Starling but ranges are totally different. Immature is dull sooty-brown on head and underparts with grey-brown eyes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in open woodland and bush below 1,600m, but also wanders to seasonally moist semi-arid areas.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Groups make a continuous chattering consisting of a warbled, burry downslur, interspersed with explosive swii notes, which are also given in flight.

images.caption: Lesser Blue-eared Starling · Plate 250

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large, dark-looking, purplish-blue starling with a long graduated tail, black mask and conspicuous creamy-white eyes. Immature is similar but duller and dark-eyed. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are common, wide-ranging, and often seen on the ground in woodland, bush country and around cultivation from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a long, complex and loud warble with both harsh and sweet notes, and mimicry. Calls swi-chew and a slightly tremulous kwerr given perched and in flight.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Rüppell’s Long-tailed Starling

images.caption: Rüppell’s Starling · Plate 251

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Darker than Greater Blue-eared Starling with dark blue-green gloss to head, mantle and upper breast. Rest of underparts dark purplish-black grading to black on belly and vent. No black spots on wing-coverts; eyes orange-yellow. Immature duller with sooty-black underparts. Two races occur: nominate (as described) is widespread; vaughani with a purple gloss to the head is endemic to Pemba Island, Tz.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Usually in flocks, and common in forest and coastal bush in the east below 1,000m. but also occurs north-east of Mt Kenya at 1,500–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: May call for long periods, often from perches within shade, a variety of short pinched notes interspersed with an oriole-like wi-tchew.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Lamprotornis.

images.caption: Black-bellied Starling · Plate 251

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Largest glossy blue starling. In good light a stunning bird with brilliant green, blue and golden reflections above, black wing spots, and iridescent deep-purple, blue and coppery underparts. Eyes pale creamy-yellow. Sexes similar, but female has bluer underparts. Immature is blackish below with random blue feathers. In flight, wings look broad and make loud swishing sound. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks occur in treetops at forest edge and in remnant woodland at 700–2,300m, and are more common in the west.

sections.heading: Voice
