sections.text: Unusual, rather outrageous call combines a mixture of explosive and variable gurgles, plops and creaks, krrrau kiau ko-chock wiow wi-eee, which may be delivered as a song for long periods.

images.caption: Splendid Starling · Plate 251

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has entire upperparts, throat and upper breast brilliant fiery iridescent violet and plum, with a snowy-white breast to vent; can appear black and white when backlit. Adult female is very different, almost pipit-like, being mottled brown and blackish above, slightly rufous on head, and white below with numerous narrow brown streaks. Immature is like female. Two races occur: nominate (mainly NUg and NKe) as described; male verreauxi (elsewhere) differs in having a white base to outer tail feathers.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common throughout the year from sea level to 3,000m, but numbers greatly increase in Mar–Sep with arrival of southern migrants.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song has no real pattern, nor does it contain particularly sweet or harsh notes, but consists of rather rambling, slurred wails, riariarowh.

images.caption: Violet-backed Starling · Plate 252

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult dark blue-black above, with white throat and upper breast merging to tawny-apricot flanks and belly; eyes creamy-yellow. Immature is duller above and dark-eyed, with small arrow-shaped spots on breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or small flocks are generally uncommon in the canopy of highland forest at 1,400–3,000m, where they often perch on exposed dead branches.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is an extraordinary refrain of very high bell-like rising and falling spitted notes, then rising again, vaguely reminiscent of Dark-backed Weaver. Flight calls include high-pitched spitted spink and chin’k notes.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Cinnyricinclus.

images.caption: Sharpe’s Starling · Plate 252

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is black and white with brilliant red eyes, in flight obvious white wing patches. Adult female has similar pattern and eye colour, but is grey on the head and upper breast. Immature like female, but grey-brown above with dark eyes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks are locally common from sea level to 1,200m, mainly in the semi-arid north and east, but wander to moist coastal woodlands.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a jumble of harsh and soft squeaks, resulting in an unmusical, formless ramble. Alarm call is a harsh and loud ti-chuk chuk-chuk.

images.caption: Magpie Starling · Plate 252

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is blue-black above including head, throat and breast extending as a ‘V’ down centre of breast. Lower breast to vent white with black crescent on lower flank; eyes creamy-yellow. Immature dull, largely brown with extensive streaking below; eyes change from brown to yellow with age. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic: local, uncommon, and restricted to highland forest at 1,800– 2,500m in central Kenya and north-eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very high-pitched calls include metallic spitted notes similar to Sharpe’s Starling, while the song is a mix of short musical slurs and spitted notes.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Cinnyricinclus. VU BROWN AND WHITE STARLINGS Two distinctive brown and white starlings in different genera.

images.caption: Abbott’s Starling · Plate 252

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large white-crowned starling, brown with iridescent green sheen above, brown with white streaks below, and white vent and undertail-coverts. Eyes white, bill black. Sexes alike. Immature is much duller brown with less streaking below and black-tipped bright yellow bill. In flight, white wing patches are obvious. Two races occur: nominate (extreme NEKe) and similar but smaller horrensis (NKe).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are locally common in semi-arid and desert country, often on the ground around habitation, at 300–1,000m in extreme northern Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song consists of various long or short rising slurs with a skirled quality, the effect being a querulous and soft sounding krrrri-kuri-kuri-koyi. Flight call is a burry koyi.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Spreo.

images.caption: White-crowned Starling · Plate 252

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is easily separated from similar starlings by creamy-white eyes, narrow white breast-band, white underwing-coverts, and white vent and undertail-coverts. Immature is duller with dark eyes and no white breast-band; differs from similar immatures by white vent. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are confiding, common and widespread in semi-arid country, open woodland and bushed grassland, including towns and gardens, from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a long ramble of rising and falling skirls and squeals. In flight, calls a purred skrrrrrri.

images.caption: Superb Starling · Plate 253

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is darker-toned and more violet-blue above than Superb Starling with red eyes (not white); lacks white breast-band and vent. In flight reveals rufous (not white) underwing-coverts. Immature is dark-eyed and much duller, with paler rufous underparts. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to Kenya and Tanzania: pairs and small flocks are common in open woodland and bush country at 500–2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a series of short, low-toned, quite musical phrases that often end with querulous rising notes. In flight, calls a throaty kurrrakurrrakurrra.

images.caption: Hildebrandt’s Starling · Plate 253

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is richer and darker than both Superb and Hildebrandt’s Starlings with orange or orange-red eyes and very dark rufous belly. Head, breast and upperparts largely glossy rich violet-blue. Immature has head and mantle dull ash-brown. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are generally uncommon wanderers in dry bush country (especially Commiphora) from near sea level to 1,300m. Most frequently recorded Aug–Mar, often associated with other rufous-bellied starlings.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is similar to Superb Starling, but louder, harsher, and broken into short phrases, rather than a long continuous ramble. In flight, calls a throaty kurrikurrikurri. PALE STARLINGS Two pale, largely brown starlings of bush country and savanna. See also vagrant Rosy Starling on p. 603.

images.caption: Shelley’s Starling · Plate 253

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is a rather distinctive ashy grey-brown starling with paler crown, black lores, white eyes and white lower breast to belly. Immature is browner with yellowish bill and dark eyes. In flight, easily separated from Wattled Starling by grey-brown (not white) rump. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are locally common in dry bush country from near sea level to 1,900m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical song is rather burry and monotonous with some notes repeated for long periods. A striking krrrrrrikrrrrrikrrrrrri is commonly heard in flight.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Spreo.

images.caption: Fischer’s Starling · Plate 253

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Non-breeding male, female and immature are the most frequently encountered: all are pale brown with darker wings and tail, and a whitish rump. At close range, they show a small area of pale yellow skin around and behind the dark eye. Greyer breeding male has extensive yellow and black skin and wattles on the head. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks are highly mobile, common and widespread throughout the region from sea level to 3,000m, often associating with cattle and plains game.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Flocks create an unusual medley of squeals, squeaks and hissing notes, without any really distinctive form or pattern.

images.caption: Wattled Starling · Plate 253

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has pale eyes, a small black bib, curved rufous streak around ear-coverts, and a rufous rump. Female is paler and duller with grey (not black) throat. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to Kenya and northern Tanzania where common in the highlands, inhabiting bushed grasslands, cultivation, villages and towns at 1,000–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A versatile sparrow, singing musical chirps and scratchy calls sometimes interspersed with canary-like upslurs, weeer.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with P. shelleyi and known as Rufous Sparrow.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Kenya Sparrow

images.caption: Kenya Rufous Sparrow · Plate 254

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has bright chestnut crown and nape, grey mantle and rump with heavy black streaks, black bib, and yellow cheeks and underparts. Non-breeding male has greyer crown and is generally paler. Adult female and immature are similar to female House Sparrow, but have longer pale buffy supercilium and are washed pale yellow below. Birds in EA are the race fulgens; recent reports of paler nominate race hybridising with House Sparrow in EKe require confirmation.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are rather local and restricted to tree-lined dry riverbeds and villages in arid country at 300–1,000m in northern Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical call is a rather loud and monotonous upslurred chirping treeet, cheritt.

images.caption: Somali Sparrow · Plate 254

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smallest sparrow in our region. Breeding male is all deep chestnut gradually grading to a darker face. Compare with Chestnut Weaver which is much larger with a well-defined black head and longer heavier bill. Non-breeding male has fine buffy edges to feathers giving scaly appearance. Immature male is irregularly and boldly mottled chestnut and buff. Adult female has typical female sparrow plumage, but small size, pale chestnut supercilium and chestnut throat patch (if present) aid identification. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a wide variety of bushland from sea level to 2,200m, often near water. Wanders widely, occurring in large flocks particularly after rains.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a continuous series of varied trills, while in flight calls chup chup chup… SPECKLE-FRONTED WEAVER Distinctive weaver with a sparrow-like appearance.

images.caption: Chestnut Sparrow · Plate 254

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small, rather sparrow-like weaver. Forecrown black speckled white, nape rufous, malar stripe black. Rest of plumage grey-brown above and pale greyish below. Sexes alike; immature slightly duller. Birds in EA are race emini.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks often feed on the ground and tend to be rather local in wooded grassland and semi-arid areas with bush cover at 400–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a rather pipit-like series of chips and trills, while flight and feeding call is a series of identical spitted notes, tsitsizizizizit…

images.caption: Speckle-fronted Weaver · Plate 254

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Classic grey-headed sparrow: rufous-brown back contrasts with grey nape and crown, whitish throat clearly separated from greyer breast and upper belly, lower belly whitish. Birds in EA are the race ugandae.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Occurs mainly west and east of Swahili Sparrow in Tanzania, often around human settlements, and extending to coast at Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Generally prefers higher rainfall areas than Parrot-billed Sparrow.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song consists of typical sparrow-like chirps, either delivered slowly or more rapidly with a seesaw effect chup chep chup chep…

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Grey-headed Sparrow

images.caption: Northern Grey-headed Sparrow · Plate 255

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Largest and darkest member of the group; uniform grey below (no white on chin) with heavy conical bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common eastern species of semi-arid bush country and open wooded grassland; less fond of settlements than some other species but does occur around Nairobi, Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls are variable, and utters higher-pitched, squeakier musical chirps than close relatives, and a monotonous ramble, chip chip tt-tt chip chet treet… which may be rather sharp and explosive.

images.caption: Parrot-billed Sparrow · Plate 255

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Northern Grey-headed Sparrow but dull brown back contrasts with more rufous rump; head and underparts darker grey with less contrasting white throat and some white on belly. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In East Africa, restricted to the Moyale area, northern Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Chirping calls are similar to Northern Grey-headed Sparrow.

images.caption: Swainson’s Sparrow · Plate 255

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Northern Grey-headed Sparrow but mantle grey-brown, more or less uniform with nape and crown; darker grey below than Northern Grey-headed. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small groups are common in bushed grassland and villages from south-western Kenya to central Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical chirps are delivered slowly, and are more downslurred and sharper than those of its close relatives chierp… chierp…chiep…

images.caption: Swahili Sparrow · Plate 255

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Fairly uniform pale grey-brown sparrow-like bird, typically with a yellow spot at base of throat (but often concealed). Pale bill and eye-ring often more obvious than throat spot. Sexes alike. Immature is browner with a buffy supercilium. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common but local in dry bush country and open woodland from near sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a repeated rising t’chepor, and call is an explosive dry chirp.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Yellow-spotted Petronia

images.caption: Yellow-spotted Bush-Sparrow · Plate 255

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Boldly marked, brown above with a broad white supercilium, white rump and two broad white wingbars. Two races occur: melanorhynchus (NUg and Ke) has white underparts with dark smudges at sides of breast; pectoralis (C to SETz) is white below with short black streaks across breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common in dry bush country (particularly acacia) and wooded grassland at 400–2,000m. Highly sociable: small flocks are found at their nesting colonies throughout the year. Feeds on the ground and is often tame.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a musical chattering medley of chirps and throaty churrs given from the nest or on the ground.

images.caption: White-browed Sparrow-Weaver · Plate 256

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Medium-brown above, finely mottled grey-brown except for white rump. Whitish throat has narrow black malar stripe running below buffy cheek and extending to side of neck; lightly mottled brownish below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in semi-desert with some trees, generally preferring drier areas than White-browed Sparrow-Weaver.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a continuous varied and scratchy ramble, usually delivered from near the nest, a mixed medley of chirrups and nasal skirls.

images.caption: Donaldson Smith’s Sparrow-Weaver · Plate 256

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Slightly slimmer than other sparrow-weavers and rusty-brown above with a chestnut crown and ear-coverts. Bold face pattern comprises white supercilium and black and white stripes on sides of throat; two white wingbars, rump brown like back. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or small groups are local and uncommon in dry bushland and woodland at 400–1,800m. Less common and much more inconspicuous than other sparrow-weavers. Often in rocky areas, quietly walking on the ground or under bushes feeding.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a very varied selection of twitters, trills and sweet canary-like notes, while the contact call is a fast high-pitched and spitted titititit titititit…

images.caption: Chestnut-crowned Sparrow-Weaver · Plate 256

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large mottled grey-brown weaver with pale blue eyes and a rufous dark-centred tail; in flight shows much rufous in wings. Sexes alike. Immature is browner and dark-eyed with a pale horn-coloured bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to northern Tanzania (occasionally occurs in Maasai Mara, south-western Kenya), where locally common at 1,100–2,000m. Breeds in large acacia trees in sparrow-weaver like nests, and present around colonies throughout year. Often tame and feeds in noisy flocks on the ground.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a mixture of nasal skirls and slurs strung together in an apparently random pattern, based on skrri skrer skrah.

images.caption: Rufous-tailed Weaver · Plate 256

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small, brown, short-tailed weaver with contrasting neat grey cap; in flight shows pale grey band at tip of tail. Two races occur: nominate (NUg, Ke and NTz) has a brown back; dorsalis (N and CTz) has a grey back. Immature has browner cap than adult, hardly contrasting with mantle.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a wide variety of bush and open wooded country at 500–1,900m, including semi-arid areas. Often remains in breeding area year-round and uses nests to roost.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song and call are a series of high-pitched piercing squeaks tseer tseer… given for long periods.

images.caption: Grey-capped Social-Weaver · Plate 257

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small attractive weaver with black cap and tail contrasting with brown back and wings, white bill with greenish tinge, and red eyes. White below with black streaks on flanks and belly (hard to see in the field). Immature has a brown crown. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks inhabit drier country than Grey-capped Social-Weaver, at 200–1,300m, including rather arid areas if large trees are present for breeding. Will wander, but also occurs around colonies when not breeding.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a very sparrow-like mixture of chirps and skirls, and feeding birds maintain a constant chipping. B S BUFFALO-WEAVERS Large weavers with heavy bills. Bubalornis are mainly black and their nests are very large constructions of dead thorn branches. Dinemellia is distinctly orange-red, brown and white. Its nest is smaller, includes more grass, and often has some thorny branches attached to the outside. All occur in small flocks, but Bubalornis may also gather in much larger numbers.

images.caption: Black-capped Social-Weaver · Plate 257

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very distinctive, especially in flight, when white head, bright orange-red rump and large white wing patches are bold and distinctive. Sexes alike. Two races occur: in northern nominate race, mantle, wings (except white primary patch) and tail are brown, and are blacker in boehmi (SEKe to CTz); they freely intergrade in contact areas.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in acacia bush country and wooded grassland from sea level to 1,400m. Often seen on the ground or calling loudly from their nest trees.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song and calls are slowly delivered, drawn-out, piercing nasal skirls that are variations of skrieril skri-skril skrieril…

images.caption: White-headed Buffalo-Weaver · Plate 257

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is deep black with a red bill and variable small patches of white on sides of breast. In flight, wings look black, but from below can show white streaks at base of primaries. Adult female is browner, mottled brown and white below, with a dull red bill. Immature is like female, but more grey-brown with heavy whitish mottling below; bill usually shows some pale red or orange. Birds in EA are the race intermedius.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common but patchily distributed in dry bush country and wooded grassland from near sea level to 1,500m. Often feeds on the ground with other species including hornbills and starlings.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually given from the colonial nest by several birds simultaneously, song is a mixture of nasal skirls chn chn chn chrerlink chrerlink…, which may continue for long periods and becomes more excited with the arrival of a female.

images.caption: Red-billed Buffalo-Weaver · Plate 257

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is black with a greyish-white bill and white streaks on the flanks. In non-breeding plumage bill is blackish with paler base. Adult female is similar to male in non-breeding plumage. Immature is dark brown above with brown and white streaked and mottled underparts, and blackish bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small parties and flocks favour dry acacia country from Lake Bogoria, Kenya, to the north-west at 400–1,300m. Several together at Naabi Hill, Serengeti NP, in Mar 2000 is the only record for Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is possibly more exuberant, varied and metallic than Red-billed Buffalo-Weaver, but is still similar.

images.caption: White-billed Buffalo-Weaver · Plate 257

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two distinct forms occur: breeding males of both are large with red eyes, heavy bill and an extensive black hood tapering to a point on the breast where variably edged chestnut. In race bohndorffi (most of Ug, WKe and NWTz) black scapulars form two linear patches, nape, breast and flanks are yellow (sometimes with a rufous wash); while paroptus (widespread in N, C and EKe and Tz) and graueri (SWUg, Rw, Bu and NWTz) have yellow backs evenly spotted black, more black on the crown and a variable chestnut wash. All females have olive-streaked backs, yellow superciliaries and yellow underparts when breeding. Non-breeding males and females have greenish-yellow heads contrasting with either an olive or greyish dusky-streaked back, yellow breast and whitish belly.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and very common from sea level to 2,500m in a wide range of habitats as well as human settlements.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: While dangling below their nests and flapping their wings, males keep up a constant chattering punctuated by higher-pitched squeaks, strange snoring churrs and short flourishes.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Much debate as to which races are valid, with some authorities subsuming bohndorffi in nominate and paroptus and graueri in nigriceps.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Black-headed Weaver

images.caption: Village Weaver · Plate 258

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has obvious creamy-white eyes that stand out within black mask which extends over forecrown and is variably edged with a chestnut wash; legs blue-grey. Two races occur: nominate (Ug and WTz to Ke) is variably washed pale chestnut on yellow underparts (becoming more yellow in east); cabanisii (SWTz) is plain yellow below and always lacks chestnut wash to nape and underparts. Similar Vitelline Masked Weaver lacks black on the forecrown, has red eyes and pink legs. Non-breeding male and female have pale eyes, blue-grey legs and quite a strong yellow wash on the breast. Immature has dark eyes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common, often in flocks, in bush country, woodland, cultivation, and a wide variety of vegetation near water, from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is very different from other masked weavers consisting of an accelerating series of both nasal and liquid notes.

images.caption: Lesser Masked Weaver · Plate 258

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has red eyes and a black mask extending below the eye but only a very narrow band above the bill, crown strongly washed chestnut, legs pinkish-red. Lesser Masked Weaver has whitish eyes and black forecrown. Non-breeding male and female have red eyes, pink legs and yellowish breast. Immature is browner than female with dark eyes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are widespread in a variety of bush and wooded habitats including semi-arid areas, from near sea level to 1,800m. Usually alone or in pairs, building distinctive onion-shaped nests with entrance hole at bottom.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Long rambling song is buzzy and scratchy, without any musical flourishes.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with southern African Southern Masked Weaver P. velatus.

images.caption: Vitelline Masked Weaver · Plate 258

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has dark brown eyes and a black mask extending from just behind eyes to upper breast, broadly edged chestnut-orange (almost blackish on forecrown). Non-breeding male and female have dark eyes and buffy breast. Immature similar but has whitish eyes. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In East Africa, mainly restricted to shores and waterside vegetation in the Baringo–Bogoria area, and at exteme north end of Lake Turkana, Kenya, but occasionally reported at Murchison Falls NP and near Fort Portal, western Uganda. Altitudinal range 350–1,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Hesitant song is somewhat jerky and terminal flourish is dry and unmusical.

images.caption: Northern Masked Weaver · Plate 258

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is mostly yellow with a green back and wings, narrow black line through eye and broad black stripe down throat; eyes very pale yellow, bill rather slender. Adult female is similar, but lacks black throat stripe. No non-breeding plumage. Two races occur: crocatus (Ug to WKe and south through N and WTz) as described; suahelicus (EKe to STz) has variable rufous wash to head. Immature is like dull female.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common in a wide variety of habitats from sea level to 2,200m, including forest edge, woodland, bushed grassland and overgrown cultivation. Most often seen slowly creeping about in cover.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Regular and familiar call is 6–7 rapidly delivered, descending whistles si si si si si si… Song begins with this and then breaks into a complex, musical and buzzy flourish before ending with cht notes that fade away.

images.caption: Spectacled Weaver · Plate 259

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Male and female both boldly marked black and yellow. Adult male has short black eyestripe and black throat contrasting with yellow (or orange-yellow) head and underparts. Adult female has black extending over crown, yellow supercilium and black line through eye. Two races occur: nominate (Ug to WKe and south to NWTz and Bu) male has orange wash to crown, and both sexes have dark slaty-olive upperparts; in melanoxanthus (EKe to N, C and ETz) both sexes are black above. No non-breeding plumage. Immature is like dull olive-backed female.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread but never numerous, singles and pairs occur in a variety of habitats from sea level to 2,250m. In the west prefers forest, remnant woodland and secondary growth, while eastern and southern birds occur in woodland and thick bush including semi-arid areas.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a rapid, short flourish, typical of a weaver, but with a strange liquid bubbling quality. Call is a spitted chwit chwit chwit…

images.caption: Black-necked Weaver · Plate 259

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Fairly large stocky weaver with a heavy bill. Adult has a black mask extending from eye downwards, variably edged rufous on breast, all-yellow crown, and pale yellowish eyes. Mantle spangled yellow and black. No non-breeding plumage. Female is dull olive-green above with broadly streaked mantle, very indistinct supercilium, and pale yellow throat and breast. Immature is like female, but more olive-brown. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in flocks in open woodland, acacia country and around settlements at 1,100–2,200m. Often breeds in large colonies in villages.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Colonies keep up a constant chattering that lacks musical quality although individuals sing a nasal burry skirl that ends in a series of chattering notes.

images.caption: Speke’s Weaver · Plate 259

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is very similar to Speke’s Weaver, but smaller with lightly mottled greenish-olive mantle (not boldly patterned black and yellow); face mask tapers to a point on the upper breast; eyes pale yellowish. Non-breeding male is quite plain olive-green above and all yellow below. Female similar to female Speke’s, but has slight pale yellow supercilium, less heavily streaked upperparts and smaller bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local and uncommon in range, breeding in small colonies in open woodland and cultivated areas at 650–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Simple and monotonous song given for long periods, based on a rising swi, followed by a nasal zhwee zhwee zhwee zhwee zhwee (rather like call of Rattling Cisticola).

images.caption: Heuglin’s Masked Weaver · Plate 259

ploceus-baglafecht.ref: Plate 260: Ploceus Weavers Iii And Grosbeak Weaver
ploceus-baglafecht.name: Baglafecht Weaver

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Four races occur, three of which were previously treated as separate species, forming two distinct groups: one in which males have a yellow crown and females a black crown, and the other in which both sexes are black-crowned. Yellow-crowned males include reichenowi (highlands of Ke, N and NETz) wherein both sexes have black back; emini (NUg and NWKe) with similar head markings to reichenowi but with a mottled green-and-black back, grey rump and white belly in breeding plumage, and uniquely in EA, a non-breeding plumage with streaked grey and black back and buffy underparts. Black-crowned group: stuhlmanni (much of Ug, Rw, Bu and NWTz) has a yellowish-green back; very similar sharpii (highlands of SWTz) has a green back. Intermediate forms of most races occur in contact zones. Immatures are mostly like dull versions of females, but often more olive above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are very common and widespread, notably in high country, but lower in north-western Uganda, occupying forest edge, open woodland, cultivation and gardens at 800–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical song is a complex buzzing churr that becomes a flourish, often then ending in another buzzy churr, and punctuated by a loud zwink zwink (also given as a call). There is little difference between the distinctive races.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly regarded as three species: Reichenow’s Weaver P. reichenowi, Emin’s Weaver P. emini and Stuhlmann’s Weaver P. stuhlmanni (including race sharpii).

images.caption: Baglafecht Weaver · Plate 260

ploceus-rubiginosus.ref: Plate 260: Ploceus Weavers Iii And Grosbeak Weaver
ploceus-rubiginosus.name: Chestnut Weaver

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is distinctive with a clear-cut black head contrasting with all-dark chestnut back and underparts, and red eyes. Wings and tail blackish, edged buffy-brown or yellow. Similar Chestnut Sparrow is much smaller with a very dark brown face grading into a chestnut nape and throat. Non-breeding male, female and immature are browner than similar female-type weavers; streaked black above, and white below with broad tawny-buff band on breast and flanks. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Wanders widely, often appearing during the rains in very large numbers. Highly colonial, building hundreds (even thousands) of nests together. Most frequent in dry woodland and bush country (particularly acacia), usually below 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is similar to other weavers, but song is unique with birds suddenly giving a very short dry fizzling call within bouts of general chattering. GROSBEAK WEAVER Unique weaver, the only member of the genus Amblyospiza.

images.caption: Chestnut Weaver · Plate 260

amblyospiza-albifrons.ref: Plate 260: Ploceus Weavers Iii And Grosbeak Weaver
amblyospiza-albifrons.name: Grosbeak Weaver

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large stocky dark weaver with a very thick bill. Adult male blackish-brown with variable white forecrown and wing patch. Three races occur: melanota (Ug to WKe and NWTz) has dark rusty-brown head contrasting with blacker upperparts, wings, tail and underparts; montana (Rw, WTz and C and SWKe to NTz) has head blackish like rest of upperparts and underparts; unicolor (E lowlands and coastal Ke and Tz) has head tinged very dark brown. Males of all races have a blackish bill, usually white on the forecrown and a small white patch at base of primaries. Female and immature are brown above, with no white in wing, heavily streaked brown and white below; bill yellowish-horn.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in flocks in swamps, but also at forest edge, in bush along rivers and overgrown cultivation, from sea level to 3,000m. Always breeds over water: nest is a finely woven fibrous dome with entrance near the top.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a random mix of very harsh nasal notes.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Thick-billed Weaver

images.caption: Grosbeak Weaver · Plate 260

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctly small weaver: breeding male has lemon-yellow nape and underparts (unlike orange-yellow of many other weavers), a small black mask without chestnut edging, and typical weaver-shaped stubby black bill. Back, wings and tail greenish; eyes brown. Non-breeding male and female are olive above with darker streaking, mostly yellow below, male with whiter belly. Immature is like pale female, but buffy and whiter below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs are rather local within range, being common but not numerous in acacia bush country, open woodland and cultivation with trees, at 400–1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a typical weaver buzz breaking into a flourish, with a rather nasal pinched quality. Each set is often introduced by a musical sweetiswiswi.

images.caption: Little Weaver · Plate 261

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is very similar to Little Weaver, but black bill is noticeably long and slender; eyes brownish. Adult female is plain rich yellow on head and underparts. Immature is like a pale female with a horn-coloured bill. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs inhabit swamps, papyrus, cultivation and a variety of woodland usually near water, at 700–1,700m. Can be common but is not gregarious.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a typical weaver buzz breaking into a flourish with a rather nasal pinched quality, and sometimes also gives a whistled sisisisisi between each sequence. CHESTNUT-BELLIED WEAVERS Three similar weavers, males with largely black heads and chestnut underparts. Colour of eyes and nape, extent of chestnut on underparts and range aid identification.

images.caption: Slender-billed Weaver · Plate 261

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has head and nape all black, bright red eyes, bright yellow mantle and deep chestnut underparts. Non-breeding male, female and immature are olive-green above with much streaking, yellowish supercilium, and yellowish underparts washed buffy-orange on breast. Immature is like pale buffy female. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and sometimes numerous at 500– 1,800m (rarely to 2,300m), preferring vegetation near water (although not restricted to it), and with evidence of erratic wandering.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is very complex and rambling with both high hissed notes and long, deep, descending snoring notes.

images.caption: Golden-backed Weaver · Plate 261

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is similar to Golden-backed Weaver, but black hood ends near rear crown; lower nape yellow, forming distinct collar. Eyes brown; underparts chestnut with yellow belly. Two races occur: dimidiatus (most of range) as described; duboisi (Rusizi Plain, Bu) is plain yellow below without chestnut wash. Non-breeding male, female and immature are browner (both above and below) than similar plumages of Golden-backed Weaver. Female Northern Brown-throated Weaver in same range and habitat has whitish eyes.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and gregarious, in a wide range of vegetation usually near water at 600–1,700m, including reedbeds, papyrus, moist thickets, and cultivation.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Breeding colonies maintain a squeaky chipping, where individuals are not discernible. Song is quite buzzing, starting with a squeaky si si si… and continuing with a weaver chatter and low nasal notes.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Yellow-backed Weaver

images.caption: Black-headed Weaver · Plate 261

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has a dark chestnut mask tapering to point on upper breast (can appear blackish around eyes and at bill base, becoming brown on throat); eyes whitish. Female rather brown-toned above, within range and habitat most similar to female Black-headed Weaver, but eyes whitish (not dark). Immature like female, but eyes dark. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in range being especially associated with water (but not restricted to it), and inhabits papyrus, reedbeds, and nearby cultivation at 900–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Quite a high-pitched weaver song which lacks flourishes and consists of various chattering notes and high-pitched squeaks.

images.caption: Northern Brown-throated Weaver · Plate 262

ploceus-xanthops.ref: Plate 263: Ploceus Weavers Vi And Cuckoo-Finch
ploceus-xanthops.name: Holub’s Golden Weaver

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large stocky weaver: adult male is mainly yellow, greener on the back and wings, with heavy black bill, pale yellow eyes and orange wash to throat. Adult female is slightly duller and lacks orange throat. Immature is greener above with indistinct streaking. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are common in a wide variety of open wooded grassland, marshes and cultivation at 900–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song starts with a few ticking notes and continues with a buzzy flourish tikatikatikatika; call is a distinctive loud and frequently repeated chup.

images.caption: Holub’s Golden Weaver · Plate 263

ploceus-bojeri.ref: Plate 263: Ploceus Weavers Vi And Cuckoo-Finch
ploceus-bojeri.name: Golden Palm Weaver

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is very bright yellow with an orange head and throat (some have darker rufous band on lower throat), dark brown eyes (often look black) and black bill. Adult female is yellow above with indistinct streaking, uniform yellow below, and has a bicoloured bill. Immature is like dull pale female. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Gregarious and common along the Kenya coast in palms, wooded areas and gardens, also inland in riverine habitat from sea level to 1,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Prolonged song is high-pitched and hissing, while the call is an explosive, very metallic, repeated chwenk.

images.caption: Golden Palm Weaver · Plate 263

ploceus-subaureus.ref: Plate 263: Ploceus Weavers Vi And Cuckoo-Finch
ploceus-subaureus.name: African Golden Weaver

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Golden Palm Weaver, but breeding male has a duller orange head, with pale red eyes (not dark). Non-breeding male has an olive wash to the head. Breeding female is similar to female Golden Palm but has reddish eyes. Non-breeding female and immature are more boldly streaked above, with yellow breast and white belly. Birds in EA are the race aureoflavus.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Gregarious and locally common from sea level to 1,800m, preferring wetter habitats than Golden Palm Weaver.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is rambling and usually has a winding-up series of soft squeaky tikotikotikotiko notes, before breaking into a set of complex flourishes, many with a canary-like quality.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Male ‘golden’ weavers from Bagamoyo to Selous GR, Tz, have dark eyes and orange restricted to crown and throat, and may prove to be a new species, ‘Ruvu or Yellow Weaver’.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Eastern Golden Weaver

images.caption: African Golden Weaver · Plate 263

ploceus-castaneiceps.ref: Plate 263: Ploceus Weavers Vi And Cuckoo-Finch
ploceus-castaneiceps.name: Taveta Golden Weaver

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has orange-chestnut bands on hindcrown and upper breast, giving a rather yellow-faced appearance; eyes dark brown. Female is greenish above with fairly heavy streaking, yellow supercilium and underparts, and bicoloured bill. Immature is like female but more olive-brown above. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to East Africa. Flocks are common but local in swamps and nearby woodland in the border area of Kenya and Tanzania, at 250–1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Simple song is very harsh and tuneless, with many hard chip notes which are used as contact calls.

images.caption: Taveta Golden Weaver · Plate 263

anomalospiza-imberbis.ref: Plate 263: Ploceus Weavers Vi And Cuckoo-Finch
anomalospiza-imberbis.name: Cuckoo-finch

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is bright yellow with a stubby black bill, olive back and wings streaked black (suggesting a heavy-billed canary). Non-breeding male is paler and duller. Adult female is very similar to a female Southern Red Bishop, but has a stubbier bill. Immature is tawny-brown above with some streaking, and dull buff underparts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: The nominate race is local and generally uncommon in wet grassland and cultivated areas from sea level to 2,000m. Usually alone or in pairs but occasionally in small flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Flight call is a fast titititit; song includes a weaver-like swi sun-suit and a long wheezy vweeeeeooooo.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Parasitic Weaver

images.caption: Cuckoo-finch · Plate 263

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A pale-billed, dark-headed forest weaver with red eyes, blackish upperparts and yellow breast to vent. Four races occur: mentalis (Ug to WKe) and kigomaensis (Rw, Bu to SWTz) have a black head contrasting with dark grey mantle and wings; throat usually black in mentalis, browner, tipped dirty yellow in kigomaensis; kersteni (coastal Ke, NE and STz) has black head uniform with mantle, wings and tail; stictifrons (lowland SETz) is more slaty-brown above, often with black and white speckled forecrown and throat; eyes brown (not red). Sexes alike, immatures duller.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in a variety of forest from sea level to 2,400m, and forages through mid-storey in pairs, small groups or with mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Wonderfully distinctive song varies regionally, but typically starts with chips, buzzes or squeaks, and continues musically with double nasal squeaks, rising and falling bell-like notes, or a rhythmic and rising wi-wi wi-chuk-chuk wi-chuk, all randomly peppered with weird bleats, trumpets and squeaky hinge noises.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some races intergrade and range limits are unclear.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Forest Weaver

images.caption: Dark-backed Weaver · Plate 264

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is similar to Dark-backed Weaver but smaller, with black throat extending to upper breast, and yellow edges to wings; eyes brown, bill black. Adult female is olive-green above with black streaking on back and obvious yellow wing edges; underparts yellow, grading to white on belly. Immature is like pale-billed, washed-out female. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Endemic to the Malindi- Kilifi area, coastal Kenya, where fast-moving flocks occur in the canopy of Brachystegia woodland in Arabuko-Sokoke Forest and north of the Galana River, where it breeds around pools in the Dakatcha Woodlands.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very noisy; large canopy parties forage and call together in a rolling sizzling mixed with sudden silences and bursts of their distinctive sharp chip chip flight call. [Alt. Kilifi Weaver] EN

images.caption: Clarke’s Weaver · Plate 264

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is bright yellow with black head, wings and tail, and chestnut cap. Adult female is similar, but crown all black. Immature is paler and duller with blackish-green head sometimes speckled yellowish. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and family groups are fairly common in highland forest at 1,200–3,000m where they creep nuthatch-like along branches, and join mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual call heard from family parties is a piercing siip siip…, given both perched and in flight. Unique but rarely heard song is a short rapid and rhythmic sizzling ending with two punctuated notes.

images.caption: Brown-capped Weaver · Plate 265

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinctive with reverse plumage of many weavers. Adult is black with rich yellow mask. Male differs from female in its black throat. Immature is dull olive-green with greenish-yellow head and throat; paler on belly. Birds in EA are the race stephanophorus.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs are shy but fairly common in undergrowth and tangled vines of highland forest and forest edge at 1,200–3,000m (usually above 1,500m).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a rapid series of descending notes ending in a dry tuneless rattle, more like a sunbird than a weaver. Contact call is a harsh, rapidly delivered zhink-zhink-zhink… BLACK WEAVERS Two similar black weavers best identified by size and eye colour.

images.caption: Black-billed Weaver · Plate 265

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is all black with pale yellow eyes (greyish in Maxwell’s Black Weaver). Adult female is heavily streaked dull dark olive above, and dingy yellow below with a strong olive-brown wash on breast and flanks; eyes pale yellow. Immature is like female, but eyes yellow in male, brownish in female. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Gregarious and common within range, it occurs at forest edges, in cultivated areas and around villages at 700–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Colonies maintain a constant cacophony of chattering and squeaking which is higher-pitched than similar-sounding weavers.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Vieillot’s Weaver

images.caption: Vieillot’s Black Weaver · Plate 265

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is distinctive with a black head, yellow underparts and stubby orange-pink bill. Three races occur: prigoginei (WUg to WBu) is washed orange on breast; elgonensis (EUg to CKe) is brighter yellow above and on underparts; and kilimensis (SKe and Tz) is greener upperparts and flanks. Female has dull olive-green with a darker face and yellowish bill. Immature is like female but has a duller bill.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs and small flocks are rather local but widespread in undergrowth and canopy of highland forest at 1,550–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is rarely heard and rather canary-like with trills and twitters, and some finch-like snoring. Call is a high-pitched zit-zit given perched and in flight. MALIMBES Striking black and red forest weavers that are easily identified by the extent of red in their plumage.

images.caption: Oriole Finch · Plate 266

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is all black with bright scarlet from forecrown to nape spreading slightly on sides of neck. Adult female is similar, but forecrown black. No red on underparts in either sex. Immature is duller version of adult. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are widespread but not numerous in canopy of good forest at 700–2,150m, where they feed nuthatch-like along large branches and often join mixed-species flocks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Perched or flying birds often give a few high-pitched downslurs and continue with twittering or sizzling notes, and an occasional upslurred whistled seeeu.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Several races described but differences are minimal.

images.caption: Red-headed Malimbe · Plate 266

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three distinct races occur in which breeding males differ as follows; leuconotus Northern Red-headed Weaver (Ug, Rw, most of Ke and NTz) has a black mask, red primary panel and white breast to vent; jubaensis Red Weaver (extreme NE coastal Ke) is almost entirely red with some black on wings and tail; and nominate Southern Red-headed Weaver (SETz) has plain red head and breast, yellowish primary panel and white breast to vent. Non-breeding males are similar to corresponding females, but may have a few random red feathers on head or upper breast. Females of northern races are greyish-brown with distinctive orange-red bill and orange-red primary panel; southern nominate female also has a red bill, but a more yellowish head and primary panel, and white breast to vent. Immatures are like females with a yellow wash to the head. Races leuconotus and nominate hybridise over much of STz.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Lone birds or pairs are widespread and locally common in a wide variety of woodland, bush country, grassland with scattered trees and gardens, from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a complex mix of high-pitched sizzling and a few chip notes, while feeding birds give a smooth chut.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Some authorities treat all three races as separate species, but the nominate race and leuconotus hybridise across a wide area in Tz. QUELEAS Weaver-like birds that often congregate in large flocks. Males in breeding plumage pose no identification problems, but non-breeding males and females are very similar to each other, and also to several weavers, widowbirds and whydahs.

images.caption: Red-headed Weaver · Plate 267

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has a black mask and red bill. Colour of crown and breast vary: pink, tawny-yellow or buff. Non-breeding male and female have streaky sparrow-like plumage with whitish supercilium and red bill. Immature is similar, but has a much duller, brownish-pink bill. Pin-tailed Whydah (Plate 283) is similar in non-breeding plumage, but smaller and smaller-billed with a much more boldly streaked head. Birds in EA are the race aethiopica.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common, widespread and sometimes abundant, but seasonally migratory and may be absent from apparently suitable areas for months at a time. Occurs throughout the region in bush country, grassland and cultivation from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a medley of chipping mixed with mournful downslurs, seu seu seu seeeeu, given around nest. Roosting flocks maintain a continuous chipping audible at considerable distance.

images.caption: Red-billed Quelea · Plate 267

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male has most of head, throat and upper breast bright red, with variable red or brown on nape. Non-breeding male and female have supercilium and throat washed yellowish; bill dark brown. Immature is like female but throat pale brown. Some authorities recognise two races: nominate (Ug, Bu, NWTz and much of Ke) with a red nape; and rhodesiae (SKe southwards) with a brown nape, but highly variable across range and often considered monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Seasonally common, often appearing immediately after the rains in tall wet grassy areas and marshland fringes at 400–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a series of chip notes that descends and accelerates before ending with a nasal downslurred sheeeeu. Other chip calls are frequently heard from feeding flocks.

images.caption: Cardinal Quelea · Plate 267

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is larger than Cardinal Quelea with a longer bill and entire head (including nape) darker red with variable black scalloping on throat. Non-beeding male, female and immature are extremely similar to corresponding plumages of Cardinal Quelea, but throat slightly whiter. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Less common than other queleas, with a patchy distribution from sea level to 1,400m. Most regular in marshy areas and wet grassland in eastern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a formless, tuneless, squealing chatter, and gives a chipping call in flight.

images.caption: Red-headed Quelea · Plate 267

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is a short-tailed black widowbird with deep orange-red shoulders bordered creamy-buff; rather confusingly named as tail only appears fan-shaped in display. Two races occur: phoeniceus (widespread) as described; zanzibaricus (coastal Ke, and coastal and ETz) is larger-billed with black tips to wing-coverts. Non-breeding male is similar to female but has orange-red shoulders. Female and immature have typical streaky brown plumage, but with a small area of pale rusty-brown at bend of wing.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread, preferring marshy areas and wet grassland from sea level to 2,300m, but also found in drier habitats (particularly in the east). Males frequently perch on reed tops and make short display flights to attract the more skulking females.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song, usually heard in display flight, is a slightly variable insect-like trilling. In flight, parties maintain a constant twittering. Marsh Widowbird Euplectes hartlaubi  21–36cm, 8–14";  15cm, 6" Two distinct races occur: breeding male humeralis (Ug to WKe) is similar to Fan-tailed Widowbird but larger and longer-tailed with orange-buff shoulders (not deep orange-red); in the nominate race (Ufipa area of SWTz) breeding male has an even longer tail and more yellowish shoulders. Very similar to Montane Widowbird, but lacks extensive pale buff in wing-coverts and ranges do not overlap. Non-breeding male is like female, but retains orange or yellow shoulders. Female and immature are streaked buffy-brown below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather uncommon in wet grassland and marshes at 1,100–1,800m, in two widely separated locations in Uganda to western Kenya and the Ufipa area of south-western Tanzania.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very distinctive song, usually delivered from a perch, consists of quiet twitters punctuated by an explosive single or double rising musical rasp zrun-tink.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Hartlaub’s Marsh Widowbird] Montane Widowbird Euplectes psammocromius  40cm, 16";  15cm, 6" Breeding male has yellow shoulders broadly bordered buff, and a long drooping tail. Non-breeding male is like female but retains yellow shoulders. Female has whitish throat and is narrowly streaked below. Monotypic. SH Common in high grassland at 1,800–3,000m around Iringa and Mbeya in STz. Voice Differs little from Marsh Widowbird, but explosive call is usually delivered singly. [Alt. Montane Marsh Widowbird

images.caption: Fan-tailed Widowbird · Plate 269

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is a rather stocky, short-tailed bishop with bright yellow shoulders, lower back and rump. Non-breeding male is like female, but has yellow on shoulders and rump. Adult female has typical female-like streaky plumage, but with a dingy uniform olive-yellow rump. Immature is like female, but rump brown with darker streaking. Birds in EA are the race crassirostris.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Usually alone or in pairs, but occurs in small flocks in non-breeding season; common and widespread in bushed grassland, marshes and cultivation from sea level to 2,300m, particularly in highlands (but at lower altitudes in Tanzania).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is typical of a widowbird rather than a bishop, a high-pitched sisisisisisi… the notes interspersed with insect-like trills and chittering. Yellow-mantled Widowbird Euplectes macroura  21cm, 8";  14cm, 5.5" Three races occur (sometimes considered two species): breeding male nominate (Ug to WKe and south through W and STz) has yellow mantle and shoulders; conradsi (Ukerewe Island, Tz) is similar but longer-tailed; distinctive race macrocercus (Ug to WKe) has yellow restricted to shoulders. Precise ranges and overlap between races not entirely clear. Non-breeding male of both forms has yellow shoulders and cannot be separated in the field. Females and immatures may show yellow fringes at bend of wing.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks are common within range, in moist grassland and cultivation at 1,000–1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Nominate race sings from a perch a high-pitched twitter tzip-tzip-tzip… followed by a louder nasal downslur weah, while macrocercus utters a more rapid introductory twittering and the downslur is more subdued or absent.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: If considered specifically distinct, the nominate race and conradsi remain Yellow-mantled Widowbird E. macroura, and macrocercus becomes Yellow-shouldered Widowbird E. macrocercus.

images.caption: Yellow Bishop · Plate 270

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very small, short-tailed, black and yellow bishop. Breeding male is much smaller than Yellow Bishop with an obvious bright yellow crown, mantle, rump and vent; yellow patches at sides of breast vary in size. Non-breeding male and female have dark ear-coverts contrasting with whiter face; underparts whitish with blackish streaking. Immature similar, but more buffy below. Birds in EA are the race taha (which includes ladoensis).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Uncommon resident and wanderer, occurring in large numbers after rains, and inhabiting reedbeds and flooded grassland at 400–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a tuneless, monotonous dry chipping with slight variation, given perched and in flight.

images.caption: Yellow-crowned Bishop · Plate 270

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Striking little bishop: breeding male has a bright red spot on forecrown, extensive yellow on lower back, rump and vent, and yellow and black streaked mantle. Non-breeding male, female and immature are small with yellowish-edged primaries; can be confused with non-breeding queleas but smaller-billed. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Highly nomadic; may appear in large numbers after rains, preferring semi-arid areas from sea level to 1,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Sizzling song is similar to other small bishops, calls zet-zet-zet, or chet, chet, chet. White-winged Widowbird Euplectes albonotatus  17cm, 6.5";  13cm, 5" Two distinctive races occur: both have white on primary and secondary coverts and on base of primaries, appearing as obvious white patches in flight. Breeding male eques (widespread) has deep chestnut-brown shoulders; nominate (mainly STz, rarely north to CKe) has yellow shoulders. Non-breeding male has streaky female-like plumage, but retains yellow or chestnut, and white on wing. Female and immature may show hint of yellow or chestnut feather edgings at bend of wing.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small and large flocks are locally common in moist grassland and cultivation from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a repeated high-pitched insect-like buzzing sisisisisisisisisisi interspersed with a dry rasping; call is a repeated twit twit, similar to many other widowbirds.

images.caption: Fire-fronted Bishop · Plate 270

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is very similar to Northern Red Bishop, but black on crown is restricted to narrow band on forecrown; brown tail extends well beyond upper and under tail-coverts. Plumage varies; either bright red and black, or orange and black. Non-breeding male, female and immature are all similar, with streaked upperparts, buffy supercilium, largely pale buffy below, with whiter throat and variable streaking on breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks of this western and southern species are locally common in marshes, tall grasses and around cultivation, often near water, at 600–1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is an exuberant dry mix of twitters and chattering interspersed with higher-pitched trills.

images.caption: Southern Red Bishop · Plate 271

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smallest of the red bishops. Breeding male is easily identified from other red bishops by mainly black underparts (occasionally shows a few red feathers on throat). Entirely red crown further separates this species from Northern and Southern Red Bishops. Non-breeding male, female and immature are very similar to female Southern Red Bishop, but slightly smaller. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are common to the east of Southern Red Bishop, but in similar habitats from sea level to 1,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is the most complex of all bishops: a variety of dry trills and twitters sometimes ending in a double descending, subdued and mournful piping.

images.caption: Zanzibar Red Bishop · Plate 271

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Breeding male is similar to Southern Red Bishop, but black on crown is more extensive; exceptionally long upper and lower tail-coverts conceal all but very tip of brown tail. Now considered monotypic, but previously some more orange and black populations in extreme NEKe were treated as race pusillus. Non-breeding male, female and immature are extremely similar to Southern Red Bishop and cannot be identified in the field.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common at 600–1,800m, occupying similar habitats to the two previous species.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Simple song is a tuneless dry chipping and trilling.

images.caption: Northern Red Bishop · Plate 271

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Larger and heavier-billed than other red bishops. In flight, breeding male shows broad rounded black wings and tail. Combination of red on crown extending to (or almost to) bill, and red band on upper breast is distinctive. Non-breeding male, female and immature are larger than other female-type red bishops, with stronger wash of tawny-brown on breast and flanks. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in bushed grassland and cultivation in generally wet areas from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is an insect-like accelerated twittering tititititrrrrrrr sometimes interspersed with a high-pitched musical squeaking.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Black-winged Red Bishop

images.caption: Black-winged Bishop · Plate 271

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two distinct races occur: breeding male ansorgei (Ug and WKe) is a thickset black bishop with an orange-red nape grading into a yellowish upper back and extending around sides of neck and on upper breast as narrow orange-red band; in friederichseni (SKe and NTz) breeding male is smaller with a broader collar on upper breast, and orange-red extends from nape to mantle and upper rump. Both races distinguished from similar red bishops by black rump and uppertail-coverts. Non-breeding male, female and immature are dark and heavily streaked black above (particularly male), with black spots at sides of breast.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local but not uncommon in tall wet grassland and cultivated areas at 700–1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Very simple songs are either nasal slurs rapidly repeated in a short series, or a dry twittering.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Races ansorgei (Northern Black Bishop) and friederichseni (Southern Black Bishop) are sometimes treated as separate species.

images.caption: Black Bishop · Plate 271

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three races occur: adult schistaceus (Ug to NWTz and east to WKe) is grey above with paler rump, narrow white line from forecrown to lower neck separating grey crown from black forecrown and underparts. White-spotted wing-coverts distinctive compared to similar Pale-fronted Nigrita. Race diabolicus (CKe to NTz) is similar to schistaceus, but slightly darker above including rump; and candidus (Mahale Mts, WTz) has whiter crown and rump. Sexes alike. Immature is fairly uniform dark grey with scaly buff edges to wing-coverts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread but restricted to highland forest in Kenya and most of Tanzania, at 1,700–3,350m. Occurs at lower altitudes in the west, including at 700m in Semliki Forest, western Uganda.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song varies locally but typically is a penetrating whistled seeu seeu seeeee or a seesawing si-so-si-so-si-so repeated from a high perch at irregular intervals.

images.caption: Grey-headed Nigrita · Plate 272

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small nigrita with a rather waxbill-like appearance. Black cap and tail contrast with brown back and wings and white underparts. Sexes alike. Immature has crown, rump and tail browner. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and small flocks are reasonably common (but often hard to see) in tall canopy of western forests and forest edge at 700–2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical song starts with a rattle and continues as a long descending trill lasting about 6 seconds. ANTPECKER A unique, small, slender-billed forest waxbill.

images.caption: White-breasted Nigrita · Plate 272

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has bill and face red, rear part of head grey, mantle and wings green, rump and tail red, and breast to vent barred and spotted dark grey (or olive-grey) and white. Five races occur: males differ in amount of red on face and breast-band colour: soudanensis (NEUg, N and EKe, and NETz) has all-red face (extending back to eye) and yellowish breast-band; very similar percivali (C and SWKe, and N and CTz) has grey around eye; belli (WUg, Rw, Bu to WTz) has grey lores and red extending to centre of olive-yellow breast-band; grotei (ETz) is similar with grey lores and red extending to centre of breast, but sides greener; and nominate (SWTz) has grey lores, red on head confined to forecrown and throat (not on breast), and breast-band greener. Intergrades occur in areas of overlap. Adult females are all paler than males with grey heads (lacking any red) and well-barred underparts. Immatures are like dull females, but may have yellowish edges to wings (beware confusion with Orange-winged Pytilia).

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in semi-arid acacia country, scrub and wooded grassland from sea level to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usual song is a quite loud and persistent series of chips, squeaks and nasal notes which are well imitated by Eastern Paradise-Whydah. Call is a loud, spitted series of identical spit-spit-spit notes.

images.caption: Green-winged Pytilia · Plate 273

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to Green-winged Pytilia, but has smaller rounder red mask extending well behind eye, and orange-edged wings; lores grey, belly olive with narrow white bars. Adult female is similar to male with orange wing edgings, but no red on head. Immature is like drab female. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local and generally uncommon but widespread resident of forest edge, miombo woodland and moist wooded grassland from sea level to 1,800m; tends to avoid dry areas.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is simpler than Green-winged Pytilia, a monotonous series of chips and squeaks, which is imitated by Broad-tailed Paradise-Whydah.

images.caption: Orange-winged Pytilia · Plate 273

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is mainly brown above with red lower rump and tail edges. Sides of face to breast red, lower breast to vent black with conspicuous white spots. Adult female is similar to male, but more washed out, with greyer face and buffy-orange sides to head and breast. Immature is largely dull brown, with a paler buffy face, dull red rump, and sooty-grey belly which may show indistinct white spotting. Birds in EA are the race macrospilotus.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Reasonably common but local inhabitant of forest undergrowth, thickets and dense herbage from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varied song is a complex mix of high-pitched sibilant trills, mournful downslurs and single extended notes. Call is a distinctive tit-tit.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Peters’s Twinspot

images.caption: Red-throated Twinspot · Plate 274

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is a mainly green twinspot, with contrasting bright red mask; breast to vent black well spotted with white. Adult female is paler than male with buffy-yellow mask. Immature is mostly dull grey-green with paler area around eyes, and can show a few indistinct whitish spots on underparts. Two races occur: chubbi (C and EKe, N and ETz) as described; male schlegeli (Ug to NWTz) has an orange-red wash to throat and breast, female has face and breast washed yellowish; they appear to intergrade in WKe.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local and rather uncommon, but also widespread from sea level to 2,150m. Particularly shy, it occurs in dense undergrowth and thick cover within forest, but also in the canopy.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a complex mix of very high-pitched and canary-like phrases with varied sibilant trills and slurs. Call is a high zit-zit… given perched and in flight.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Green-backed Twinspot

images.caption: Green Twinspot · Plate 274

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has uniform greyish-olive head, and dark crimson on back, wings, rump and flanks; underparts mainly olive-grey with paler throat, eye-ring pinkish-red. Female very similar, but lacks eye-ring and has slightly less red on wings and flanks. Immature is duller with brownish-olive back. Three races occur: nominate (NKe) as described; kilimensis (NEUg, W and CKe, and NETz) is paler below; and ruwenzori (WUg to WBu) is greyer on head and underparts. Red-faced Crimsonwing has red, or buffy, mask. Female Shelley’s Crimsonwing has red (not black) bill.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread and common but shy, with a patchy range mainly at 2,000–3,000m, occasionally as low as 1,500m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a high sibilant tsit-tsit…, which can break into a rapid delivery of even higher-pitched notes.

images.caption: Abyssinian Crimsonwing · Plate 275

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two distinct races occur: adult male nominate (Ug to WTz and east to CKe) has head, breast and flanks red, with red rump and black tail; eyelids bluish-white (distinct when breeding), bill blue-grey with pink cutting edge. Adult female is similar, but has bold white spots from breast to vent. Immature is dark slate above, with variable red wash to head, breast and rump; rich dark brown below; bill blue-grey. Race cana (East Usambara Mts, NETz) has upperparts (and sometimes nape) dark grey, not black.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or family groups often feed on forest trails at dawn and dusk and are locally common in forest, secondary growth and moist thickets at 700–2,150m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Whistled song is rather sibilant: starts with a short note, then a short series of rising notes, and longer series of rising upslurs, si-sisi-su-wii si-sis-swiswiswisiwiswi, with emphasis on the final note.

images.caption: Red-headed Bluebill · Plate 276

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three races occur: adult males vary only in tone of brown or grey-brown upperparts; all are easily identified by bright red cheek patches. All adult females are brown above (except for blue rump and tail), but extent of blue on face and underparts varies: nominate (Ug and Rw east to WKe) has most blue, extending over sides of face, neck, breast and flanks; brunneigularis (widespread in Ke and NETz) has brown sides to face and neck; ugogensis (elsewhere in Tz) is similar to brunneigularis but paler. Immature is like dull female. In areas of overlap with Blue-breasted Cordon-bleu female ugogensis differs in its pale brown (not blue) cheeks.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very common and widespread in virtually all habitats except forest interior, from sea level to 2,300m. In area of overlap with Blue-breasted Cordon-bleu, Red-cheeked prefers more lush habitats and miombo woodland.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Rhythmic but lazy song consists of 4–6 high-pitched lispy notes with the last one lower, longer and more burry. Contact call is an oft-repeated high-pitched siii siii…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Previously described race littoralis is now subsumed in brunneigularis.

images.caption: Red-cheeked Cordon-bleu · Plate 277

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has an entirely bright blue head, breast and flanks, and a bright pink bill. Adult female is similar to other female cordon-bleus with brown on crown, but may show diagnostic deep pinkish-red bill. Immature is paler, with brownish breast and dark grey bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread but never really numerous, in semi-arid country from sea level to 1,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Complex and varied song has a peculiar metallic twang; calls are stronger and less lispy than other cordon-bleus, and retain a metallic timbre.

images.caption: Blue-capped Cordon-bleu · Plate 277

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Brightly coloured red-billed waxbill with long pointed tail. Adult male has russet-brown head with blue face marks, deep violet-blue breast to vent, and black tail. Adult female is similar above but paler, with pale blue or whitish lines above and below eyes; underparts pale russet-brown, variably barred white especially on flanks. Immature is fairly uniform dull warm brown, with plain face, dark bill, blue rump and black tail. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common within range, inhabiting open woodland, bush and cultivation, as well as semi-arid areas, from near sea level to 2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song often starts with a strong high trill which continues as a rising metallic squeaking sit-t-sit sit siiiiiiii; call is a metallic explosive zeet which may be repeated.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Uraeginthus.

images.caption: Purple Grenadier · Plate 277

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Male of widespread race ruberrima is mostly wine-red including crown (although crown browner when worn); upperparts reddish washed brighter on the rump and tail edges, and belly buffy grey-brown. Bill has pinkish-red sides and grey culmen. Female is largely brown, with red rump and duller bill. Both sexes may show small white spots at sides of breast. Immature is dull brown with some red on rump. Three other races occur, intergrading in contact zones: in extreme NEKe birds with a red crown and pinkish-brown back may be somaliensis; in NKe some show a brown crown as in Ethiopian race brunneiceps, and in SETz birds are brown-crowned and paler as in Mozambique race rendalli.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: The commonest firefinch in a wide range of habitats including human settlements from sea level to 2,400m
