sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varied song is a mix of chip notes and rising upslurs, chep chep de-zwizwi, also chick-pea-pea-pea, a song mimicked by Village Indigobird. Also a downslurred seeu.

images.caption: Red-billed Firefinch · Plate 278

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has more contrasting upperparts than Red-billed Firefinch with a distinct brown mantle, red rump and black tail. Both sexes have slate-grey bill, black belly and black undertail-coverts; small white spots often at sides of breast. Two races occur: congica (WUg to WTz) has head and underparts pinkish-red, and browner upperparts on female; haematocephala (NEUg, Ke and ETz) has head and underparts more red than congica, and female is washed browner on the head. Immature dull brown, paler below, with blackish vent.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather shy within woodland, thickets and overgrown cultivation, from sea level to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song varies locally but is typically dry trills interspersed with bunting-like suwee suwee suwee suwee notes. Calls is a sharp pit-pit-pit which is mimicked by Variable Indigobird.

images.caption: African Firefinch · Plate 278

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Red-billed Firefinch with pink sides to bill, but crown, nape and mantle uniform earth-brown. White bars on breast variable and often hard to see; rump and base of tail red; undertail-coverts buffy-brown. Sexes alike, immature much browner. Birds in EA are the race lateritia.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in overgrown cultivation and lush vegetation near water, at 600–1,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a mixture of rising and falling chipping notes, interspersed with short sibilant upslurs, chip chip weee weeee…; alarm call is a repeated metallic chip.

images.caption: Bar-breasted Firefinch · Plate 278

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two races occur: male nominate (NEUg to WKe) is extremely similar to male African Firefinch with brown back, red rump, and black tail and vent. May show white spots on sides of breast. Best identified by preference for drier habitats and rapid purring call. Male jamesoni (EKe and Tz) has head, back and underparts rosy-pink. Females (of both races) are paler than males with greyer crown and ear-coverts, and red loral spot; underparts orange-pink (nominate) or pink-buff (jamesoni), barred blackish on undertail-coverts. All have slate-grey bill. Immature is browner, with some red on rump.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Local in dry bush country from sea level to 1,500m, but in more lush habitats near the coast.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song varies but is often a bunting-like si..syee-syee-syee-syee-syee on one pitch, frequently interrupted with a fast purring trill which is mimicked by Purple Indigobird.

images.caption: Jameson’s Firefinch · Plate 278

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Male is deep wine-red including mantle; wings brown, lower breast, belly and vent black; bill dark with purplish-pink base to lower mandible. No white spots on underparts. Female is browner above with greyish head and red lores; underparts pinkish with black belly and vent. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Generally uncommon in wooded grassland and edges of cultivation at 800–1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song starts with a sharp dry clicking, breaks into squeaky rhythmical slurs and ends in a single long note, sisisi see-susu-sisi-si weeeeeee.

images.caption: Black-bellied Firefinch · Plate 278

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small and colourful waxbill, with a pale grey head and upper breast, olive-green mantle and wings, red rump, blackish tail and yellow belly. Upper mandible black, lower mandible red. Immature is paler with dark bill. Three similar races occur: nominate (extreme NEUg) as described; kilimensis (WUg to Ke and south to CTz) is slightly darker; and stuartirwini (S and ETz) has head more blue-grey.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common at forest edge, in highland grasslands and around cultivation at 900–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a short series of slurred, whistled squeaks and nasal notes; call is a high-pitched lispy siii siii siii…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly in the genus Estrilda.

images.caption: Yellow-bellied Waxbill · Plate 279

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult is finely barred dark brown on brown above, including rump and tail; bright red streak through eye and waxy red bill. Four races occur and differ in general tone of pinks and browns, density of fine barring, and intensity of pink or red on underparts: adesma (Ug to NWTz, and WKe) is greyish-brown with strong barring, pink on underparts, but no red belly patch; massaica (CKe to CTz) is browner overall, with red confined to belly patch; minor (EKe to NETz) has a white throat and pink belly patch; and cavendishi (STz) has a pinkish-white throat and large red belly patch. Immature is paler with a blackish bill.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small to large flocks are very common and widespread away from forest interior and arid habitats, from sea level to 3,000m, often feeding in long grass near water.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Foraging birds usually maintain contact with irregular dry squeaks and chips; song consists of a paired tikatik-wheez tikatik-wheez, with the last note burry and upslurred.

images.caption: Common Waxbill · Plate 279

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Common Waxbill with red streak through eye and finely barred brown upperparts, but has blackish bill, crimson-red rump, and red edges to wing-coverts and tertials. Immature is plain brown, darker above than below, lacks red eyestripe and has duller red rump. Birds in EA are the race centralis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common resident and wanderer, occurring in thickets, damp grassland and marshy shores from sea level to 1,800m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song structure is similar to Common Waxbill, although the notes are nasal and more clearly defined, consisting of musical chips forming a regular rhythmic pattern: wi-chi wi-chi wi chi-chi… Also a low churr and a nasal chipping in flight.

images.caption: Crimson-rumped Waxbill · Plate 279

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Common Waxbill but cleaner and pallid-looking, with jet-black rump and tail, latter narrowly edged white. Bill and streak through eye red; faint barring above may be visible in good light. Very pale pinkish-buff below, whiter on throat. Immature is duller, with blackish bill. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in west, less so in Kenya and north-western Tanzania, in both dry country and thicker vegetation near water at 800–1,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a loud somewhat metallic chipping, and song is similar but more subdued and punctuated by long single upslurs soyiiiii…

images.caption: Black-rumped Waxbill · Plate 279

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather pale-looking waxbill with bright red bill, red rump, black tail and yellowish-fawn underparts. Four races occur: nominate (NUg to WKe) has ashy-grey head, pale yellowish-buff underparts and variable pink patch on lower belly; roseicrissa (SWUg to Bu and NWTz) has an olive-brown crown and mantle, whitish underparts with pink belly patch; marwitzi (C and SWTz) is like roseicrissa but darker, more tawny-olive above; benguellensis (extreme SWTz) has a grey crown, bright buff underparts with pinkish breast and yellow belly patch. Pink belly patch can be absent in females. Immature is generally paler with dark bill.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common, but patchily distributed in mainly lush habitats, forest clearings, wet grassland and overgrown cultivation at 700–2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a loud, energetic, rolling and rhythmic nasal series of chips and squeaks; call is a short nasal downslurred sieu.

images.caption: Fawn-breasted Waxbill · Plate 279

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Black-capped, grey and white waxbill with red rump and flank patch. Very similar to Kandt’s Waxbill, but underparts white with a faint grey wash. At close range has fine dark barring on back and wings; red and black on both mandibles. Female has less red on flanks. Immature is plainer and duller than adult, with slight brownish wash and all-dark bill. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common at forest edge, in secondary growth, marshy areas and cultivation, below 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Small flocks frequently call a high-pitched and sibilant sii-sii-sii-sii…, and rarely heard song consists of rising and falling tinkling notes.

images.caption: Black-crowned Waxbill · Plate 280

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Black-crowned Waxbill but overall appearance is much darker, especially on underparts which grade from whitish throat to dark grey breast and black vent and belly; at close range has fine dark barring on back and wings; red on flanks is more extensive than Black-crowned Waxbill. Bill has red on lower mandible only. Female is similar but has smaller red flank patch. Immature is duller and browner than adult without red on flanks. Two races occur: nominate (WUg to Bu) as described; keniensis (EUg to CKe) is similar but slightly browner above.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common high-country species inhabiting forest edge and nearby grassy clearings at 2,000–3,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a loud, persistent and slightly metallic sii-sii-sii, often from perch and always in flight.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Black-headed Waxbill E. atricapilla of West and Central Africa.

images.caption: Kandt’s Waxbill · Plate 280

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Black-cheeked Waxbill with pinkish-grey finely barred upperparts, black mask, red rump and black tail. Black-faced Waxbill differs in slightly larger black area on chin (‘black face’) and overall darker appearance; belly to vent black in male; uniform with rest of underparts on female. Immature is like dull adult. Birds in EA are the race delamerei.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in range, inhabiting open woodland, acacia country, scrub and cultivation, mainly at 1,000–1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call and song is a long high-pitched rising upslur seeeeeeeeii…, a less frequent double tsee-tsee and quiet twittering.

images.caption: Black-faced Waxbill · Plate 280

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Paler than Black-faced Waxbill, with black mask confined mainly to cheeks (only a very narrow black line on chin); belly to vent usually pinkish-grey in both sexes. Immature is less pink than adult. Two races occur: nominate (widespread) as described; kiwanukae (SKe) is overall more pink, with grey belly and undertail-coverts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in semi-arid bush country at 100–1,000m, occasionally to 1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is much harsher than Black-faced Waxbill and consists of repeated dry chips and short dry rattled trills.

images.caption: Black-cheeked Waxbill · Plate 280

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very small bright waxbill. Adult male is olive-brown above with red bill and eyestripe, red uppertail-coverts and blackish tail. Two races occur: nominate male (Ug, NWTz and WKe) is bright orange-yellow below; male clarkei (Rw and CKe south to STz) is mostly yellow below; both have olive-green barring on flanks. Female is duller and paler, and lacks eyestripe. Immature is drab with a dark bill, dull brown upperparts and buffy-brown below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in small flocks, and very active inhabitant of reedbeds, marshy grassland and cultivated areas from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Most frequently heard calls are short repeated and complaining nasal downslurs, which are usually paired. Song mixes these notes with long decending rattled trills or a series of random spitted metallic notes tit tit tit tit…

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Orange-breasted Waxbill

images.caption: Zebra Waxbill · Plate 280

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Sandy-brown waxbill with a rather large stubby blue-grey bill; blackish primaries, rump and tail; buffy-white below. Immature similar but has browner tail. Birds in EA are the race orientalis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in semi-arid bush and dry wooded grasslands from sea level to 1,900m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Flight call is a loud, harsh, hollow-sounding tink-tink…, but from perch may utter an extended dry rattle.

images.caption: African Silverbill · Plate 281

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to African Silverbill but with grey head, white-speckled cheeks, pinkish-brown upperparts, white rump and blackish tail. Washed peachy-pink below. Immature is duller than adult, without white spotting on cheeks, underparts washed buffy on breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small wandering flocks are patchily distributed from near sea level to 1,900m, occurring in open wooded grassland, bush and semi-arid acacia country.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In flight utters a soft downslurred seeu, while the song is a series of these notes which rises and falls and is occasionally mixed with sharp metallic notes. QUAILFINCH AND LOCUSTFINCH Small, dumpy, short-tailed waxbills (despite their names) found in flocks on the ground. They crouch motionless and are often difficult to see until flushed, when they suddenly fly away together calling.

images.caption: Grey-headed Silverbill · Plate 281

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is cryptically marked above, but has distinctive face markings, a tawny-rufous breast and belly, and barred flanks. Taxonomically complex with different authorities dividing the 11 races into three ‘groups’ which are sometimes regarded as distinct species. EA has one representative from each group. Across NUg and WKe (rare) ugandae (Black-faced Quailfinch) has a plain back and white chin; in CKe and most of Tz muelleri (African Quailfinch) has mottled upperparts, white chin and bold white spectacles; and in SUg, Rw, Bu and NWTz dorsostriata (Black-chinned Quailfinch) has mottled upperparts and a black face including chin. All females are duller, immatures even paler. All show small white corners to tail in flight.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Usually in pairs or small flocks in open grassland (both dry and wet) from sea level to 3,000m. They often drink at pools and lakeshores, but are shy and difficult to see on the ground, flying up quickly when flushed and calling before dropping down again a short distance away.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: When flushed, individuals within the flock utter a burry and metallic tchink-tchink…

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Birds on the Ufipa Plateau, SWTz, are thought to be race fuscata which is in the Black-chinned group; they differ from dorsostriata in being blacker above, and more chestnut on the lower breast and belly.

images.caption: Quailfinch · Plate 281

spermestes-cucullata.ref: Plate 282: Mannikins, Cut-Throat Finch And Java Sparrow
spermestes-cucullata.name: Bronze Mannikin

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small with blackish head and breast contrasting with dull brown nape, mantle and wings; head and breast have variable amounts of iridescent green or purplish-bronze. At close range small glossy dark green patch on shoulder and sides of breast; lower breast to vent white, with dark barring on flanks. Dark grey upper mandible and pale grey lower mandible. Two races occur: nominate (Ug to WKe) as described; scutata (C and EKe south through Tz) lacks green patch at side of breast. Races intergrade over a wide area. Immature is plain brown above with darker wings and tail, paler brown below grading to buff on vent.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Commonest mannikin, widespread in all habitats except desert and forest interior, from sea level to 2,200m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song and calls consist of rapidily delivered short burry chips which rise and fall in tone, sometimes becoming a churr. Similar twittering is frequently given in flight.

images.caption: Bronze Mannikin · Plate 282

spermestes-bicolor.ref: Plate 282: Mannikins, Cut-Throat Finch And Java Sparrow
spermestes-bicolor.name: Black-and-white Mannikin

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small, smart mannikin, with two races that are sometimes considered specifically distinct. From Ug to Bu and east to WKe, adult poensis (Black-and-white Mannikin) is black and white without any contrast between head and mantle; flight feathers and rump barred black and white (plain on Bronze Mannikin), bill pale blue-grey. Immature is very dark brown above and paler tawny-buff below. From CKe to E and STz, adult nigriceps (Red-backed Mannikin) is similar, but mantle, tertials and wing-coverts are chestnut-brown. Immature is brown above with rufous wash, and paler below with buffy flanks.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common at forest edge, in lush thickets and around cultivation, from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls are similar to a white-eye, but marginally harsher, more mournful, whistled downslurs tsiu tsiu…

images.caption: Black-and-white Mannikin · Plate 282

spermestes-fringilloides.ref: Plate 282: Mannikins, Cut-Throat Finch And Java Sparrow
spermestes-fringilloides.name: Magpie Mannikin

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar to Bronze Mannikin but larger; black on head extends over nape contrasting with brown back and wings, and plain black rump and tail. Breast to vent white with black smudges at sides of breast and variable small black, white and rufous flank markings. Bill is blackish above and blue-grey below. Immature is dull brown above with darker rump and tail, buffy below with indication of darker breast patches; bill all dark. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Very local and uncommon in forest edge, secondary growth and cultivation, occurring in two widely separated areas, from sea level to 1,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls are similar to Black-and-white Mannikin but louder with whistled downslurs longer and less mournful: tsiu rsii tsiu tsii… CUT-THROAT FINCH A distinctive waxbill of semi-arid bush.

images.caption: Magpie Mannikin · Plate 282

amadina-fasciata.ref: Plate 282: Mannikins, Cut-Throat Finch And Java Sparrow
amadina-fasciata.name: Cut-throat Finch

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has bright red crescent-shaped ‘cut’ across throat, otherwise brown with bold scaly blackish markings and variably sized chestnut patch on belly. Adult female is similar but lacks red ‘cut-throat’ and has little or no chestnut on belly. Immature male shows indication of red throat streak. Two races occur: alexanderi (widespread) as described; nominate (extreme NEUg and NWKe) is similar but paler and more cinnamon with finer scaly markings.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in flocks, mainly in semi-arid country, but wanders erratically, occurring less frequently in farmland and on the coast, from sea level to 1,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song consists of short and abrupt phrases mixing nasal notes and squeaks. [Alt. Cut-throat] JAVA SPARROW A locally common waxbill introduced to Pemba and Zanzibar.

images.caption: Cut-throat Finch · Plate 282

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two races occur: breeding males of both have a blue-black sheen, with dark brown wings and red or orange-red feet, but differ in bill colour; centralis (widespread) has a white bill; amauropteryx (coastal Ke and Tz) has a red bill.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: By far the most common and widespread indigobird, in a wide variety of habitats from sea level to 2,000m, closely matching the range of its host, Red-billed Firefinch.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Male song is a two-tone chick followed by simple clear rising whistles pea pea, as well as a chick-pea-pea-pea which may rise and fall. Pattern uttered frequently between phrases of its own chattering song.

images.caption: Village Indigobird · Plate 284

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Fairly large green and yellow canary with a heavy pinkish-horn bill; malar stripe olive-green (not black). Upperparts greenish with darker streaking, does not show contrasting yellow rump in flight. Female duller, breast often washed greener with faint streaking. Immature has less distinct head markings. Birds in EA are the race sharpii.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or singles are common in wooded grassland, moist bush country and cultivated areas from sea level to 2,400m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song varies from a rather rapid high-pitched sparrow-like chirping (in the west) to sweeter, varied refrains (mainly in the east). Calls a loud rather gravelly trill chrirrrrir.

images.caption: Brimstone Canary · Plate 285

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has bright yellow forecrown and supercilium; narrow dark line through eye and strong black malar stripe create well-marked face pattern. Bright yellow rump contrasts with streaked greenish mantle; underparts bright yellow. Three races occur: barbata (Ug to Bu, and SWKe to CTz) as described; nominate (EKe and ETz) has hindneck and ear-coverts greyish; samayilae (SWTz) is similar, but ear-coverts darker olive. Females are slightly duller and paler, immatures are like females with some breast streaking.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Small flocks are common and widespread in open woodland, bush country and cultivation from sea level to 2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a rather monotonous refrain which may continue for long periods, but is broken into short phrases, si-yu sisi si yu, with embellishments.

images.caption: Yellow-fronted Canary · Plate 285

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three races occur: adult male maculicollis (NEUg and NKe) has distinctive white belly and vent, olive-green malar stripe and some streaking on flanks; nominate (SEUg, WKe and Tz) has a much smaller area of white on the belly and is best separated from Yellow-fronted Canary by olive-green (not black) malar stripe; taruensis (CKe to CTz) is more yellow below than maculicollis. All races show contrasting yellow rump in flight. Female maculicollis has a white belly, but is paler than male with variable streaking on breast and flanks. Female nominate is like female maculicollis but less white on belly. Immatures are like females but paler and buffier below. Races intergrade widely in C and SKe.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Prefers drier areas than Yellow-fronted Canary, usually in bush country at 400–1,800m, but to 2,650m in northern Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Attractive song is high-pitched and continues for long periods but is broken into complex phrases which vary a little and last about 5 seconds.

images.caption: White-bellied Canary · Plate 285

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is a brightly coloured highland canary with a golden-yellow forecrown, two bright yellow wingbars and an obvious yellow rump in flight. Two races occur: nominate (NEUg, Ke and NTz) as described; sassii (SWUg to STz) has more yellow in the tail. Females are duller with variable streaking below. Immatures are more buffy-brown with extensive streaking below.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in flocks at 1,600–4,300m in cultivation, forest edge and moorland.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: In flight, gives a short rapid trill of about five low notes, tiririririr; long rambling song has a strange tinny tone.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with southern African Cape Canary S. canicollis.

images.caption: Yellow-crowned Canary · Plate 285

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Dull brown fairly plain seedeater with two narrow buffy wingbars, olive-green edges to primaries, and a very heavy bill; mostly brown below with variable flank streaking. Three races occur: tanganjicae (WUg to Bu and WTz) usually lacks white forecrown; kilimensis (EUg and SWKe to NTz) is similar but darker on throat; albifrons (CKe) has white on forecrown. Sexes and all ages alike.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Rather shy, but not uncommon in highland forest and bamboo at 1,200–3,000m, mainly above 1,700m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Calls a high thrush-like seeep, given perched and in flight. Song is a series of high-pitched hissed notes usually broken into short repeated phrases.

images.caption: Thick-billed Seedeater · Plate 285

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to African Citril with a black face, but bright yellow supercilia join as a broader band on forecrown; plain yellow below. Female has bright yellow forecrown and supercilium with olive-green cheeks; plain yellow underparts can be washed greenish on sides of breast with some fine streaking on flanks. Immature is generally more olive-brown with darker brown streaking above and below. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in farmland, gardens and forest edge below 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song a high-pitched series, interspersed with sit-sit notes and a buzzy zwee.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with African and Southern Citrils.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Yellow-browed Citril

images.caption: Western Citril · Plate 286

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A black-faced canary with bright yellow supercilia which may meet as a narrow band across black forecrown; yellow below (except perhaps a few narrow dark streaks on lower flanks). Female lacks black face, has less distinct supercilium and is streaked below. Immature similar but more olive above. Birds in EA are the race kikuyensis.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common in Kenya highlands where it occurs in pairs and small flocks in farmland, gardens and forest edge to 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is often a complex series of short phrases, very similar to Reichenow’s Seedeater but more pinched and slightly nasal. Also a series of diagnostic falling piped notes, wee-aay-wee-pay-weee-e-thu.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Western and Southern Citrils.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Abyssinian Citril

images.caption: African Citril · Plate 286

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A grey-faced canary (not black) with streaked underparts. Two similar races occur: both sexes in nominate (SEKe to STz) have grey face and lack yellow supercilium; brittoni (WKe) has grey restricted to chin, greener ear-coverts and indistinct supercilium. Sexes similar. Immature is more olive-brown above and paler below than adult with heavier streaking.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in farmland, gardens and forest edge below 3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is basically similar to African Citril but shows more variation and a little more hurried delivery.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with African and Western Citrils.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: East African Citril, Grey-faced Citril

images.caption: Southern Citril · Plate 286

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to race brittoni of Southern Citril, with streaking above and below, but has short pink conical bill (not straight and pointed). Male has greenish sides to face and dark grey lores. Female similar but has paler grey lores. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Uncommon and restricted to papyrus beds and nearby vegetation at 900–1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a broken series of short phrases each slightly varying but typically including a series of rattle-like identical notes, tit’t’t’t’t’t, quite different from other African citrils.

images.caption: Papyrus Canary · Plate 286

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Streaky brown seedeater with yellow rump, whitish supercilium, and buff or whitish throat; density of streaking on underparts varies. Yellow rump is conspicuous in flight. Sexes and immature similar. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Flocks are common and widespread in open woodland, bush country and cultivation, from sea level to 2,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Typical canary song is loud and continuous with little variation, the same notes and occasional trills being repeated for long periods.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly known as Yellow-rumped Seedeater Serinus reichenowi.

images.caption: Reichenow’s Seedeater · Plate 286

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Very similar to Reichenow’s Seedeater, but generally darker above with less distinct supercilium and variable blackish mottling on throat. Sexes and immature similar. Two races occur: somereni (SWUg to NWTz and rarely WKe) as described; lwenarum (SWTz) is similar but paler on upperparts.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Similar to Reichenow’s, but has more westerly range.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a long rambling similar to Reichenow’s Seedeater, but harsher and more varied.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Black-throated Canary

images.caption: Black-throated Seedeater · Plate 286

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A heavily streaked seedeater with bold facial pattern of either creamy-buff or yellow, well-defined supercilium, and variable greenish or yellow edges to primaries. Three races occur: graueri (SWUg to Bu) is darkest with a creamy-buff supercilium and often green edges to primaries; nominate (Ke and NTz) is similar, but overall tone of underparts is paler. In SWTz distinctive race whytii (Yellow-browed Seedeater) has a bright yellow face, wing edgings and tail; underparts pale greyish, with blackish-streaked breast and flanks. Sexes and immature similar.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in highlands at 1,300–4,300m, in moorland heath, forest edge, rank vegetation, gardens and cultivation.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song has a rather forced thrush-like quality and often ends in a soft rattle; either repeated short phrases, or an attractive continuous refrain. Cheerful call is a loud upslurred whistle siyuya. Race whytii is similar but lower-pitched; call is siyuuee.

images.caption: Streaky Seedeater · Plate 287

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Best identified by combination of streaked brown upperparts, long white supercilium, brown sides to face, and fairly heavily streaked underparts including on chin and throat. Sexes alike. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: In East Africa, restricted to rocky hills and escarpments with scattered bush and woodland at 1,600–2,000m. Pairs are shy and inconspicuous unless singing; non-breeders may occur in small flocks and move actively while feeding.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song often begins with djee t’what or djee tu-waa and continues with a prolonged rambling including much mimicry. Also an interrogatory call siyuah.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with Reichard’s Seedeater.

images.caption: Stripe-breasted Seedeater · Plate 287

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large canary with a heavy pinkish bill. Adult male is similar to Southern Grosbeak-Canary, but more distinctly streaked above, with stronger yellow supercilium and white lower belly; ranges do not overlap. Female and immature are brown above with darker streaking and bright yellow rump; underparts off-white with heavy brown streaks on breast and flanks, and resembles a giant Reichenow’s Seedeater. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Pairs or family groups are uncommon in semi-arid bush and desert country of northern Kenya below 1,600m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Varied calls include a rapid seu-seu-seu-seu-seu-seu…, with the same note repeated 10–20 times, also suweer and an upslurred tuweeer both of which are similar to Southern Grosbeak-Canary.

images.caption: Northern Grosbeak-Canary · Plate 288

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: In range only likely to be confused with Brimstone Canary, but larger, with a very heavy pink-horn bill and contrasting yellow rump. Sexes virtually alike, but female can show more fine streaking on the breast. Immature is similar to female but has a duller rump. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles and pairs are rather local in Commiphora and acacia bush country, especially along dry river courses.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Call is a piped, loud and far-carrying si’tiri siiyu, and song is a series of repeated short phrases with a mournful piping, tinny quality. BUNTINGS Often with colourful underparts (especially males), buntings have small pointed bills and boldly marked heads. Pairs or small flocks feed on the ground, but fly to cover if disturbed. In open woodland, grassland and bush country, all frequently sing from exposed perches.

images.caption: Southern Grosbeak-Canary · Plate 288

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is rufous with black streaking above, and has black and white striped head, black throat and rich cinnamon breast to vent. Female is duller with subdued head pattern. Immature is plainer than female, with mostly brown-streaked head and duller brown underparts. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Widespread but seldom numerous in rocky areas, cliff bases and escarpments with small trees and light cover at 400–3,000m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a monotonous repeated scratchy phrase of mainly falling notes, lasting about 2 seconds, si siri si stri.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Cinnamon-breasted Rock Bunting

images.caption: Cinnamon-breasted Bunting · Plate 288

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has striped face pattern, and crown, nape and upper breast are finely streaked pale grey, black and white. Wings are extensively edged warm rufous (conspicuous in flight). Female and immature are largely brown, with darker brown streaking on head and upper breast. Birds in EA are the race saturatior.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Locally common in rocky arid and desert country at 375–800m in northern Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is a series of short repeated phrases, siti tiri tiri si tiou or similar variations.

sections.heading: Taxonomy note
sections.text: Formerly considered conspecific with north-west African House Bunting E. sahari.

images.caption: Striolated Bunting · Plate 288

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male has white stripes above and below eyes, plain chestnut mantle (lightly mottled greyish in fresh plumage), two white wingbars, grey rump and white-edged outer tail. Underparts bright golden-yellow (more orange-yellow on breast), with whitish flanks and belly. Female is similar but duller, immature paler with more subdued brown and buff head pattern and indistinct streaks on breast. Birds in EA are the nominate race.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Singles or pairs are common and widespread in wooded grassland and moist bush country from sea level to 2,300m.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Individual songs vary, but are typically a series of 4–5 downslurs, siu siu siu siu siu, chip-chip choo chip-chip choo or cheree cheree cheree cheree cheree all with a high-pitched and far-carrying quality.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: African Golden-breasted Bunting

images.caption: Golden-breasted Bunting · Plate 289

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Adult male is similar to Golden-breasted Bunting, but chestnut-brown mantle is broadly edged pale buffy-grey creating a scaly appearance, rump paler grey and more white in outer tail. Female is duller. Immature is much paler with browner head pattern, very little yellow on underparts and dark brown streaks across breast. Monotypic.

sections.heading: Status and habitat
sections.text: Common and widespread in dry bush country from sea level to 1,200m (occasionally 1,800m) to north and east of Golden-breasted Bunting range.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Song is similar in form and pattern to Golden-breasted, but hurried not relaxed in delivery: siu siu siu siu siu siu siu and swit swit swit chee t’choo t’choo t’choo. Also a distinctive piped upslur, p’yuuu, given in flight or perched.

sections.heading: Other names
sections.text: Somali Golden-breasted Bunting

images.caption: Somali Bunting · Plate 289

sections.heading: Key facts
facts: 1-2 (1 is the norm in East Africa)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: GREATER GALAGO) cresierBusnbaby) plus tail: 1ft 2in-1ft 8in (36-49cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Similar in size to a small cat, with large eyes, prominent ears and a bushy tail. The coat colour ranges from grey to brown. A melanistic variety which is dark chocolate brown is easily seen at tented camps in the Masai Mara in Kenya. The fur is thick and woolly, especially on the tail, which is carried erect like a cat’s when the galago is moving around on the ground. The second toe of the hind limb has a distinct claw which is used for grooming. Males are heavier than females. The large-eared greater galago is exclusively nocturnal and primarily arboreal, sleeping in the tops of trees amongst dense foliage.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Greater galagos are very noisy at right, particularly during the breeding season. The most commonly heard call is like that of a baby crying (hence he name bushbaby) and may be ‘epeated 50-100 times per hour, 1elping to space individuals and acting as a contact call. The sound is somewhat similar to the call of the tree 1yrax (see page 99). Galagos also spit, itter various low growls and scream when alarmed or threatened.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Woodlands, evergreen forests and savanna, coastal bush and cultivated areas where there are trees. Greater galagos are abundant in coastal districts and occur in mountainous

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Exclusively nocturnal and primarily arboreal. The greater galago is solitary or lives in small family groups of adult females and their offspring, with each family moving within a separate home range (which may partially overlap one another). Breeding males occupy a territory including the home ranges of two or three different groups of ‘emales. Both males and females mark heir home range with secretions from a bare Pei glandular patch on their chest, together with urine and secretions from the genital region deposited on aerial pathways. A mother and her young, and sometimes also the oreeding male, sleep together during the daytime in dense foliage, with the male alternating between the various families within his territory. Greater galagos begin their activity cycle at dusk, with adults foraging on their own among fruiting trees and those exuding gum. Bouts of feeding interspersed with periods of resting and dozing continue throughout the night, with the various individuals making their way back to one of a number of favoured sleeping sites high up among the foliage. Galagos can make prodigious leaps from the ground up into the trees, and walk and run along the branches like monkeys. They hop like kangaroos when on the ground or walk ina rather ungainly and awkward fashion with their hindquarters and tail raised.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Galagos breed annually, with the resident male monopolizing mating opportunities within his territory. Up to three young (depending on the region) are born in a leafy nest concealed among the tree tops, or in a hole in the trunk of a tree. A single young is the normal litter in East Africa, while twins are common in southern Africa. The young cling to their mother’s back while she forages, and suckle for the first three months. They remain in close association with her until they are six or seven months old, when the next offspring is born. By this time they are able to forage on their own.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Mainly fruit, seeds, flowers, nectar, gum, grubs and insects. They also at times take small reptiles, birds’ eggs and nestlings.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Young and adults are preyed on by eagles, owls, and snakes. Adults are occasionally taken by leopards, and young by genets and palm civets.

images.caption: Large-eared Greater Galago
A melanistic, dark chocolate brown variety of the large-eared greater galago is easily seen at Mara River Camp in the Masai Mara National Reserve, Kenya.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: SENEGAL GALAGO esserBusibaby plus tail: 8-10in (20-25cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The Senegal galago has huge eyes, highly mobile ears and a greyish yellow coat. It is half the size of the large-eared greater galago (see page 16), with larger, more pointed ears and a more slender tail. Its hands and feet each have five digits equipped with flat nails, except for the second digit on each foot, which has a curved grooming claw.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Senegal galagos have some 25 recognizable calls, ranging from a loud chattering to a shrill whistling. The contact call is a loud bark – quite different from the screaming cry of the large-eared greater galago. When alarmed they spit and chatter. Males utter a loud scream while pursuing oestrus females.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Coastal forests, acacia and riverine woodlands, and montane forests up to greater galago and the Senegal galago are frequently found together, though the Senegal galago is more commonly associated with thorntree country.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Strictly nocturnal, foraging for an average of six hours a night. Related females and their young live in groups of up to eight in overlapping home ranges of 3-9 acres (1.2-3.6 hectares). Adults forage on their own, but family members usually share the same daytime sleeping sites. Galagos mark their home ranges with urine, and adult males defend an exclusive breeding territory and generally avoid contact with other males. A male’s territory may overlap that of a number of adult females, and he may at times share the families’ communal sleeping sites; otherwise they sleep alone. On waking, galagos lick themselves and groom one another before leaving the sleeping area to forage. They mostly feed in the trees, but do descend to the ground at times in search of food. Galagos are particularly active during two foraging peaks early and late in the night. They often call to one another during the first hour of activity, and family members gather together again near the sleeping site before dawn to groom and socialize prior to going to sleep. A galago can rotate its head 180 degrees and its large eyes are especially adapted to gain the maximum amount of light, aided by a special layer of retinal cells called the tapetum lucidum. This facility enables them to leap about in the trees and capture insects during the darkest nights. Galagos are prodigious jumpers and can easily negotiate a gap of 15ft (4.5m) when moving from tree to tree; a leap of up to 23ft (7m) is within their range. They use their tail to balance as they jump, at first holding it straight out and then curling it up over their back.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Two births are possible each year, with a birth peak during each of the two rainy seasons. Females usually have their first baby when they are one year old, thereafter giving birth to twins. They usually mate and conceive again within a few days. The young are born with hair and with their eyes open. A mother stays continuously with her twins for the first few days and will change the nest if unduly disturbed, transporting each baby in her mouth. Initially the young cling to the fur of their mother’s belly, and then ride on her back. They eat gum and catch insects by one month old and are weaned at six to ten weeks. Galagos are fully grown at four months.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: The gum of certain trees (particularly acacias) is an important part of a galago’s diet, together with nectar, petals, fruit and seeds. They are very quick, grabbing insects on the wing with their long fingers, and taking eggs, nestlings and lizards.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Galagos remain hidden during the daytime and are very agile, making it difficult for a predator to catch them, as long as they stay in the trees. They are also highly vigilant, uttering alarm calls which alert other galagos to the presence of danger, and will mob any predator that approaches them. They are very vulnerable when moving about on the ground, and the main threat is posed by owls, genets and large snakes. Opposite: the Senegal galago is half the size of the large-eared greater galago (see page 16), with larger, more pointed ears and a more slender tail. It is the commonest and most widespread of the galagos.

images.caption: Senegal Galago

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Tumbili females: 6½-9lb (3-4kg) plus tail: 11–12in (27-–30cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The commonest of the East African monkeys, with a black face rimmed with white hair and a greyish coat. The tail has a black tip and males may be distinguished by their bright blue scrotum and vivid red penis.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A troop makes various chirping and twittering calls, and individuals squeal or scream if frightened. When a predator is sighted troop members respond with a distinctive stuttering alarm call which may vary according to the type of predator, with leopards, martial eagles and pythons each eliciting a somewhat different call.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Vervets are found anywhere with fairly large trees or clumps of bush, favouring acacia woodlands bordering streams, rivers and lakes. They also occur in mountainous country up to heavily forested areas.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal, arboreal and terrestrial. Vervets are gregarious, usually living in troops of 5-30 individuals, though these are sometimes as large as 50 or 60. A troop consists of a number of distinct families, each comprising a group of related females and their offspring, with individual families ranked in a well-established hierarchy. The families within a troop co-operate in defending their shared home range against males from other troops. They are assisted in this by a number of mature male troop members who compete with one another for breeding rights. Vervets forage in a well-defined home range, spending much of their time on the ground, sometimes wandering short distances out into the grasslands. When disturbed they gallop for the safety of the nearest bushes or trees. They can swim well when necessary and roost in trees during the night. Females remain in their natal troop, but young males must leave and attempt to ingratiate themselves into a new troop. Their efforts are resisted by both male and female residents, and their best chance of being accepted is if they transfer with other male relatives (or males of a similar age), or try and join a troop that has previously accepted males from their natal group. These young males often have to transfer between troops a number of times before finally managing to establish themselves and breed.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Vervets give birth to their young at all times of the year. Newborn infants are carried by clinging to their mother’s belly fur, and begin to climb about among the bushes at one month old. They start feeding on solid food at two months.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Omnivorous, feeding on fruit, buds, seeds, flowers, roots and gum from various species of acacias, as well as insects, grubs, small reptiles, eggs and nestlings. During the rainy season vervets are quite often seen feeding on fresh grass shoots. They can be very destructive to crops, particularly fruit and maize.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Vervets are preyed on by leopards (the sight of which provokes an outburst of coughs and ‘checkering’ notes), caracals, servals, large eagles such as the martial eagle, crocodiles and pythons. Male baboons sometimes kill and eat young vervets. During the rainy season, vervets are often seen feeding on fresh grass shoots and they can be very destructive to crops, particularly fruit and maize.

images.caption: When alarmed, vervets seek refuge in trees and bushes, repeatedly uttering distinctive stuttering alarm calls, which may vary according to the type of predator.
Vervet Monkey

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: BLUE or SYKES MO Kima or Nchima females 8-10lb (3.5-4.5kg) plus tail: 2ft 4in–2ft 11in (70-90cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Two distinct races of this species occur in East Africa, namely the blue monkey (Cercopithecus mitis stublmanni) and the Sykes monkey (Cercopithecus mitis albogularis). The blue monkey is bluish grey to black in colour with greyish eyebrows and cheeks and a very long black tail. The Sykes differs in having a greyish coat and distinctive white collar around the throat and chest. The long tail is carried in a slightly arched position and is curled in a loop over the back during grooming. Males are considerably larger and heavier than females. The blue or Sykes monkey is a forest species, occurring in both eastern and southern Africa. Its coat colour and facial markings vary considerably. This is a male blue monkey (Cercopithecus mitis stuhimanni).

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Widely distributed and common in evergreen forested regions up to people of the Mau forest in Kenya used to kill and eat large numbers of these monkeys as their staple diet, and traders offered high prices for their beautiful fur. Consequently, they were nearly exterminated in this area.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and gregarious; primarily arboreal, but where undisturbed they will forage on the ground for fresh green shoots. They are usually found in family troops of 10-20 individuals, but sometimes in larger groups. each other and live in a home range presided over by a mature male. Young males are forced to leave their natal troop but do not form bachelor groups, wandering on their own in search of the opportunity to take over a harem for themselves. It is thought that when a male takes over a troop he kills the offspring of the previous territory holder, thereby ensuring that Left: Male blue or Sykes monkeys are considerably heavier than females. Below: Black-cheeked white-nosed monkey or red-tailed monkey (Cercopithecus ascanius schmidti), frequently seen associating with blue monkeys at Kichwa Tembo Camp in the Masai Mara.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Breed all year round with a peak in births during the rainy season. The young grow more slowly than other species of monkeys. Infants first begin to leave their mother at one month old, and attain their adult coat colour at two to three months.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Omnivorous: leaves, fruit, berries, flowers, shoots, insects and nestlings.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Preyed on by leopards, golden cats, crowned eagles and pythons.

the females come into season. Shyer and less adventurous than the vervet (see page 20), blue and Sykes monkeys prefer to keep in the shade. They often associate with other species, and at Kichwa Tembo Camp in the Masai Mara are regularly seen mingling with a troop of black-cheeked white-nosed monkeys or red-tailed monkeys (Cercopithecus ascanius schmidti, also known as copper-tailed monkeys).

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Nyani females 30-44lb (14-20kg) plus tail: 1ft 4in-1ft 7in (40-47cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A large, heavily built monkey with a dog-like head and olive brown coat. The tail points straight up at the base and then loops over. Males have very powerful canines measuring up to 2in (Scm) long. Older males have a well-developed erectile mane or cape around their neck and shoulders. Baboons have excellent hearing and eyesight, and are capable of distinguishing colours.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Olive baboons have a wide range of vocalizations, including deep murmurings, grunts and barks. During social fracas, individuals often cry out with piercing screams and squeals. When a predator such as a leopard or lion is detected, baboons utter a loud, challenging bark, alerting every member of the troop to danger.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: A widespread species found in acacia woodlands, open plains in the vicinity of trees or rocky outcrops, riverine forests and mountainous country up to access to water.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Baboons are diurnal and gregarious. They are equally at home foraging in the trees or on the ground, and are usually found in troops of from 10-100 individuals, occupying a home range larger troops of 150-200 individuals may occur where food is plentiful. A troop is composed of a number of family units, consisting of a group of related females and their offspring. Each family in the troop is ranked according to a dominance hierarchy, and within each family the mother is the dominant individual, followed by her youngest child. Young males leave their natal troop when they are four years old and transfer to another troop, thereby helping to prevent inbreeding. Baboon society is highly Male baboons have very powerful canines measuring up to 2in (5cm) long. They will rally to the defence of the troop if threatened by predators. complex and is based on the ability to forge relationships with other troop members, rather than on outright aggression. Though the large males do not (as was previously thought) lead the troop, they are vital to its well-being, rallying to its defence when threatened by predators, and males have been known to inflict serious injury on, and sometimes even to kill, a full-grown leopard. Baboons sleep in trees or rocky outcrops, to which they return at dusk, transferring from one favoured site to another every few days. Daily activity begins an hour or so after dawn with troop members mutually grooming one another. They then wander for up to 6 miles 10km) through the bush and savanna searching for food. Unlike other monkeys, baboons generally leave the safety of trees and gallop off overground when approached by humans.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Baboons breed throughout the year. Females give birth during the night and the single young is carried under its mother’s chest, clinging to the long fur. At six weeks old the infant starts to ride jockey-style on its mother’s back. By the time they are three months old infants form play groups with young of a similar age, presided over by their mothers. They begin taking food for themselves at five to six months, at which time the adult coat colour appears. They are weaned at eight months, but remain closely attached to their mother until they are one and a half years old.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Baboons are highly opportunistic omnivores, feeding on grass, herbs, leaves, seeds, roots, tubers, fruit, bark, sap and honeycomb. They also take insects, spiders, scorpions, worms, crabs, lizards and the eggs and young of ground-nesting birds. The larger adult male baboons sometimes kill more substantial prey such as hares, newborn gazelles and young impalas, and are occasionally cannibalistic. A troop can be very destructive to agricultural crops.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Preyed on by leopards, lions, hunting dogs, jackals, crocodiles, large eagles and pythons. But the troop’s mobbing response is usually an effective deterrent against predators, allowing baboons to feed in the open in relative safety. Top: female olive baboon and infant. The young are weaned at eight months, but remain closely attached to their mothers until they are one and a half years old. Bottom: an infant begins riding jockey-style on its mother’s back at the age of six weeks. Olive baboons waiting to drink at the Mara River, Masai Mara National Reserve, Kenya. sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Nyani females 30-37|b (14-17kqg) plus tail: 1ft 4-1ft Zin (40-48cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The yellow baboon has a yellowish brown coat and is somewhat lighter in build with more slender limbs than the olive baboon (see page 24); males lack the distinctive mane of their larger relatives.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Bush country with baobab trees, rocky outcrops and woodlands.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and gregarious. See the description under olive baboon for other details.

images.caption: Baboons will stand up on their hind legs when alarmed, or to keep track of other troop members.
The yellow baboon occurs in Tanzania and the eastern part of Kenya, where it can be seen in Amboseli and Tsavo National Parks.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: WHITE COLOBUS cucrez Mbega mweupe or Kuluzu (10-15kg), though can be up to 44lb plus tail: 28-34in (70-85cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A handsome black and white monkey with a long, white, tasselled tail. Colobus differ from other monkeys in the absence of a thumb, which is reduced to a short stump (the name colobus comes from a Greek word meaning maimed or mutilated). Their pendantlike white tails were once highly prized as fly whisks, and together with their skins were used to decorate the traditional costumes of certain tribes. Skins were also made into rugs and mats. It is said that East Africa was exporting 2 million colobus skins in the late 1800s. In 1972, curio shops in Kenya had a stock of 27,000 skins, while Ethiopia had 200,000 skins for sale. As a result colobus were almost exterminated in parts of Africa. Colobus are distinguished from all other monkeys by the absence of a thumb, which is reduced to a short stump.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Males mark their territories by uttering guttural, far-reaching roars – ‘rurr, rurr, rurr’ – particularly at dawn and dusk. This sound is also used as a contact call. Family members make various soft clicks, purrs and snuffles when communicating with one another. A loud nasal snort is used as an alarm signal.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and gregarious, usually in family troops of up to five females, accompanied by three or four young of various ages, and a dominant male who has exclusive breeding rights with the females. In some instances there may be more than one male, but these are subordinate to the dominant male. At times a number of troops associate together at a rich food source in suitable habitat, with colobus reaching their highest densities in montane forests. Young males leave their natal troop and are mature at four years old. They either become solitary or join up with other bachelors, staying on the periphery of the breeding troops until they succeed in displacing a resident male and taking over his harem. Colobus spend most of their waking hours foraging among the tree tops or grooming. After leaving the tree in which it slept, a troop often wanders to a suitable site where individuals can sun themselves, advertising their location to other troops in the vicinity, with family members engaging in intense grooming sessions. The troop then makes its way to the place where it will feed for the day, resting and grooming during the hotter hours. Later in the afternoon they feed again before returning to their sleeping tree. Colobus are extraordinarily agile, leaping from tree to tree and using the rebound of the branch they land on to gain distance for the next jump. They are somewhat clumsy on the ground.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Colobus breed all year round with a birth peak during the rains. Newborn young have pink faces and a white coat, attaining their adult colour at three months. All the troop members seem to enjoy handling and carrying infants, and compete for the chance to hold them. By the time they are six months old young colobus can climb and jump proficiently and can feed themselves, though they may continue to suckle for up to a year, sometimes longer.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Mainly leaves from a limited range of trees; also fruit, lichens, moss, bark, seeds, grass, insects and mineralized earth. Their ability to digest more mature and coarser foliage and unripe

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: They are preyed on by leopards and large eagles. Male colobus can be very aggressive and will challenge an eagle that tries to snatch a young troop member; they are also more than a match for the ¢ largest of domestic dogs.

images.caption: Black and White Colobus

By the time they are six months old, young colobus can climb and jump proficiently and can feed themselves, though they may continue to suckle for up to a year, sometimes even longer. Colobus spend most of their waking hours foraging among the tree tops or grooming. fruits and seeds from just a few species of trees enables them to live in relatively small ranges in a wide variety of habitats. Colobus can eat a quarter to a third of their body weight per day. They obtain water from hollows in tree trunks and by licking droplets from branches.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Jackals are thought to be the ancestor of modern domestic dogs. The side-striped jackal may be distinguished from other jackals by its less pointed face, rounder ears, white-tipped tail and a diagonal white stripe along the flank, which may not always be prominent. Males are somewhat larger and heavier than females. The side-striped jackal is less common than the black-backed jackal. Side-striped jackals are primarily nocturnal, though they are occasionally seen in the early morning.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Makes a loud bark as a contact call, and growls when alarmed or threatened.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Lightly wooded country and savanna, preferring areas offering good cover

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Side-striped jackals are primarily nocturnal, though they are occasionally seen in the early mornings. They are thought to pair for life and maintain a territory, but little is known of their habits.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Breed seasonally at the time of the rains, often choosing an old aardvark hole, termite mound or hiding place among rocks as a den site. See black-backed jackal (page 33) for other details.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Side-striped jackals feed on carrion, small rodents, hares, ground birds, eggs, reptiles, insects, fruit and berries. They sometimes bury food for consumption later.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Adults are killed by leopards, and pups by eagles and large snakes.

images.caption: The side-striped jackal can be distinguished from the other two jackal species by the diagonal white stripe along its flank and its white-tipped tail.
Side-striped Jackal

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A dusky, yellowish or rufous-grey jackal, with a dark tip to its tail.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A high-pitched or repeated howl of varying length and intensity is used to announce the presence of territory holders, and as a contact call between family members, which helps to promote bonding. Golden jackals bark when alarmed and growl when threatened.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Most commonly seen on the open plains but also found in bush country. Golden jackals occur in large numbers on the Serengeti plains. A pair of jackals will co-operate when hunting gazelle fawns: while one attacks the fawn, the other distracts the mother.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Nocturnal and diurnal, often seen searching for food in the early morning and evening. Golden jackals mate for life and are strictly territorial. In the Serengeti they predominate at carcasses during the daytime, while black-backed jackals are found in greater numbers at night kills.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Breed annually during the rainy season. Pups emerge from the den at two weeks and are fed on insects and meat regurgitated by their parents. Members of the previous litter often stay on, gaining experience in parenting and promoting their own genetic interests by helping to raise their younger siblings. Pups begin acquiring their golden coat at one month old. A significant number of litters are lost due to flooding of the den site.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Omnivorous, taking carrion, young antelopes up to the size of topi calves, as well as figs, desert dates and other fruits and berries.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Leopards occasionally kill adults, and eagles and large snakes prey on pups. Above: golden jackal pups playing at their den site, Ngorongoro Conservation Area, Tanzania. Left: golden jackal with freshly killed gazelle fawn.

images.caption: Golden jackals are both nocturnal and diurnal, often seen searching for food in the early morning and evening. They occur in large numbers on the Serengeti plains, Tanzania.
Golden Jackal
Golden Jackal
Golden Jackal
Top: golden jackal, Lake Magadi, Ngorongoro Crater, Tanzania. Golden jackals sometimes manage to kill flamingoes when they mass in very shallow water at the edge of lakes.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: (Silver-backed Jackal) Bweha nyukundu or Bweha shaba plus tail: 11-14in (28-35cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: This is the commonest of the three jackal species found in East Africa. Fox-like in appearance, the black-backed jackal has larger ears, a black (not white) tip to its tail and shorter legs than the side-striped jackal (see page 30). The sexes are similar, but males are a little larger.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A distinctive, high-pitched, yelping bark, particularly when in the presence of the larger cats such as leopards, or if otherwise alarmed or excited. A similar call is used as a form of territorial marking, and a pair of jackals and their offspring frequently create a howling chorus, which helps rally and bond the family.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Savanna, open plains, light woodland and semi-desert.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Black-backed jackals are mainly nocturnal, though they are often seen during the daytime, particularly in the early morning. Usually in pairs or family parties, but sometimes solitary. Adult black-backed jackals pair for life, and both partners help to defend their territory, marking it with urine, faeces and their presence. They are highly intelligent and well known for their wariness and cunning.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: The pups are born during the dry season in an old termite mound or a crevice amongst rocks, and the female frequently moves her pups to a new den site. Both parents help to raise the young, and the pups first appear above ground at two weeks old. Initially the adult male does much of the foraging, regurgitating food for the female and the pups. The previous litter of pups sometimes remain with their parents to help provision their younger relatives, and their help may be crucial to the number of puppies that survive, freeing both parents to hunt for food while the den is guarded. By three months they have acquired their adult coat coloration and are no longer so dependent on a den. At six months they are able to hunt for themselves, though they still gain much of their food from their parents and older siblings. By eight months they are fully grown and may leave to try and establish themselves in their own territory.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Black-backed jackals are opportunistic omnivores, scavenging from kills made by larger predators, as well as killing small prey for themselves. They hunt newborn gazelles and impalas, rodents and ground birds, as well as taking eggs, reptiles, insects, fruit and berries. Jackals can be a pest, stealing small livestock, domestic poultry and anything else small and edible.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Leopards frequently kill jackals, and pups are taken by large eagles and pythons. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Distinguished by their huge bat ears, long legs and a long, bushy, black-tipped tail. The forefeet have long claws for digging up insects. Sometimes referred to as Delalande’s fox.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A variety of calls, including soft ‘who-who’ contact notes for summoning cubs. They bark when alarmed, and growl or hiss when threatened.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open plains, light woodland and sandy scrub bush.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Primarily nocturnal, and usually seen in pairs or family groups. Bat-eared foxes generally mate for life, with each pair occupying widely overlapping home ranges. The home range is of necessity temporary, due to the variable and seasonal availability of insect prey and the need to select the best denning sites before each new breeding season. Bat-eared foxes sometimes gather at optimum feeding grounds with little overt aggression. They are often encountered huddled together at the mouth of the resident burrow, which may have several entrances and is usually located in an old termite mound. Bat-eared foxes groom each other and their young, The bat-eared fox may be distinguished by its huge bat ears, long legs and long, bushy, black-tipped tail.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a birth peak at the time of the rains and females are capable of breeding in their second year, The young are born in the resident burrow, emerging at two to three weeks. They begin to follow their parents at 10-12 weeks and the adults sometimes find and share food with dependent cubs. At this stage the family becomes more nomadic and ranges widely, possibly increased feeding requirements. Cubs become independent at about seven months, by which time they are fully grown. Bat-eared foxes have 48 small, pointed teeth adapted to an insectivorous diet. In areas where they occur, grass-eating harvester termites are an important part of their diet. They also feed on beetle larvae, grasshoppers, scorpions, spiders, safari ants and millipedes, as well as taking small mammals, eggs and nestlings, reptiles and fruit. Bat-eared foxes locate subterranean insects by listening for them with their huge ears, then digging them up with their long claws. They eat large quantities of winged termites (alates) released from mounds during the rains, at times leaping high into the air to catch them.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Bat-eared foxes are quick and extremely agile, zig-zagging at hig speed for the nearest burrow if pursued by a predator. However lions, leopards and hyaenas all occasionally kill them, and large birds of prey and larger snakes take adults and young. Top: the young first emerge from the den at 2-3 weeks and begin to follow their parents at 10-12 weeks. Left: bat-eared foxes have 2-5 young which are born in the resident burrow. Cubs become independent at about seven months, by which time they are fully grown. Below: bat-eared foxes are primarily nocturnal, though they can sometimes be seen foraging for insects on cool or overcast days.

sections.text: HUNTING DOG wie doe plus tail: 1ft-1ft 4in (30-40cm) have been recorded) Hunting dog puppies constantly pester adult pack members for food. This yearling is yawning in response to the puppy’s begging behaviour, indicating that it has nothing to regurgitate.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Hunting dogs (or wild dogs as they are also known) are medium-sized, dog-like carnivores with large bat ears and a white-tipped tail. Their scientific name Lycaon pictus means painted or ornate wolf, aptly describing their distinctive, tricoloured coat markings of yellow, dark brown and white. Each animal has a unique coat colour and can be individually recognized. Hunting dogs possess only four toes on each foot, lacking the dew-claw of true dogs (though it can be seen beneath the skin on X-rays).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A mournful, bell-like hoot is used as a contact call to help reunite pack members that become separated. When greeting each other, hunting dogs emit strange bird-like twittering sounds of excitement. A gruff bark signals alarm, bringing the whole pack to its feet.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: A variety of habitats from open plains to light woodland and bush country dense forests. Once recorded at the top of Mt Kilimanjaro, which is

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Hunting dogs are primarily diurnal, pack-hunting predators, hunting at dawn and dusk, though it is not unusual for them to be active on moonlit nights. Their basic lifestyle is that of nomadic wanderers ranging over vast areas in search of prey, being sedentary only when raising pups. Their home range can be anything km), with the smaller ranges being the norm in areas supporting resident prey, and larger ones in places like the Serengeti plains where prey is nomadic. A pack usually consists of three to ten adults, often accompanied by a number of sub-adults and puppies. Hunting dogs are highly social; packs containing 20-40 individuals were not uncommon in earlier times. They are coursers, sometimes chasing gazelles for distances of up to 3 miles (Skm) at speeds of 30mph (48kph), even up to 40mph (64kph) for brief periods. Having run their prey to the point of exhaustion, they grab it by the tail, hind leg or groin and then disembowel it. Small prey such as Thomson’s gazelles are dispatched quickly. But if the prey is large and the pack small, death may be a slow process, causing the hunting dogs to be reviled by man and wrongly typecast as cruel, wanton killers. Large animals such as wildebeest or zebras

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: A pack breeds annually, usually when prey is in plentiful supply. Each pack is led by a male and female known as the dominant or alpha pair. These two monopolize breeding in the pack. The pups are usually born in an old aardvark or warthog burrow, and all the adults and yearlings help to raise the litter by protecting them from predators and regurgitating food for them on returning from a kill. By the time the pups are 10-12 weeks old they are strong enough to abandon the den site and follow the pack wherever it wanders. Young females emigrate from their natal pack as a group when they are about two years old, as they cannot breed in the same pack as their mother. Males usually stay in their natal pack longer than their sisters, but as numbers increase they too may leave. New packs are formed from the merging of these single-sex groups of wandering adults. Usually only the dominant female in each pack breeds, giving birth to a single litter of 5-12 puppies annually. If a subordinate female produces a litter, the dominant female may try to kill the puppies.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Hunting dogs usually hunt animals the size of Thomson’s gazelles and impalas as well as a variety of smaller

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: They are occasionally killed by lions, and puppies are sometimes taken by hyaenas or large birds of prey. Contrary to popular belief hunting dogs are not known to attack man. Previously a common species in most wildlife areas throughout Africa south of the Sahara, fewer than 5,000 hunting dogs (perhaps as few as 3,000) remain due to a policy of extermination conducted by farmers, hunters and even game departments, as well as disease and loss of suitable habitat. Canine distemper and rabies have greatly reduced hunting dog numbers in the Masai Mara and Serengeti during the last few years. Today they are Africa’s most seriously endangered large carnivore.
