sections.text: Fungo plus tail: 1ft 2in–1ft 5in (35-42cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Though commonly referred to as the civet ‘cat’, civets are not cats but are related to the mongooses. They are the size of a medium-sized dog, and at first glance look like a raccoon, with a black face mask, clean white muzzle and greyish brown coat marked with black stripes and spots. They have non-retractile claws and powerful jaws with broad, crushing molars. The hind legs are longer than the forelegs, giving them a characteristic high-rumped gait. When alarmed, civets raise the 4in (10cm) long hair of their spinal crest, which runs the whole length of the body to the tip of the tail. Males are larger and heavier than females. Opposite: civets are nocturnal and terrestrial, favouring areas providing good cover for lying up during the daytime. They will defend themselves when threatened or cornered, raising their spinal crest to make themselves look bigger.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: The contact call is a ‘ha-ha-ha’ sound. Civets utter various growls and panting noises when interacting with one another, and spit, cough and growl when cornered. Kittens have a gruff, coughing contact call.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Favour areas providing good cover for lying up during the daytime, particularly riverine forests, savanna woodlands, and rocky hillsides. Rarely found in very dry areas.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Nocturnal and terrestrial. Civets are usually encountered foraging on their own and are presumed to be solitary, moving around on well-used pathways and living in overlapping home ranges. Individuals of both sexes mark their home range by depositing piles of faeces at regularly used latrines during their nocturnal wanderings, and also by smearing pungent anal gland secretions by everting their anal pouch and rubbing it against suitable scent posts such as the trunks of trees. This enables them to signal their presence in an area and avoid unnecessary contact with other civets. For many millennia civetone, as the perineal gland secretion is known, was used as the basis for perfumes, and civets were kept in captivity and ‘milked’ of their civetone on a regular basis for this purpose. Civets are rather unspecialized hunters, and are not particularly quick, so they must try and surprise their prey and then pounce on it. They do not have a well-defined killing bite like the members of the cat family, relying instead on their powerful jaws to grab their prey haphazardly, biting and then shaking it with great vigour, sometimes dropping it and then shaking it again, which may prove sufficient to kill it. Large prey is often dispatched with a final bite to the skull. Civets lack the shearing carnassial teeth used by cats to slice through the flesh of their prey, instead holding a carcass down with their forefeet and tearing off pieces of flesh. During the daytime they lie up in tunnels in the long grass or conceal themselves in hollows or rocky crevices, or under fallen trees.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Civets prey on a wide range of species, including small antelope, hares, domestic cats, ground birds, reptiles, amphibians, insects of all kinds, aquatic invertebrates, carrion, fallen fruit and berries.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Females give birth in their second year, selecting a suitable hole as a nest. The kittens are well developed at birth and their eyes open within a week. They remain hidden in the nest for the first two weeks, but are highly mobile by one month, when they begin eating insects and meat. Young civets are weaned at around three months, and both sexes are mature by one year old.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Civets will defend themselves when threatened or cornered, raising their spinal crest to make themselves look bigger. Leopards kill adult civets as prey, and so probably do hyaenas. Jackals, caracals, honey badgers, genets and mongooses are all thought to kill young civets.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A badger-like animal with a black coat and a whitish grey mantle running from the top of the head along the back. The coat is short and coarse and the skin fits loosely, providing protection from attack by large predators and from the effect of bee stings. Honey badgers possess extremely strong curved foreclaws, which can measure up to 1½in (4cm), Sexes are similar,

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Pairs of honey badgers grunt as a contact call, and utter high-pitched growls, barks and screams when threatened.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Mainly nocturnal, but sometimes seen in the early morning or at dusk, particularly where undisturbed, aN nN Usually found in pairs or solitary. They sleep in burrows in the ground or among rock crevices. During their nocturnal wanderings they deposit faeces and smear anal gland secretions against rocks and stumps as well as on the ground to mark their home range. Honey badgers move with a distinctive rolling gait as they scour the land for food, frequently pausing to flip over stones, investigate burrows and dig into the ground. They can be extremely aggressive if threatened and may inflict serious injuries with their sharp teeth and strong claws. When provoked they also release a foul smelling skunk-like secretion from their well-developed anal glands, which may cause intense irritation to the eyes of an attacker. Honey badgers will feign death if all else fails. Predators usually avoid honey badgers. They are extremely powerful makes them very difficult to catch hold of without sustaining injury.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: They breed at all times of the year, and the young are born in a burrow lined with grass and leaves. Little else is known of their reproductive behaviour.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Omnivorous, feeding on a wide range of prey, including insects, fish, reptiles, eggs and nestlings, small mammals, fruit, berries and roots. They sometimes take carrion and will scavenge from refuse dumps around camps and lodges. Honey badgers are excellent tree climbers, breaking into beehives to feed on honey and the larval stages contained in beeswax. They are sometimes assisted in locating bee hives by a bird called the Honey Guide Undicator indicator). By flying ahead and calling repeatedly, the honey guide leads the honey badger to the hive. This co-operation benefits the honey guide by providing access to wax and grubs.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Predators usually avoid honey badgers, and with good reason. Apart from their strength, aggression and the potency of their anal gland secretions, their loose skin makes it very difficult for an attacker to catch hold of them without sustaining injury. and their loose skin

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A weasel-like mongoose with a long, slender body, short legs and a very long, black-tipped tail (almost as long as the body). The greyish brown coat is sleeker and shorter-haired than that of most mongooses. The tail is carried straight out, with the black tip curled up or held vertically like a flag when the mongoose is angry or alarmed. It has piercing sandy red eyes and sharp claws adapted for climbing.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: The contact call is a soft ‘hoo’. They growl or churr repeatedly when alarmed.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: All types of country except deserts. Slender mongooses seem to prefer dense cover in the vicinity of water and rock-strewn hills up to 10,000ft

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Primarily diurnal and terrestrial. Slender mongooses are most commonly seen hurrying through the rocks or crossing a game path. They are generally solitary creatures, with males defending a territory which usually overlaps the home range of more than one female. Slender mongooses are quite often active at dusk and on moonlit nights. The normal gait is a fast walk or quick trot, gliding along with long tail trailing and black tip raised. They are very agile and excellent climbers. If pursued they sometimes take refuge in trees, and will readily scavenge from a leopard’s kill. They rest up during the night in termite mounds, rocky crevices, burrows, thickets or holes in trees. The slender mongoose has a slender body, short legs and a very long, black-tipped tail. It is primarily diurnal and terrestrial.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: A male locates an oestrus female by her scent, and may accompany her for up to a week. Females can have two or even three litters a year, and give birth for the first time in their second year. A mother is fiercely protective of her young, which are weaned at about two months and are capable of living independently at ten weeks old. Young adults sometimes continue to associate with their mother.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Highly predacious, feeding on small rodents, young hares, eggs, nestlings, birds, snakes, insects and occasionally fruit and berries.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: The main predators are probably large eagles; occasionally also taken by leopards.

images.caption: Slender Mongoose

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The dwarf mongoose is the smallest African carnivore. The coat colour varies from reddish brown to yellowish grey. Males are slightly heavier than females.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Dwarf mongooses have a wide range of calls adapted to the needs of living in a group. Pack members frequently utter rather quiet plaintive ‘peeps’ as a contact call while foraging, and are often to be heard twittering in excitement and curiosity. When seriously alarmed they utter a short harsh ‘tchrr’, which is liable to send the whole pack fleeing for the nearest termite mound or hole. Dwarf mongooses growl and spit when cornered. The dwarf mongoose is the smallest African carnivore.

sections.text: Diurnal and terrestrial. Dwarf mongooses are gregarious, living in packs of up to 15 individuals with a dominant male and female in each pack. sections.text: Forage during the daytime, mainly taking insects (particularly beetles), grubs, grasshoppers, spiders, scorpions and termites; also snails, small reptiles, rodents, eggs and nestlings, as well as fruits and berries. Dwarf mongooses drink regularly, but can go without water if necessary. Left: a pack of dwarf mongooses lives in a permanent territory, with up to 30 termite mounds serving as nest sites and dens. But emigration is risky, and leaving one’s natal pack incurs a greater risk of predation opportunities. Females are more likely to stay on in their natal pack than are males. Membership of a pack provides protection for an individual, with pack members taking it in turns to watch for danger, alarm-calling if a predator is sighted. Dwarf mongooses are often seen early in the morning and in the evening, sunbathing at the entrance to their burrows, grooming and socializing with one another. They often stand on their hind legs to look around, and are very quick and agile; they can also climb trees and swim if necessary.
Predation Birds of prey are always a threat, particularly chanting goshawks; so too are snakes. Dwarf mongooses are occasionally taken by leopards and the smaller cats.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Nguchiro miraba or Kicheche plus tail: 7-11in (18-28cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Banded mongooses are greyish brown in colour with dark vertical body stripes. This is the mongoose most commonly seen by visitors to East Africa. The sexes are similar, though males are slightly larger and heavier than females.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Pack members keep in contact by constantly twittering, churring, chattering, chirping and whistling to one another as they forage. A loud strident ‘churr-churr’ is used as an alarm call, and when seriously threatened banded mongooses hiss, spit, snap and growl, arching their backs and erecting their fur.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Savanna and associated bush country, preferably with termite mounds. They are sometimes seen foraging in the open grasslands. The banded mongoose is a social species, active during the daytime and retreating to termite mounds at night.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and terrestrial. The banded mongoose normally lives in packs of 5-20 individuals, sometimes even 30 or 40, though these larger packs eventually split up. Each pack contains a number of adult males and females, and there is no dominant pair: several males and females mate at the same time of the year. Each morning, on emerging from their burrows, pack members sunbathe, play and groom; they mark various prominent objects (including each other) around their sleeping den with secretions from their anal glands, and visit communal latrines. They then move off to forage as a group, often fanning out across the ground, all the while digging with their strong claws and congregating at a particularly rich source of insects such as a pile of elephant droppings or old predator kill. A pack may travel 1-2 miles (1.6-4km) in a day, sometimes twice this distance while searching for food. They rest under bushes or in termite mounds during the hottest part of the day, foraging again in the afternoon before retiring for the night (usually in a termite mound). When two packs meet at the common boundary of their territories they may fight and chase one another, with the smaller pack usually retreating. Mongooses stand bolt upright when alarmed or if trying to locate other pack members and show little fear.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Typically three or four females come into oestrus at the same time and mate with a number of different males. The young are usually born during the rains when insects are most abundant, and are suckled communally with all the pack members grooming and playing with the babies, as well as acting as babysitters and helping to feed them. The young begin to travel with the pack at approximately five weeks old, But despite all the care they receive, probably less than 50½ of all juveniles survive the first three months. The adult coat colour appears by two to three months. Young males usually transfer to another pack in an attempt to gain breeding rights for themselves,

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Mainly insects; particularly beetles, grubs, grasshoppers, ants, spiders, scorpions, and termites; also snails, birds’ eggs and nestlings, small rodents, snakes, fruits and berries. Mongooses have the habit of throwing hard edible objects such as eggs, snails and millipedes backwards between their legs to smash them open against a rock, stone or tree. They drink where water is available, but can exist without it during dry periods.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Banded mongooses are preyed on by the larger birds of prey and sometimes by leopards. A pack of mongooses will bunch together and mob predators the size of martial eagles and jackals, lunging furiously and swarming in a teeth-snapping wave towards their larger foe. At times young lions catch and play with mongooses before killing them, though they do not eat them. Banded mongooses stand bolt upright when alarmed or when trying to locate other members of their pack. Spotted hyaenas have immensely strong jaws and powerful molar teeth, which enable them to crush bones and feed on the marrow will consume anything remotely edible.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Spotted hyaenas have a rather bear-like appearance and are the largest and most powerful of the three species of hyaena found in Africa. They have large, rounded ears and a sloping back, and the short, bushy tail is carried erect and flared in aggressive situations. With increasing age, the spots become less obvious. Females are larger than males and are further distinguished by the presence of a pair of enlarged dark nipples after their first cubs have been born. Spotted hyaenas possess the strongest jaws of all land predators, equipped with extraordinarily powerful molar teeth for crushing bones. They have blunt, non-retractile claws adapted for the long-distance chase and are the most abundant large mammalian predator in Africa. The spotted hyaena is the most numerous and adaptable of East Africa’s large predators.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Hyaenas are extremely vocal, giving voice to a rich variety of grunts, growls, cackles and screams when gathered at a kill. These peels of maniacal laughter gave rise to the name ‘laughing hyaena’. The contact call is a characteristic wailing whoop, uttered with the head to the ground and repeated five to ten times. This can carry for more than 3 miles (Skm).

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Widespread in a variety of habitats from semi-desert and dry bush country to moist savanna and forested regions

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Primarily nocturnal and terrestrial. Hyaenas are commonly seen during daylight and are highly opportunistic, scavenging and killing at any time of Spotted hyaenas have blunt, non-retractible claws adapted for long-distance chases in pursuit of prey. Here a hyaena peers up ata the day or night if the opportunity arises, though they generally rest up between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. They are usually found in clans of 5-30 individuals, consisting of adult females and their offspring, together with a number of unrelated males. Females remain in their natal clan for life, while males leave and join up with other nomadic males, eventually becoming resident in a new clan after a transitional period requiring considerable submissiveness. Females lead the clan in hunting and defence of territory, and are dominant over the males, with the most dominant females usually being the biggest and most aggressive hyaenas. Sons of dominant females outrank all clan members except their mother, way i) and are able to remain in their clan longer than their male age-mates. This may confer advantages on them when they transfer to another clan, including being better fed and more confident. Clan members recognize each other by scent. They mark grass stems with secretions from their anal glands, scratch up earth with their forefeet, leave scent from inter-digital glands as they walk, and deposit their bone-white droppings on conspicuous sites. Formerly despised as cowardly scavengers, hyaenas are now known to be formidable predators, capable of making their own kills either singly or in groups. They hunt by chasing prey animals such as wildebeest and zebras to the point of exhaustion before disembowelling them. Hyaenas can gallop at speeds of 25-30mph and even a solitary hyaena is quite capable of pulling down a full-grown wildebeest. A hyaena can comfortably eat 33lb (15kg) of meat ata sitting, and crack open the heaviest bones to feed on the marrow. This calcium-rich diet is the reason for their distinctive white droppings. During the day hyaenas often lie in the water at the edge of muddy pools to keep cool. They have excellent hearing and a highly developed sense of smell, which they employ to good advantage when seeking out carcasses on which to feed. In folklore hyaenas are associated with witches, who are believed to ride about at night on their backs.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: For many years hyaenas were thought to be hermaphroditic (possessing both male and female sex organs), due to the fact that the external labia of the female are swollen in the form of a false scrotum, and the clitoris is long and erectile, making it indistinguishable from the male’s penis. Copulation takes place by the male inserting his penis into an enlarged opening in the female's clitoris, which connects with the merged urinogenital duct. The reasons for these strange adaptations are still being debated. The young are born throughout the year, and females usually give birth to two cubs in an abandoned aardvark or warthog burrow, generally with a narrow entrance to prevent predators (including male hyaenas) from entering the den. The cubs are well developed at birth with their eyes open and their canines and incisor teeth already cut. It has recently been discovered that siblings of the same sex fight for dominance, and the death of one of the cubs within-the first month is not uncommon. Siblings of the opposite sex co-exist peacefully. After a few weeks the cubs are transferred to a communal den occupied by several females and their young. Cubs are black at birth, with the spots gradually becoming more obvious. They are seldom provisioned or guarded by clan members other than their mother (despite being related to some of them), and males play no part in cub rearing. Young hyaenas suckle until they are 12-14 months old, by which time they can accompany their mother on hunts and compete at kills. Males leave their natal clan at around two years old.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Hyaenas prey on both large and medium-sized herbivores such as wildebeest and Thomson’s gazelles, and the young of most of the larger antelope. They are very efficient feeders, eating everything except for the rumen contents and the horns of their prey, all of which is digested completely within 24 hours. Highly adaptable, they will eat anything vaguely edible, including people, and have been known to bite off the face of a person sleeping in the open. A number of deaths are reported each year in East Africa.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Hyaenas occasionally kill each other during inter-clan battles, and lions (particularly males) sometimes kill them at disputes over a carcass, though they do not eat them. Young hyaenas are occasionally attacked and killed at their den by a belligerent male lion, and male hyaenas sometimes kill and eat cubs. Spotted hyaenas are capable of killing prey the size of an adult wildebeest or zebra.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Smaller, lighter in build and rarer than the spotted hyaena (see page 50), with pointed upright ears, not rounded ones. The coat is sandy grey with vertical black stripes, and an erectile mane of long hair along the back. The front of the face is black. The aardwolf (Proteles cristatus) looks very similar to a striped hyaena, but is much smaller and primarily insectivorous. Male striped hyaenas are somewhat larger than females.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: The long-distance contact call is said to be a raucous howl. Unearthly moans, shrieks, groans, growls and giggles are uttered when individuals compete for food at a carcass.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Woodlands, rocky hillsides bordering savanna, dry bush country and semidesert. They are widely distributed, but everywhere very uncommon. Like the leopard, the striped hyaena occurs both in Africa and Asia.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Strictly nocturnal, lying up in caves, burrows, under dead trees or tucked away in dense cover during the daytime. The fact that adult striped hyaenas generally forage alone and are rarely seen together initially led people to think that this species was primarily solitary. But it has since been shown that a number of adults may share and defend the same home range, which is marked by anal gland secretions pasted on to grass stems. Small groups of (possibly related) adult females often occupy the same den and rear their cubs communally, with older offspring participating by keeping watch over the young and bringing food back to the den for them. Individuals wander widely in search of food, but are not particularly quick, running briefly at speeds of up to 30mph (S0kph) when chasing smaller prey such as African hares and gazelle fawns, though with little success. A number of striped hyaenas sometimes gather at a carcass to feed, though they are much less common and shyer than spotted hyaenas, and in general are rather timid, giving way to lions and avoiding their larger spotted relatives. They will, however, steal kills from leopards and cheetahs, and if threatened erect their manes to make themselves look bigger, as well as producing offensive anal gland secretions to deter an attack.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: The external genitalia do not show any of the extraordinary modifications seen in the spotted hyaena. Striped hyaenas breed at all times of the year, and females usually have their first litter of cubs when they are three years old. The young are born in a burrow or in a cave with their eyes closed. They suckle for up to a year, but begin to accompany their mother foraging when they are six months old. It is not yet known if males help to raise the young.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Insects, reptiles, ground birds and nestlings, small mammals the size of young antelopes, fruit and particularly carrion. Surplus food is sometimes stored in cover or at the sleeping den. Striped hyaenas drink regularly when water is readily available, but can go without for long periods during the dry season. Sometimes take livestock.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Occasionally killed by lions, and shot or poisoned by man. If cornered they will defend themselves courageously, erecting their mane to make themselves look bigger.

images.caption: The striped hyaena is smaller and lighter than the spotted hyaena, with pointed, upright ears.
The aardwolf looks very similar to a striped hyaena, but is much smaller and primarily insectivorous.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Simba females 250-300lb (110-135kg) plus tail: 2ft 4in–3ft 3in (70cm-1m) females 15-20 years Most adult male lions have a well-developed mane, and weigh up to 500lb (225kg). Lionesses are smaller, lighter and lack a mane.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Unmistakable. Females are smaller than males and lack a mane. Males begin to show a noticeable growth of mane at one and a half years old; it is fully developed by the time they are five or six. Some males never grow particularly fine manes and in certain areas (e.g. Tsavo National Park in Kenya) they do not grow names at all. Lions have a claw-like horny spine in their tail-tuft.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Lions roar to mark their territory and as a contact call between pride members. In dry conditions a roar can be heard for up to 3 miles (Skm), and when the air is moist the sound travels even further, perhaps as far as 5–6 miles (8-10km). They use a variety of sounds in aggressive situations from a deep rumbling growl to explosive grunts, snarls and hisses. A lioness calls her cubs with a soft, throaty ‘eoaw ugh’, repeated several times. Cubs grizzle and ‘eaow’ repeatedly when distressed. Lions are the only t ruly social members of the cat family, living in groups known as pri des which consist of a number of related females

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Lightly wooded country, rocky outcrops, thornbush and thickets bordering open plains. Lions generally avoid densely forested areas.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Nocturnal and diurnal, hunting mainly at night and at dawn and dusk. Lions are the exception among the cat family in that they are social, with adult males and females living together in groups called prides. The core of each pride is a number of closely related females (usually two to six, sometimes up to 12) and their cubs, together with a coalition of two to four (up to six) mature males who are often brothers or cousins but are not related to the females. Lionesses usually remain in their natal pride for the whole of their lives, while all young males are forced to leave, usually when they are two or three years old, thereby preventing inbreeding. Until they are big and powerful enough to attempt to oust males from another pride, these young males must lead the life of nomads. Pride territories may be as small as 8 sq miles (20 sq km) in high-density lion areas such as the Masai Mara, or as large as 150 sq miles (400 sq km) in marginal habitats such as parts of the Kalahari region in southern Africa, where prey is scattered and migratory. Young lionesses may also become nomadic, particularly if there are already a large number of adult lionesses in their pride, and at times manage to form a new pride by excising part of their natal territory and expanding into the periphery of other prides’ territories. Lions mark their territory by roaring and scent-marking with urine and anal gland secretions. Pride males rub their manes against bushes and spray them with urine, and all pride members claw the trunks of trees, leaving scent from their inter-digital glands, a habit that also helps to sharpen their claws. Serious fights over territory sometimes result in the death of a lion. When a coalition of new males ousts the existing pride males there is often a lengthy transitional period within the pride. Small cubs are invariably killed by the new males, thereby ensuring that the lionesses quickly come into oestrus again, allowing the new males to sire their own cubs rather than investing their time protecting the offspring of the previous pride males. Lions spend 16-20 hours per day resting, usually in a shady place, thereby avoiding heat stress. If the grass is long or if they are unduly bothered by biting flies, they will even climb into trees. Lions usually bolt when confronted by humans on foot, though females with young cubs can be particularly dangerous and may charge, Nomadic males try to kill any young cubs

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: A lioness usually has her first litter of cubs when she is three to four years old, thereafter producing a new litter of two to four cubs once every two years if the cubs survive. If the cubs die, she comes into oestrus within as little as four weeks. However, if the cubs have been killed by nomadic males it usually takes three months for the lioness to conceive, allowing time for the strongest coalition of males to to the males at Lioness with eight-month-old cub. A lioness gives birth to 2-4 cubs in thicket or rocky outcrop, and introduces them to other members are 6-8 weeks old. the safety ofa Deere) assume control of the pride territory before she becomes pregnant. All the members of the cat family are thought to be induced ovulators, with copulation helping to stimulate ovulation; a mating pair may copulate two to three times an hour for several days (usually two to six days). A lioness gives birth to her cubs in a place of concealment such as a thicket or rocky outcrop, where they remain hidden for the first six to eight weeks. and their eyes open towards the end of the second week. Females with young cubs allow them to suckle communally; in doing so each lioness is promoting her own genetic interests by helping to raise her relatives’ offspring. Cubs first eat meat at six weeks old and are weaned at six to eight months. They are reasonably competent hunters at two years old, but still rely on the pride for their survival and continue to grow until they are at least four or five years old.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Prey selection varies according to habitat and season. Lions are capable of overpowering a wide variety of herbivores, including wildebeest, zebras, topi, hartebeest, warthogs, buffaloes, giraffes, impalas and gazelles. Lions usually kill their prey by strangulation, though very large animals such as buffaloes are suffocated by one of the lions clamping its jaws over the animal’s mouth and nose. When plenty of food is available lions gorge themselves, with males eating up to 90lb (40kg) on an empty stomach, while lionesses can consume 60lb (27kg). This is four to five times their average daily requirement, and is an adaptation to a ‘feast or famine’ regime – predators can never be sure of when they will next eat.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Old or sick lions are sometimes killed and eaten by hyaenas. The young are preyed on by hyaenas, leopards and jackals. Lions attacking a young cow buffalo. Lions are stalkers, relying on stealth to get close to their prey (usually within 65 ft (20m) before launching an attack, reaching speeds of 35-40mph (50-60kph), though chases longer than 200-300yd (180-275m) are rare. The lionesses do most of the hunting, but often have to give way a kill, particularly if the prey is a small animal such as a warthog. But the pride males are more tolerant of the small cubs, who are their offspring and might otherwise fare badly at a kill. Even so, starvation is the main cause of death among lion cubs, and together with predation and infanticide by nomadic males, accounts for a mortality rate of 50-60½ during the first year. Though visitors are sometimes shocked by the bullying tactics of males at a kill, the division of labour within a pride does work to the advantage of the whole group. While the females hunt, the pride males ensure the integrity of the territory, thereby helping to create optimum conditions for the lionesses to rear their cubs.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Has a prominent necklace of spots and bars across its chest; spots on the torso and upper limbs form a pattern of rosettes. Its long tail is two thirds the length of its body, and the tip is pure white on the underside. Leopards are less frequently seen than cheetahs, though they are far more numerous. They are the most adaptable, least specialized and most numerous of the world’s big cats, and are found in Africa and Asia. Black leopards or ‘panthers’, as they are sometimes called, are simply melanistic leopards (the product of a recessive genetic trait), most commonly seen in dense forested habitats at higher altitudes. They can be born to parents with the normal coat colour, and despite the darkness of their coat the spots and rosettes are still discernible. Female leopard with four-month-old male cub. Leopards are highly opportunistic and will hunt by day or night if undisturbed.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A deep, rasping cough similar to the sound of wood being sawed. Leopards make this call at the beginning and end of their nocturnal wanderings, thereby signalling their presence in a area while helping to avoid contact with one another. Mothers call their cubs with a gruff ‘eaow’ or an abrupt sniffing sound called prusten. Leopards hiss loudly when approached by baboons or other predators such as hyaenas, warning them to keep their distance. If this fails they snarl, cough or grunt (and charge or flee).

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Leopards inhabit a wide variety of terrain from thick forests, rocky outcrops and bush country bordering open plains, to semi-arid scrub and deserts. They are found at all altitudes, and favour riverine forests and woodlands.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Primarily nocturnal, but where undisturbed they also hunt during the day, particularly when a female has cubs to feed. Leopards are terrestrial and arboreal, occasionally to be seen sunning themselves on anthills or rocky outcrops in the early morning or evening. Both males and females are solitary, associating only long enough Dich to mate. Males are territorial, spray-marking bushes, rocks and fallen trees with urine and secretions from their anal glands; and further defining their territory by calling and clawing the bark of trees. A male’s territory may overlap the home range of one or more females, who, even if related, tend to avoid one another as adults. Leopards are highly opportunistic hunters, obtaining their prey by stealth and ambush, attempting to get within 15-30ft (4.5-9m) of their quarry before rushing forwards and pouncing on it. They can accelerate to 38mph (60kph), but avoid long chases unless almost certain of success (e.g. when chasing a young impala or warthog). Leopards are unbelievably strong and are capable of dragging a 1001lb (45kg) carcass up into a tree clasped in their mouth. They use their incisors to pluck fur or feathers from prey such as African hares or guineafowl before feeding. By storing their kills in trees leopards are able to avoid the larger lions and hyaenas, and can feed until all but the skin and bones have been consumed. They drink regularly when water is available, but can survive without water by drinking the blood and body fluids of their kills, and by remaining nocturnal to avoid heat stress. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: distinguished from leopards by the distinct black ‘tearmarks’ running from the inner corners of their eyes to the edges of their mouth. They have the build of a muscular greyhound, and lack the rosettes and stocky physique of the leopard. Adult cheetahs are unable to retract their blunt, dog-like claws fully, though the dew claw on their wrist is extremely sharp and is used to help snag and trip their prey. The claws of young cheetah cubs remain semiretractile for up to six months.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Cheetahs have a high-pitched, birdlike contact call which sounds like a chirrup and is almost a whistle. They purr loudly when contented, and growl, spit and hiss when threatened or angry. Cheetahs cannot roar.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open plains, savanna and dry bush country.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Cheetah are diurnal and terrestrial, seldom hunting after dark. Females are solitary except when mating or when accompanied by cubs, and in areas where prey is migratory wander seasonally within a large home range of up to 400 sq miles (1,000 sq km). Male litter-mates sometimes stay together as adults, and a single male may form a partnership with one or two unrelated males. These male coalitions (numbering up to three individuals) have greater success in defending small exclusive territories (and the breeding rights | ee ™ that go with them) than do solitary males, as well as being able to bring down larger prey such as yearling wildebeest. Males will fight over ownership of a territory and coalitions sometimes kill or seriously injure single rivals. Cheetahs hunt mostly during the first few hours of morning and the last few hours of evening, though mothers accompanied by cubs will often hunt in the middle of the day as well, when the risk of interference from lions or hyaenas is at a minimum. Hunting strategy varies according to the habitat and the prey being sought. Generally, cheetahs single out a particular animal and then try to stalk to within 50-60yd (45-55m) of it before chasing. They can run at a maximum speed of Cheetahs, like other big cats, have specially adapted carnassial (cheek) teeth for shearing through the skin and flesh of their prey. before accelerating for the final dash. Prey is tripped and often hooked with the sharp dew claw; the rest of the claws are permanently exposed to give better traction when chasing and cornering. Cheetahs kill their prey by strangulation, and where possible drag it into cover to avoid detection. They very rarely scavenge. They are mild natured, and have never been known to attack humans in the wild.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Up to six cubs are born in a hollow created by their mother’s body in long grass or among tall vegetation in a marsh, or at the edge of a thicket. Their eyes open by the time they are two weeks old, and they remain hidden for the first six weeks. A mother often moves her cubs from one hiding place to another during this period, carrying them in her mouth. Young cheetahs have a mantle _ their hunting skills. Cubs begin following their mother when they are six weeks old, though at first they remain behind when she chases prey. By the time they are four to six months old their mother begins releasing young gazelles to them, allowing them the chance to practise months before they learn how to administer a killing bite quickly and effectively. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Caracals are the heaviest and most powerful of the small cats, with a rufous or fawn-coloured coat. They are short and stocky with long legs, large paws and a short tail. The long tufted ears give them a lynx-like appearance and they are sometimes known as the desert lynx. The sides of the muzzle and ear tufts are black. Sexes are similar, though males are larger and heavier.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Not very vocal; said to use a hoarse bark as a contact call. They growl, spit and hiss when alarmed or angry.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Dry bush, open woodlands, rocky outcrops and stony hill country.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Mainly nocturnal, but also active early in the day and in the late afternoon where undisturbed by man. Caracals are solitary, avoiding contact with other adults and marking their home range by spraying urine tinged with anal gland secretions on to bushes. They are hunters of legendary power and agility, combining the strength of a leopard with the leggy bird-hunting skills of a serval. Caracals will cover a kill with vegetation or store it in a tree to feed on it again, and will scavenge from old carcasses,

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Breed year round with a birth peak during the rains. The young are born in a cave or burrow or under a log, and their eyes open during the second week. They start eating meat at four to six weeks, are weaned at five months and are independent by the time they are a year old.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Caracal prey on a large variety of species up to the size of impalas. They commonly take hyrax, hares, rodents, francolins, guineafowl, sandgrouse, pigeons and doves, as well as small antelopes such as steenbok and klipspringers, which they kill by strangulation in the same way as the big cats.

images.caption: The caracal may be distinguished from all other African cats by its tufted ears. It is renowned for its strength and agility. Predation Adults are occasionally killed by leopards and perhaps lions; the young are vulnerable to large eagles. Caracals are good climbers and seek refuge in trees if chased by dogs. They have been shot, trapped and poisoned by farmers throughout their range for killing livestock and poultry.
Though primarily nocturnal, the caracal will hunt by day when not disturbed by humans.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Mondo females 18-26lb (8–12kg) plus tail: 11-16in (25-40cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: When seen at a distance the serval looks a little like a small cheetah, though its long legs, large ears and short tail are distinctive. Servals are spotted and streaked along the back of the neck and shoulders. Melanistic (black) varieties occur in some highland areas.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A high-pitched, repeated cry used as a contact call. They also growl, spit and hiss when angry or frightened.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Long grass areas near streams or marshes, among scattered bush with good grass cover, and montane

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Primarily a nocturnal species, though quite often active during the early morning or evening and on overcast days. Servals are solitary, with females living in overlapping home ranges, but avoiding contact with one another. Males defend a territory which includes the home ranges of more than one female. Both sexes mark bushes with urine and rub secretions from the corners of their mouths on to grass stems, to notify other servals of their whereabouts The serval’s large ears help it to locate small mammals and birds hidden without actually meeting. They are usually seen high-stepping through long grass in search of food, and though primarily terrestrial, will climb trees to escape danger. They employ their large ears to help them locate prey hidden in the grass, and are exceptionally quick and agile, leapin go into the air and pouncing on small rodents and ground birds before bending forward to dispatch them with a bite. Birds are regularly taken on the wing, sometimes from a standing jump. Servals use their long forelimbs to snag mole rats and hole-nesting birds, and stalk along the fringes of marshes to hunt for frogs and waterfowl? They curl up in the long grass or at the base of small bushes to rest during the day, and are so well camouflaged that they are almost impossible to detect. in the long grass.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Breed annually, the young being born amongst tall vegetation or rocky crevices, or concealed in a hollow in thick cover. A female moves her cubs regularly and brings small prey back to them. Cubs suckle for three to four months and are independent by the end of their first year.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Rats, mice, game birds, hares, young antelopes, frogs and lizards.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Servals are sometimes killed and eaten by larger predators such as leopards and occasionally by hyaenas. The young are taken by all the larger predators, large mongooses, ratels, large eagles and snakes. Right: the serval has long legs and a short tail and, from a distance, looks a little like a small cheetah. Below: the serval is primarily nocturnal, although it may be seen high-stepping through the long grass in the early morning or late afternoon.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Resembles a large, leggy domestic cat with greyish or sandy-coloured coat and a ringed tail with a black tip. The coat colour seems to vary to suit the habitat. Dark stripes may or may not be visible, but are usually most prominent on the legs, and are sometimes well defined on the torso as in a domestic tabby cat. The backs of the ears are a distinctive rusty red colour. or sandy-coloured domestic cat, with a ringed, black-ti

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Courting wild cats caterwaul like domestic cats, and share many of the same vocalizations.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Widely distributed over much of Africa, particularly in scrub bush country and the edge of grasslands, as well as in mountainous habitats up to periphery of human settlement and scavenge during the night for scraps of food. Wild cats interbreed with domestic cats and were domesticated by the Egyptians from 4000 BC.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Nocturnal and generally difficult to observe. Little is known about the social system of the African wild cat, though it is thought to be similar to that of the European wild cat (Felis silvestris), with adults being solitary except when mating or when a female has kittens. A male’s territory overlaps the home ranges of two or three females, who tend to avoid contact with one another. Wild cats mark their home range with urine and anal gland secretions as well as secretions from glands situated at the corner of their mouths, which are rubbed against grass stems and twigs. They are sometimes to be seen early in the morning lying at the entrance to a burrow in the open grasslands (e.g. the Serengeti plains), but must be careful to avoid conflict with the larger predators. In less open terrain wild cats sleep during the day under fallen trees, in dense thickets or in rocky crevices. They climb well and will sometimes rest in trees or use them as a refuge from predators.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Wild cats in grassland environments feed principally on mice and grass rats, as well as birds, frogs, reptiles, large insects, and animals up to the size of hares.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Leopards, caracals, servals and honey badgers are all known to kill wild cats. Kittens are preyed on by all of these species, and by smaller carnivores such as civets, genets, large snakes and jackals. A mother will try to defend herself and her young by looking as fierce as possible, raising her fur, arching her back, flattening her ears, hissing, spitting and lashing out with her claws.

They breed throughout the year, with a peak during the rains when rodents are at their most abundant. A female gives birth at a den similar to those used as daytime hiding places. She brings back mice and birds for the young to feed on when they are just a few weeks old and by the time the kittens are two to three months old they begin to accompany their mother when she hunts. Young females have their first litter in their second year, and males are fully mature by the time they are two or three years old.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Unmistakable: the largest land mammal. Male elephants weigh almost twice as much as females and have a more rounded forehead and heavier and longer tusks; females have a pointed forehead. Tusks are upper incisors which become visible at two to three years of age, and continue to grow throughout an elephant’s life. The record length of a tusk along the curve is 11ft 6in (3.5m), and the record weight of a single tusk is 235lb Elephants are highly social animals and live in family units consisting of a number of related adult females and their calves. Family members often touch one another, and greet by the lower-ranking animal inserting the tip of its trunk into the other’s mouth.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Elephants have a wide range of vocal communication. It has recently been discovered that herds keep in contact by emitting loud (103dB), very low frequency (14-35Hz) calls which carry at least 1/2 miles (2.5km). The ‘throaty’ rumbles and growls that humans can hear are used as a greeting. Bellowing, trumpeting and screaming all signal various degrees of alarm and aggression.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: A wide variety of habitat from savanna and semi-arid bush to montane forests.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal. Elephants are gregarious, living in family groups of 10-15 individuals, consisting of related cows and their offspring, led by an old female known as the matriarch. Family units sometimes join up to form larger herds when searching for fresh vegetation during the rainy season. Elephants spend 16 hours a day feeding, interspersed with visits to suitable mud wallows, after which they often shower themselves with dust and rub against trees or boulders, all of which helps to remove ticks and keep their skin in good condition. In the middle of the day, a herd seeks the shade of riverine hickets or clumps of trees, emerging again to continue feeding as the emperature cools around three or our o'clock in the afternoon. Adults generally sleep in a standing position, though they do sometimes lie down bulls have been seen propping hemselves up against termite mounds 0 snooze). Young calves generally sleep lying down. All elephants secrete a thick, strong-smelling substance called temporin from temporal glands situated on either side of the face, midway between the eye and the ear. Temporin has an individual odour and is secreted throughout the year by cows; it is thought to help individuals to recognize each other and maintain contact and is first visible when a calf is about six months old. Adult males secrete temporin only at particular times of the year, when they are said to be in ‘musth’ (a Hindi word), constantly dribbling smelly urine down their legs, which causes their penis and sheath to turn green. Musth signals a marked rise in production of the male hormone testosterone, leading to an upsurge in aggression and heightened sexual activity. Increasingly confined to smaller and smaller areas, elephants can cause rapid and dramatic changes to their environment, often to the detriment of the other species dependent on trees and bushes for food and shade. For this reason elephants are culled in some parts of Africa to keep the population at manageable levels and maintain the diversity of species in wildlife areas. sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Bull elephants leave their natal herd when they are 12-15 years old and form loose associations of up to 15 individuals with other bachelors. They begin competing for the chance to breed by the time they are 25 years old, joining the family units at various times to test the females for oestrus by scenting them with their trunks. Mature bulls of 35 years or older monopolize breeding opportunities within the various populations, with each bull coming into musth at a different time of the year. In this way they are able to fertilize receptive cows throughout the year, locating Young bull elephants engage in mock battles known as ‘jousting’, a ritual which helps establish their position in the male dominance hierarchy. They leave their natal herd at puberty, when they are about 12-15 years old, and form loosely associated bachelor herds with other bulls. them by the loud oestrus rumbles that they utter when they are ready to mate. A cow first conceives when she is 10-11 years of age, and in optimum circumstances will continue to produce a calf every four or five years for the rest of her life. She gives birth standing up, and the calf suckles from the pair of breasts between its mother’s forelegs, sometimes standing on its hind legs to reach her teats. Calves weigh 250lb (1 15kg) at birth and are small enough to pass under their mother’s stomach for the first year. They suckle for at least four years and continue to grow throughout their lives.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Grass, leaves, reeds, seed pods, wild fruits, bark and roots. Elephants day, and drink 30-60 gallons

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Due to their enormous size, adult elephants are immune to predation, though lions, hyaenas and crocodiles will kill young or sick elephants. By far the most devastating ‘predator’ has been man, slaughtering 700,000 elephants during the 1980s for their ivory. There are thought to be approximately 600,000 elephants remaining today, and the trade in ivory is banned worldwide.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The plains zebra has broad, widely spaced stripes which are generally browner in colour in females, and jet black in stallions. The subspecies Boehm’s zebra (Equus burchelli (Common or Burchell’s Zebra) boehmi) of southern Kenya and Tanzania has brown shadow stripes between the main stripes. Each zebra has a unique coat pattern. The contact call is a peculiar barking noise which sounds rather like a cross between a dog barking and a donkey braying. Zebras snort abruptly alarmed or nervous, and adults squeal when threatened or bitten. Foals wail Open grassy plains, wooded grasslands and semi-arid grass bush Diurnal and nocturnal, though generally more active during the daytime. Zebras are gregarious, and are usually found in groups of up to six females accompanied by their offspring, and a mature male who is the dominant member of the group. Young males leave their family group at between one and three years of age, and join bachelor herds of from two to ten males (sometimes more), consisting either entirely of young or older males, or of a mixture of all age groups. Seniority in these bachelor herds is age-based. sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Stallions acquire females by abducting young mares from another family. This happens at the onset of a female’s first oestrus, when she is one to two years old. These young females adopt a very obvious and distinctive stance when they come into oestrus, standing with their legs apart and their tail lifted. Competition for females is intense and a dozen or more stallions fight for possession of young mares, making it almost impossible for the harem male to withstand their challenge. Older females conceal oestrus, and only adopt this stance when about to mate with the harem male. Females give birth in the vicinity of their family group; foals can stand within 10-15 minutes, walk shortly afterwards and run within the hour. Plains zebras waiting to cross the Mara River during the migration. Plains zebras gather into huge herds while migrating, though individual families (consisting of a number of females, their young, and a harem stallion) remain intact.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Lions, hyaenas and hunting dogs are all capable of killing both adult and young zebras, while leopards and sionally cheetahs take foals. When threatened, a zebra family bunches together and moves off, with the stallion bringing up the rear. This is often sufficient to deter a fully fledged attack by pack-hunting hyaenas and hunting dogs. If not, adult zebras are capable of delivering a bone-crushing kick, and have been known to smash the jaw of a pursuing predator. Added to this, their teeth are razor sharp and can snap a man’s arm.

Food Zebras are grazers but do not ruminate, relying on large quantities of coarser vegetation, which they are able to process rapidly. They are highly adaptable, selecting the seed head and stem of the longer grasses during the dry season, and feeding on short green grass during the rains. Zebras prefer to drink daily, often making their way to water during the middle of the day.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The largest of the zebras, the Grevy’s can be distinguished from the plains zebra (see page 84) by its large head and bat ears, its narrow, close-set stripes and unstriped belly. The thin circular stripes on the rump form a distinctive ‘target’. Grevy’s zebras are sometimes found in mixed groups with plains zebras. The Grevy’s, the largest of the zebras, is found in north-eastern Kenya and southern Ethiopia. It has large bat ears, narrow, close-set stripes and an unstriped belly.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Grevy’s zebra is the most northerly representative of the zebra family, inhabiting the dry savanna and arid bush country of northern Kenya and southern Ethiopia.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal. Grevy’s zebras adopt a very different form of social organization to plains zebras. Groups of five to ten females and their foals wander in overlapping home ranges which include the territories of a number of territorial males. Social grooming is almost absent, and herds seem to lack cohesion or well-defined social bonds. Young males stay in their mother’s herd until they are three years old and then leave to join other bachelors. They are fully mature and capable of holding a territory at six years old. Stallions mark the boundaries of their territory by defecating and urinating at dung middens, by calling and by their physical presence. Bachelors often mingle with the female herds while searching for good grazing, and are tolerated by territory holders as long as none of the females is in oestrus, Large mixed herds of up to 200 individuals sometimes form during the dry season migrations, and may gather at waterholes. These big herds generally disperse for the duration of the dry season to avoid competition for scarce grazing. Territorial males often remain on their territory year round, waiting for the females to return at the onset of the wet season, when most breeding takes place.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Foals are born throughout the year with a peak during the rains. Females usually have their first foal when they are three years old. Newborn foals gain their feet within 10-15 minutes and can run within the hour. Mothers with young foals congregate in nursery herds, sometimes in the company of heavily pregnant mares and mares with older young.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Grevy’s zebras graze on the stems and seed heads of various grass species, browsing on herbage during the dry season when grass is in short supply. They drink daily if water is available, but can go without drinking for two or three days when necessary. During prolonged drought they will dig for water in the river beds.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Lions prey on adults and young, while leopards and hyaenas sometimes take foals. Grevy’s zebra herd, Samburu Game Reserve, northern Kenya.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The white rhinoceros is a huge animal, larger but lighter than a hippo. The name ‘white’ rhino is a misnomer from the Dutch word weit meaning ‘wide’, due to the wide, square mouth which is adapted for grazing. In fact all rhinos are greyish or greyish brown in colour, The white rhino is much bigger and heavier than the black rhino (see page 94) – double its weight at times – and is further distinguished by a large hump on the hind neck. The length of the front horn averages 24in

sections.text: High-pitched squeals, grunts, bellows and snorts,

sections.text: Their natural habitat is grassy savanna country, but both the northern and southern races of the white rhino were virtually exterminated earlier this century. sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: White rhinos are more placid and sociable animals than black rhinos. They are found singly or in small parties of females and their young, with breeding females living in overlapping home ranges. Adult males are generally solitary and territorial. They drink and wallow daily where possible, but can go for a few days without water during dry spells. The white rhino is a slower creature than the black rhino, but can still gallop at 25mph (40kph) and trot at 18mph (29kph). When alarmed the calf of a white rhino trots off in front of its mother, while a black rhino calf

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Births are recorded throughout the year. Copulation lasts for 30 minutes, usually after hours of preliminary mounting. A cow isolates herself in thick cover to give birth and remains hidden with her calf for several days. The newborn calf weighs about 150- 175lb (70-80kg) and continues to suckle for the first year, although it begins eating grass at two months. Whenever a cow gives birth, her previous calf moves away and often attaches itself to a cow without a calf or joins other calves of a similar age.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Their size makes adults immune to predation. Lions and hyaenas do kill young rhinos, though females will attack a predator with their horns in an attempt to defend their calves.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Unmistakable, prehistoric-looking creature with a two-horned head. The front horn occasionally over 40in (102cm);: the rear horn measures 13-16in (33-40cm), occasionally over 20in (50cm). Males have a shorter, thicker front horn than females. Rhino horn is composed of a tightly packed, fibrous protein called keratin (also found in skin, nails and hooves), which grows from the skin but is unattached to the skull. Black rhinos have three hoofed toes on each foot and a pointed prehensile upper lip adapted for browsing. The spoor or footprint is rounded at the back, whereas that of the white rhino (see page 92) is sharply indented. Black rhinos are noticeably smaller than white rhinos, Powdered rhino horn has for centuries been used as a medicine in Asia and the Far East, and is considered to have almost supernatural healing powers for a wide variety of Fewer than 2,500 black rhinos survive in the wild. It is estimated that there were 65,000 black rhinos in the 1960s; today they are severely endangered and less than 2,500 survive in the wild.

sections.text: A variety of habitats from savanna and semi-arid bush to montane forests up for areas with scrub and thick bush.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Most active early morning and evening, also during the night. Adults are usually solitary, living in a well-defined home range which is marked by characteristic dung piles or middens. The dung is scattered at these sites by a scraping motion of the hind feet, and males also mark bushes by spraying them with urine. The home ranges of males and females tend to overlap, but males may or may not defend part of their range as an exclusive territory. Their eyesight is poor, but their hearing and sense of smell are highly developed. Black rhinos are surprisingly quick and agile charging at speeds of up to 30mph (48kph), and can about-turn at full gallop. They are mainly active in the morning and the evening, lying down to rest during the hotter hours. They drink, wallow in mud and dust bathe daily where possible, as well as searching out suitable salt licks. Rhinos use their front horn to defend themselves and to dig for salt and

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a peak in breeding activity during the rainy season. Females usually have their first calf when they are about six years old. It is not uncommon for a number of males to congregate around an oestrus female and serious fighting may take place as the bulls compete for the chance to mate. Generally the largest bull ends up asserting his dominance. Calves weigh up to 100lb (45kg) at birth, gain their feet after ten minutes or so and can walk within three hours. They stay with their mother until the next calf is born (two to four years). At this point the older calf is usually driven away, but often returns later or is temporarily adopted by another female. Males mature at 10-12 years of age. Adult rhinos are too big to be vulnerable to predators, but the young are sometimes taken by lions and hyaenas.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Black rhinos browse on a wide variety of plants, in some areas up to 100-200 species, such as acacia seedlings and branches of euphorbias (which are broken off with the horn),with a preference for herbs and shrubs, particularly legumes. During the rains they occasionally take grass.

During the dry season they may be forced to travel up to 12 miles 19km) to drink and wallow, but can go without water for three to five days. Predation Their large size means adult rhinos are generally immune to predation, but crocodiles may pose a danger to a rhino crossing a river. Lions and hyaenas occasionally kill young rhinos, but females can horn and kill predators in defence of their young.
Because of the threat of poachers, armed game rangers monitor the movements of rhinos in the parks and reserves.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Hyrax are rabbit-sized, tailless animals. These two species both occur in similar rocky habitats and are often found together. The rock hyrax is bigger and has a squarer head than the yellow-spotted rock hyrax, which is more lightly built and has a more pointed face with a white spot over each eye. The coat of the rock hyrax is coarse and brownish in colour; that of the bush hyrax is soft and grey, like that of the tree hyrax (see page 99), The rock hyrax has an oval patch of yellow hair in the middle of the back, while the yellow-spotted rock hyrax and tree hyrax have a whitish patch; this patch is the site of a scent gland. Hyrax share a common ancestor with the elephant, aardvark and dugong. Their feet have rubbery pads on the underside, adapted to climbing, with four toes on the forefeet and three on the hind feet. The peculiar hoof-like nails are similar to those of elephants; the claw-like inner toe of the hind foot is used for grooming. Hyrax possess two permanently growing upper incisors which are curved and tusk-like, and serve as potent fighting weapons. Males have internal testes; females have two teats between the forelegs, though these may be lacking in some species of tree hyrax, and two or four teats on the belly. Sexes are similar, though males are more thickset and have longer incisor tusks.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Males have a genus-specific, far-carrying, oft-repeated territorial call, usually heard in the early morning and evening. Both sexes utter a high-pitched screech when alarmed.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Savanna and semi-desert. Hyrax live among boulders, rocky outcrops and other similarly rugged terrain with small caves and crevices for them to hide in. The rock hyrax also occurs in Sinai, Syria and Arabia and is the animal referred to in the Bible as the coney.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Generally diurnal due to their rather slow metabolism. They are often seen sunning themselves early in the morning, sometimes huddled together or piled on top of each other for warmth. Gregarious, usually in colonies of 10-30 individuals representing a number of different families. Each family is composed of a territorial male and a group of related females and their young. Families live in overlapping home ranges, though the core of each home range is defended by the territorial male. Colonies of rock and yellow-spotted rock hyrax often exist side by side with little overt aggression, though the larger rock hyrax takes priority over its smaller neighbours at drinking sites or dust-bathing locations. Hyrax are excellent climbers and are capable of walking on the thinnest of branches (particularly the yellow-spotted rock hyrax). Numerous sweat glands keep the rubbery soles of their feet moist, giving them increased traction and enabling them to run up steep rock faces, They feed during the morning and afternoon, and groom and dust bathe regularly.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a seasonal peak in births during the rainy season. The young are usually born in rocky crevices and are well developed at birth – fully raired and with their eyes open. They start to eat solid food almost immediately, although they are not weaned for one to five months. Females remain in their natal range when fully grown, while young males disperse as adolescents at one and a nalf to two years old. Males do not form bachelor groups, and must wait heir chance to take over a territory.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Rock hyrax are predominantly grazers. They eat rapidly while in the open to avoid predation. The yellow-spotted rock hyrax is a browser, feeding on plant material from a wide variety of bushes and trees.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Preyed on by leopards, caracals, servals, larger eagles, owls and snakes. The Verreaux’s eagle or black eagle is well known as a hunter of hyrax. A pair of these birds will often hunt together, swooping down to pluck a hyrax from its rocky home. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The southern tree hyrax is similar in size and general appearance to the rock hyrax (see page 96), but has longer, softer fur. The coat colour is variable, but is usually browner than that of the rock hyrax. Tree hyrax have an oval white patch in the middle of the back, surrounded by erectile hair. This is the site of a scent gland, and during aggressive interactions the hair is erected and an aromatic secretion released. The tree hyrax and the yellow-spotted rock hyrax share a common ancestor, with the tree hyrax having adapted to a more specialized way of life.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Well known for the highly repetitive, ear-piercing screech uttered at night as a means of marking its territory. Both sexes call, but males are louder and can be heard up to 2 miles 3km) away.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Montane forests and woodlands up to very high densities in suitable forest habitats.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Nocturnal and either solitary or in monogamous pairs. Tree hyrax rest in hollows in trees during the day, emerging at night to feed and use communal latrines situated at the base of trees. They are highly adaptable and can also live a diurnal, rock-dwelling existence in rugged country at high altitudes.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a seasonal peak in births during the rainy season. The young are born in a hole in a tree and are well developed at birth with their eyes already open.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Tree hyrax feed on a wide variety of vegetable matter, eating large quantities of leaves, twigs and fruit as well as lichens and grass. They can consume the equivalent of a third of their body weight each day.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Preyed on by leopards, caracals, servals, civets, larger eagles, owls and pythons. Tree hyrax are traditionally hunted for their soft fur to make blankets and capes.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Savanna, grasslands, semi-arid bush, and highland areas up to 8,500ft

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Strictly diurnal. Warthogs are gregarious, usually in groups consisting of a single adult female, one or two generations of her offspring, and at times a mature male. Sometimes two or more related females and their young share a home range, and these groups or ‘sounders’ may number 5-15 individuals, with arger groups evolving when food i D most readily available. Young males form loose associations with other bachelors until they are fully grown at four years old. At this age they become solitary and begin to breed. Adult males usually associate with the sounders only when consorting with an oestrus female. Warthogs live and breed in old termite mounds, usually commandeering the burrows created by aardvarks. Each sounder moves to and fro between as many as ten different burrows, which are occupied on a first come, first served basis. During the heat of the day warthogs seek shade or rest in mud wallows. They avoid cold and wet conditions by remaining in their burrows until the temperature rises. They feed at any time of the day, but particularly during the early part of the morning and later in the afternoon. They are often to be seen feeding down on their front knees, which allows them to clip the green shoots close to the ground. Warthogs are surprisingly quick, running at speeds of up to 35mph (56kph) when chased by predators, though they are more usually seen trotting in a characteristic fashion with their tails held ramrod straight like

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Mating usually takes place towards the end of the long rains and there is a peak in births during September- October, at the beginning of the short rains. Despite being born hairless the piglets look just like miniature adults. The female remains underground with her young for much of the first week. The litter emerges during the second week, and straight away begins Male warthog with red-billed oxpeckers. Warthogs have three distinctive facial growths, more prominent in males, which help to protect the eyes and face from injury when the animals ‘joust’. feeding on the grass around the den. Piglets start to try and follow their mother at five to six weeks of age, but continue to suckle for three to four months, by which time the bulk of their diet is grass. They are weaned at six months.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Adults are preyed on by lions and leopards, and at times by hyaenas and hunting dogs. The young are killed by all the larger predators and larger eagles, with up to 50½ mortality during the first year. Warthogs occasionally turn to face an attacker, and may inflict serious injuries on an inexperienced or careless predator with lightning thrusts of their razor-sharp lower tusks. A female warthog usually gives birth to 2- 4 piglets (rarely as many as 6-8) after a gestation period of 5½ months. She uses an underground den, usually an old aardvark burrow. The young begin to try to follow their mother when they are 5-6 weeks old and are vulnerable to all the rains in the Masai Mara, Kenya. This strategy is effective against most predators, though a hungry lion will sometimes dig a warthog out of its burrow. Adult males urinate in their mud wallows, probably as a way of signalling their presence in the area; and both sexes mark objects within their home range, using secretions from tusk and preorbital glands; they also frequently rub scent on to one another. Warthogs are grazers, preferring short green grass. During the dry season they use their tough, disc-like snouts and heavy upper tusks to dig up bulbs, roots and tubers. They also take fallen fruit, and occasionally eat carrion and grass from the stomachs of carcasses abandoned by predators, as well as sifting through the vegetation in elephant droppings. They tend to avoid cultivated areas but are at times destructive to crops.
