sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Hippos are distantly related to pigs and have four webbed toes on the front and hind feet. They are second only to the elephant in terms of weight and possess a formidable set of permanently growing canine tusks, with those in the lower jaw measuring up to 1ft 8in (50cm). The name hippopotamus is derived from a Greek word meaning ‘river horse’, due to their rather horse-like profile when partially submerged. Their skin is traditionally used to make whips, which are called kibokos in East Africa and sjamboks in southern Africa.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Hippos communicate with a variety of raucous bellowing noises, oinks, snorts and grunts. They suck in their breath and make a menacing hiss when threatened.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Rivers, lakes and swamps, preferably with sandy banks to lie on and access lo grassy areas as foraging sites. Hippos have wide mouths and massive lips as an adaptation to hippo can consume 100|b (45kg) of grass per night. The bristles on feel its way and measure its bite when feeding at night.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Nocturnal and diurnal. Hippos are gregarious, and are usually found in groups of 10-20 females and their young, together with a territorial male who has exclusive breeding rights with the females. The dominant bull forces adolescent males to leave the herd when they are seven to eight years old, and some males live in bachelor groups or remain solitary. Larger herds of 50-100 hippos are not uncommon, and during periods of overcrowding or when very dry spells occur they may gather in their hundreds. Hippos spend much of the day partially submerged on sand banks, and produce an oily red secretion to protect the thin epidermis of their 2in (Scm) thick skin from overheating and drying out in the sun. They can stay beneath the water for periods of one to five minutes, and are capable of snoozing while submerged, resurfacing to breathe automatically, Hippos generally walk on the bottom rather than swim. They emerge from the river shortly after dusk via well-worn ‘hippo trails’ carved into the steep banks. Individuals can eat approximately 100lb (45kg) of food per night, sometimes wandering on a round trip of up to 5 miles (8km) in search of suitable grazing before returning to the river at dawn. During their nightly wanderings bulls advertise their presence by vigorously wagging their thick hairy tails while defecating, thus scattering dung and urine against bushes and the bases of trees (and the hippo trails leading to and from the water). On meeting, territorial bulls turn their backs and shower each other with dung and urine before continuing on their way. Non-damaging ritualized fights involving two combatants in open-mouthed jousting contests sometimes degenerate into more serious affairs, and their razor-sharp tusks can cause gaping wounds and even death. Hippos are surprisingly quick on land and in the water, galloping at 18mph (30kph) if threatened, and capable of outrunning a man over short distances. They can about turn in full flight (but are unable to jump) and generally retreat to the safety of the water when alarmed. Hippos are said to cause more human deaths than buffaloes, elephants or rhinos.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Apart from whales and dolphins, hippos are the only mammals to mate in the water. There is a birth peak during the rains, and a cow usually moves away from the herd when she is ready to calve, giving birth in shallow water or close to the river bank on land. The mother remains alone for one to two weeks with her at birth and can suckle underwater, surfacing to breathe every few seconds. Calves begin grazing at five months and are weaned towards the end of their first year. Young females remain in their natal herd and produce their first calf when they are about ten years old.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Grazers, preferring short green grass and creating neatly cropped lawns with their huge wide lips.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Lions occasionally attack adult hippos, and crocodiles sometimes take calves, though a healthy hippo is capable of killing a predator with one bite from its massive jaws. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Giraffes are the tallest mammals in the world with males sometimes growing to more than 18ft (5.5m), and females to 16ft (4.9m). Despite their size, giraffes – like humans – have only seven neck vertebrae. The Masai giraffe, which occurs in southern Kenya and Tanzania, has a pattern of jagged-edged reddish-brown coat markings, with spots running down the legs to below the knee. Both sexes have short, skin-covered horns which are solid bony outgrowths from the skull, unlike true horns. The ends of the horns are tufted in females and hairless in males. Due to their great height and excellent vision, giraffes are often quick to spota predator on the move. Right: Masai giraffe browsing on whistling thorn. All giraffes have a long – 18-20in (45-50cm) – prehensile tongue which enables them to reach into vegetation that would otherwise be inaccessible. Below: Masai giraffes among thornbush country near Seronera Lodge, Serengeti National Park, Tanzania. Giraffes can gallop at speeds of up to 35mph (56kph). During adolescence, male giraffes establish a dominance from of fighting called ‘necking’. Serious fights are rare female is present. Female giraffes do not ‘neck’.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Usually silent, occasionally uttering harsh coughs, rumbles and grunts.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open acacia woodlands, wooded grasslands, desert grass-bush, and scrub and coastal forests up to 6,500ft

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal. Giraffes are usually found in parties of 5-20 individuals, but sometimes in groups of 50 to 100 roaming large, overlapping home ranges. Though giraffes are gregarious they rarely interact with one another and do not form bonds. Consequently a group may be made up of any combination of sexes and ages. Instead of defending a territory, adolescent males establish a dominance hierarchy by a ritualized form of fighting called ‘necking’. Contestants stand flank to flank and then swing their heads at each other's bodies, entwining their long necks, with the winner sometimes mounting the loser in a display of dominance. Serious fights between adult males are rare and occur only when an oestrus female is present. sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: A female isolates herself among the thorn thickets to give birth, and remains standing throughout. The calf mother stays with her calf for the first few days, allowing it time to imprint on her. Calves join a creche on emerging from hiding, often staying on high, bush-covered terrain while their mothers go off to feed. Young giraffes suckle until they are a year old, and continue to grow for the first seven to ten years of their lives.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Giraffes are ruminants, browsing on trees and bushes, particularly on acacia leaves, pods and soft thorns, using their mobile upper lip and 18- 20in (45-50cm) prehensile tongue to reach among the foliage. If succulent vegetation is available they can exist for long periods without drinking, producing hard, marble-sized droppings as a way of conserving water. When a giraffe does drink it has to spread its stilt-like legs wide apart in order to reach the water. But this is only part of the problem! A giraffe’s head is 7-10ft (2.1-4m) above its heart, necessitating a carotid artery more than 6ft (1.8m) long. To prevent it from fainting when suddenly raising its head while drinking, the giraffe has a complex network of highly elastic and absorbent blood vessels in the brain, and special valves in its arteries and veins to prevent the blood rushing to or from the brain when it lowers or raises its head. Twiga The reticulated giraffe is found in dry acacia woodlands and desert grass-bush, north of the Tana River in the Northern Frontier district of Kenya. It is slightly smaller and less dependent on water than the Masai giraffe, and has a beautiful brick-shaped, liver-red coat pattern, demarcated by narrow white lines. sections.text: By hunting in a group lions occasionally manage to kill adult giraffes, usually by surprising them when they are lying down during the night. Female giraffes will often defend their young calves courageously by lashing out with their plate-sized feet, and adult giraffes have been known to kill or seriously injure lions. Despite this, in some areas more then 50½ of young calves fall prey to lions and spotted hyaenas. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A strangely fashioned, bearded antelope with a heavy-looking head, long face, humped back and the long, wispy tail of a horse. The tail has long been Bull wildebeest about to engage in a horn-to-horn ‘jousting’ contest during the annual rut taurinus prized as a ceremonial fly-whisk by tribes such as the Masai. Both sexes have horns, those of the males being heavier, with a more pronounced boss at the base. Severe outbreaks of a viral disease known as rinderpest or cattle plague were the scourge of the Serengeti’s wildebeest and buffalo herds prior to a successful veterinary campaign during the 1950s to create a disease-free buffer zone among cattle living on the periphery of the Mara and the Serengeti. By 1960 the disease was under control and the wild herds expanded rapidly to their present numbers. However, wildebeest carry malignant catarrh, which is spread to cattle by contact with afterbirths and post-natal fluids when the wildebeest are calving. Mortality among cattle may be high. in June.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Adult males grunt loudly, and large herds sometimes erupt in a noisy collective chorus of grunts and froglike oinks. They snort when alarmed.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open grassy plains, wooded grasslands and acacia thickets. Wildebeest do not occur in Uganda.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal. Wildebeest are gregarious, at times massing into vast herds numbering hundreds of thousands of animals. The largest concentrations of wildebeest are to be found in the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem, an area of 10,000 sq miles (26,000 sq km) lying astride the Kenya–Tanzania border. This is the home of 1.5 million wildebeest and 250,000 zebras, commonly referred to as ‘the migration’. The wildebeest’s annual pilgrimage takes them on a circuitous journey from their wet-season pastures and ancestral calving grounds on the short grass plains of southern Serengeti, to dry-season holding areas in the west and the north, particularly the Masai Mara in Kenya where the herds congregate from July to October. The wildebeest begin to leave the southern plains at the beginning of the dry season at the end of May, and the annual rut takes place in early June as the herds move westwards into the longer grass areas and acacia woodlands of the Western Corridor. The bulls set up small temporary territories which are marked with urine and dung piles, the animals’ presence and their distinctive grunting call. Each territory holder attempts to anchor a harem of females long enough to mate with whichever of them are in oestrus. Males controlling adjoining territories perform a challenge ceremony by dropping to their knees, head to head, horns touching, before returning to the centre of their territory. Young males join the ranks of bachelors during their second year, but only when they are five to six years old are

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a seasonal peak in calving during the rains, though the exact timing varies from one area to another. Synchronization of the rut in the Serengeti in June is thought to be triggered by the full moon. This produces the amazing spectacle of 400,000 calves, 80½ of which are born on the southern plains in a two- to three-week period in February and March. Cows give birth in the open and calves are capable of gaining their feet faster than any other ungulate, standing within three to five minutes. They retain their buff-coloured natal coat for the first two months and stay with their mother throughout their first year. Each dry season up to a million wildebeest migrate from the Serengeti in Tanzania to the Masai Mara in Kenya, where they can usually find adequate grazing and water.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Wildebeest are grazers, and have broad muzzles adapted to feeding on short green grass with a high leaf to stem ratio, which is abundant in areas of alkaline soil such as the Serengeti plains. During the dry season, when the moisture content of the grass is minimal, they prefer to drink daily.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Preyed on by all the larger predators, with cheetahs and leopards taking calves and occasionally yearlings. Wildebeest cows sometimes manage to defend their young from a single hyaena or hunting dog, but are rarely successful in warding off an attack by more than one of these predators. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A large, long-faced, buffy-brown antelope with a pale belly and whitish rump. Both males and females have bracket-shaped horns. Their upright posture is accentuated by the high shoulders and sloping back.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Territorial males grunt, and both sexes snort loudly when alarmed.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Grassy plains, open woodlands, dry scrub bush and hills up to 6,500ft

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal. Coke’s hartebeest are gregarious, usually in small groups of up to ten females and their young. Female herds roam over a large home range which may include within it a number of male territories through which they wander. Sometimes a group of females will reside permanently in an area with a single male territory holder. Old males may be solitary. Territory holders mark their range by urinating and depositing droppings at regular dunging sites. They also horn the ground, rub their facial glands on the soil and stand conspicuously on Coke’s hartebeest lacks the plum-coloured thigh patches which distinguish the topi. Both termite mounds and other prominent places to advertise their presence. Young males leave their natal group when they are two years old and join a bachelor herd. This may number up to 30 individuals, including older males who have lost or temporarily abandoned their territory. By the time a male is three to four years old he can begin to compete for a territory of his own. During the dry season the females and territory holders often form larger herds in areas of good grazing, dispersing again with the onset of the rains.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Hartebeest give birth throughout the year, with peaks during the dry season. Females have their first calf during their third year. They leave the herd and seek cover when giving birth; calves lie out for the first week or so, and suckle for up to four months. in an area with a single male territory holder; or they may roam over a large home range which includes a number

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Strictly grazers, preferring medium-length grasslands and selecting the leafy portion of the grass. Hartebeest prefer to drink daily, but can go without water for extended periods. Male and female hartebeest have bracket-shaped horns, though those of the male, shown here, are heavier.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Lions, spotted hyaenas and hunting dogs take adults and young, while leopards and cheetahs prey on calves. A hundred years ago hartebeest were the most widely distributed of the larger open-country antelopes. Loss of habitat and hunting by man has since greatly reduced their numbers. of male territories.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Rather similar in appearance to Coke’s hartebeest (see page 120), but darker brown in colour with plum-coloured thigh patches and a less elongated forehead. Adult males are somewhat darker than females. Horns are present in both sexes and are less widely spreading than in the Coke’s hartebeest. The topi is one of a number of rather similar races or subspecies, namely the tiang (subspecies tiang) found in southern Sudan and Ethiopia, and the tsessebe or sassaby (subspecies /unatus) found from Zaire southwards as far as the Kruger Park in South Africa.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Topi are very alert, snorting loudly when alarmed. Males emit a destinctive clicking sound when courting females.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open grassy plains, wooded grasslands, coastal areas and scrub No ins) Topi can be distinguished from the rather similar Coke's hartebeest by their handsome

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal, feeding intermittently in the early morning and afternoon, resting and ruminating during the heat of the day; they feed again during the night. Topi are often found in large herds of more than 100 individuals in both dry and wet seasons, and mass in very large numbers in areas of good grazing during the dry season. Where topi congregate year round in large numbers such as in the grasslands of the Ishasha plain in Queen Elizabeth National Park in Uganda, males establish temporary territories whenever the herds become static. In areas where green grass is patchy in its distribution they are more sedentary, with herds of 10-15 females and their young moving within the territory of a single territorial male. In the Masai Mara in Kenya, males fight for possession of small temporary territories in traditionally favoured areas during the rut of February- March. Groups of females enter the ‘lekking grounds’, as they are known, when they are in oestrus, mating with the most centrally positioned territory holders. Males mark their territory with urine and piles of dung, and by rubbing their facial (pre-orbital) and foot (inter-digital) glands on the ground. They also stand conspicuously on termite mounds and other similar elevated sites to advertise their presence. Rival males challenge each other by dropping to their knees and butting horns together.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: In the Masai Mara calves are born during the short rains of October- December. Females either seek cover or calve in the open near to other topi, and the young normally gain their feet within ten minutes. Calves form nursery herds of up to half a dozen young, which stay together while their mothers move off to feed. For the first few weeks the calves retreat to cover and hide at night after suckling from their mothers. Initially topi calves look rather similar to the young of Coke’s hartebeest, developing their distinctive purple thigh patches only after a few months. They are weaned by the time they are six months old.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Topi use their long, narrow muzzles and mobile lips to graze selectively for the newest grass growth in medium length grasslands, preferring the green shoots and leaves, and avoiding the mature sections of the grass. They can exist without drinking when feeding on green pastures, but during the dry season drink almost daily. Topi give birth annually during the short rains of October-December, when the grass is green, nutritious and plentiful.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Adults are preyed on by lions, hyaenas and hunting dogs, and leopards and cheetahs take calves, as do jackals at times. Hyaenas in the Masai Mara patrol the topi breeding grounds during the daytime and regularly kill males that have lain down to rest, grabbing them by the shoulder and pulling them onto their side, before transferring their hold to the flank or belly. Other hyaenas are usually quick to appear and help to disembowel the topi. Right: initially topi calves look rather similar to young Coke’s hartebeest, developing their distinctive purple thigh patches only after a few months. They are weaned by the age of six months.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A commonly seen, medium-sized, toffee-brown antelope with large ears. Males have beautiful, lyre-shaped horns measuring approximately 1ft 8in-2ft 1in (50-65cm). A tuft of black hair on the lower part of the hind legs above the hooves (fetlock) is the site of a scent gland.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: The male impala’s larynx and skull have evolved to amplify sound, and during the rut territorial males (and sometimes bachelors) can often be heard making resonant nasal snorts and guttural trumpeting noises. ‘Roaring’, as it is known, carries for up to a mile (1.6km) and is made as the males chase each other about and try to round up females. Mothers use a soft bleat to call their calves. If a calf has been taken by a predator the mother makes a louder clicking bleat of distress while searching. The alarm call is a loud, nasal snort.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Acacia woodlands and riverine thickets. Impala are commonly found along the transitional zone between woodlands and grasslands. They can survive in quite dry areas, but are usually within a few miles of water.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Mainly diurnal, resting in the open during the night except for a period of heightened feeding activity for a few hours after midnight. During the daytime impala are at their most active in the early morning and late afternoon. Females and their young form herds of 6-100 individuals which move around a large home range, passing through areas occupied by territorial males. The largest herds are seen during the dry season when breeding is at a minimum, with up to 200 individuals in a herd. Territory young sex, nibbling each other’s coats with their incisors. They are not particularly fleet-footed nor renowned for their stamina, with a top speed of 38mph (60kph). Access to some degree of cover may be important to impala asa means of avoiding predators such as wild dogs, hyaenas and cheetahs. When alarmed they take flight in a series of spectacular bounding jumps and are capable of leaping 10 feet (3m) in the air, and an incredible 36 feet (11m) in breadth. This often has the effect of confusing a predator that has singled out a victim among a herd, and may enable it to escape.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Impala in East Africa breed throughout the year with a peak in births during the rains. Females have their first calf when they are two years old, and retreat to thick cover to give birth. Calves often stay hidden for a number of days, after which they join a creche of calves of a similar age and their mothers. A male’s horns emerge during the third month. Calves are weaned at four to five months old.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Mixed feeders, capable of adapting to a variety of food sources according to the habitat and the season. In some areas they are almost completely short-grass feeders, while in others they mainly browse on the foliage of bushes and trees. Generally, feed predominantly on grass in the wet season, and take more browse during drier times when the nutritional content of the grass is at its lowest. They drink daily where possible, but can go without water when the vegetation is green and high in moisture.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Adults are preyed on by lions, leopards, cheetahs, hunting dogs, hyaenas and crocodiles. The young are commonly taken by leopards and cheetahs, and at times by jackals, baboons, martial eagles and pythons. Below: male impala sometimes fight vigorously by locking their horns and pushing against one another in battles to establish dominance.

They also deposit scent from a gland on their forehead by vigorously rubbing their faces against low bushes, as well as thrashing the bushes with their horns. Male calves are forced to leave their natal group at the age of seven to eight months and join a bachelor herd comprising both roung males and non-territorial males. These bachelor herds stay on the periphery of the breeding herds, with individuals ranked in a dominance hierarchy. When a territorial male is ousted from his territory he rejoins the ranks of bachelors, enabling him to devote more time to feeding and allowing him to regain condition and eventually challenge for a territory again, often the same one he previously occupied. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Largest of the gazelles, with fawn or tan upper body and white belly. Grant’s gazelles lack the distinct black body stripe of the smaller Thomson’s gazelle (see page 134), and the white on the rump reaches above the tail and on to the hips. Males are the size of an impala (see page 126) and have powerfully developed necks and long, diverging horns. smaller and have shorter, thinner horns. A number of subspecies which may be distinguished by their horns occur in East Africa: these are robertsi, petersi and brighti. Roberts’ gazelle is found from the Serengeti plains in Tanzania to the Loita plains in Kenya and westwards to Lake Victoria. Horns grow upwards and then widely outwards with downward-pointing tips. Peters’ gazelle occurs in the coastal regions of Kenya. It has short, narrow and nearly straight horns. The fawn body Female Grant's gazelle, Buffalo Springs Game Reserve, Kenya. Grant's gazelles lack the distinct black body stripe of the Thomson’s gazelle and the white on the Grant's rump extends above the tail.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Males utter a nasal bleat as a threat and when herding females. The alarm call is a loud nasal snort. Grant's gazelles bleat loudly in terror.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open plains, wooded grasslands, savanna, arid thornbush country and montane grassland up to 8,200ft

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal, mainly feeding in the morning and afternoon. Grant's gazelles are gregarious, in parties of 5- 15 females and their offspring, usually with a mature territorial male in attendance. Young males and nonterritorial males form small bachelor herds. The social structure varies according to the habitat and seasona availability of food, with large mixed herds numbering 300-400 forming o1 the open plains of the Serengeti. Herd size is smaller in more bushed habitat. Grant’s gazelles often range widely in mixed herds during the dry season, and in the wet season are commonly seen in the company of Thomson’s gazelles. Young males leave the female herds and join a bachelor herd at about a year old, and begin competing for a territory when they are three. Territorial males do not use their pre-orbital glands to mark their territory in the manner of Thomson’s gazelles, but instead create dung middens, thrash their horns on bushes and clumps of grass, and stand conspicuously as a way of advertising their presence. Rival males perform an unusual display called ‘head-flagging’, turning the head abruptly to one side while standing laterally to show off their massive neck muscles; and sometimes males fight horn to horn. Gazelles are among the fleetest of all mammals, reaching speeds of 50mph

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Grant’s gazelles breed throughout the year with birth peaks at the end of both dry seasons. Females leave the herd to give dirth and fawns lie up on their own for the first month, visited regularly by heir mothers, who clean and suckle them. When they finally emerge, the young gazelles often stay in creches wi th calves of a similar age and their mo hers. They are weaned by six months. Females begin breeding in t leir second year.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Grant’s gazel es browse and graze, eating leaves and shoots as well as feeding on sl ort green grass during the rainy season. They are completely independent of water, obtaining sufficient mo isture from their food.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: All the larger predators occasionally kill adult Grant’s gazelles, though less often than they do Thomson’s gazelles and impalas, probably due to their speed and stamina. Servals, caracals, roney badgers, eagles and pythons all ake fawns, but jackals are probably heir most important predator. A mother gazelle is often successful in thwarting an attack by a single jackal, out if there are two jackals one is able to chase the fawn while the other harasses the mother. Female Grant’s gazelles leave the herd to give birth and calves lie up on their own for the first month.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Commonly referred to as a ‘tommy’, this is a small gazelle with a prominent black body stripe. Both sexes have horns, but those of the female are small, thin, spiky and often malformed. The male’s horns are heavier and annulated, measuring approximately

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A loud nasal snort when alarmed. Mothers and fawns bleat as a contact call.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open short grass plains, acacia woodlands and bushed hillsides up to occur in huge numbers in the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem, with more than 400,000 in the Serengeti population alone.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal, feeding mainly in the morning and afternoon. Thomson’s gazelles are both gregarious and migratory, and as such form no lasting ties between adults. They are the most water-dependent of the African antelopes, preferring areas of short green grass rich in protein. Gazelles in the Serengeti ecosystem Female Thomson’s gazelles have short, spiky horns which they use to defend their adequate pasture and water. In general Thomson’s gazelles form loose associations of 5-50 females and their young, with a territorial male in attendance. But the female herds are constantly moving and only stay in a male’s territory for a few hours or so – just long enough for him to mate with any of them that are in oestrus. Mixed herds containing males and females of all ages vary in size from less than a situated in front of their eyes. They also deposit droppings and urine at dung middens situated in the centre and along the perimeter of their territory to denote ownership. Nonterritorial males form bachelor herds usually of 5-15 individuals, though ‘stotting’ or ‘pronking’. Tommies usually do this when danger threatens ) signalling to a predator that it has been seen. It has also been suggested that it is a way of exhibiting their ‘fitness’ to a predator, discouraging a chase, as well as helping to communicate the danger to other gazelles. Gazelles of all ages also occasionally stot as a form of play.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a peak in births during the rainy seasons. Under optimum conditions two fawns may be born in a year and females conceive again within a few weeks of giving birth. Young gazelles lie out for the first two weeks with their chin to the ground. This behaviour, combined with the natural camouflage of their coat colour, makes them very difficult to detect on the open plains and helps them to avoid predators. Mothers visit their fawns several times a day to allow them to suckle, and they are weaned by three months old. Females mature at one year old, males at one and a half.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Thomson's gazelles both graze and browse, preferring short green grass whenever it is available. If grazing is lush they can go without drinking, but during the dry season they often travel many miles to drink, and supplement their diet with the foliage of shrubs and bushes. Right: male Tommies challenge each other by locking horns and pushing against one another in trials of strength. plains and often forcing a predator to abandon the chase. A mother gazelle will try to defend her young against predators such as jackals and martial eagles, butting at them with her sharp, spiky horns. For this reason, jackals hunting in pairs have greater success in taking fawns; while one jackal attacks the fawn the other tries to keep the mother at bay.

Male Tommies joust head to head as a way of establishing dominance as sub-adults or during territorial disputes as mature males. Adults and young sometimes jump high into the air in a series of stiff-legged, bouncing leaps called dozen to many hundreds, even thousands during migration, when breeding is at a minimum. Territorial males mark the ends of grass stems and twigs with black, tar-like secretions from pre-orbital glands

Tommies are very fast, reaching speeds of up to 50mph (80kph). They are commonly preyed on by cheetahs, leopards and hunting dogs. Predation Preyed on by the whole range of predators from lions, leopards and crocodiles to baboons and pythons. In areas such as the Masai Mara and Serengeti, Thomson’s gazelles are the primary prey of cheetahs and hunting dogs for much of the year. sections.text: -GERENUK or females 75lb (33kg) plus tail: 10–12in (25-30cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Stilt-like legs and elongated neck distinguish this elegant gazelle from other members of its tribe. (The word ‘gerenuk’ means ‘giraffe-necked’ in the Somali language.) Gerenuk are typically seen browsing on branches up to 6ft (1.8m) high, standing on their wedge-shaped hooves, supported by their strong hind legs, while resting their forefeet on the edge of the bush. The gerenuk’s rather small, pointed head is accentuated by its large ears. Males are heavier than females and have thick, S-shaped horns. Gerenuk have very long necks and will stand up on their hind legs Males (above) have horns; females (left) do not.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Males make a rumbling sound during aggressive social interactions, and females and calves bleat as a contact call. The alarm call is a short soft buzzing sound or whistle. When startled gerenuk utter a loud bleat of fear.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Dry thornbush country, semi-desert scrub and stony hillsides up to 4,000ft

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Mainly diurnal, feeding in the early morning and afternoon. Gerenuk seek the shade of bushes during the heat of the day and ruminate. They are gregarious, usually in small groups consisting of two to five females, their young and a territorial male. Gerenuk are sometimes seen in pairs, and both males and females are not uncommonly found on their own. Young males leave their mothers when they are one to one and a half years old, and remain in a bachelor herd until they are at least three to five years of age, old enough to compete for a territory. Gerenuk are localized and sedentary in their movements, occupying a home range of 0.4-1.2 square miles (1-3 sq km). Territorial males mark their range by depositing tar-like secretions from their preorbital glands on to twigs and dry grass stems. Males and females defecate and urinate at the same spot, one after the other, which also helps to establish their presence in an area. The gerenuk’s ability to feed up to a greater height than similar herbivores, and to withstand waterless conditions, enables it to compete successfully in desert-like conditions.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Gerenuk breed throughout the year with a peak in births during the rainy season. A female leaves the herd and seeks dense cover to give birth. The calf can stand within the hour, but remains hidden for the first few weeks. Young gerenuk are

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Strictly browsers, feeding on leaves, twigs, buds, shoots and flowers of thornbushes, shrubs and trees. Gerenuk use their long, pointed tongues and mobile lips to strip the small leaves from the thornbushes and can go for long periods without drinking, obtaining sufficient moisture from their food during the driest spells.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Preyed on by leopards, cheetahs and hunting dogs, less commonly by lions

Calves are taken by jackals, the smaller cats, larger eagles and pythons. Gerenuk tend to try and conceal themselves by standing motionless among the bushes if they detect the presence of a predator, and despite their rather stilt-like movements they can run surprisingly fast. They are heavily hunted in Somalia for food.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Nyati or Mbogo plus tail: 2ft-2ft 4in (60cm–70cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A large, dark brown, cow-like animal with horns. Males may be distinguished by the thickening at the broad base of their strongly down-curved horns, which forms a heavy boss. The record length for a set of horns belongs to a cow and is more than 60in (1.5m).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Belch-like grunts, bellows and clicks. Mothers grunt when calling their calves, and calves bleat when separated.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Grassy plains, thickets, forested regions and mountainous country up far from water, preferring to drink daily.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Nocturnal and diurnal where undisturbed. Buffaloes are gregarious, occupying a large permanent home range. The biggest herds are a feature of the rainy seasons, breaking up into smaller groups and staying close to water during the dry season. Older bulls often associate in small bachelor groups of five to ten individuals, or remain solitary for much of the year. The mixed herds are a movable collection of sub-groups, each containing a number of related cows and their offspring. Status within these breeding herds is determined by fighting ability, with males and females ranked in separate dominance hierarchies. High-ranking individuals travel and feed in the front and centre of the herd, thereby gaining access to the best grazing and maximum protection from predators. Females move up in rank when they have a calf. Young bulls leave their natal group at three years of age but remain in the main herd, associating with age-mates while avoiding conflict with dominant bulls. Bulls are usually seven or eight years old by the time they have fought their way up the dominance hierarchy and are permitted to breed. Males are sometimes seen fighting during the rutting season (towards the end of the long rains), facing off and clashing ‘boss-to-boss’, interlocking their horns and pushing against each other in a trial of strength. Buffaloes mainly feed during the early morning, evening and at night. They mud-wallow or lie up in the shade of trees, bushes or long grass during the heat of the day to chew the cud. Cattle egrets often associate with buffaloes, picking up insects disturbed by the movement of the animals through the grass, while oxpeckers (tick birds) pick ticks and biting flies from their skin and prise off pieces of dead skin and flesh from open wounds. months. The young calves are vulnerable to attack by lions and hyaenas, though the size

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a seasonal peak in calving during the long rainy season. Cows have their first calf at five years old and calve every two years thereafter. They either give birth among the herd while it is resting or seek cover. A calf gains its feet within ten minutes, but is unable to walk properly for several hours and must remain hidden until it is strong enough to accompany its mother back to the herd. Calves generally suckle for at least the first five months, sometimes until they are nearly a year old.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Predominantly grazers, feeding on taller grasses, and at times browsing on leaves and foliage, particularly in the dry season. They can drink up to 642-9 gallons (30-40 litres) of water a day and regularly seek out salt licks (including termite mounds) to obtain minerals and trace elements.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Being a member of a herd provides a formidable defence against predators, and individuals rally to help one another when attacked. Nevertheless lions kill both male and female buffaloes, often seeking out bulls in the smaller bachelor herds. But a healthy bull is incredibly strong, and sometimes proves more than a match for a group of lions. Calves, cows and old and sick animals are at times taken by hyaenas, and crocodiles have been known to attack and drown buffaloes. When wounded, adult buffaloes defend themselves bravely against human adversaries and predators. Below: bulls fight during the rutting season by pushing horn to horn in a trial of strength

sections.text: Taurotragus Oryx Pofu aces cae ae Young bull eland with oxpeckers. Eland are by far the largest of the antelopes, and a really big bull can weigh up to a ton.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A huge antelope with thin, transverse body stripes and a prominent dewlap on the throat which terminates in a tuft of hair. Similar in size and weight to the giant or Derby eland (7aurotragus derbianus) of Central Africa, but with much smaller horns. Old bulls have a dense mat of hair on the forehead and are greyer than young bulls and cows. The horns have one or two spirals, and measure approximately 1ft 8in-2ft 1in (S0-65cm), with the record standing at 3ft 7½in (1.1m). The horns are more robust in males, – but longer in females.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open grassy plains, dry thornbush country and mountain grasslands up forests.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Eland are diurnal and nocturnal, and are usually found in loose herds of 10-40 females and calves, often accompanied by one or more mature bulls. Older males are frequently solitary for much of the year, and young males form separate bachelor herds, maturing at five years old. Eland are nomadic, wandering in search of food over a large home range; at times during the rainy season they form into herds of more than 100 individuals, though they are not an abundant species. They can exist without drinking, avoiding heat stress during very dry periods by seeking the shade in the daytime and feeding at night and during the early morning. Their great bulk also helps to lessen the speed at which their body temperature rises, and water loss is further decreased by concentrating their urine and faeces. If water is available they drink every day or so. Eland are slow by comparison to other

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Breed throughout the year with a peak in births at the end of the dry season. Newborn calves lie up among thick cover during the first two weeks, after which they form a creche with other youngsters and stay close together.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Eland browse and graze, feeding on the foliage of trees and bushes, fruits and seeds, as well as eating grass – particularly during the rainy season, when it forms the bulk of their diet. They are sometimes seen snapping off branches with their horns to feed on the leaves and buds. Like oryx (see page 154), eland rely on the moisture from succulent plants to sustain them during the dry periods.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Lions are the main threat to adult eland, taking females more frequently than the huge males; hyaenas and hunting dogs also occasionally attack adults. Calves are vulnerable to all of the larger predators, particularly lions and hyaenas, though cow eland sometimes manage to defend their young successfully against hyaenas. They are hunted by man for their highly edible meat, and are ranched commercially for this purpose in some parts of Africa. prominent tuft of hair on forehead.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The second tallest antelope after the eland, with a distinct hump at the shoulder, and a coat marked with up to ten narrow white body stripes. Males have a long neck mane and beautiful spirally twisted horns measuring approximately males have two and a half to three spiral turns to their horns, which are a prized hunting trophy.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Males have a gruff bark, which is similar to but louder than that of a bushbuck.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Kudu are still a common species in the wildlife areas of southern Africa, but due to loss of suitable habitat they are uncommon in East Africa. They prefer mixed scrub woodland and acacia bush country in lowland areas, and rocky wooded terrain in hill country.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Nocturnal and diurnal, hiding during the day when persecuted. Kudu are gregarious, and are most commonly seen in small groups of four to six cows and calves, and separate bachelor herds of three to five males. Females stay in their natal herd at maturity, while males leave at two years old. They are mature by the time they are five and their horns are fully developed when they are six years old. Older bulls are often solitary and defend a territory during the breeding season which may overlap the home ranges of two or three cow herds. Sometimes a number of female families join together to form a single herd of up to 20-30 individuals during the rainy season, but these are only temporary associations. When undisturbed kudu feed at night and in the early morning and evening, resting up in cover during the hotter hours of the day. They have excellent hearing and can be very secretive. When alarmed they make off with their tail curled up over their back to reveal the white underside, providing a visual alarm signal for other herd members to follow. Males run with their horns laid back to avoid snagging them on overhanging branches. They are very agile and can leap an 8ft (2.4m) fence blocking their path.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a peak in births during the rainy season, and females seek cover when giving birth. Calves remain hidden for the first two weeks, then join the herd during the daytime. They continue to lie out at night for another two weeks and suckle for up to six months.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Kudu are browsers, eating the leaves, shoots and flowers of a wide variety of plants. They also feed on fruit, vines, seedpods and small amounts of grass. They drink where water is readily available but can subsist in waterless regions by feeding on succulents. They can be destructive to cultivation and vegetables.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Lions, spotted hyaenas and hunting dogs kill adults and young, and leopards take yearlings and calves. The smaller cats, eagles and pythons prey on young calves.

images.caption: Greater kudu bull, young and cow at Lake Bogoria, Kenya: flamingoes in the background.
Greater kudu bull browsing. Old males have two and a half to three spiral turns to their horns, and are often solitary.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Bongo or Ndongoro females 440–550|b (200-250kg) plus tail: 1ft 8in–2ft (50-60cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Large, thickset, reddish brown forest antelope with prominent narrow white stripes running vertically down the back. Similar in appearance to the bushbuck (see page 149), but much larger. Males become a darker blackish brown with age. Males and females have lyre-shaped horns with pale tips and one and a half spirals. Those of the male are very stout and measure approximately 2ft 6in (75cm); those of the female are more slender.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Grunt and snort during aggressive interactions and bleat or moo when distressed. The alarm call is loud and resonant, rather similar to that of a bushbuck.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Nocturnal and partially diurnal, Bongos are extremely shy and rarely seen except by visitors to the various night-viewing lodges in the Aberdare forest in Kenya. They are nonterritorial and are usually found in small parties of related females and their calves, though at times larger herds of 30-50 animals occur. These larger herds are temporary and often form when the females are accompanied by young calves after the calving season. Bulls are usually solitary and generally only seek the company of females when breeding. Bongo feed mainly at night or in the cooler hours of the day, lying up in dense cover during most of the rest of the daytime. They frequent mud wallows and are attracted to salt licks.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a peak in births in the Aberdare population from July to Female bongo (foreground) are lighter in colour with less robust September. Young lie up in cover to protect themselves from predators.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Mainly foliage of young trees and bushes, the pith and decaying wood from fallen trees, and charcoal and rotten fruit. Bongo will use their horns to dig up roots and sometimes stand on hind legs to reach the vegetation.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Adults are occasionally taken by leopards and hyaenas, and calves are preyed on by leopards, golden cats and pythons. They are hunted for their meat by man and defend themselves bravely when cornered. A cow sometimes manages to save her calf when attacked by hyaenas or dogs. sections.text: Pongo females 55–110lb (25-50kg) plus tail: 10in (25cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A medium-sized antelope with a distinctive white throat patch and white chest band. Males are dark brown; females a lighter reddish brown. vertical white stripes and spots on the back and flank may not always be evident and varies regionally. Only horns, which are stout, relatively straight, have a single twist and light-coloured 57cm). Coat colour and size differ considerably area to another, males and females becoming darker with age.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Males make a clicking sound when courting females. Both sexes bark loudly when alarmed.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Forested areas, dense bush and riverine thickets up to 10,000ft (3,000m). Usually found near water.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Primarily nocturnal, but sometimes seen feeding during the daytime A pattern of the males bear tips, from one with both where undisturbed. Bushbuck are the only solitary, non-territorial African antelope, though they sometimes gather in small groups. Individuals within a given locality know and greet one another. Bushbuck are rather shy, and are most commonly seen in the early morning or evening. They lie up and ruminate for much of the daytime in thickets. secretive habits help them to lessen competition for food and avoid predation. They swim * strongly and can clear a 6/ft (2m) fence. If cornered or wounded, bushbuck defend themselves bravely.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Bushbuck breed throughout the year. Females give birth in thick cover, and calves remain hidden for the first three to four months. They are weaned by the time they are six months old but stay with their mother until her next calf is born.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Predominantly browsers on the leaves and shoots of bushes, and the bark of trees and acacias, as well as fruit and berries. Also feed on lush green grass and herbs, and regularly visit salt licks. Bushbuck can be very destructive to agricultural crops and gardens.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Preyed on by leopards and crocodiles, and occasionally by lions. The young are sometimes taken by the smaller cats, pythons and the crowned eagle.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Korongo females 530lb (240kg) plus tail: 2ft 1in (65cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Horse-sized antelope with a black face mask, tufted ears and longish buff-brown coat. Roans have a short mane running from the chin to the chest, and backward-curving horns measuring approximately 2ft Gin (75cm) in the male; those of the female are shorter.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A horse-like snort when alarmed. They also bleat with fear.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open plains, dry bush savanna and light woodlands.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal. Roans are found in herds of 5-20 females and their young, which move intermittently within a traditional home range, overlapping the territories of a number of mature bulls. Non-territorial males live in bachelor herds. During the dry season roans often gather into larger herds to take advantage of the best pastures. Females are organized into a dominance hierarchy based on age, and at times the dominant animals spar with one another, jousting with their horns. Males leave their natal herd when they are two or three years Female roan antelope, Shimba Hills Game Reserve, Kenya.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Roans breed throughout the year, and females have their first calf when they are two years old. They seek cover to give birth, rejoining the herd after a few days but staying within a few hundred yards/metres of their calf’s hiding place. A cow locates her calf early in the morning and once or twice at night to allow it to suckle. Calves are weaned by six months.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Predominantly grazers, but also browse on leaves, seed pods and herbs, and have been known to submerge their heads completely to feed on underwater plants. Where possible they drink daily or at least every other day. They chew bones to obtain minerals, particularly calcium and phosphorus.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Adults are rarely killed by predators, but young are taken by leopards, hyaenas and hunting dogs. Roans will defend themselves bravely if attacked.

They mark their range by depositing dung and by digging up the soil with their horns, as well as marking the ground with secretions from glands situated between their toes. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A large, handsome antelope with white facial stripes and backward-curving horns, those of the male measuring approximately 3ft 4in (1m), and the female 2ft 6in (75cm). Mature males are black with a contrasting white belly and rump; females are chestnut brown with shorter, less robust horns. Sables are somewhat smaller and lighter than roan antelope (see page 150).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Bulls snort and sometimes bellow when herding females. The alarm call is a loud, horse-like snort. Both sexes bleat when fearful.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Thick bush, dry open woodlands and adjacent grasslands; usually in the proximity of water.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Sables are often found in larger troops than roan antelope, usually in herds of 15-30 individuals, though during the dry season they may form herds of up to 70. These larger herds tend to split up when food is readily available during the rainy season, gathering again on the most s productive horns, but those of the male are longer and more robust. pastures § in the dry season. Females form stable hierarchies within each herd and normally remain in the area where they were born, occupying overlapping home ranges of 4-10 sq miles (10-25 sq km), which include the territories of a number of bulls. Young males are forced out of their natal herd by the territorial bull when they are three to four years old, remaining in a bachelor herd until they are five years old and can begin to compete for a territory of their own; some bulls remain solitary. A territorial bull usually brings up the rear of the herd, whose movements are dictated by the dominant or alpha female. When a herd tries to leave a bull’s territory, he may try to block its path, with or without success. During the rutting season males pursue oestrus females and court them by tapping between their hind legs with a foreleg. Sables can be very ageressive, and battles over territory are occasionally fatal.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Some populations breed year round, while others have a peak in births late in the rainy season. Cows have their first calf in their third year, and individual cows leave their herd to give birth in dense cover. The calf moves to a new hiding place each day to avoid building up an odour and making itself vulnerable to predation. Older calves stay together in nursery herds, and are weaned at six to eight months.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Sables are primarily grazers, supplementing their diet with leaves and herbs. They drink regularly and are never far from water.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A greyish or buff-coloured antelope with long, spear-like horns, measuring up to 2ft 6in (75m) in oryx found in northern Kenya; females have longer horns than males. Oryx have black and white facial markings, and a black side stripe running along their flank and the tops of their forelegs. The belly is white. Two subspecies occur in East Africa: the beisa oryx (subspecies beisa), and the smaller, browner, less distinctly marked fringe-eared oryx (subspecies callotis).

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Females summon their calves with a soft, lowing sound. Oryx grunt aggressively when provoked, and bleat when agitated.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: The beisa oryx inhabits arid semidesert bush and scrub north of the Tana River in the Northern Frontier District of Kenya, westwards to northeastern Karamoja in Uganda. The fringe-eared oryx is found in similar country, as well as in Open grassy woodlands, prefert ing rather denser, Samburu Game R Reserve, K Kenya.: O Oryx are lessia other large East African antelope, and can survive in semi-deser less dependent on water than an thorny areas. It occurs south-east of the Tana River and south of the Aberdare Mountains in Kenya, southwards into northern Tanzania.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal. Oryx are gregarious and famed for their fighting spirit. They are shy, wary antelopes usually found in herds of 5-15 individuals, composed of a mature male with several females and their young. Bulls are sometimes solitary. Larger mixed herds also occur, consisting of cows and calves, nonbreeding bachelors and a dominant bull. Males and females form independent dominance hierarchies, and in the more sedentary populations, groups of females and calves wander within a large home range overlapping the territories of a number of males. Males are mature at five years old, when they begin to challenge for a territory of their own. Bulls fight savagely during the rut and have thickened skin at the top of the shoulders to help absorb blows from the pointed horns of their rivals. Oryx are less dependent on water than any other large East African antelope, drinking regularly when water is readily available, but otherwise sustaining themselves by feeding on succulent plants. sections.text: Calves are born at all times of the year, though females in the same herd often calve within a few months of each other. Females isolate themselves from the herd when giving birth, and calves remain hidden for the first four

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Grazers and browsers, taking grass, other plants and the shoots of trees and bushes. In desert environments, oryx feed on thick-leaved plants, wild melons and similar ground fruits, as well as digging for succulent roots, tubers and onions.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Adults are preyed on by lions, hyaenas and hunting dogs, and the young are taken by all of the larger predators. Oryx rely on their speed and stamina to avoid predators. They rarely turn and defend themselves, but have been known to kill predators and humans by spearing them with their horns. Mothers defend their calves bravely.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A dwarf antelope only slightly larger than a hare, with a very reduced tail. The coat is greyish brown with an orangy wash and dark flecks. Dik-dik have a conspicuous pre-orbital gland Dikidiki situated in front of each eye, and a prominent tuft of long hair on the forehead. Males have small, spiky horns measuring approximately 3in (7.5cm). Females are without horns and are slightly larger than males. Guenther’s dik-dik is found only in the northern part of Kenya and north-eastern Uganda. Other details as for Kirk’s dik-dik. plus tail: 2in (Scm) Slightly larger and commoner than Guenther’s dik-dik, with a less elongated nose and somewhat browner coat. The two species occasionally interbreed where their range overlaps in northern Kenya.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A ringing ‘zick-zick’ sound is used as a contact call, giving rise to the name ‘dik-dik’, Females whistle softly during courtship. When alarmed dik-dik make explosive nasal alarm whistles, often as a duet by pairs, which may help to reinforce the pair bond. Kirk's dik-dik. If detected by a predator, dik-dik bound away, jinking this Way and that to escape capture.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Acacia thornbush country bordering savanna grasslands; scrub and bushes alongside intermittent watercourses and rivers; also thickets on stony ground and rocky slopes.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Dik-dik are nocturnal and crepuscular, being active at dawn and dusk. They live in monogamous pairs and are usually accompanied by the latest calf and sometimes also by the previous year’s offspring. They are commonly seen feeding around the bases of bushes in the early morning and evening, seeking the shade during the middle of the day. The elongated, trunk-like nose is an adaptation to living in hot, arid country, allowing dik-dik to pant rapidly through the nose as a form of evaporative cooling. A pair of dik-dik stays close together for much of the time and the extent and location of their territory changes little over the years. Males in particular mark their territory by depositing secretions from their pre-orbital glands on to the tips of prominent grass stems and twigs, and each pair creates a series of large dung piles by constantly urinating and defecating at Kirk’s dik -dik. Dik-dik avoid predators by concealing themselves in vegetation

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: A female can produce two young ina single year, conceiving again within two weeks of giving birth. The young remain concealed for the first two to three weeks and are rarely seen, constantly changing their hiding place. Calves are weaned at around three months and are fully grown at one year old, by which time they have already left their parents. Male offspring are forced to vacate their natal range at an earlier age than females due to harassment from their father; they must then search for their own territory. Females usually breed in their second year.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Browsers and very selective feeders. They generally eat leaves, shoots, herbs, flowers, seeds and fruit, at times standing on their hind legs to reach a particularly nutritious food source. They are completely independent of water, obtaining sufficient moisture from their food.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Small, chunky-looking antelopes, characteristically seen standing on the tips of their squared-off hooves. Their coat is a greyish yellow-brown with black speckling. Only the males have horns, which are short and spiky, measuring the subspecies schillingsi (found in southern Kenya and Tanzania), where females also have horns. Klipspringers have a prominent gland in front of each eye (pre-orbital). They are almost twice the size of dik-dik. Females are larger than males.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: The alarm call is a loud, nasal whistle, often given in duet by a pair, which is thought to help in pair bonding.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Confined to rocky areas associated with bush cover on hillsides, isolated granite kopjes and mountainous Klipspringers are found in both dry and moist environments.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and partially nocturnal. Klipspringers are usually seen in pairs, sometimes accompanied by a calf Klipspringers are both diurnal and partially nocturnal. They stand on the tips of their squared-off hooves and can move with extraordinary agility over the rockiest terrain.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Births are recorded throughout the year, probably with a peak in the rainy season. Calves remain hidden for the first few months, and are weaned at four to five months. Both sexes are mature at one year of age.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Klipspringers browse on the leaves and shoots of shrubs and bushes, and take fruit and flowers as well as some grass during the rainy season. They can go without drinking, obtaining sufficient moisture from their food.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Principally leopards, caracals and large eagles, and to a lesser extent hyaenas and jackals. Baboons probably find and kill fawns at times. Klipspringers pair for life, defending a territory of 20-40 acres (8-16 hectares). They keep a constant look-out for predators, p

images.caption: (which may remain hidden) and at times the previous offspring as well. A pair defends a territory of 20-40 acres (8-16 hectares), and probably mates for life. Klipspringers are most commonly seen standing motionless on rocky outcrops, all four feet close together. In this way they advertise their presence to neighbouring territory holders and remain alert to the ever-present threat of both aerial and ground-dwelling predators. Klipspringers are rather shy, moving away over the most precipitous terrain with breathtaking agility on the tips of their hooves in a characteristic bouncing gait. Both males and females frequently mark their territory by depositing secretions from their pre-orbital glands on to twigs, and by regularly depositing dung and urine at dung middens situated along the periphery of their territory. Young males leave their natal territory of their own volition to establish a separate territory.

sections.text: Superficially similar to a small reedbuck (see page 165), with reddish brown or yellowish brown coat, and a distinctive, short, fluffy, black tail. Oribi have a very distinct scent gland beneath each ear, marked by a large black spot of bare skin. Males have short, slender, upright horns measuring approximately 4¥2in (11.5cm). Females lack horns, and are slightly larger and heavier than males.

sections.text: A repetitive, high-pitched whistle when alarmed.

In areas providing good cover they live in monogamous pairs and defend a joint territory. sections.text: The young are generally born during the rainy season and two births are possible in a year. Females have their first calf in their second year. Calves lie up among rocks or clumps of vegetation to avoid detection and are weaned by the time they are four months old.

sections.text: Adults and young are preyed on by leopards and caracals; occasionally by cheetahs and hunting dogs. The young are taken by jackals, servals, large eagles, pythons and sometimes male baboons.

At other times they hide from predators by lying up among rocks, tufts of grass or in shallow depressions. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A small, tan-coloured antelope with large ears and a very short tail. Steenbok are smaller than oribi (see page 160) and lack the black spot beneath the ear of that species. Males have small, mainly smooth, straight horns that are widely spaced, Females are slightly larger than males.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: A rather silent species, which snorts when alarmed.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Wooded savanna, dry scrub bush and semi-desert areas. Steenbok are far commoner in southern Africa than in East Africa, though they are quite frequently seen in parts of the Serengeti National Park in Tanzania.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal; predominantly nocturnal in areas near to human settlement. Rather shy and more commonly seen singly than in pairs. Each adult lives in a small home range which it marks with secretions smeared on to the tips of dry grass stems from glands situated in front of each eye (pre-orbital). Individuals also defecate at regularly used dung (Steinbok) middens, which help to define the borders of their territory. Steenbok are active in the early morning and late afternoon, resting up during the hotter hours of the day in clumps of long grass or in the shade of rocks. When alarmed they hide by crouching with their chins to the ground and their large ears folded back. If flushed steenbok run off in a low, bounding gait, zig-zagging to avoid capture.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Browse and graze on the foliage of woody plants, and eat forbs, seed pods, fruits and berries, as well as short green grass during the rainy season. Steenbok are independent of water, obtaining sufficient moisture from their food.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Breed at all times of the year, with a birth peak during the first half of the rains. Females can have their first calf by the time they are one year old,

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Leopards, cheetahs, hunting dogs, caracals, large eagles and pythons all take young and adult steenbok; they are also occasionally killed by lions and hyaenas. Calves are preyed on by servals, wild cats, civets, jackals, baboons and honey badgers. Females will try to defend their young against predators up to the size of a jackal.

Calves remain hidden for much of the time, and are weaned by three months.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A large, shaggy-coated, rather deer-like antelope with a distinctly musky odour; the older males usually have darker coats. Only males have horns, which diverge widely at the base and are strongly ringed, measuring approximately 2ft 2in (65m). The defassa waterbuck (subspecies de/assa) may be distinguished by its completely white rump, while the common waterbuck (subspecies ellipsiprymnus) has a horseshoe-shaped white ring on the rump. Apart from this the two races are identical. where the two subspecies overlap (e.g. in Nairobi National Park in Kenya and Lake Manyara National Park in Tanzania). The common waterbuck has a distinctive horseshoe-shaped white ring on the rump. Males have strongly ringed horns; females have no horns.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Females call their calves with a soft bleat or ‘muh’ sound: calves bleat in response. Waterbuck snort loudly when alarmed.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Grasslands bordering thickets and riverine woodlands, marshlands and lakesides, broken scrub-bushlands and moist mountain moorlands. As their name implies, waterbuck are never far from water.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal and nocturnal. Waterbuck are gregarious, living in groups of 5-20 individuals. Larger herds of 50 or more animals are not uncommon in suitable habitat such as Lake Nakuru National Park in Kenya. Mature males usually hold a territory for all or part of the year, while females and calves live in rather loose social groupings, either moving in the vicinity of a number of territorial males or staying with just one male. The same females do not always associate together, seemingly joining and leaving a herd at will. Young males become members of a bachelor herd towards the end of their first year, maturing sufficiently by the time they are six or seven years old to challenge for a territory. Bachelor herds can number from as few as three males to up to 20 or more, and so long as they show the required appeasement gestures bachelors are tolerated by territorial males and graze among the females. Waterbuck are rather localized in their movements, usually staying within a mile or so (1.5-2km) of where they were last seen. Though somewhat slow they are capable of prodigious leaps, and when alarmed make off in a high-stepping, stiff-legged trot. Sweat glands on their body produce an oily secretion which helps waterproof their coats and gives rise to their strong, musky odour. Common waterbuck, Buffalo Springs Game Reserve, Kenya. Waterbuck are the most water-dependent of all antelopes. Young male common waterbuck, Samburu Game Reserve, Kenya.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Waterbuck breed throughout the year, with a peak in births during the rains. Females have their first calf when they are three years old and seek cover when giving birth. Calves lie out in long grass or at the base of bushes for about a month, and are three times each day by their mother so that they can suckle. They are weaned at six to seven months. Young females tend to stay in their natal herd.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Prefer medium and short green grasses with a high protein content. During the dry season they supplement their diet by browsing on herbs and the foliage of bushes.
