sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: A medium-sized, yellowish-brown antelope with a white underbelly and a prominent scent gland below each ear (marked by a black spot of naked skin). Males have forward-curving horns.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: When alarmed, reedbuck utter a shrill, repetitive, nasal whistle, with pairs duetting at times.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Prefer the cover of reed beds among marshy ground, and long grass tussocks fringing intermittent watercourses in open grasslands. Sometimes occur in hilly regions more commonly associated with the mountain reedbuck (Redunca fulvorufula).

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Mainly nocturnal, but sometimes active during the early morning and evening, particularly during the dry season. They feed on the taller, less palatable grasses shunned by similar-sized plains-dwelling antelopes. The bohor reedbuck is generally solitary or in small groups. Male territories overlap the home ranges of a number of females and their young. Adult females generally avoid contact with one another, but in the wake of grass fires or during drought, when cover is at a minimum, reedbuck are often seen together in small parties. Young males are evicted during their first year and form small bachelor herds at the periphery of the male territories. They mature at four years old. Reedbuck rest up in the middle of the day in reed beds or amongst tall grass or bushes. They are shy and secretive, crouching low in the grass to avoid detection. When disturbed reedbuck burst from cover in a rocking-horse gait with their tail fluffed out to show the white underside.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: There is a seasonal peak in births during the rainy season. Females begin breeding at two years old and isolate themselves when giving birth. A calf remains hidden for the first two months, and its mother visits it once or twice a day to clean and suckle it. The calf finds a new hiding place after each visit. Male bohor reedbuck have forward-curving horns. Reedbuck are shy and secretive, crouching low in the grass to avoid detection.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Adults are preyed on by all the larger predators, and the young are taken by leopards, cheetahs, jackals, servals, large eagles and pythons.

images.caption: The bohor reedbuck has a prominent scent gland beneath each ear, marked by a black spot of naked skin. Food Feed mainly on grass, but also browse on leaves and buds during the dry season. Where vegetation provides adequate moisture they can go without drinking, but in dry periods they drink regularly during the daytime.
Bohor Reedbuck

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Grey or greyish rufous in colour, with a bushy tail which is often held curled up over the body, possibly as a shade against the sun. Ground squirrels have coarse, bristly coats, not soft, furry ones like their tree-dwelling relatives. Their ears are small and they have elongated hind feet. The claws are long, stout and only slightly curved as an adaptation to life on the ground. Unstriped ground squirrels can be distinguished from Geoffrey’s ground squirrel (Xerus erythropus) by the absence of a white side stripe. Males are larger than females.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: The contact call is a high-pitched whistle. Ground squirrels growl or scream when alarmed.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Open dry savanna, sandy bush country and semi-desert areas. The unstriped ground squirrel feeds on vegetable matter, insects, scorpions and at times reptiles, eggs and nestlings.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Strictly diurnal and terrestrial. Ground squirrels are gregarious and live in colonies. They are mostly active in the mornings and afternoons, remaining in the shade during the hotter parts of the day. Each squirrel has its own hole within a colony of up to a dozen animals (sometimes up to 30). Unlike other members of the squirrel family, ground squirrels seldom climb trees, living in burrows 4-6ft (1.2-1.8m) in length which they excavate for themselves. There are often several entrance and exit holes to the dwelling place. Ground squirrels frequently stand upright to gain a better view of their surroundings, and in times of danger bolt for the safety of their burrow in typical squirrel fashion, with their long tail held out straight behind them. They are often seen sitting upright with their forefeet clasped around a food object, and will store food for hard times.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: The young are born in a burrow, and are naked and helpless at birth with their eyes closed. They first emerge from the burrow at about six weeks

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Ground squirrels feed on grass, leaves, seeds, nuts, fruits, roots, bulbs, insects, scorpions and at times small reptiles, eggs and nestlings. They can be damaging to crops such as maize, ground nuts and cassava.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: They are preyed on by smaller members of the cat family, jackals, honey badgers, larger mongooses, large eagles and snakes. Ground squirrels administer a painful bite, which due to high levels of bacteria in their salivary glands may become infected and cause septicaemia.

images.caption: Unstriped Ground Squirrel

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Nungu or Nungunungu plus tail: 5in (12cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Unmistakable, with a distinct crest of long erectile hair extending from the top of the head to the shoulders. The rest of the upper parts are armed with long black and white spines and sharp quills measuring up to 1ft (30cm). The tip of the short, banded tail has a ‘rattle’ of hollow, open-ended quills. Porcupines possess strong curved claws for digging and are Africa’s largest rodent.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: The loud, rattling noise made by a porcupine when alarmed is caused by the vibration of the quills at the tip of its tail. Porcupines grunt intermittently when foraging and utter a loud, growling roar when attacked.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Most types of country, including mountainous terrain up to 6,500ft (2,000m). They do not occur in dense rain forests or marshy areas.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Primarily nocturnal, though occasionally seen at dawn or dusk. Usually solitary or in pairs; sometimes in family parties of up to six individuals. Their eyesight is said to be rather poor. Porcupines may travel considerable distances in search of food. They sleep during the daytime in burrows or caves among rocky outcrops. If alarmed or attacked porcupines stamp their feet, raise their crest and rattle their tail quills. If pressed they will charge backwards and embed their sharp erect quills into their adversary. They cannot ‘shoot’ their quills.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: throughout the year. Only one pair breeds in each group: the other members may copulate, but the females do not conceive. When mating, the female flattens her quills and raises her tail, allowing the male to mount her. The young are born in the sleeping burrow, which is lined with grass and leaves. They are well developed at birth and covered with

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: All types of plant material, particularly roots, bulbs, tubers, fallen fruit and the bark of trees. They are not averse to carrion and gnaw bones for their mineral content (and perhaps also to sharpen their teeth). Porcupines can be very destructive to crops.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Lions and leopards occasionally kill porcupines, but at times suffer festering wounds due to quills becoming lodged in their paws or muzzle. The tips of the quills have tiny barbs which cause them to hold fast or even work their way deeper into the flesh. Porcupines are killed by man for their meat, and are considered a delicacy by some tribes.

images.caption: Porcupines are primarily nocturnal, though they are occasionally seen at dawn or dusk. soft quills less than 1in (2.5cm) in length. They remain below ground for the first two weeks, during which time their quills harden. They suckle for one to two months, and are fully grown at two years old.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: CAPE Aine Sungura plus tail: 3-5in (7–12cm)

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The Cape hare has long, round-tipped ears measuring approximately 3in (7.5cm), and a short, fluffy tail which is black on top, white below and along the sides. The upper body is brownish yellow, flecked with black and the throat and belly are white. Unlike those of rabbits, hares’ hind legs are considerably longer than their forelegs.

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Generally silent, though they will stamp their forefeet when angry. Males growl when courting or during fights with other males, and females call their young with a soft piping sound. They utter a high-pitched scream when trapped or wounded.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Primarily nocturnal, though sometimes active at dusk. Hares are solitary and sedentary, while rabbits are social. The Cape hare lives in a large home range of a square mile (2.5 sq km) or more and is commonly seen at night along the roadside. They keep their fur clean by regular grooming and dust-bathing. Unlike rabbits, hares do not excavate burrows, preferring to lie up in a ‘form’ of flattened vegetation created by their body among tussocks of grass, under logs or in clumps of bushes. A hare’s best chance of avoiding predators is to crouch motionless with its large ears folded back on its body. Even when discovered they still often outwit a pursuer with a high-speed jinking run, reaching speeds of up to 40mph

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Hares breed all year round. The female does not build a nest for her young, which are born in thick cover. Known as leverets, the young are fully furred at birth with their eyes open, and can run when they are only a few hours old. They are independent by the time they are a month old.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Primarily grass, though they also eat buds, twigs, bark, fungi, fruit and berries. Both hares and rabbits re-ingest some of their own droppings. These are soft and rich in vitamins, unlike the hard faecal pellets which they expel as waste products.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Leopards search for hares among thickets and under fallen bushes, and cheetahs and wild dogs also prey on them. Jackals, caracals, servals, large birds of prey, snakes and the larger mongooses all take both adults and young at times, though a mother hare will chase and kick smaller predators in defence of her young. Unlike rabbits, hares are usually solitary and sedentary. They do not excavate burrows but lie up in a ‘form’ of flattened vegetation, under tussocks of grass, logs or bushes.

images.caption: Cape Hare

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Terrapins, tortoises and turtles are reptiles belonging to the order Chelonii. They are correctly referred to as chelonians – meaning that they are encased within a bony protective shell, which may be soft or hard, and either flat, knobbed or hinged. Chelonians have been in existence since before the advent of the dinosaurs, and fossil chelonians from Germany date back to 210 million years ago. The Chelonian shell evolved over time from a combination of the spine, ribs and bony plates derived from the skin. The inner part of the shell is fused to the rib cage, necessitating the repositioning of the shoulder blades and hips inside the rib cage. The upper part of the shell is called the carapace and the lower part the plastron. Tortoises are those species that live on land, while turtles live in the sea and terrapins are found in fresh water. The aquatic chelonians have more flattened shells than their land-dwelling relatives, and their feet are webbed or flipper-like. Being by necessity rather slow, most chelonians are herbivorous, lacking the speed to capture moving prey, though some of the aquatic forms are able to catch fish or feed on invertebrates such as sponges and molluscs. They do not possess teeth, but have a horny, parrot-like beak. All chelonians lay eggs, which are generally soft-shelled in the aquatic forms and hard-shelled in tortoises and the soft-shelled terrapins. The eggs are laid in a concealed nest on land and incubated by the heat of the sun. In many species The marsh terrapin withdraws its head sideways into its shell, leaving the side of its face visible. Omnivorous, it takes water vegetation, insects and frogs. the sex is determined by the ege incubation temperature, with females being produced at the higher temperatures of The marsh terrapin belongs to the family Pelomedusidae, containing the side-necked terrapins, all of which withdraw their head sideways into the shell, leaving the side of the face visible. They are olive brown in colour with a hard, thin, flattened shell. The neck is long and the head large, and their hind feet are webbed, with five claws. Males are larger, and have longer tails and narrower shells than females.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Wherever there are freshwater pools, marshes, intermittent watercourses and puddles.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Commonly seen resting and sunning themselves on rocks at the edge of still water, sometimes with three or four terrapins of different sizes stacked on top of each other. During dry spells they burrow into the mud and aestivate until the next rains. Even though they lack teeth, terrapins will bite if handled roughly, as well as defecating a stream of foul-smelling waste products from their cloaca. sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Omnivorous, eating water vegetation, insects and frogs, and the occasional small fish and mollusc.

sections.text: Terrapins mate in the water with the male pursuing the female and attempting to ride up on top of her, grasping the edge of her shell with his feet. He then rubs the two small tentacles situated beneath his chin on the back of her head, and squirts water through his nostrils on to her face. With courtship completed they mate. The young hatch after three to three and a half months, usually when it has rained and the ground becomes soft. The mother plays no part in protecting her eggs or the hatchlings.

sections.heading: Predators
sections.text: Hyaenas, civets, monitor lizards and ground hornbills.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: The largest African lizard, with a stout body, powerful limbs and strong, curved claws. The laterally compressed tail is marked with black and yellow bands and is much longer than the body. The skin colour is somewhat variable, being generally greyish or a muddy olive brown interspersed with lighter spots and blotches. The belly is pale with dark bars. Like crocodiles, monitors are at their most colourful when wet. patterned in black and bright yellow, and look rather like young crocodiles. Only three of the world’s 30 species of monitor occur in Africa. The largest monitor (and the world’s largest lizard) is the Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensts) of Java, which grows to a lenght of about 10ft (3m) and a Monitors are sometimes called leguaans.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Usually found close to thick vegetation bordering rivers, lakes and marshes.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Monitors can move surprisingly quickly when disturbed, switching from a ponderous reptilian walk to a tail-thrashing sprint across the ground. Males wrestle vigorously with one another as a way of determining dominance and to lay claim to a territory. They are quite at home in the water and are powerful swimmers, using their long tail as both an oar and a rudder as they glide through the water. During the day they often lie up in lush vegetation or among dry leaves near to rivers, and sometimes rest in trees, leaping straight into the water when startled. It is not uncommon to see a monitor lizard sunning itself on the rocks in a river. They can be very aggressive if cornered, lashing their serrated tail from side to side in defence, scratching with their sharp claws, and inflicting deep bites with their rounded, peg-like teeth which are adapted for crunching up their prey. The only venomous lizards in the world are the two species of Gila monster which are found in the southern part of North America. However, a bite from a monitor lizard is quite likely to become infected due to bacteria on their teeth.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: scavengers, foraging for whatever they can find, including crabs, mussels, frogs and fish from freshwater pools, as well as insects, ground nestlings and young water birds. The ‘relish all kinds of eggs, raiding birds’ nests, digging up terrapin eggs and plundering crocodile nests while the females are away. Young monitor lizards avoid deep water and hunt for food among the reed beds, using their sharp, recurved juvenile teeth for catching frogs and insects.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: The female monitor lizard excavates a hole in the ground with her strong claws or uses an old burrow as a nest site for her eggs. Sometimes she digs a hole in an active termite mound, laying 20-60 large, white, soft-shelled eggs. The termites quickly repair the damage to their nest, leaving the eggs to incubate inside it at a constant temperature and humidity. Incubation time varies, but it can take up to a year before the young hatch and dig themselves out. The female monitor lizard excavates a hole in the ground with her strong claws or uses an old burrow or even an active termite mound as a nest site for her eggs.

sections.heading: Predators
sections.text: Large eagles such as the martial eagle regularly prey on monitor lizards, and they are sometimes killed by crocodiles and pythons. Monitors are killed and eaten by man, and some tribes use their fat for medicinal purposes. Their handsome skins are made into shoes and handbags.

images.caption: The Nile monitor is the the largest African lizard – in exceptional cases it grows to 6ft (1.8m) in length. It is a powerful swimmer.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Sometimes known as rainbow lizards, agamas are probably East Africa’s most commonly seen lizards. They are plump, medium-sized to large lizards with cylindrical or flattened bodies and well-developed limbs, large triangular heads and rather thin necks. Their eyes have round pupils and movable eyelids, and they have two fang-like teeth in the upper jaw. The tail is longer than the body and cannot be shed or regenerated. Males are often brightly coloured, while females and juveniles are cryptically coloured to match their habitat.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Savanna and rocky outcrops, particularly in arid regions. Most agama lizards are terrestrial, some are rock-dwelling and a few species (e.g. Agama atricollis) live in trees. Agama agama is usually found among rocky outcrops or stone buildings, or scurrying around termite mounds. A male rock agama displaying himself prominently on a rock to advertise his claim to his territory and to try and attract females.

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Diurnal. Agama lizards often form colonies, and parties of rock-dwelling agamas are commonly seen pressed against sheer rock faces early in the morning, soaking up the sun’s rays to help regulate their body temperature. Some species are solitary or are found in pairs. Agamas are extremely quick and are excellent climbers, making spectacular leaps when racing from rock to rock. Male agama lizards exhibit gaudy combinations of head and body colours during the breeding season, courting females and defending their territory. A male’s territory usually overlaps the home ranges of a number of females, and a dominant male will choose a conspicuous point in his territory which to display, vigorously bobbing his head up and down as a threat, and chasing away defeated rivals. Males of some species have frills, crests or throat fans to make themselves look Agama lizards can often be seen sunning themselves in th ‘cold-blooded’ creatures to regulate their body Lempeeuee from shila

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: All the African species lay soft-shelled eggs, excavating a hole in soft ground as a nest. The young lizards must fend for themselves, and cannibalism among males has been reported. A female often lays two clutches of eggs annually.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Insectivorous, mainly feeding on ants and termites, as well as beetles, flies and moths. They sometimes repeatedly leap forward to snatch flies from the fur of mammals resting among rocks, such as lions, steenbok and hyrax. Some species supplement their diet with seeds and leaves.

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Snakes, birds of prey (such as rock kestrels and bateleur eagles), small mammals and even young leopards on occasion manage to catch agama lizards. Their only defence is to run for safety among crevices in rocks or holes in the earth, or to flatten against the ground in an attempt to conceal themselves. The bright attire of male agama lizards rapidly fades to match the surrounding environment when they are threatened. sections.heading: Identification
sections.text: Three species of crocodiles occur in Africa: the dwarf or broad-nosed crocodile of Zaire (Osteolaemus tetraspis), which inhabits small pools; the African slender-nosed or long-nosed crocodile (Crocodylus catapbractus), which is found in West and Central Africa and is occasionally recorded in Lake Tanganyika; and the Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus), the commonest of the three species and the one described here. Crocodiles are unmistakable, with a tail that is 40½ of the total length and has two raised dorsal keels. The body is covered with large, bony plates and horny scutes. Crocodiles and the North American alligator look very similar, but can be distinguished by the fact that in crocodiles the fourth tooth of the lower jaw is visible when the mouth is closed, while in the alligator it is hidden in a socket. Crocodiles have 66 peglike teeth adapted to grabbing hold of their prey. Their eyes and valved nostrils are situated on the top of the head, allowing them to make a stealthy approach through the water so as not to disturb potential victims. They have short legs with webbed hind feet, and adults are a uniform dark olive to grey colour with a yellow or cream belly. The young are lighter in colour, being greenish with irregular black markings. Crocodiles and alligators are the closest living relatives of the dinosaurs. They have the most advanced brains and hearts (with four chambers) of all the modern reptiles, and are more closely related to birds than to other reptiles. Even so, crocodiles have changed little in form or function over the last 65 millior years. The Nile crocodile has short legs: the forefeet are unwebbed, the hind feet

sections.heading: Voice
sections.text: Males roar during disputes over territory, and growl in anger. Young ‘yelp-squawk’ when they are ready to be released from the nest and if alarmed or distressed.

sections.heading: Habitat
sections.text: Large rivers, lakes and swamps (except at high altitudes).

sections.heading: Habits
sections.text: Unlike the mammals, which regulate their temperature from within, reptiles rely on the sun, moving in and out of 1e shade to maintain an optimal temperature. Where undisturbed crocodiles rest during the early part of ie day on sand bars or rocks to bask in the sun and absorb the heat from 1e ground on which they are lying. If it is very hot they open their mouths 0 help cool themselves by the process of evaporative cooling, losing noisture through the mucous membranes of their mouths. The broad, strong tail acts as both an oar and a rudder, propelling them effortlessly through the water, with the webbed hind feet allowing for careful manoeuvring. The nostrils are clamped shut before submerging and a flap of skin (the gular flap) at the back of the mouth can be closed to allow them to open their mouths to feed beneath the surface without swallowing water. Crocodiles are capable of a surprising turn of speed on land and can raise themselves high enough off the ground to gallop over short distances. Some of the largest crocodiles in Africa are found in the Grumeti River in Serengeti National Park in Tanzania, where each year the migratory wildebeest come to drink during the dry season and some are preyed on by the crocodiles.

sections.heading: Food
sections.text: Catfish are an important source of food, and fish probably forms 80-90½ of the diet of most crocodiles. The larger crocodiles also prey on impalas, gazelles and bushbuck that come to the river's edge to drink, and take animals the size of full grown wildebeest and zebras, particularly if they try and cross. Even buffalo are at times taken by big crocodiles. When the animal is drinking, the crocodile attacks by lunging out of the water and throwing its head sideways with jaws open wide to try and grab the startled animal by the head, neck or leg. If successful it pulls the prey into the water and drowns it. Crocodiles have also been seen using their tail to good effect, dislodging nestling birds from overhanging vegetation and sweeping fish to within range of their jaws. Dead hippo and other animals that have died or drowned are also consumed. Often a number of crocodiles gather at a large carcass, each grabbing hold of it with their teeth and then rotating their whole body by spinning on their long axis to twist and yank a portion free. Smaller animals such as Thomson’s gazelles are repeatedly thrashed against the surface of the water to break them into manageable pieces before being swallowed. Crocodiles have 66 peg-like teeth adapted to grabbing hold of their prey. To feed, they must tear chunks of meat from a carcass, sometimes spinning round to wrench off a portion. site against predators (including other crocodiles – particularly males) for the next 90 days, going without food, though she may visit the water to drink. Three months later the young crocodiles begin to emit high-pitched cheeping noises from within the eggs – the sound is audible up to 65ft (20m) away. On hearing this the female digs open the nest and releases the hatchlings, which use a special egg tooth to break through their shells. Then their mother gently transports them to the water’s edge in the elastic gular pouch of her throat so that they can clean themselves. The young crocodiles remain in a creche area in shallow water for up to two months, existing on insects and other small creatures. When alarmed they utter high-pitched distress calls, prompting their mother to gather them up in her mouth if they are in danger. Crocodiles can ‘choose’ the sex of their offspring by controlling the temperature of the nest. Cooler produce female crocodiles, while hotter temperatures of 88-93°F (31-34°C) produce males – the opposite of what happens in chelonians (tortoises and allies, see page 169).

sections.heading: Predation
sections.text: Adult crocodiles are so large that they are almost immune to predation, though males are sometimes injured and may die from wounds inflicted in territorial disputes. They occasionally risk injury by attacking hippo calves, and adult hippo will at times shove a basking crocodile out of their way with their massive jaws, forcing them back into the water. Crocodile eggs and newborn young are preyed on by hyaenas, mongooses, large eagles, herons, storks, pelicans, catfish and in particular monitor lizards. For this reason probably only 1½ of young survive. Crocodiles have long been hunted for their skins to make shoes and handbags (only the soft belly skin is used), and consequently their numbers have been greatly reduced. Nowadays crocodiles are farmed commercially for this purpose.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Many of the animals included in this book are to be found in Uganda, a country I first visited in 1995, twenty years after coming to live in Africa. In Uganda you can still enjoy watching wildlife in almost total isolation, as until quite recently it was off limits to most safari operators, due to years of civil war. All of that has changed now, and Uganda is home to a number of animal species that visitors will not see elsewhere in East Africa, such as the Uganda cob and Jackson’s hartebeest. The cob is a handsome antelope similar in size and appearance to an Nguruwe females 286-449|b (130-204kg) years The giant forest hog prospers in Queen Elizabeth National Park, where the scarcity of large predators allows it to feed in the open during the daytime. impala and, as in that species, only the males have horns. Their breeding habits are of particular interest in that they breed throughout the year, occupying traditional breeding grounds known as leks. Dominant males strut and whistle as a means of advertising their territories, challenging rival males and mating with oestrus females in both Queen Elizabeth and Murchison Falls National Parks. Jackson’s hartebeest is darker brown and has more robust upright horns than its relative the Coke’s hartebeest, found in Kenya and Tanzania. An unexpected highlight of our visit to Queen Elizabeth Park was the chance to see giant forest hogs. Though sometimes shy and predominantly nocturnal, giant forest hogs were for years relatively easy to observe in the Aberdares in Kenya. But recently people have reported an alarming decline in the population, attributed to predation by lions, which have been introduced into the Aberdares. At Queen Elizabeth National Park, where there are fewer predators, the giant forest hogs seem to be thriving.

sections.text:
Moderate-sized, slender-bodied and narrow-headed; snout narrowly rounded. Eyes large. Mouth V-shaped, narrow, its width ~1.5 times length. Lower jaw with 5 rows of blade-like, comb-shaped anterolateral teeth. Pectoral fins narrowly triangular and semi-falcate. Anal fin smaller than dorsal fin and set just behind it. Peduncle long and slender. Caudal-fin postventral margin deeply notched in adults and subdivided into upper and lower parts; lower lobe short and strong in adults but weak in young. Body pale grey to brown, darker dorsally and paler ventrally; fins sometimes dusky and usually with trailing white edges. Attains 180 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Sparsely but widely distributed in warm-temperate and tropical seas, except possibly eastern Pacific. WIO: Kenya, South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal), northern Madagascar, Nazareth Bank, Aldabra, Mauritius, Geyser and Zélée coral banks (NE Mozambique Channel) and southwestern Mediterranean Sea (rare).

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Litters of 13–26; size at birth 40–43 cm TL. Males mature at 123–157 cm TL, and females at 142–178 cm TL; fecundity is much lower in this species than in H. griseus. Little-known, primarily deepwater, over continental and insular shelves and slopes, at 90–621 m, usually on or near bottom, but occasionally moving to near surface or inshore in tropics. Likely feeds on small- to medium-sized bony fishes, cephalopods and crustaceans. Uncommonly taken on line gear and in trawls; of relatively minor importance to fisheries, probably used for human consumption and as fishmeal. Apparently uncommon to rare, thus affected by a variety of bottom fisheries; often misidentified as juveniles of H. griseus. IUCN Red List conservation status Near Threatened.

images.caption: Hexanchus nakamurai, bigeyed sixgill shark, 100 cm TL (Nazareth Bank).
Hexanchus nakamurai, bigeyed sixgill shark, 89 cm TL (South Africa). · AD Connell © NRF-SAIAB

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Body small, moderately firm, cylindrical, not compressed, and slender. Head somewhat depressed, flattened and subconical; head width ~2.4 preoral length; snout flattened-conical, not bulbous. Upper teeth generally with 2–4 pairs of cusplets, with cusps greatly expanded. Two or 3 horizontal rows of greatly enlarged hook-like denticles on flanks above and slightly behind pectoral fins. Denticles on head not in longitudinal rows, but denticles on flanks and tail arranged in regular or semi-regular longitudinal rows; scattered denticles on base of 2nd dorsal fin. First dorsal-fin origin over pectoral-fin inner margins; 1st dorsal-fin spine stout, lower than fin apex. Second dorsal fin much larger than 1st, fin apex rounded-angular, and rear margin deeply concave; 2nd dorsal-fin spine stout with tip posteriorly curved to become diagonally vertical. Vertebrae 83; spiral valve turns 8 or 9.

Body greyish above and below, dorsal surface paler but ventral surface not conspicuously dark, except underside of snout and abdomen blackish; caudal-fin tip with conspicuous black bar. Flank and caudal photophores conspicuous; flank photophore base just behind 2nd dorsal-fin spine, with anterior branch long and broad, much longer than posterior branch. Attains 27 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: WIO: Kenya to South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal) and Madagascar (off Toliara).

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Viviparous with yolk sac. Males mature at 22–27 cm TL, and females at 25–27 cm TL. Little known, dwarf-sized; found in deep water at or near bottom, at 200–500 m. No interest to fisheries but apparently caught as a bycatch. IUCN Red List conservation status Least Concern, although bottom-trawl fisheries occur in its range.

images.caption: Etmopterus sentosus, thorny lanternshark, 20 cm TL (N Mozambique). · PC Heemstra © NRF-SAIAB
Etmopterus sentosus, thorny lanternshark, 26 cm TL; rows of enlarged denticles above pectoral fin (inset) (Mozambique). · O Alvheim © IMR

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Diagnosis as for family. Teeth small and tricuspidate, similar in both jaws; tooth count 28–33/22–34. Vertebrae 207–243; spiral valve turns 18.

Body yellowish with distinctive pattern of dark brown spots in adults, or with dark saddles and black spots alternating with vertical white or yellowish stripes in juveniles. Attains 250 cm TL (possibly >3.5 m TL).

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Indo-Pacific (widespread). WIO: Persian/Arabian Gulf, Red Sea, Gulf of Aden to South Africa (Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal), Madagascar, Mauritius, Maldives, India and Sri Lanka; elsewhere to Indonesia, southern Japan, Marshall Is., Australia New Caledonia and Samoa.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Oviparous, with large dark brown to purplish black egg cases with fine hair-like fibres that anchor to substrate; egg dimensions approximately 13–17 cm long, 8 cm wide, 5 cm thick. Litter size likely >2, as multiple egg cases have been found in a single oviduct. Inshore shark of tropical continental and insular shelves, from intertidal zone, coral reefs and offshore sediments, to ~62 m deep. Usually solitary, but also found in large aggregations (up to ~50) over sand near reefs, but young seldom seen. Slow but strong-swimming; probably nocturnal, feeds mostly on molluscs (gastropods and bivalves) but also small bony fishes and crustaceans. Commonly taken throughout its range in nearshore fisheries by bottom trawls or longlines, and often sold in local fish markets; captured in smaller numbers by prawn trawls in Australia. Also kept in public aquaria. IUCN Red List conservation status Endangered due to fishing and coral reef degradation, but assessed as Least Concern in Australia where it is abundant.

images.caption: Stegostoma tigrinum, zebra shark, ~120 cm TL, subadult (South Africa); 58 cm TL, juvenile (Bahrain). · Source: CFSA
Stegostoma tigrinum, 37 cm TL, immature male (South Africa). Source: Bass et al. 1975

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Diagnosis as for genus. Fins rounded; dorsal fins equal-sized. Tooth count 24–27/22–27; vertebrae 135–143; spiral valve count 15.

Body uniformly dark brown, but paler ventrally. Attains 75 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: WIO: Kenya to Mozambique, Madagascar, and possibly Seychelles and Mauritius.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Reportedly common off East Africa, but poorly known. Assumed oviparous, as one female that lived for at least 33 years in an aquarium laid infertile egg cases. Nocturnal in captivity; diet presumably similar to other members of the family. Probably landed in inshore artisanal and commercial fisheries.

images.caption: Pseudoginglymostoma brevicaudatum, shorttail nurse shark, ~65 cm TL, female (SW Indian Ocean).

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Diagnosis as for family. Vertebrae 153–174; spiral valve turns 68–73.

Body with prominent pattern of white or yellow spots between vertical and horizontal stripes reminiscent of checkerboard pattern, offset by background colour of dark grey, bluish or brown above, becoming white below. The largest living fish, attains at least 18 m TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Circumglobal in tropical to temperate seas, including Red Sea. WIO: South Africa (Western Cape) to Sri Lanka and northwards to Pakistan.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Viviparous with yolk sac, without placenta; litters large, up to 300 embryos; size at birth 55–64 cm TL; gestation period and pupping grounds unknown. Males mature at 7–9 m TL, at ~20 years; females mature at ~10 m TL, at 27 years or more. Diet of this huge filter-feeding shark includes plankton, copepods, jellyfish, and pelagic crustaceans such as crabs. Gulps and feeds, often while hanging vertically, by drawing in water at high velocity by expansion of gill cavity, unlike the more passive method of basking sharks. Oceanic, to >700 m deep, but usually found at or near the surface, from close inshore, including bays and lagoons, to far out at sea. Prefers areas of mixing layers of cool upwelled oceanic waters. Highly migratory, often making long-term transoceanic migrations. A docile species that has at times been the subject of regional artisanal fisheries; has become a popular attraction for ecotourism in recent years. IUCN Red List conservation status Endangered; currently protected under CITES.

images.caption: Rhincodon typus, whale shark, 3.5 m, juvenile (South Africa). · Source: CFSA
Rhincodon typus, whale shark, 60 cm TL, juvenile (Taiwan).
Rhincodon typus, whale shark, juvenile (SW India). · KV Akhilesh © CMFRI
Figure 11 A whale shark, Rhincodon typus. © M Fraser

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Pectoral fins nearly straight and narrowly rounded. Mouth parabolic, without lip folds; teeth oblique, with small secondary cusp posterior to primary cusp, and with symphysial teeth; tooth count 41–45/37–48. Vertebrae 453–477.

Body metallic pale blue to dark blue or grey, above and on fins, changing to white below level of pectoral fins. Attains 3.8 m TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Tropical to temperate waters of Indo-Pacific. WIO: Gulf of Oman, Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, Arabian Sea, Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal), Maldives and Sri Lanka.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Historically confused with thresher shark A. vulpinus in the Indian Ocean, resulting in few reliable records of this species from the region. Oceanic, epipelagic, and apparently rare in inshore waters of Indian Ocean. Behaviour and biology poorly known, and virtually unknown in WIO. Reproduction in the Pacific is possibly aseasonal; gestation <1 year, with litters of 2; the Gulf of Aden may be used as pupping grounds. Taken as a bycatch in longline fisheries where it occurs. IUCN Red List conservation status Endangered globally.

images.caption: Alopias pelagicus, pelagic thresher, ~100 cm TL (Japan).
Alopias pelagicus, 2.8 m TL, immature female (South Africa). Source: Bass et al. 1975

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Diagnosis as for genus. First dorsal-fin origin over pectoral-fin inner margins; 2nd dorsal fin minute. Tooth count 20–28/ 20–28; vertebrae 170–187.

Body grey to dark blue-grey, sometimes brownish, blackish or bronzy dorsally, and abruptly white ventrally; eyes very black; pectoral fins black-tipped underneath, with or without black axillary spot on body near rear edge of pectoral fins; albinism recorded. Attains 6.4 m TL, but most adults <6 m TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Worldwide in most temperate and tropical seas. WIO: Kenya to South Africa, Madagascar, Seychelles, Réunion, Mauritius, southern India and Sri Lanka, and possibly Red Sea; records from Arabian Sea and Persian/Arabian Gulf need confirmation.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: One of the greatest known distributions for a shark; this wide geographic and habitat distribution has given rise to multiple synonyms. Generally uncommon but locally common in some areas; principally pelagic, but known from surfline to >1 250 m deep. Individuals are known to make transoceanic movements: in the Indian Ocean, tagged white sharks have travelled from South Africa to Australia and back within a span of months. Litters of 2–13; size at birth 110–160 cm TL; gestation period assumed >1 year. Feeds on a variety of bony fishes and elasmobranchs, other vertebrates (seabirds, pinnipeds and cetaceans), cephalopods and crustaceans. Larger individuals are a spectacular ambush predator of marine mammals, patrolling close to bottom and then launching upwards to strike prey close to surface, sometimes becoming airborne in the process. Relentlessly sensationalised in the media, particularly regarding infrequent but dangerous interactions with humans; paradoxically now the subject of dive tourism. IUCN Red List conservation status Vulnerable; a protected species in South Africa and in other countries outside the region due to historical persecution and its highly valued jaws and teeth.

images.caption: Carcharodon carcharias, white shark, ~ 4 m TL, mature male (South Africa). · Source: CFSA
Carcharodon carcharias, jaws of a large specimen (South Africa).

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Head broad; dorsal fins subequal. Slightly enlarged denticles on midback from above pectoral-fin origins to 1st dorsal fin, and denticles on dorsal surface of pectoral fins not enlarged. Buccal papillae inconspicuous; club-shaped papillae on tips of claspers. Tooth count 40–43/38–41; vertebrae 90–112.

Body yellow-brown to grey-brown background dorsally, with numerous small brown spots; characteristic horizontal dark bar or C-shaped mark on both dorsal fins; white spot absent or variably present at origin of either dorsal fin (never at origin of both fins); large pale or white spots above pectoral fins; paler ventrally. Attains at least 27 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: WIO: northern Tanzania, Zanzibar, southern Kenya (few records) and southern Mozambique.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Smallest of the Holohalaelurus sharks. A single female specimen, along with several male specimens, was included in the original description of H. melanostigma, with differences between male and female specimens attributed to sexual dimorphism. However, additional male specimens were later collected and readily identifiable with the female specimen previously collected, thus justifying the separation of this species from H. melanostigma. Very rare, known only from five museum specimens; biology unknown, presumably singly oviparous. Possibly a single population, recorded from 238–353 m, on upper slope.

images.caption: Holohalaelurus grennian, grinning Izak, 26 cm TL (Mozambique). · O Alvheim © IMR

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Body robust. Ridges over eyes. Nasal flaps end well before mouth. Vertebrae 124–140.

Body pale grey background dorsally, with dusky grey-brown saddle markings which fade with age and may be absent in adults; paler and unspotted ventrally. Attains 110 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Indian Ocean: South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal), Mozambique and Comoros in WIO (patchy); records from Kenya and Gulf of Aden may be of a separate species (cf. Springer 1979; Heemstra et al. 2006); elsewhere, records from Vietnam appear to be of an undescribed species.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Oviparous, pairs of egg cases laid; size at hatching ~20–22 cm TL; matures at 70–80 cm TL. Common, found on continental shelf and upper slope, over sand and mud bottom, at 40–600 m. Ontogenetic segregation, with immature individuals reported to be a relatively common bycatch in KwaZulu-Natal prawn trawls in South Africa; adults may live deeper or north of the trawl grounds. Feeds primarily on crustaceans (shrimp and lobsters) and cephalopods, but also bony fishes and elasmobranchs. Known prey item of the coelacanth (Latimeria chalumnae) in Comoros. A discarded bycatch of bottom trawlers.

images.caption: Cephaloscyllium sufflans, balloon catshark, 20 cm TL (South Africa). · AD Connell © NRF-SAIAB
Cephaloscyllium sufflans, 42 cm TL, immature male (South Africa). Source: Bass et al. 1975

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Diagnosis as for genus. Nictitans internal; no interdorsal ridge. Tooth count ~50/44.

Body bronzy to grey-brown above, paler below; dorsal and caudal fins with dusky tips (especially in young). Attains 130 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Indo-Pacific (patchy). WIO: Persian/Arabian Gulf, South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal) to Tanzania (Zanzibar) and Kenya.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Viviparous with yolk-sac placenta; litters of 2–15 (average ~10); size at birth 33–35 cm TL; gestation period <12 months. Matures at ~95 cm TL. Found in relatively deep tropical and warm-temperate seas, along continental shelf and upper slope, at 40–230 m. Diet includes bony fishes and cephalopods. A bycatch of numerous fisheries, especially the trawl fisheries in WIO region.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Medium-sized with slender body, short head, and snout moderately long and bluntly angular in lateral view; internarial space narrow. Eyes large; interorbital space narrow. Mouth short, upper lip folds longer than lower folds. Teeth molariform and asymmetric, with cusps reduced to low point. Paired fins moderately sized. Trailing edges of dorsal fins denticulate, without bare ceratotrichia. First dorsal fin broadly triangular, with posteroventrally sloping rear margin, and midbase closer to pelvic-fin bases than to pectoral-fin bases. Anal-fin to caudal-fin space greater than 2nd dorsal-fin height. Caudal-fin lower lobe not falcate in adults. Vertebrae 129–142.

Body grey or grey-brown above, paler below; usually many white spots on dorsal surface, but no dark spots or bars. Attains 117 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Northwestern and western central Pacific and Indian oceans. WIO: Kenya.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Viviparous with yolk sac; litters of 1–22 (mostly 2–6), varying with geographic region and mother’s size; size at birth 20–35 cm TL; gestation period 10–12 months. Matures at 60–80 cm TL, depending on region. Wide-ranging, but reports may represent more than one species. Occurs in temperate to tropical continental waters, from intertidal and subtidal areas, and commonly close inshore, especially over mud or sand bottoms. Feeds on bottom-dwelling crustaceans, fishes, polychaetes and sipunculid worms. Considerable fisheries interest, especially off Japan; used for its meat and oil.

images.caption: Mustelus manazo, starspotted smoothhound, 53 cm TL (Taiwan). · © H-C Ho, NMMB-P

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Large-sized, fusiform body; snout moderately long and broadly rounded. Upper lip folds inconspicuous. Upper teeth broad, with erect to moderately oblique triangular cusps, with strong serrations and coarser serrations basally; lower teeth broad but with erect, more slender cusps, and no serrations. Pectoral fins large, semifalcate. Interdorsal ridge present. First dorsal fin moderately large, semifalcate; origin usually over or slightly before pectoral-fin free rear tips. Second dorsal-fin origin over or slightly behind anal-fin origin. Tooth count 12–14/12–14; vertebrae 216–231.

Body bronzy, dark grey or brown dorsally; inconspicuous white band on flanks; all fins (except 2nd dorsal fin) with distinctive white tips and rear margins; white ventrally. Attains 3 m TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Indo-Pacific (widespread but fragmented). WIO: Red Sea, Kenya to South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal), Madagascar, Comoros, Aldabra, Seychelles, Mascarenes and Chagos.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Litters of 1–11 (average 6); size at birth 63–81 cm TL; gestation period ~12 months; biennial reproductive cycle. Males mature at 160–180 cm TL, and females at 160–199 cm TL. Occurs in tropical waters over continental and insular shelves, from surface to ~800 m deep. Has localised movements, with strong preference for offshore islands, coral reefs and offshore banks, but also found in lagoons and well offshore; young are restricted to shallower water close to shore. Feeds on a variety of midwater and bottom fishes and cephalopods. A known bycatch in areas where it occurs, especially around the WIO islands where it is abundant. Potentially dangerous to humans (although few, if any, attacks have been attributed to it). IUCN Red List conservation status Vulnerable.

images.caption: Carcharhinus albimarginatus, silvertip shark (South Africa). · © P Timm
Carcharhinus albimarginatus, 83 cm TL, male (central Mozambique). Source: Bass et al. 1973

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Moderate-sized, fairly stocky body; snout moderately long and broadly rounded. Eyes usually round and fairly large. Anterior nasal flaps weakly expanded, low triangular lobes. Upper lip folds short and inconspicuous. Upper anteroposterior teeth with narrow cusps, with serrations, and crown feet with coarser serrations and often low distal cusplets. Gill slits moderate-sized. Pectoral fins moderately large, narrow and falcate. Interdorsal ridge weak or absent. First dorsal fin relatively tall and semifalcate; origin usually over or just before pectoral-fin free rear tips. Second dorsal-fin origin roughly over anal-fin origin. Tooth count 28–30/27–29 (usually 28/28); vertebrae 211–221, precaudal vertebrae 110–119.

Body grey dorsally; 1st dorsal fin plain or irregularly white-edged; pectoral fins, 2nd dorsal fin, pelvic fins and anal fin with dusky tips; caudal-fin rear margin with conspicuous broad black edge; white ventrally. Attains 255 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Indo-Pacific. WIO: Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, Kenya to South Africa, Madagascar, Seychelles, Mauritius and India.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Litters of 1–6; size at birth 45–60 cm TL; gestation period 12–14 months. Males mature at 130–145 cm TL, aged 7–9 years; females mature at 122–137 cm TL, aged 7.5–11 years; maximum age 25 years or more. Coastal-pelagic, on continental and insular shelves and in adjacent oceanic waters, from surface and intertidal zone to at least 100 m. Common on coral reefs, often in deeper areas near drop-offs to open sea, in atoll passes, and in shallow lagoons adjacent to areas of strong current. Active, strong swimming, social species found in groups or individually; prefers clear water and shows site fidelity, forming daytime schools or aggregations in favoured areas. Feeds mostly on small bony fishes, but also cephalopods (squid and octopus) and crustaceans. Can be aggressive to humans, yet a very popular subject of dive ecotourism. Caught in multi-species tropical fisheries. IUCN Red List conservation status Endangered.

images.caption: Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos, grey reef shark, 68 cm TL (Mozambique). · O Alvheim © IMR
Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos, 68 cm TL, female (NW Madagascar). Source: Bass et al. 1973

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Large-sized, fairly slender body; snout long and pointed, internarial width 1.5–1.8 in preoral length. Eyes small and circular. Anterior nasal flaps low and inconspicuous. Upper lip folds usually long and conspicuous. Teeth fairly small; upper anterolateral teeth mostly erect, with narrow cusps, serrated or partly serrated, and no cusplets; lower teeth with narrow cusps and no serrations. Gill slits long. Pectoral fins falcate. No interdorsal ridge. First dorsal fin relatively large, semifalcate; height >2.2 in interdorsal space; origin over or slightly after pectoral-fin free rear tips. Second dorsal-fin origin over or slightly after anal-fin origin. Tooth count 15–18/14–17 (usually 16/16); vertebrae 155–185.

Body greyish to bronzy dorsally; inconspicuous white band on flanks; all fins (except pelvic fins) black-tipped in large juveniles and adults, and plain in young (<80 cm TL); white ventrally. Attains 3 m TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Circumglobal, including Mediterranean Sea, except not eastern Pacific. WIO: Pakistan, Gulf of Oman, Gulf of Aden, Red Sea, Mozambique, South Africa (southwestern Cape), Madagascar, Comoros (Mayotte I.), Amirante Bank, Seychelles, Réunion, India and Sri Lanka; not known from Persian/Arabian Gulf.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Litters of 3–15; size at birth 60–75 cm TL; gestation period 12–15 months; biennial reproductive cycle. Males mature at 159–203 cm TL, and females at 170–200 cm TL, aged 8–10 years for both sexes; maximum age 17–19 years. Common, coastal-pelagic, in warm-temperate to tropical waters, close inshore off beaches, in bays and off river mouths, from surface to at least 75 m deep offshore (but usually above 30 m). Some segregation by size and sex. Active, schooling shark that often leaps ‘spinning’ from water as part of its frenzied feeding run. Feeds mostly on a variety of fishes, but also cephalopods. Captured frequently in commercial and recreational fisheries. Not considered dangerous to people, but possibly troublesome to divers when spearfishing. IUCN Red List conservation status Vulnerable.

images.caption: Carcharhinus brevipinna, 179 cm TL, male (South Africa). Source: Bass et al. 1973

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Large-sized, heavy-bodied; snout very short and bluntly rounded, internarial width 0.7–1 in preoral length. Eyes circular and small. Upper lip folds short and inconspicuous. Upper teeth large, broad and triangular, and saw-like with serrations and no cusplets; lower teeth triangular and narrower, erect to slightly oblique, and with weak serrations. Pectoral fins large and broad, triangular to semifalcate. No interdorsal ridge. First dorsal fin large and broadly triangular, its height up to 3 times 2nd dorsal fin; origin over or slightly after pectoral-fin insertions (sometimes nearer their free rear tips). Second dorsal fin relatively high; origin before anal-fin origin. Inconspicuous caudal keels. Tooth count 25–29/25–29; vertebrae 198–227, precaudal vertebrae 101–123.

Body grey to grey-brown dorsally; inconspicuous white band on flanks; juveniles with dusky to black fin tips, and adults with indistinct fin markings; caudal-fin upper lobe with dusky anterior and posterior margins, whitish between. Attains 3.4 m TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Cosmopolitan in most tropical seas and commonly enters freshwater rivers and lakes. WIO: Persian/Arabian Gulf, Somalia to South Africa (Eastern Cape), Zanzibar (Tanzania), east coast of Madagascar, Seychelles, Lakshadweep and India; regional range includes great distance up Zambezi River (Mozambique).

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Often confused with the pigeye shark C. amboinensis or Ganges shark Glyphis gangeticus. Litters of 1–13 (mostly 6–8); gestation period 10–11 months; size at birth 56–81 cm TL. Males mature at 157–226 cm TL, age ~25 years; females mature at 180–230 cm TL, aged 14–22 years; maximum age 29–32 years, possibly >50 years. Coastal, estuarine, riverine, and lacustrine tropical and subtropical; usually close inshore, from surfline to usually <30 m but recorded to 152 m. Commonly occurs in hyposaline and hypersaline lagoons and bays, river mouths, and near surfline; the only wide-ranging shark that penetrates far into freshwater and is able to exist there for long periods. Migrates seasonally in some portions of its range; uses estuaries and river mouths as pupping grounds. A versatile and opportunistic predator with a varied diet comprising bony fishes, elasmobranchs, sea turtles, birds, dolphins, whale offal, terrestrial mammals and invertebrates. Caught in fisheries throughout its range, but rarely targeted. Lives well in public aquaria displays, for which there is increasing demand. May be the most dangerous species of tropical shark (particularly in warm turbid waters), and one of the three most dangerous sharks by number of recorded attacks on people. IUCN Red List conservation status Near Threatened.

images.caption: Carcharhinus leucas, bull shark, 2.4 m TL, mature male (Australia). · Source: CFSA
Carcharhinus leucas, bull shark, 155 cm TL (Mozambique). · O Alvheim © IMR

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Moderate-sized; snout short and bluntly rounded, internarial width 0.9–1.1 in preoral length. Eyes horizontally oval. Anterior nasal flaps nipple-shaped. Upper lip folds short and inconspicuous. Upper teeth narrowly triangular, erect to oblique, and with coarse serrations basally; lower teeth erect, with narrower cusps, with fine serrations. Pectoral fins moderately large, narrow, and falcate. No interdorsal ridge. First dorsal fin large, falcate; origin usually over pectoral-fin free rear tips. Second dorsal fin relatively large; origin about over anal-fin origin. Tooth count 23–28/21–27; vertebrae 193–214.

Body pale brownish grey dorsally; conspicuous white band on flanks; 1st dorsal fin and caudal-fin lower lobe with large black apical blotch and brilliantly highlighted proximally with white, and other fins generally with less prominent black tips or thin edges; white ventrally. Attains 180 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Indo-Pacific. WIO: South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal) to Red Sea, Persian/Arabian Gulf, Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka, as well as Madagascar, Comoros, Seychelles, Mauritius, St Brandon Shoals, Maldives and Lakshadweep; possibly enters eastern Mediterranean Sea through Suez Canal.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Litters of 2–4; size at birth 33–52 cm TL. Males mature at 91–100 cm TL, and females at 96–112 cm TL; biennial reproductive cycle. Occurs in tropical and subtropical waters; common in very shallow inshore areas on or near coral reefs and reef flats, but also found in mangroves, near reef drop-offs and occasionally close offshore. Occurs singly or in small groups or aggregations, but not strongly schooling. Feeds on small fishes, also crustaceans, molluscs and cephalopods. Predators of this species include large groupers and other sharks. Not a major target but regularly caught in fisheries where it occurs. Not regarded as dangerous to humans yet has bitten people swimming or wading in the vicinity of reefs; a popular subject of ecotourism and aquarium displays. IUCN Red List conservation status Vulnerable.

images.caption: Carcharhinus melanopterus, blacktip reef shark (Hawaii). · © JE Randall, Bishop Museum

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Upper lip folds long and prominent (as long as or longer than lower folds); prenarial snout long, 4–5.4% TL; usually >8 enlarged hyomandibular pores on each side of head just behind angle of mouth. Teeth generally smooth-edged, but with some irregular low cusplets. Tooth count 23–27/23 or 24; vertebrae 121–162.

Body greyish or bronzy dorsally; pectoral fins with pale margins, and 1st dorsal fin and caudal-fin upper lobe sometimes dark-edged; white ventrally. Attains 178 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean Sea (one record off Italy) and Indo-Pacific (widespread). WIO: South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal) and Madagascar to Red Sea, Socotra, Persian/Arabian Gulf, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Lakshadweep and Maldives.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Litters of 1–8 (usually 2–5); size at birth 25–39 cm TL; gestation period ~12 months. Males mature at 68–72 cm TL, and females at 70–81 cm TL, both sexes at ~2 years; maximum age at least 8 years. Abundant, inshore and offshore over continental shelf, from shore to ~200 m deep; often found off sandy beaches, at midwater or near bottom, and sometimes in estuaries, but does not tolerate low salinities or range into freshwater. Feeds primarily on bony fishes, but also squid and crustaceans. Often preyed on by larger sharks. One of the most common sharks in inshore waters where it occurs; taken by artisanal and small-scale commercial fisheries and offshore fishing fleets by longline, hook and line and bottom trawl; used for its meat and fins, and as fish meal. Harmless to people. IUCN Red List conservation status Vulnerable.

images.caption: Rhizoprionodon acutus, milk shark, 67 cm TL, female (Persian/Arabian Gulf). · Source: CFSA
Rhizoprionodon acutus, milk shark, 33 cm TL, male (Red Sea). · © SV Bogorodsky
Rhizoprionodon acutus, 99 cm TL, mature female (South Africa). Source: Bass et al. 1975

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Diagnosis as for genus. Mouth slanted downward in lateral view. Eyes horizontally oval. Teeth similar in both jaws, with erect to semi-oblique, triangular central cusps, flanked by pair of conspicuous cusplets or pointed blades, and no serrations; tooth count 42–50/42–48. Vertebrae 208–214.

Dorsal and lateral surfaces of head, trunk and tail greyish brown, becoming paler ventrally; flanks usually with few scattered dark spots; conspicuous white tip on 1st dorsal fin and caudal-fin upper lobe, and sometimes 2nd dorsal fin and caudal-fin lower lobe, as well as underside of pectoral-fin tips. Attains 213 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Indo-Pacific. WIO: South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal) to Red Sea, Gulf of Oman, Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka, as well as Madagascar, Comoros, Aldabra, Seychelles, Maldives and Lakshadweep; not known from Persian/Arabian Gulf.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Litters of 1–5; size at birth 52–60 cm TL. Matures at 104–109 cm TL, with mating having been observed in the wild; maximum age at least 25 years. Occurs on continental and insular shelves, to ~330 m deep (commonly <40 m); associated with reefs and coral lagoons, in clear waters, on or near bottom and resting in caves and crevices, and occupies a small home range. Feeds on small bony fishes, cephalopods (octopus) and crustaceans. Caught in line and net trawl fisheries near shallow reef areas; used for its fins. Popular subject of ecotourism, may be curious and approach divers, and occasionally aggressive towards humans when food stimulus present. IUCN Red List conservation status Vulnerable.

images.caption: Triaenodon obesus, 139 cm TL, mature male (South Africa). Source: Bass et al. 1975

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Large-sized, with front margin of head curved, and with prominent median and lateral indentations; rear margins of head long, angled posterolaterally, and generally broader than mouth width. Preoral snout length 1/5–⅓ head width; well-developed prenarial grooves in front of nostrils. Rear edge of eyes slightly ahead of upper symphysis of mouth. Anterior teeth with moderately long, smooth or occasionally weakly serrated cusps; posterior teeth mostly cuspidate and not keeled or molariform. First dorsal fin moderately falcate, its origin above or slightly behind pectoral-fin insertions, and free rear tip anterior to pelvic-fin origins. Second dorsal fin low, less than anal-fin height, with shallowly concave rear margin, and inner margin long, about twice fin height, and ending slightly before upper caudal origin. Pelvic fins not falcate, with straight to slightly concave rear margins. Anal fin larger than 2nd dorsal fin, and moderately long, its base 4.3–6.4% TL; anal-fin origin well ahead of 2nd dorsal-fin origin, and rear margin deeply concave. Tooth count 30–36/30–35; vertebrae 174–209.

Body pale grey-brown to bronzy dorsally, white ventrally; pectoral-fin tips dusky to black. Attains 4.2 m TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Circumglobal in warm-temperate to tropical seas. WIO: South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal) northwards to Red Sea, Persian/Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, and eastwards to Seychelles, Maldives, India and Sri Lanka.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Genetic evidence suggests multiple subpopulations. Litters of 15–31; size at birth 42–55 cm TL. Males mature at 140–165 cm TL, at ~10 years; females mature at ~212 cm TL, at ~15 years; maximum age ~35 years. Coastal-pelagic and semioceanic, over continental and insular shelves and in adjacent deep water, from intertidal zone and surface to at least 275 m deep, but often approaching close inshore and entering enclosed bays and estuaries. Forms large schools at different stages of its lifecycle, though solitary individuals of both young and adults also occur. Feeds on a wide variety of fishes, but also invertebrates (especially cephalopods). Perhaps the most common hammerhead shark in the tropics and once abundantly available to inshore artisanal and small commercial fisheries as well as offshore operations; caught as a bycatch and in target fisheries (including illegally targeted) with a variety of gear; used less often for its meat than for its highly valued fins. Young and sometimes adults are displayed at large aquaria. IUCN Red List conservation status Critically Endangered globally, due to heavy fishing pressure in many regions.

images.caption: Sphyrna lewini, scalloped hammerhead, 71 cm TL (Seychelles). · O Alvheim © IMR
Sphyrna lewini, scalloped hammerhead, aquarium (Hawaii). · © JE Randall, Bishop Museum

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Disc slightly wider than long, widest near midlength; anterior margin truncated, sometimes with median bulge. Teeth small, in up to 50 rows. Dorsal fins rounded at apices; 1st dorsal fin larger than 2nd. Tail short, stout; lateral skin fold on tail usually ridge-like, extending from about midbase of 2nd dorsal fin to lower peduncle. Caudal fin broad, with slightly sloping upper lobe. Males without skin flap in clasper glans region.

Disc grey, yellowish to reddish brown background dorsally, with close-set brownish black spots; dorsal fins brownish black with white edges. (Colour variation in this species needs more study, as the number, size and arrangement of darker spots on the dorsal surface vary, such as no spots in specimens from South Africa, but smaller and more regularly arranged spots in specimens from Mauritius.) Attains 65 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: WIO: South Africa (Eastern Cape) to southern Mozambique, Tanzania (Zanzibar), Madagascar, Seychelles and Mauritius.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Specimens ~25 cm TL almost sexually mature. Recorded from intertidal zone to ~440 m deep, and also from estuaries in South Africa. Feeds on fishes and cuttlefish.

images.caption: Torpedo fuscomaculata, blackspotted torpedo, 7 cm DW, 10 cm TL (South Africa).
Torpedo fuscomaculata, blackspotted torpedo, 28 cm TL (South Africa). · PC Heemstra © NRF-SAIAB
Torpedo fuscomaculata, 27 cm TL (South Africa). Source: Whitfield 1998

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Rostrum relatively slender, with sides nearly parallel near base; rostrum width at base 1/10–1/7 its length. Pairs of rostral teeth 23–34; lateral teeth moderately flattened, elongated, with double posterior edges and groove on posterior edges in adults. First dorsal-fin origin somewhat posterior to pelvic-fin origins but ahead of pelvic-fin insertions. Peduncle with no secondary keel below main keel.

Body greenish or greyish brown to olive dorsally, pale or white ventrally. Attains at least 5.4 m TL, possibly 7.3 m TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Indo-Pacific, with localised extinctions probable. WIO: extant in southwestern Red Sea to Gulf of Aden, Persian/Arabian Gulf to Gulf of Oman, and off Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka; also East Africa off Kenya, Mozambique and Madagascar; presumed extinct from South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal) and Mascarenes (Everett et al. 2015).

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Probably the largest sawfish species, but large individuals have become rare. Life history poorly known; presumably more tolerant of cooler waters than other Pristis species. Lecithotrophic viviparity, with litters of ~12; size at birth ~80 cm TL. Matures at 3–4.3 m TL, at ~9 years. Inhabits inshore coastal waters, estuaries and freshwater river systems, most common in shallow waters, but to ~70 m deep. Feeds on small schooling fishes, crustaceans and other benthic invertebrates. Presumed extirpated from many areas of its native range due to intensive inshore gillnet and trawl fisheries and habitat loss. IUCN Red List conservation status Critically Endangered.

images.caption: Pristis zijsron, green sawfish, adult male (South Africa). · PC Heemstra © NRF-SAIAB
Pristis zijsron, green sawfish, 3.9 m TL, adult female (South Africa). · © DR King
Pristis zijsron, green sawfish, 91 cm TL, dorsal view (Bahrain). · © JE Randall, Bishop Museum
Pristis zijsron, 109 cm TL, immature male (South Africa). Source: SSF 1995

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Diagnosis as for genus.

Body bluish grey to brownish dorsally, with numerous pale spots scattered over body, fins and tail (markings most pronounced in juveniles); mostly white ventrally. Attains 270 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Indo-Pacific (widespread). WIO: South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal) to Arabian Sea, Red Sea, Persian/Arabian Gulf, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Seychelles, Madagascar, Réunion and Mauritius; elsewhere to east coast of India, Philippines, Taiwan, southern Japan, Australia and New Caledonia.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Viviparous with yolk sac and supplementary uterine fluid; litters of 2–11; size at birth 46–48 cm TL. Males mature at 150–175 cm TL, females mature at ~180 cm. Uncommon but widely scattered; coastal, demersal, found close inshore on sandy and muddy bottoms and around coral reefs, possibly to ~90 m deep. Diet includes crustaceans (crabs) and other shellfish. A target species and bycatch in multiple artisanal and commercial fisheries throughout its range; traded in Asia for its fins. Harmless to people and a popular exhibit animal in public aquariums. IUCN Red List conservation status Critically Endangered globally; Near Threatened in Australian waters.

images.caption: Rhina ancylostomus, shark ray (SW India). · KK Bineesh © CMFRI
Rhina ancylostomus, shark ray, 100+ cm TL, adult (South Africa).
Rhina ancylostomus, 54 cm TL, juvenile (Oman).

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Disc margin beside eyes concave; thorns not set on raised ridges; 1st dorsal-fin origin slightly behind pelvic-fin origins. Vertebrae 144–164.

Body pale grey to yellowish brown dorsally and ventrally; dorsal surface with few large white spots loosely arranged in 2 rows on each side of trunk, and well-defined dark spot surrounded by 4 white spots at base of each pectoral fin. Attains 3 m TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: WIO records: Mozambique to Arabian Sea, Red Sea, Persian/Arabian Gulf, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Madagascar, and Seychelles. Indo-Pacific: tropical eastern Indian Ocean and western Pacific Ocean.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Probably a species complex of 3 or 4 difficult-to-distinguish species; smaller individuals are easily misidentified with R. laevis. Very little known about its behaviour and biology. Litters of 7–19; size at birth 46–50 cm TL. In the Pacific, males mature at 110–130 cm TL, and females at ~150 cm TL. IUCN Red List conservation status Critically Endangered.

images.caption: Rhynchobatus australiae, bottlenose wedgefish, 115 cm TL (Qatar).

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Disc rather narrow; anterolateral margins almost straight to slightly concave. Snout bluntly triangular and moderately long, preorbital length ~12% TL; 2 well-developed folds at rear edge of spiracles. Small tubercles around eyes and spiracles, and in two groups on shoulders; small blunt tubercles in median dorsal row.

Body plain coloured dorsally, white ventrally. Attains at least 75 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: WIO: Tanzania (Zanzibar).

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Known only from two specimens (75 cm TL male and 20.5 cm TL female; depth of capture unknown); very similar if not identical to A. ocellatus, except for its plain colour and slightly concave anterolateral margins. IUCN Red List conservation status Near Threatened.

images.caption: Acroteriobatus zanzibarensis, male holotype (Zanzibar). Drawn from photograph

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Disc rather narrow and moderately long, anterolateral margins almost straight to slightly concave; disc length 41–42% TL, disc width ~1.3 in disc length. Snout triangular, sharply pointed and long, preorbital length 15–16% TL. Eyes about twice size of spiracles; 2 distinct folds at rear edge of spiracles. Denticles minute (skin smooth to touch), but with small tubercles on rostrum, around eyes and spiracles, and 1 or 2 on each shoulder; larger, irregular tubercles in median dorsal row.

Body plain dark olive-brown; margins of pectoral fins and pelvic fins somewhat dusky; snout noticeably translucent on each side of rostral cartilage; white ventrally, but with conspicuous dark blotch on underside of snout. Attains at least 127 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: WIO: South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal) to Kenya.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Biology unknown. Rare; occurs offshore, at 75–253 m. Likely taken in local fisheries.

images.caption: Rhinobatos holcorhynchus, slender guitarfish, 42 cm TL (South Africa). · © ST Fennessy, ORI/SAAMBR
Rhinobatos holcorhynchus, 45 cm TL, male (South Africa). Source: SSF

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Disc narrow and moderately long, anterolateral margins slightly convex to almost straight; disc length ~40% TL, disc width ~1.4 in disc length. Snout bluntly triangular and somewhat short, preorbital length ~13% TL; 2 folds at rear edge of spiracles, inner fold rudimentary. Small tubercles on rostral ridges, and around eyes and spiracles; large blunt tubercles in median dorsal row.

Body plain tan dorsally, and margins slightly paler; large translucent area on each side of snout; white ventrally. Attains 171 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: WIO: Red Sea, Gulf of Oman, and probably Gulf of Aden and other areas of northeastern Arabian Sea; reports from Mediterranean Sea and elsewhere in Indo-Pacific need confirmation.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Litters of up to 10; size at birth ~29 cm TL; males mature at ~83 cm TL. Coastal, in shallow inshore waters and sheltered bays, to ~40 m deep; young observed in very shallow water washing onto beach with breakers and then sliding back into water. Aggregates during spawning. Feeds mostly on small crustaceans. A target species and utilised bycatch mainly in artisanal fisheries.

images.caption: Glaucostegus halavi, Halavi guitarfish (Red Sea). · © SV Bogorodsky
Glaucostegus halavi, Halavi guitarfish, 84 cm TL (Red Sea). · © JE Randall, Bishop Museum
Glaucostegus halavi, ~1 m TL, mature male (Red Sea).

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Large-sized with very broad disc, DW ~1.4 times disc length and 80–85% TL; pectoral-fin apex acutely angled. Snout triangular and long, length 19–23% TL and 4.8–5.1 times interorbital space; angle anterior to spiracles ~85°. Teeth sharp, cuspidate; 35–40 in upper jaw. Pelvic-fin anterior lobes long, extending to or beyond rear edge of posterior lobes. Tail relatively short, shorter than distance from snout tip to rear edge of cloaca, and narrow at base and not attenuated distally or else slightly broader at midlength. Ventral surface densely covered with small denticles. Dorsal surface with 2–7 small orbital thorns, no nuchal thorns, ~15 in median row on tail to 1st dorsal fin, and 2 interdorsal. Predorsal caudal vertebrae 53–56.

Disc dark grey dorsally and ventrally; pores on ventral surface black. Attains 190 cm TL (females reach larger sizes than males).

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Southern Africa: Namibia (Lüderitz) in southeastern Atlantic, to South Africa, Mozambique, Kenya and off Madagascar in WIO.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text: Size at hatching <27 cm TL; slow-growing. Males mature at 125–134 cm TL, and females at 171–190 cm TL. Uncommon, in scattered localities; occurs on outer continental shelf to slope, at 50–970 m. Diet includes fishes (rattails, round herring), crustaceans and squid.

images.caption: Dipturus springeri, roughbelly skate, ~45 cm TL (Mozambique). · © P Bouchet, MNHN
Dipturus springeri, roughbelly skate, 27 cm TL, ~21 cm DW, neonate (South Africa). · AD Connell © NRF-SAIAB
Dipturus springeri, roughbelly skate, juvenile (South Africa). · © DA Ebert, MLML

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Disc moderately narrow, DW 56–63% TL; anterior margins not convex. Snout very acute and relatively long, length 15–17% TL. Teeth in upper jaw 31–35. Eye diameter greater than interorbital space. Pelvic-fin anterior lobes relatively long, not reaching rear edge of posterior lobes. Tail moderately long,

length 52–56% TL, and slender at base and attenuated distally.

Interdorsal distance greater than length of 1st dorsal-fin base;

1st dorsal fin anteriorly set. Dorsal surface with 1–4 small

orbital thorns, 1 interspiracular, 1 or 2 nuchal, in 3–5 irregular

rows on tail between base and 1st dorsal fin, and 2 interdorsal.

Predorsal caudal vertebrae 47–53.

Disc dark brown dorsally, with symmetrically arranged,

small, bicoloured ocelli and sooty blotches on disc, pelvic fins

and tail; pale grey ventrally. Attains at least 61 cm TL.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: WIO: Mozambique to Kenya.

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text:
Known from few specimens; 2 mature females

measured 60 and 61 cm TL. Occurs on outer continental shelf

and uppermost slope, at ~200–500 m.

images.caption: Okamejei heemstrai, East African skate, 22 cm DW, eye detail inset (Mozambique). · O Alvheim © IMR
Okamejei heemstrai (Mozambique). © P Bouchet, MNHN

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
Disc rhomboidal, about as long as wide; pectoral-fin anterior margins weakly concave, lateral apices narrowly rounded to angular, and posterior margins broadly convex. Snout broadly triangular, with small apical lobe; distance from snout tip to maximum disc width 33–43% DW. Tail extremely long, 2.9–3.5 times DW, usually with 1 stinging spine. Disc mostly smooth, with band of small flat denticles extending from head onto tail; central disc with 1 or 2 enlarged heart-shaped thorns. Tooth count 26–40/27–44; oral papillae 4 or 5 in two transverse rows.
